News.title: Man admits drugging and raping wife for 20 years
News.content:
A man accused of drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge for more than 20 years has admitted 60 offences against her.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, had already admitted some counts at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, including rape.

The wife watched proceedings from the public gallery supported by members of her family.

The husband, in his sixties, became visibly emotional as he repeated the word guilty to dozens of charges - including multiple counts of rape, assault by penetration and administering a substance with intent - and at one point was invited to sit down in the dock by the judge.

Twelve other men deny multiple serious sexual offences against the same woman.

The husband, from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, will be sentenced for the counts he has admitted at the conclusion of the trial.

A 13th man previously admitted sexual offences against the woman.

The husband's offending against his wife, who he was married to for decades, took place over a period going back to 2004, while the accusations involving the other men range from September 2018 to November 2025.

The other defendants are:

Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport

Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport

Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester

Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester

Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport

Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport

Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode

Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire

Richard Townsend, 37, from Rochdale

Karl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, Somerset

Daniel Rayner, 42, from, Whitstable, Kent

David Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, Derbyshire

The trial is due to continue in the coming weeks.

News.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of his father
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Speaking to the Times newspaper, external shortly before formally taking over as prime minister, Burnham said it was "a sadness, because he would be [proud]".

He continued: "The way I look at it, it's his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn't know it."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

News.title: Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today'
News.content:
The House of Lords is currently debating the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at Â£100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than Â£100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two Â£36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap on individual donations made by UK residents.

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

News.title: Member of UK armed forces dies in road traffic incident in Ukraine
News.content:
A member of the UK armed forces has died in a road traffic incident in Ukraine, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has announced.

The individual's family has been informed and has "requested a period of grace before further details are released", the MoD's statement said.

The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands.

The British government has previously acknowledged a small number of personnel in Ukraine to support Kyiv's armed forces and provide security to diplomatic staff.

It is not known which service the individual was in or what their role was.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting shared his "deepest condolences" with their loved ones, writing on social media: "This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our armed forces."

A 28-year-old paratrooper, who died while watching the testing of a new defensive capability away from the front lines in December, was the first member of the armed forces killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

On Sunday, a Russian drone hit and damaged a train in Yahodyn, near the Ukraine-Poland border - shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through on a different train on the same line.

The UK's national security adviser Jonathan Powell was among those on board.

No casualties were reported. Russia's defence ministry said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company said the drone's intended target "could have been the diplomatic train".

The UK has been one of Ukraine's closest allies during the war.

Ukraine was the location of Andy Burnham's first overseas trip as prime minister in August, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats".

Chairing his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, Burnham also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for Scalp missiles.

News.title: Staff slept while patient killed at NHS mental health unit
News.content:
Staff falsified records, slept and were on their phones on the night one patient was killed by another on an NHS mental health unit in east London, an inquest has heard.

Hugo Flint-Cahan, 34, was being treated at Newham Mental Health Centre (NMHC), run by the East London NHS Trust (ELFT), when he was fatally attacked by 22-year-old Rolando Torres-Pena.

Hugo's family say they have been shocked by the "dangerous" failures in his care.

The Trust told the coroner they had addressed some of the issues raised in the inquest, and are launching an investigation into the staff whose failings have been identified.

In a narrative conclusion, the coroner found Hugo was unlawfully killed which was contributed to by neglect, recommended four members of staff be referred to their regulator and that the Metropolitan police review their investigation into what happened that night.

Hugo, who had been a patient at the NHMC for six months, was strangled in the early hours of 3 January 2023 by Torres-Pena who had arrived on the ward five days earlier.

Torres-Pena pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility. He was given a hospital order without time limit.

A coroner criticised repeated failures by the Trust in a number of patient deaths - not just Hugo's.

Graeme Irvine, the Senior Coroner for East London, said it was like "ground hog day" as he heard evidence of "the same" errors, "over and over again," including the falsification of patient observation records and slow emergency responses.

News.title: Oasis confirm second leg of reunion tour after weeks of social media teasers
News.content:
The band's 2025 comeback got off to a shaky start before an E minor chord was even strummed, with fans criticising the ticket sales process after being asked to queue for hours, with some finding themselves having to pay hundreds of pounds more than they expected.

The fiasco triggered a UK government response. Following an investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Ticketmaster agreed to several voluntary changes, external, including telling fans 24 hours in advance if a tiered pricing system is in use and giving clearer information about ticket prices while people wait in the queue, as well as not using misleading ticket labels.

Demand and expectation were huge among fans, old and new. But the band delivered, with the BBC's review saying they hadn't sounded so good since the 1990s.

Mid-way through the world tour, Noel told TalkSport that he and his bandmates had been "blown away" by the response to their return after 16 years away.

Last week, another emotional documentary chronicling the tour - and featuring the reconciled brothers' first joint interview since their acrimonious split in 2009 - was released in UK cinemas, following its premiere in Venice.

In it, Noel confirms the band is "not a power struggle any more".

On Monday, following the announcement, he told the same radio station, external that booking part two of the comeback tour had been a no-brainer.

"We were having such a great time that, why wouldn't you?" he said, while confirming there would be no new music off the back of it.

News.title: Immigrants held in small outdoor cages at 'Alligator Alcatraz' in Florida, investigators find
News.content:
In its response included in the investigation report, DHS officials said Florida - not the federal government - had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility.

The facility was established by the state of Florida through an executive order signed by DeSantis, but the federal government paid for operational costs.

In January, the OIG conducted a surprise inspection at the detention facility, which had become one of the most notorious immigration detention centres in the US. The OIG is an independent internal watchdog at DHS. The current inspector general was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term.

In 2025, the detention facility was built over the course of eight days in the Everglades, a protected wetland known for its alligators. Trump once joked that immigrants held there would need to learn "how to run away" from the reptiles at the facility, which civil rights groups have decried as inhumane.

In June 2026, DeSantis said the facility would close as it was only meant to be temporary.

According to the OIG report, between July 2025 and January 2026, the facility kept 79 immigrants in the small metal enclosures, describing them as "calming areas" for people to "deescalate and have time alone". They were held there from periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, at least once as a disciplinary measure, OIG said.

"The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report stated.

News.title: Former top civil servant received pay-off of nearly £860,000
News.content:
A former top civil servant received a record pay-off of nearly Â£860,000 after he was forced out of his job by Sir Keir Starmer, just 14 months after the then-prime minister appointed him.

Lord Wormald left his role as cabinet secretary and head of the Civil Service in February by "mutual agreement" following months of media reports suggesting Downing Street was unhappy with his performance.

The Cabinet Office's accounts, external show there was "contractual compensation" of Â£332,897 and "additional severance" of Â£526,598.

The BBC understands the size of the pay-off was partly to cover Lord Wormald's pension contributions as his removal from office essentially cut his civil service career short.

He also was compensated for a mandatory "waiting period" following his departure from government. As cabinet secretary he would have had regular access to sensitive information about national security, foreign policy and the UK economy.

His salary for the period 1 April 2025 to 13 February was between Â£210,000 and Â£215,000, according to the accounts, bringing his total for the year to more than Â£1m.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: "We do not comment on HR matters.

"The permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office received a ministerial direction from the then-prime minister to proceed with the payment to the former cabinet secretary. Their exchange of letters is a matter of public record."

The accounts state Sir Keir authorised the "special severance package" on 16 February.

A note in them also states: "The former cabinet secretary elected to take early payment of his pension.

"The majority of the total severance payment was used to ensure he could access the full value of his pension that would have been due at normal retirement age, rather than it being reduced for early payment."

The BBC has approached Lord Wormald and Sir Keir for comment.

Conservative shadow Cabinet Office minister Alex Burghart said: "Chris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin.

"This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers' money by Labour."

The UK's top civil servant sits next to the prime minister during cabinet minister meetings, which usually take place weekly in Downing Street when Parliament is sitting.

They are responsible for ensuring policy decisions are put into action and are ultimately responsible for all civil servants in Great Britain.

At the time of his appointment in December 2024, Sir Keir said Lord Wormald would be tasked with "the complete re-wiring of the British state to deliver bold and ambitious long-term reform".

As a career civil servant, some questioned whether he was the best person to reform the Civil Service.

Lord Wormald was replaced in February, making him the shortest-serving cabinet secretary in the history of the post.

The FDA Union, which represents senior civil servants, responded to his departure by criticising "anonymous briefings" against him and called his treatment "a new low for this government and its relationship with the Civil Service".

Lord Wormald was replaced by Dame Antonia Romeo.

He was later given a seat in the House of Lords in one of Sir Keir's last acts as prime minister.

Lord Wormald will be an independent crossbench peer and is scheduled to formally take his seat on Thursday.

News.title: Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say
News.content:
The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

The nationalist leaders from Plaid Cymru, Sinn FÃ©in and the SNP - who want their countries to leave the United Kingdom - signed an agreement on Monday which said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

But while Scotland's John Swinney and Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill called for referendums at a joint press conference, Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable for one in his country.

Labour and Reform accused Plaid of wanting to break up the UK.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth's governments later backed a separate agreement agreed to work together on pressing UK government on "fairness" in funding and powers.

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

All three met on Monday as representatives of their parties. Sinn FÃ©in president Mary Lou McDonald also attended.

The memorandum of understanding said: "For people watching across these islands - for people watching around the world - there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end.

"No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.

"We recognise that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time."

News.title: Speedboat killer jailed for attack on girlfriend
News.content:
Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs.

The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July.

The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison.

He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date.

Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel.

He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman.

According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening.

In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument.

In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar".

News.title: No police collusion in sectarian murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
News.content:
An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers.

However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night.

The report, published on Monday, external, highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect.

Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997.

The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded.

The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle.

"However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order.

"They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers."

Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed â both at the scene and in the days that followed.

"The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said.

The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate.

The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately Â£33m.

The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades.

Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner.

The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public".

On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view.

Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill".

However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view".

News.title: This is what women in sport look like - female athletes hit back
News.content:
Female athletes have spoken out against a controversial sports gambling advert starring actress Sydney Sweeney.

The advert has gone viral online and features American Sweeney naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.

It has sparked a strong reaction, with many female athletes criticising its sexualisation of women in sport, and how they are being defined by their appearance rather than their achievements as sportswomen.

Amy Hunt, who became a four-time European champion earlier this summer, referenced the advert after she ran a season's best 22.10 seconds to finish fourth in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday.

"Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt said in her post-race interview with BBC Sport.

Referring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, she added: "21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening."

American actress Sweeney, 29, starred in the television series Euphoria and her films include Anyone But You and The Housemaid.

The backlash has included many other athletes from a range of sports posting videos of themselves competing or training, and describing the frustrations and struggles they have faced throughout their careers.

The trend was started by American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted a montage of herself training with the caption, "I don't know what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what women in sport look like."

Kramer told BBC World Service's Newshour show she "did not expect" the reaction to her post and "just wanted to uplift women and remind them that you may see these types of ads but remember that this is not the only thing that matters".

She said it was "so cool" to see "all the incredible athletes hopping on this trend, uplifting themselves, uplifting each other", adding she was used to getting "very demeaning and objectifying" messages from men because of competing in a leotard as a gymnast.

Kramer added: "Unfortunately being objectified pretty much my entire career, it made me feel strong enough to post about this and to stand up for the women that don't want to be objectified and don't want to be looped into this unfortunate narrative that's been pushed for a long time."

News.title: Key convicted Palestine Action member on the run
News.content:
A key member of Palestine Action, who is currently on the run, has been convicted in his absence over a break-in that caused damage put at Â£1.2m to an arms firm.

Sean Middlebrough, 33, originally from Liverpool, absconded in October last year after being granted bail for his brother's wedding. The self-proclaimed revolutionary communist has since sent messages to supporters describing himself as a "prisoner of war".

His trial began this summer in his absence and last month the jury convicted him of criminal damage by a majority of nine-to-one.

Prosecutors told the court Middlebrough had helped to plan and organise the August 2024 break-in at Elbit Systems in Bristol, a British defence firm with an Israeli parent company. The break-in happened 10 months before the government banned the group under counter-terrorism powers.

News.title: Uganda will now take part in Harry's Invictus Games after King's reassurance
News.content:
Uganda's military leaders have confirmed their country will take part in Prince Harry's Invictus Games for wounded veterans, after saying last week they were going to pull out of the event.

The change of heart follows a phone call with the King's principal private secretary, Sir Clive Alderton, who told them the King had "no problem" with Uganda's participation in the games.

This support from Buckingham Palace is likely to be seen as an olive branch, helping Prince Harry with his sports events for injured service men and women.

It had seemed that Uganda's involvement would be a victim of the fall-out over a letter sent on behalf of the King clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

Uganda's military chief, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said the withdrawal had been made so as "not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III".

But it seems that a private conversation between Sir Clive Alderton and General Kainerugaba has resolved any worries about the King not being supportive of Uganda taking part in the games, which are being held in Birmingham next year.

According to a spokesman for Uganda's military, Sir Clive had "encouraged the CDF [Chief of Defence Forces] to proceed with preparations" to take part in the games.

"In the telephone conversation, General Kainerugaba appreciated the King's message and clarity provided by Buckingham Palace on the subject, promising that the UPDF [Ugandan People's Defence Force] would resume preparations to participate in the upcoming games," said the Ugandan military spokesman.

It is not clear whether the Palace initiated the change of plan by calling the Ugandans, or whether it was the Ugandans who first contacted the Palace for their views.

General Kainerugaba, son of Uganda's president, had announced last Wednesday the withdrawal from the games in a social media post on X.

"We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval," said the general's announcement.

That approval now seems to have been provided, opening the way for Uganda to take part. The country had only been announced as a participant in July.

Rob Owen, CEO of the Invictus Games Foundation, welcomed the news that "Uganda has confirmed it will continue to be part of the Invictus community".

"Uganda became our 26th nation earlier this year, joining a growing movement that provides year-round recovery opportunities for wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans across the world," said Owen.

This change of minds ends a row which had been linked with the letter sent by the Palace about the status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, which had made clear that they were private citizens and could not carry out official royal engagements.

It had given an impression of tensions as Prince Harry and Meghan settled into life in the UK.

A royal source said there was now a "positive outcome" for all sides and thanked the Ugandans for their understanding.

Where there is any uncertainty about the role of the Sussexes, organisations are welcome to seek guidance from the Palace, said a royal source.

News.title: Chief coroner calls for inquiry into Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
The chief coroner overseeing inquests into the deaths of two men killed in the attack on a Manchester synagogue is to ask the government to hold a public inquiry instead.

Judge Alexia Durran, chief coroner of England and Wales, said she would write to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to recommend the inquests be converted into a public inquiry after being told some MI5 material could not be heard in open court because of national security concerns.

Inquests were planned into the deaths of Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, following the attack by Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, on Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Manchester last October.

Inquests have no mechanism to hold secret or private hearings, excluding press and public.

News.title: Opera singer leads Scottish takeover of the Last Night of the Proms
News.content:
When opera singer Nicky Spence took to the famous stage of London's Royal Albert Hall for the Last Night Proms, just a tartan scarf hinted at his roots.

But when he ripped off his "boring black trousers" to reveal a pair of tartan trews during a rendition of Donald, Where's Your Troosers? there was no doubt of his heritage.

It was part of Scotch Snap - a medley of traditional and modern classics - which the Dumfries native combined with dance moves and a series of patriotic outfits.

And it ensured the audience were treated to performances of The Proclaimers' I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles) and Bacara's Yes Sir, I Can Boogie alongside the more traditional Rule Britannia! and Sit Down, Your're Rocking the Boat.

News.title: Henry Pollock ‘open to every opportunity’ amid Northampton contract talks
News.content:

Henry Pollock has said that he is “open to every opportunity” with the England back rower yet to sign a new contract with Northampton Saints.

Pollock’s deal with the Gallagher Prem club is due to expire at the end of this season and, while The Independent understands that talks are progressing well and there is confidence at Saints that he will re-sign, the 21-year-old is yet to agree terms.

The youngster was described as a £1m player by Eddie Hearn, who oversees his commercial deals under his Matchroom agency, though is expected to be in line for a deal worth around £450,000 a year.

Pollock insists, though, that is keeping an open mind, hinting that he hopes to play abroad and potentially try another sport in the future.

“I'm very much at the minute working through different scenarios and different avenues I can take,” Pollock explained. “The big thing for me is making sure that my management are happy with it and they're doing all that stuff.

“I'm open to every opportunity. I'm not going to say no to stuff that I think will be good for my career and good for me. I'm very young but I'm still very open to lots of new things.

“Obviously, Northampton's been so great to me. I've stayed here, I've been here my whole career and they've made me who I am. For me to stay here would be so special. Obviously, I know it's not as easy as that and I know there's lots of moving parts that come into play.

open image in gallery Henry Pollock is open to alternative opportunities ( PA )

“I think for me, you almost have to be quite selfish in that aspect think what's right for you. If that is staying here, then that's great. I'll be here for however long. If it's not, then I'll be open to new opportunities. I'll be open to doing different things, selfishly I think it's down to me at the end of the day. I definitely want to go and live in different countries, explore new sports, explore new avenues. Again, that's all down to the management team. I'm just speaking to them loads and assessing my options and seeing what's right for myself.”

Pollock, who did not specify which other sports he might wish to explore, became Matchroom’s first rugby client when he signed with Hearn’s agency in March, though his contract with Northampton does not fall under their purview.

The player insisted that the promoter’s declarations about his value were a good thing.

open image in gallery Eddie Hearn signed Henry Pollock as a clientearlier this year ( Getty )

“I don't see it as pressure,” Pollock stressed. “I see it as him doing his job.

“He's the best sports promoter in the world. The reason he's the best is because he gets his client what he deserves.If he's saying that about me then for me it's just noise.

“Eddie's been great for me and he's given me so many avenues to get into. The way that he can give me access to loads of different stuff has been amazing. I have no bad words about him. The sport of rugby needs to change and hopefully this is a change.”

Northampton are due to open their Prem campaign against the Newcastle Red Bulls next Friday. Director of rugby Phil Dowson is hopeful that Pollock’s deal is done soon.

“We’re getting closer. As you can imagine it’s complex. There’s a few moving parts that we need to put together. But I’m hopeful. As I said before, he wants to stay and we want to keep him. Obviously there’s some negotiations going between that but those two things are very positive.

“It would have been good to have it sorted three weeks ago but that’s the case across the board. There’s lots of guys out of contract and that can be weighing in the back of their mind in how we managed and how we talk to them and their agents. What I’m always impressed by is with how professional the lads are in terms of still having a job to do. The best way of getting paid is to play well so that’s what we expect the lads to do.”

Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil sued Columbia University on Monday, alleging it failed to address harassment against him and other members of a pro-Palestinian campus group and retaliated against them when they reported it.

The university's “deliberate indifference” led to the doxing of multiple group members and Khalil’s detention by immigration agents, according to the civil rights lawsuit filed in federal court in New York City.

The university declined to comment on the lawsuit, but said in an email that “creating a campus environment where every member of our community feels welcome, supported, and safe is fundamental to who we are as a University.”

“Columbia is committed to protecting our community from discrimination and harassment, and responding promptly and appropriately when concerns arise,” it said.

Khalil also sued Columbia last year to block the release of student records to a congressional committee.

A former graduate student at Columbia University, Khalil gained prominence as a spokesperson for student activists protesting Israel's actions in Gaza.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested him at his campus apartment in March 2025, and he quickly became the face of the Trump administration's crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrators.

Khalil spent 104 days in a Louisiana immigration jail, missing the birth of his first child, before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered his release. His deportation case remains active.

Khalil's lawsuit says Columbia “refused to correct disinformation” about him while he was detained, “allowing a false narrative about his conduct and role to persist and further enabling peer-on-peer harassment of other Palestinian students and students with perceived shared Arab and/or Muslim ancestry.”

Instead of investigating reports of harassment, the university retaliated by characterizing events by a pro-Palestinian campus group as security risks and revising disciplinary policy to target criticism of the Israeli government, according to the lawsuit.

It accuses Columbia of civil rights violations, requests a court order restoring Khalil's access to the campus and ending the Palestinian group's suspension, and seeks damages “to be determined at trial.”

It also names the pro-Palestinian group and its president, Mohammad Zubairi, as plaintiffs.

A man has pleaded guilty to drugging and raping his wife over a 20-year period without her knowledge.

Earlier this year, he admitted to various sexual offences against his wife on dates between 2022 and 2025 including rape and sexual assault.

On Monday the husband, who is in his 60s, from Stockport, Greater Manchester, admitted similar offences dating back to 2004 including administering a substance with intent to stupefy or overpower his wife between 2004 and 2025.

The defendant cannot be identified to protect the anonymity of his wife.

Wearing a dark grey suit, blue shirt and blue tie, he broke down in tears at one point as he entered his pleas from the dock at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court and was allowed to sit down to answer the remaining charges.

His wife sat in the front row of the public gallery and was surrounded by family members.

The defendant also previously pleaded guilty to sharing intimate photographs or film of his wife, without her consent, for sexual gratification.

Twelve co-defendants all deny various allegations involving the same woman.

Reform UK has been accused of trying to “distract” voters from controversy over the party’s financial affairs after it launched a small boats mobile “game”.

Nigel Farage’s party announced the launch of its own mobile game on Monday, in a move that has been branded a “stunt and a gimmick” by political opponents.

The game, called Small Boat Scramble, will allow players to take command of a Royal Navy vessel to stop migrant boats reaching Britain.

The party said players will face “small boats, mega-dinghies and, every so often, a Boriswave”, with the person with the highest score over the next month set to win £5,000.

But the launch of the game comes as Reform is facing serious questions over two £36 million donations from crypto billionaires, which were made public over the weekend.

open image in gallery Nigel Farage’s party announced the launch of its own mobile game on Monday, in a move that has been branded a “stunt and a gimmick” by political opponents ( PA )

Questions have been raised over the legality of the donations, given the two benefactors - Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne - could be covered by a cap on overseas donors put in place by the Representation of the People Bill.

Labour accused Reform of launching the “game” as an attempt to “distract from the sleaze and scandal engulfing Reform UK”.

“While Reform play games, this Labour government is bearing down on small boat crossings, with arrivals this summer at their lowest level for six years,” a Labour Party spokesperson said.

“Nigel Farage is scrambling yet again to distract from the sleaze and scandal engulfing Reform UK - and the multiple police investigations into the party’s finances. Instead of stunts and gimmicks, he should come clean and answer the serious questions facing his party.”

Reform UK has also launched a SmallBoatWatch app, which allows users to track the number of migrants crossing the Channel each day.

open image in gallery Nigel Farage said he did not want to talk about the details of the two crypto billionaire donors to Reform UK (Will Colebourne/PA) ( PA Wire )

“SmallBoatWatch puts the facts in the hands of the public. People shouldn't have to rely on politicians' promises to understand the scale of this crisis. Instead they can see it for themselves,” Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said.

“And Small Boat Scramble lets people have a bit of fun with a very serious issue. The British public are sick of watching politicians talk while the boats keep coming.”

Meanwhile, Nigel Farage has admitted the £72 million donated to his party over the weekend may not be legal under upcoming legislation to clamp down on foreign political donors.

The government’s Representation of the People Bill will be backdated to March 25 and also apply to donations made in the first year that someone moves back to the UK, raising concerns over the location of Mr Delo ad Mr Harborne.

Mr Delo had been based in Hong Kong but stated in April he would move back to the UK to bypass limits on foreign donors, while Mr Harborne was resident in Thailand before reportedly registering to vote in Hampshire in June.

open image in gallery Questions have been raised over the legality of the donations, given the two benefactors - Ben Delo (pictured) and Christopher Harborne - could be covered by a cap on overseas donors put in place by the Representation of the People Bill. ( The Ben Delo Foundation )

Mr Farage told the BBC on Monday that while he believed the two donations were “compliant” with the law as it stands, suggested they would not be acceptable as a result of a law change.

He went on to say that if the donations were deemed impermissible retrospectively, Reform UK would advocate a cap on trade union funding to political parties, which would serve as a major blow to Labour.

"Both these donations are 100 per cent compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Mr Farage said.

He was subsequently asked whether Mr Delo and Mr Harborne were resident in the UK on 25 March, as this status would affect their donations.

Mr Farage replied: "I’m not going to go into their particular details. All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.

"Now, there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally. Well, that simply cannot be.”

Max Verstappen has admitted he came close to stepping away from Formula 1 before extending his deal with Red Bull last month, despite holding discussions with rival teams.

Speaking to German publication Bild after agreeing a deal until 2030, the four-time world champion discussed retirement thoughts and confirmed talks took place with McLaren.

"You have to take every conversation with another team seriously," Verstappen said. "But in the end, I was closer to quitting Formula 1 than to signing with another racing team."

"You either quit or you don't, so it's a 50/50 decision," he added. "I seriously considered calling it quits. But at the end of the day, I just love racing."

The 28-year-old won four consecutive F1 titles from 2021 to 2024, but remains winless this season. He sits sixth in the standings following Sunday's runner-up finish at the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, 147 points adrift of Mercedes leader Kimi Antonelli.

open image in gallery Verstappen has not won a race this season ( Getty )

Verstappen stated he did not sign his new Red Bull agreement last month owing to any external pressure.

"If both parties want to work together long-term, why wait?" he said. "The criticism doesn't bother me. I don't care what others think of me.

"The only thing that matters is how my family, my management, the team, and I feel about it. I have to be able to get along with myself, and I can."

Verstappen added that he has nothing left to prove to himself in F1.

"I'm a four-time world champion, and after my first title, I'd already achieved everything I ever wanted," he said. "I don't race for the history books, but for myself, the team, and our fans. Because of that, the decision was ultimately made quickly."

Unlike Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, 45, Verstappen does not anticipate competing into his 40s.

"I don't think so, but that's impossible to predict," he said. "I'll keep racing as long as I enjoy it."

The F1 calendar resumes in two weeks at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, while a late call is expected to be made on whether the season can finish with races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid concerns over the ongoing Middle East conflict.

Bob Mackie, the iconic fashion designer whose visually bold Hollywood creations defined 1970s glamour, dressing Carol Burnett in eccentric costumes and Cher in her most daring outfits, has died at the age of 87 on Monday.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," read a post shared across his official social media channels.

"His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Dubbed the "Designer to the Stars," Mackie earned nine Emmy Awards and a Tony Award, alongside three Oscar nominations, including one for Barbra Streisand’s sheer batwing gown in "Funny Lady."

His legacy was formally recognized in 2002 when he was inducted into the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences' Hall of Fame.

He created memorable dresses for high-profile figures such as Madonna, Barbra Streisand, Sharon Stone, Diana Ross, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, alongside stage costumes for Pink.

open image in gallery Bob Mackie ( Getty )

Notably, when Marilyn Monroe sang her iconic, sultry rendition of "Happy Birthday" to President John F. Kennedy during a Democratic National Committee fundraiser, she wore a sheer, embellished dress originally conceived in a Mackie sketch.

Bob Mackie’s distinct aesthetic continues to inspire contemporary style icons

His artistic touch remains visible in modern fashion, inspiring figures like Kendall Jenner and Bella Hadid.

Today, archival pieces from his collection are frequently worn by stars including Anya Taylor-Joy, Miley Cyrus, and Zendaya, who chose a vintage Mackie gown to pay tribute to Cher at the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony.

Taylor Swift embraced his signature showgirl aesthetic for her 2025 album "The Life of a Showgirl" by wearing original Mackie creations.

open image in gallery Taylor Swift wore original Mackie creations for her 2025 album ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ ( PA Media )

Sequins and elaborate trimmings were central to Mackie’s signature look — earning him colorful monikers such as the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones, and the Guru of Glitter.

Yet his underlying core principle was simple: "You don’t try to change anybody, you just try to make them look better than ever," he told The Associated Press in 2018.

Beyond screen and concert stages, Mackie left a significant mark on Broadway, designing costumes for "On the Town" in 1971 and "Moon Over Buffalo" in 1995.

He also dressed Burnett for "Putting It Together," Debbie Reynolds for "Debbie" in 1976, Liza Minnelli for "Minnelli on Minnelli" in 1999, and earned his Tony Award for his work on "The Cher Show."

Sydney Sweeney isn’t just the star of Euphoria – she’s now the star of a new highly sexualised ad campaign for sports betting app Novig that has officially gone viral.

It shows the 29-year-old in a variety of sporty poses, including sitting naked on top of a basketball hoop, using footballs to push up her cleavage and wearing just shoulder pads with a football placed over her crotch area.

“Sports”, “sports”, “sports,” she says on repeat. “Think you like sports? Prove it,” is her catchphrase, encouraging the viewer to start betting.

It comes only a year after her American Eagle campaign, which featured the slogan “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” and was criticised for appearing to use the language of eugenics.

open image in gallery The advert features Sweeney, nude, and in a number of provocative positions ( Novig )

Her latest ad is instead being accused of sexualising women in sport and is also offending a lot of people, including several high-profile athletes. Retired four-time Olympic gold medallist Olympic swimmer Ariarne Titmus said she was “infuriated” by this “bulls***” brand marketing.

“How do we live in a world where monetising a women’s [sic] body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?” she wrote on Instagram.

We want to encourage girls to do sport, not pile more pressure on them

Ex-Olympic runner Hannah Williams called it a “disgrace for women in sports”. British track star Amy Hunt also went for the jugular at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday, saying: “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women’s sport looks like!”

She added: “When you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty. It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time, definitely” - it’s “hard work, blood, sweat, tears”.

But Sweeney isn’t sorry. Instead, she has “responded” to the backlash by sharing a series of Instagram Stories on Sunday that highlight professional sports stars who have posed naked or semi-naked in the former American monthly sports magazine ESPN, seemingly in a bid to prove double standards.

open image in gallery The actor does not seem fazed by the outrage this advert, and her other previous questionable appearances, have caused ( Novig )

The images she shared include tennis players Serena Williams and Caroline Wozniacki and even former American football player Jason Kelce, the younger brother of Taylor Swift’s husband, Travis.

Sweeney might have been trying to point out a double standard, but her insinuations of snobbiness doesn’t wash for me.

The aim of Sweeney’s latest ad is to get men to download the sports-only market predictions app, and it’s plain dishonest to wrap it up in some kind of tongue-in-cheek support for women in sport.

And it’s the last thing mums of daughters like me need. Seeing naked Sweeney all over sports like an OnlyFans performer is not a great role model for my young daughters, especially given the trend of girls dropping sports after puberty.

By age 14, girls drop out of sports at two times the rate of boys, according to US research shared by organisations like the Youth Sport Trust, and it’s driven by body changes, declining body confidence, and a fear of being judged that knocks their confidence.

More than 1 million girls in the UK lose interest in sport as teenagers, according to research by Women in Sport

More than 1 million girls in the UK lose interest in sport as teenagers, according to research by Women in Sport in 2022 – and it’s low self-belief and body image concerns that are doing the damage.

That’s why Sweeney, a Gen Z poster girl, shouldn’t be sexualising women in sport – which she’s doing with 100 per cent success.

It sets an impossible bar which will result in tweens and teens – and even grown women – feeling inadequate and not attractive enough on the playing pitch or in the PE class.

As girls approach puberty, there’s already a gnawing worry about how you look as your body changes and your hormones run wild. Sweeney’s epic naked marathon isn’t going to help with any of that, and I doubt the creators of this campaign gave it a second thought. But it matters, and here’s why.

open image in gallery Sweeney’s new  has faced criticism from sports stars ( Novig )

If my 10-year-old daughter Lola, who plays netball at school, saw the photos of Sweeney sitting in the basketball hoop naked, the message she would likely take is that sport is about looking “hot”.

We want to encourage girls to do sport, not pile more pressure on them. But despite the visibility of women’s sports since events like the 2023 Women’s World Cup, according to the UK’s charity Women in Sport, it’s still boys who dream of being top sportspeople – 53 per cent of them last year, while for girls it dropped from 38 per cent in 2024 to just 23 per cent in 2025.

Too many girls are disengaging from sport as it is, so please, Sydney Sweeney – stop trying to double down on your choices and pretend that you’re the one who is a victim of hypocrisy and double standards. We don’t need to hear about how unfair it is that you’re degraded for posing in nothing but football socks, while a famous man would be praised.

Because reducing women in sport to visual objects is just another way of packaging women’s bodies to be commodified and objectified. It places physical attractiveness on a pedestal rather than celebrating talent.

I hope my girls don’t see this ad – and focus instead on remembering their PE kit and their enjoyment of taking part in sport, which takes them out of their heads. What girls and teens need is healthy self-esteem, positive body image, and self-belief – not harmful stereotypes and Sweeney’s objectification of women in sport.

All our reviewers are either resident destination experts or travel writers that specialise in hotels. News.title: Asia on high alert as El Niño threatens new Dengue epidemic
News.content:
Countries from Brazil to Taiwan are bracing for a surge in dengue driven by the “supersized” El Niño, as the UN warns this year’s weather phenomenon could be the strongest on record.

Both the virus and the Aedes mosquitoes that transmit it are especially sensitive to heat – and the El Niño is expected to push global temperatures to new highs.

“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” Antonio Guterres, the UN Secretary General, said last week. “The ​science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”

The weather phenomenon – a periodic warming of sea surface temperature in the eastern Pacific, caused by weakening trade winds – alters rainfall and temperature patterns across the globe. That, in turn, causes extreme weather like droughts, heatwaves, floods and typhoons – which then trigger events including wildfires, crop failures and a collapse in affected fisheries.

But it can also have a major impact on the transmission of disease, including dengue – and countries across the world, especially in Asia and Latin America, are bracing for outbreaks.

In July, Brazil’s Ministry of Health sent an alert warning states that arboviruses like dengue, chikungunya and Zika could surge later this year, and urged officials to ramp up disease surveillance and mosquito control programmes.

The increase will likely peak in 2027: the biomedical research institute Fiocruz has estimated that Brazil will see 1.7 million dengue cases next year, driven by El Niño.

News.title: ‘Your home is your palace’: Queen Elizabeth II’s housekeeper answers reader questions
News.content:
Was there one surprisingly simple trick used in the palace that made things feel instantly more polished?

Jay, West Midlands

Making sure you have a routine is the best way for everything to feel polished. At the palace, the team is trained, and everyone has the right tools and time to do their job... They learned how to lift things safely and how to be confident when they were around the Royal Collection. When you’re cleaning historic areas such as palaces and castles, you have to make sure you don’t overdo it. We had a daily routine that ensured we didn’t over-clean everything.

What is the royal protocol for dealing with ironing and maintaining perfectly crisp sheets without using harsh, eco-unfriendly chemicals?

Saleem, London

Much of what would be classed as royal protocol are things we would do in our own homes. For linen, you need to treat it well and look after it by not washing it at too high a temperature or using too much detergent. Make sure the products you’re using are eco-friendly, not only for the environment, but also to care for the linen. For historic linen, it needs to be handled very gently, as it can tear quite easily.

Did the Queen get involved in any of the details of housekeeping?

Peter, East of England

I was very blessed. The Queen did leave it up to me to make those decisions because she trusted me to keep her home and the other royal residences clean and up to a great standard. I kept in touch with her, making sure the team was involved. We would have regular update meetings to ensure everyone knew what was happening and when. There was planned cleaning throughout the year depending on what was occurring, making sure certain areas were protected or closed off, for example.

I would feel very stressed cleaning around objects of great value, history and sentiment. How do you avoid disasters?

Catherine, North West

It’s important the team feels confident when cleaning those areas. We achieve that through training and building their confidence.

In the castle, we introduced a cleaning schedule that covered different areas within the state apartments – and it meant that we didn’t over-clean. The structure of this schedule was important. Every day, we would ensure we vacuumed and damp-dusted; there were no actual chemicals or any what I call “wet chemicals”. On a Monday, for instance, we would clean vases. On a Tuesday, we would do the fireplaces. On a Wednesday, it would be light fittings.

It’s crucial the team is given the right amount of time to clean, so that they don’t feel rushed or stressed. But we also have to remember that accidents happen. And if an accident happens and it was just an accident, then what can you do? It’s just one of those things.

Ultimately, making sure people are trained and confident is the key.

With limited time, what are the housekeeping priorities?

David, South West

My housekeeping priorities when at home are to make things look really tidy quickly. Putting your newspapers away, fluffing the cushions up, tidying the curtains, making sure your washing is cleared and the dishwasher is on – these are all things that will make a big difference, even if you haven’t had time to get your mop or vacuum out.

When are you satisfied a room is clean?

D, North West

I am quite a hard taskmaster and I do like perfection, but equally, that comes with making sure people understand the guidelines and what’s expected of them, after being trained properly.

I like to be visible and around the team, showing them what I’m looking at. I would get them to sit on a toilet and then shut the door, so they could see what’s behind the door – or sit in the bath, because that way you can see what other people are seeing when they’re using it. If you’re cleaning and rushing around, you don’t always see those little details.

News.title: Woeful Man Utd have no excuses, Carrick is under big pressure
News.content:
Afterwards Haaland talked about City’s “personality, character” and that was exactly what United lacked. They did not adapt a tactical plan to combat 10-man City’s desire to keep their wingers high and wide, and break with intent and still try and attack.

It was telling that so little did City’s new head coach Enzo Maresca worry about United that he did not add a defensive player, and when he took off Rayan Cherki at half-time, he replaced him with the equally creative Iliman Ndiaye who impressed. Maresca knew United needed space to run in behind and denied them that. It was that simple.

City also struck the post with United goalkeeper Senne Lammens tipping an Enzo Fernández shot against the frame of the goal, and the visitors were worthy winners as they preserved their perfect start to the season to draw level on points with leaders, Arsenal.

City handled the occasion and the – admittedly toothless – opposition superbly under their new head coach and will clearly be Arsenal’s closest challengers this season.

Maresca delivered a masterclass. For Carrick? This was a disasterclass. An object lesson in how not to use a man-advantage. And now United will have to endure even more City songs after being outplayed at home like this.

Was it complacency? Was it inability? Was it a damning lack of courage, confidence, belief even? On the pitch and in the dugout United were far too passive. This was not how a big team plays and Carrick needs to wake up.

The former midfielder did so well last season to guide United into Champions League qualification but so far this campaign he has given the impression that his job is done. Rather than that the real work starts now.

News.title: Redemption Sunday for Hull and Woad as Europe reclaim Solheim Cup
News.content:
The quiet but steely 22-year-old, who everyone seemed to have forgotten was a rookie, punched her fist when she held the decisive two-footer, before the customary hug with opponent Auston Kim and then being mobbed by her team.

“This was really important,” Woad said. “I mean, I was pretty disappointed and felt like I was kind of letting everyone down. Then the captain kind of spoke to me and said that I was third on [the most] birdies [made]. So I just had to trust that and that’s golf sometimes. And it ended up I got the winning putt.”

Some will claim that Woad was only the match-winner on a technicality. Carlota Ciganda in the penultimate game had not finished off her win against Jennifer Kupcho, but when Woad tapped in, the Spaniard was three up with three to go and was guaranteed a half. So the acclaim Woad received was granted. Not that anyone in the Europe camp cared.

The previous evening they had returned to their team room feeling slightly down that they did not hold the advantage, Kupcho holing a 91-footer on the 17th and a 30-footer on the 18th to deny Ciganda and Céline Boutier. And their mood was not helped when videos appeared on social media of the Americans taking crates of beer on to the bus back to their hotel. Yet that foolish scenario only offered extra incentive. “At least we’ll be the ones taking crates of beer on to our bus this evening,” Mel Reid, the assistant captain, said quite pointedly.

News.title: Lando Norris fumes at virtual safety car rules for costing him Spanish GP win
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix, the first time the race has been held at the all-new, purpose-built street circuit, the Madring. The track has developed a reputation in its short life for being a bit of a tricky one. Some have gone so far as to call it a “car killer”? Is it living up to that reputation? Probably, especially if you look at some of the lower formulae that have run on it.

It has also increasingly become the case for the Formula One cars, too. The first couple of practice sessions on Friday revealed little to worry about. As the drivers began to push, though, from final practice and qualifying, the mistakes and crashes happened. The biggest so far was Oliver Bearman but also a smaller one for Lewis Hamilton.

There will almost certainly be some kind of incident in the race, but whether we see red flags, safety cars and so on remains to be seen. A bigger and perhaps more significant question will be how much overtaking will take place on this track. The drivers are not optimistic. The theory goes that if tyre degradation is high then there will be, because you will have significant pace offsets between worn and fresh tyres. The problem is that the leaders tend not to differ to greatly from one another on strategy these days...

Perhaps George Russell, who qualified down in sixth and has little to lose, will be brave and put on a set of hard tyres to start with. Russell has work to do yet again. He was not miles off Antonelli in qualifying when it came to pace, but given how close it was in the top six, finds four cars between himself and the championship leader, who just missed out on pole to McLaren’s Lando Norris.

Norris said it was the best lap of his life and seemed to come from nowhere. He improved more than a second from Q2 to Q3 and continues his fine form in 2026. He will start alongside Antonelli with Max Verstappen in third, Lewis Hamilton in fourth and Charles Leclerc in fifth, before Russell.

News.title: Tora Bora’s last midwife struggles under Taliban rule as aid runs dry
News.content:
The small clinic, crowded with pregnant women, sits in the shadow of Tora Bora in eastern Afghanistan. Twenty-five years ago, those mountains commanded the attention of the world’s most powerful military. Roughly 15 miles from the clinic, in the Tora Bora cave complex, Osama bin Laden was believed to be hiding as American bombs rained down in the hunt for the architect of 9/11.

Today, another consequence of the West’s long entanglement with Afghanistan is playing out beneath those same mountains – in the struggle to keep mothers and babies alive.

In the baking courtyard of Gandab Kharoti health centre, dozens of women enveloped in sapphire blue burqas sit shoulder to shoulder beneath trees waiting to see Shila Ibrahimi, a 27-year-old midwife.

The women rest against walls, dusty, barefoot children play, and mothers cradle sick babies beneath folds of cloth. Some have walked for hours through the mountains to reach her.

Among them is Fawzia, 30, seven-and-a-half months pregnant with her seventh child. Suffering from headaches, she has walked for miles through the heat.

Her husband works far from the village, so she makes the journey with her children and mother-in-law, hoping the Taliban do not stop her for the crime of travelling without a male escort.

Under the Taliban’s morality rules, women face restrictions on travelling alone, while UN monitors have documented the regime’s morality inspectors ordering some health facilities not to treat unaccompanied women.

But enforcement varies and Fawzia says nobody challenged her on her journey here. Asked where she would give birth if the clinic closed she says: “We have nowhere else to go. We cannot afford that. We are poor.”

News.title: Springboks look like World Cup champions elect… again
News.content:
In doing so, Erasmus while still relying on his veteran performers, managed to expose some of the next generation to invaluable white heat pressure, including Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Morne van den Berg and Cameron Hanekom, who all look to the manor born.

And the substance of the series victory is heightened by the fact it came against a regenerated and rejuvenated All Blacks side, who rediscovered their high-octane and relentless attacking identity under new coach Dave Rennie. At times the handling and precision of the All Blacks were so sumptuous that it felt like they might be in a position to level the series in Baltimore.

But the narrative of the previous two Tests continued. At key moments they were let down by their discipline and turnovers in attack to gift the Springboks’ transition ball, and their directness, backed by their power both in collisions and set piece enabled them to pick up points much more easily than their opponents.

At the end, the scoreboard ran away from the All Blacks, which was harsh on them. But one had wondered if they would be able to maintain their intensity at the end of the first half, when it took 32 phases for Will Jordan to score a try to cut the deficit to three points.

A junior football match in Wales descended into chaos as a brawl broke out on the sidelines, with adults and children getting involved in the altercation during a youth match

Footage shared shows two adult men on the pitch. A player then appears to kick towards one of the men as other individuals try to break up the fight.

The confrontation continues on the sidelines. One appears to kick the other, who ends up on the ground.

A number of adults and young players are subsequently seen wading in, while some of the stunned spectators — including young children — can be heard crying out "woah, woah" and "calm down".

Dyfed Powys Police and the West Wales Football Authority have now launched a formal investigation into the incident, with the governing body confirming in an official statement that the matter is being treated "extremely seriously", reports Wales Online.
