World.title: Stakeholders seek stronger investment to reduce maternal, newborn deaths
World.content:
Stakeholders have called for stronger investment, quality healthcare and sustainable domestic financing to reduce preventable maternal and newborn deaths in Nigeria.

The World Health Organisation (WHO), the Gates Foundation and the National Assembly made the call at the national inauguration of the Incentives to Increase Maternal and Newborn Care Services Utilisation (INSEMN) initiative in the State House, Abuja, on Monday.

The calls come as Nigeria continues to confront a high burden of maternal and newborn mortality, with evidence showing that demand-side measures such as financial incentives are most effective when combined with skilled health workers, functional facilities, reliable commodities and referral systems.

The INSEMN initiative seeks to encourage pregnant women to access antenatal, skilled delivery, and postnatal services through incentives such as Mama Kits, bags, and essential items for newborns.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The WHO Representative in Nigeria, Pavel Ursu, said the incentives could encourage families to seek essential maternal and newborn services, but stressed that increased attendance must be matched by quality care.

Mr Ursu said women must find safe, respectful and timely services when they arrive at health facilities, supported by trained health workers, essential medicines and supplies and functional referral systems.

He said primary healthcare remained critical to the initiative because it brought lifesaving services closer to families, built trust and connected communities to the wider health system.

According to him, strong primary healthcare is the foundation for Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and sustained improvement in maternal and newborn health outcomes.

Mr Ursu urged stakeholders to ensure that no woman was left behind, particularly women in rural communities, adolescent girls, women living in poverty and families in underserved areas.

He said national progress must reach every state, local government area and community.

He also called for a review of maternal and perinatal deaths, with lessons from such reviews acted upon quickly.

He stressed the importance of state and local ownership and sustainable domestic financing, saying that lasting progress must be rooted in Nigerian institutions, ownership, and accountability.

He also commended Nigerian health workers for their dedication, describing their service as heroic and calling for greater investment and support for the workforce.

Similarly, Uche Amaonwu, Nigeria Country Director at the Gates Foundation, said the ultimate measure of the initiative should be whether more mothers and babies survived and fewer deaths from preventable causes were recorded.

Mr Amaonwu said the initiative is important because it would encourage pregnant women to attend antenatal care, deliver safely with skilled birth attendants and receive the care they and their newborns needed.

He said the Mama Kits, bags and newborn items being introduced under the initiative would help encourage women to use health facilities and access essential services.

He said improving maternal and newborn health is central to the Gates Foundation’s work, noting that one of its aspirations is that no mother or child should die from a preventable cause.

He pledged the foundation’s continued collaboration with the Nigerian government and other partners to achieve the goal.

On financing, Ipalibo Banigo, Chairman of the Senate Committee on Health (Secondary and Tertiary), said that sustainable domestic financing is essential to strengthening primary healthcare and improving health outcomes.

Ms Banigo said the National Health Insurance Act had provided for a Vulnerable Group Fund to provide health insurance coverage for children under five, pregnant women, internally displaced persons, persons with disabilities, and retirees.

She said budgetary provision had been made for the fund in 2023 and 2024, describing it as an important step toward expanding financial protection for vulnerable Nigerians.

The senator also said members of the 10th NASS had pursued measures to strengthen sustainable domestic health financing, including a proposal to increase the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) allocation from one per cent to two per cent of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

According to her, increased funding will strengthen financing for primary healthcare, disease control, health insurance and emergency health services.

She also referred to efforts to amend the Sugar-Sweetened Beverage-related legislation and the Customs and Excise framework to generate resources for the screening, treatment and prevention of non-communicable diseases.

She stressed that for health financing to produce meaningful results, funds must not only be appropriated but also be released, disbursed, accounted for and monitored.

She pledged the Senate Committee on Health’s commitment to follow up on the utilisation of health funds to ensure they translate into improved services and better outcomes for Nigerians.

She said the reforms under the Renewed Hope Agenda for Health were designed to improve the health and well-being of Nigerians, save lives and strengthen public confidence in the health system.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the speakers agreed on the need to move beyond simply increasing the number of women accessing health facilities to ensuring that the services they receive are timely, affordable, safe and of good quality.

World.title: Group tasks media, CSOs to intensify checks on illicit financial flows
World.content:
The Africa Network for Environment and Economic Justice (ANEEJ) has called on civil society organisations (CSOs) and the media to intensify efforts to expose and curb illicit financial flows (IFFs), warning that the diversion of public resources is undermining Nigeria’s economic development and public welfare.

ANEEJ Executive Director, David Ugolor, said illicit funds moved out of Nigeria through fraudulent transactions had deprived the country of resources that could have been invested in critical sectors, including infrastructure, healthcare, education and job creation.

Mr Ugolor spoke at a two-day training workshop for CSOs and media partners organised by ANEEJ in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State. The workshop ended at the weekend.

He said the consequences of IFFs were ultimately borne by ordinary Nigerians, who are left with poor public services and inadequate infrastructure despite the huge resources available to the government.

“Illicit financial flows have deprived Nigeria of resources that could have been channelled into infrastructure, healthcare, education, job creation and other critical public services,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

N14bn alleged loss

Mr Ugolor cited the Benin-Sapele-Warri Road project as an example of how financial irregularities could translate into hardship for citizens.

He alleged that N14 billion was diverted from the project, leaving citizens to bear the consequences of its failure.

PREMIUM TIMES could not independently verify this claim.

However, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Minister for Works, David Umahi, wants the contractor handling the road arrested for failing to complete it despite having received N14 billion.

He, however, said the persistence of illicit financial flows showed that stronger citizen participation and public scrutiny were needed to complement the work of the agencies.

He called on CSOs and the media to collaborate to investigate suspicious financial transactions, trace stolen assets, and demand accountability from public institutions.

IFFs, terrorism

The Operations Coordinator of the SecFin Project, Philippe Pacaud, also called for stronger collaboration with civil society organisations in tackling illicit financial flows.

Mr Pacaud warned that illicit funds moved from Nigeria and other African countries could be channelled into criminal activities, including corruption and terrorism.

Representing the NFIU Chief Executive Officer, Hafsat Bakari, Chinedum Odenyi said CSOs have important roles to play in advocacy, research, public awareness, policy engagement and community mobilisation in the fight against financial crimes.

He said the role of CSOs would become increasingly important as Nigeria prepares for its 2027 evaluation of its anti-money laundering, counter-terrorism financing and counter-proliferation financing framework.

Building investigative capacity

The workshop featured presentations and interactive sessions on illicit financial flows and financial crimes in Nigeria; the country’s legal and institutional framework for combating IFFs; investigative journalism; media ethics; legal risks; source protection; and digital security.

Participants also developed investigative story ideas and reporting plans focused on illicit financial flows.

Resource persons included Mr Pacaud; Abdullahi Shehu of SecFin Africa; Taiwo Adebayo of the Institute for Security Studies; Aisha Bantam of the NFIU; Adedayo Kayode, managing consultant at Aideasbanc Consulting Limited; and the Editor-in-Chief of PREMIUM TIMES, Musikilu Mojeed, represented by Mr Adebayo.

The workshop was organised under ANEEJ’s project to strengthen the capacity of CSOs and the media to combat illicit financial flows, with support from the European Union through the SecFin Africa Project.

World.title: Another woman arrested for brutalising 7-year-old daughter with hot knife
World.content:
Another woman arrested for alleged ‘brutal abuse’ of her 7-year-old daughter.

Security operatives in Anambra State have arrested a woman, Ogechi Ofoma, who brutally assaulted her seven-year-old daughter with a hot knife in the state.

The police spokesperson in the state, Tochukwu Ikenga, disclosed this in a statement on Monday.

This latest incident occurred days after another woman, Anulika Onyeanusia, was arrested in the state for allegedly using sex toys on her eight-year-old daughter as well as circulating the child’s pornographic video.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Police receive report of fresh case

Mr Ikenga, a superintendent of police, said the state police command received a fresh report on 13 September that Mrs Ofoma brutally abused her daughter, inflicting severe bodily injuries on the minor.

The spokesperson said the incident occurred in Obosi, a community in Idemili North Local Government Area of the state.

“The prompt intervention of security personnel from the Ibollo Community, Awada-Obosi, and concerned residents led to the child’s rescue and the arrest of her mother, Mrs Ogechi Ofoma, 32,” he said.

“Preliminary information indicates that the child was allegedly subjected to severe physical abuse, including injuries reportedly inflicted with a hot knife.”

Mr Ikenga said the police command in the state has condemned the incident and vowed to ensure that those responsible were prosecuted.

The spokesperson said the Commissioner of Police in Anambra State, Nnanna Ama, has commenced collaboration with the state Commissioner for Women Affairs and Social Welfare, Chinyere Onyekesi.

He explained that the collaboration with the ministry was to ensure that the victim received urgent and appropriate medical care, protection, and all necessary welfare support.

Mr Ikenga said the police in the state have praised the vigilance, courage, and public-spirited intervention of the Ibollo Community security personnel and residents whose swift action helped save the child from further harm.

He added that the intervention also enabled the immediate commencement of police action.

The spokesperson said the police command has assured the public that the investigation would be “thorough, professional, and uncompromising.”

“The welfare, safety, and best interests of the child remain paramount, and the command will continue to work with relevant agencies to protect vulnerable persons and ensure accountability in accordance with the law,’’ he stated.

World.title: Ekiti Poll: Like PDP, SDP candidate withdraws petition against Gov Oyebanji’s re-election, party kicks
World.content:
There was a mild drama at the Governorship Election Petition Tribunal sitting in Ado Ekiti on Monday as the Social Democratic Party (SDP) candidate in the 20 June election, Adedayo Alade, through his counsel, Umar Abdullahi, announced the withdrawal of his petition challenging the victory of Governor Biodun Oyebanji against the party’s wish.

Another drama also played out at the tribunal during the cross-examination, as an SDP agent and witness, Toluwalope Oluwandabira, could not identify the name of the party’s flag bearer in the election. He was brought to the tribunal to give evidence in respect of the poll.

The three-member tribunal panel, chaired by Abubakar Idris Kutigi and comprising Aminu Tukur and Maurice Okediya, struck out the petition accordingly.

The People’s Democratic Party (PDP) candidate in the election, Oluwole Oluyede, who was the runner-up, withdrew his petition in the same manner.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

During Monday’s proceedings, Umar Abdullahi, counsel to the SDP candidate and second petitioner, disclosed that he had filed a Motion on Notice dated 12 September before the tribunal, notifying it of his client’s intention to discontinue with the petition.

Confounded by the development, Adewole Adebayo, counsel to the SDP and 1st petitioner, said the withdrawal was like an ambush, having been unaware of the candidate’s decision to step aside from the case, maintaining that he won’t oppose the application, since his backtracking would not in any way impede the party from pursuing the case.

Commenting further on the abrupt withdrawal of the candidate, Mr Adebayo said the party remains unfazed, adding that “If he (Alade) stands his ground and says he wants to withdraw or discontinue, then we will have no reason to stop him. If he withdraws and decides to go home, he is free; it doesn’t stop us from continuing with the case.”

But Adetunji Oso, counsel to Mr Oyebanji and 2nd respondent, argued that he would not oppose the application on the premise that it was undertaken in firm alignment with the provisions of the Electoral Act, 2026 and that the candidate only exercised his legal right.

In his ruling, Mr Kutigi said, “The tribunal grants the application, having considered the Motion on Notice of the second petitioner in respect of his intention to withdraw from the petition. His name is hereby struck out of the petition”.

Meanwhile, during the proceedings, the SDP, which went ahead with the case, called seven witnesses to prosecute its case after the panellists resumed from a 30-minute recess, which had been taken for the party to assemble its witnesses.

In his testimony before the tribunal, a witness, Julius Bamisaye, who raised the issue of alleged massive vote buying, said he noticed people sharing money but couldn’t ascertain precisely the amount being shared to sway voters or the actual persons responsible.

Another witness, Awoleye Samuel, revealed that, though there were skirmishes at the polling unit among contending forces, where he served as the party’s agent, he clarified that this didn’t affect the successful conduct of the election.

In the petition filed by the Action Alliance(AA), the party’s Chairman and the State Collation Agent, Sunday Ajayi, during cross-examination, stated that he was not issued any appointment letter to oversee the election, but claimed that he got the mandate of his party to serve in that capacity, being the number one party man in the state.

After calling seven witnesses, counsel for the petitioners requested a short adjournment, which was granted by the tribunal, as it was not opposed by counsel for the respondents.

At this stage, Mr Oso, counsel to Governor Oyebanji, told the tribunal to be mindful that an election petition is sui generis, and prayed the panellists to impress on the petitioners not to foot-drag and waste the time of the tribunal on this premise.

“My lord, they are hampering us. You have to tell them to present their witnesses who could give evidence based on where they worked during the election, timely. We can’t waste the time of the court.”

Petitioners not coerced to withdraw petition

Meanwhile, Mr Oso has dismissed claims in some quarters that the petitioners were withdrawing their petitions through coercion or intimidation, clarifying that the governor, who doubles as the chief security officer of the state, would not undermine, nor take action that could hinder the free operation of the tribunal to dispense justice in the matter expeditiously.

World.title: When the pulpit becomes political currency, By David Nzekwu
World.content:
The confusion that followed the Abuja event also reveals the fragility of religious representation. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria reportedly moved to distinguish itself from the similarly named charismatic body. The clarification mattered because public authority often depends on who can plausibly claim to speak for whom. Nigeria’s Christian population is vast and diverse. No conference, however grand its titles or extensive its claimed network, owns the political conscience of believers. Bishops may endorse; Christians may disagree. Spiritual office does not transfer the citizen’s vote.

The most dangerous moment for a religious institution is not necessarily when political power attacks it. It may be when political power embraces it so warmly that the institution forgets why it exists. Persecution can clarify conviction; patronage often dissolves it. The church rarely loses its moral authority in one dramatic surrender. More often, it trades that authority away gradually – one invitation, one title, one endorsement and one photograph with power at a time.

That is why the decision of the Charismatic Bishops Conference of Nigeria to endorse President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for re-election in 2027 deserves more than partisan applause or outrage. At its 2026 synod at the National Christian Centre in Abuja, held alongside the International Communion of Charismatic Archbishops, Bishops and Apostles, the conference did not merely pray for the president or urge the government to govern justly. Its President-General, Archbishop Leonard Bature Kawas, declared that the bishops would stand with Tinubu even beyond 2027 and announced the conference’s support for a second term.

A president is entitled to seek re-election. Citizens and organisations are entitled to support him. Religious leaders do not surrender their civic rights when they enter the pulpit. Yet a profound difference exists between a cleric expressing a personal political preference and a gathering of bishops placing collective spiritual authority behind an officeholder. The first is citizenship. The second risks turning a blessing into a campaign instrument.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The reasons reportedly offered for the endorsement make the problem more troubling. The president was praised for supporting the emergence of Christian governors, for his party’s elevation of a born-again Christian and preacher to national leadership, and for the First Lady’s visible faith. These may carry symbolic meaning for some believers, but symbolism is not governance. The number of Christians close to power does not tell a struggling family whether food has become affordable. It does not tell a frightened community whether it is safer, a patient whether a hospital works, or a child whether a public school can provide a meaningful education.

Governments should be judged by what they do for citizens, not by the denominational identities of those admitted into their inner circles. Once religious representation becomes a substitute for public performance, faith is reduced to patronage and citizenship to sectarian arithmetic. The crucial questions disappear: Are Nigerians safer? Are institutions stronger? Is opportunity expanding? Is public money being used responsibly? In their place comes a smaller, more convenient question: Are people like us sufficiently close to power?

That is a poor question for democracy and an even poorer one for the church.

Max Weber’s idea of charismatic authority helps explain the attraction. Charismatic authority rests less on rules or institutions than on the exceptional qualities that followers attribute to an individual. It can animate communities and inspire sacrifice, but it is also unstable and resistant to accountability. Nigeria’s religious and political cultures are deeply familiar with this form of power. The celebrated preacher commands loyalty through anointing, testimony, and personal magnetism. The political leader commands it through spectacle, symbolism and the aura of indispensability.

When these two charismatic systems meet, they should not automatically validate each other. The pulpit ought to remind the podium that power is temporary, stewardship is measurable, and every leader remains answerable to moral law and the people. Politics, for its part, should protect the freedom of religion without purchasing religious approval. In Abuja, however, the two forms of charisma appeared to enter a closed circuit: spiritual prestige offered political legitimacy, while political access offered religious leaders visibility and influence. The politician acquired a borrowed halo; the bishops gained proximity to the state.

The citizen, whose welfare should be central to both public morality and democratic debate, was pushed to the edge of the picture.

This is why the issue is not whether Christians may participate in politics. They should. Faith that says nothing about justice, poverty, violence, corruption, and human dignity is merely private sentiment dressed in sacred language. Nigeria needs religious leaders who can challenge cruelty, defend the vulnerable, demand honest government and help citizens resist hatred. The church does not need to be apolitical to be prophetic. But prophecy is not the same as partisanship, and access is not the same as influence.

A prophetic church speaks truth to power whether the occupant of office is a friend or a foe. A partisan church adjusts its moral vocabulary to protect its preferred candidate. A prophetic leader can pray for a president while questioning his policies. A partisan leader mistakes proximity for progress and ceremonial recognition for national renewal. The difference lies not in whether the church enters public life, but in what it carries into that life: an independent conscience or a negotiable endorsement.

The Christian tradition itself offers a demanding standard. Jesus rejected the conversion of spiritual mission into worldly domination, declaring that his kingdom was not of this world. The earliest Christian witness did not depend on imperial patronage for its authority. It spoke from a moral distance that made both service and rebuke possible. That distance was not withdrawal; it was freedom. It allowed the church to minister to rulers without becoming their ornament, and to serve society without becoming captive to the state.

Once that distance collapses, accountability collapses with it. A church that has publicly invested its prestige in a political leader will struggle to confront that leader’s failures without admitting its own misjudgment. The endorsement creates a moral debt. Silence then becomes easier than criticism, flattery safer than truth. What begins as access ends as self-censorship.

The political class understands this bargain. It has learnt that a religious platform can deliver what an ordinary rally cannot: the suggestion that political preference carries divine approval. The language of testimony replaces the discipline of evidence. Loyalty is presented as faithfulness. Dissent begins to look like disobedience. The voter is no longer merely asked to assess a candidate; he is subtly invited to regard the candidate as heaven’s choice.

That is unfair to voters, dangerous for politicians and corrosive to faith. No endorsement delivered at a synod can replace the verdict of citizens at the ballot box. No clerical title can exempt an administration from scrutiny. And no politician benefits in the long run from being surrounded by religious figures who bless more readily than they question. Leaders insulated from uncomfortable truth eventually become prisoners of praise.

The confusion that followed the Abuja event also reveals the fragility of religious representation. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria reportedly moved to distinguish itself from the similarly named charismatic body. The clarification mattered because public authority often depends on who can plausibly claim to speak for whom. Nigeria’s Christian population is vast and diverse. No conference, however grand its titles or extensive its claimed network, owns the political conscience of believers. Bishops may endorse; Christians may disagree. Spiritual office does not transfer the citizen’s vote.

Nor is this episode an isolated lapse. Religious intervention in Nigerian politics has long moved between moral advocacy, sectional calculation, and outright political alignment. What appears different now is the openness of the exchange. Arguments once framed around national balance are increasingly expressed as an inventory of access gained and loyalty owed. When such conduct is cheered, televised and repeated, it hardens into a system. Future politicians learn that religious endorsement can be cultivated. Future clerics learn that collective blessing can purchase relevance.

Systems reproduce the incentives that sustain them. Soon, every government seeks its choir of clerical validators, while every ambitious religious platform seeks its route to the presidential villa. The public square becomes crowded with titles but empty of moral courage.

The cost is borne by ordinary Nigerians. Citizens already live with too many institutions governed by relationships rather than rules. They see contracts influenced by connections, justice delayed by status and opportunity rationed through proximity. If the church mirrors this culture instead of challenging it, it forfeits the very distinction on which its public credibility rests. A lobbying organisation may negotiate access. A church must answer to a higher obligation.

Nigeria still has religious leaders whose authority was earned through sacrifice, service and principled consistency. Their voices matter precisely because they are not easily recruited into anyone’s campaign. They understand that moral influence grows from independence, not intimacy with power. This is the moment for them to insist that the church’s public role is to illuminate conscience, not instruct ballots; to assess power, not adorn it; and to defend citizens, not secure privileged access for clerics.

The remedy is not silence. It is principled engagement. Religious bodies can publish non-partisan assessments of government performance. They can convene candidates for serious debate, educate voters, monitor elections, resist violence and advocate policies that protect human dignity. They can pray for leaders without campaigning for them and meet public officials without becoming their public relations machinery. Most importantly, they can apply the same moral standard to every party and every officeholder.

The pulpit’s authority is strongest when no politician can take it for granted. Its blessing should comfort the afflicted, not decorate the powerful. Its voice should be free enough to commend what is right today and condemn what is wrong tomorrow, without consulting yesterday’s endorsement.

Political power is temporary. The church’s moral witness is meant to outlast every administration. To exchange that inheritance for proximity is a remarkably poor bargain. Once the pulpit turns charisma into political currency, it may discover that the transaction enriched the politician while impoverishing the church.

A blessing that can be bought is no longer a blessing. It is currency. And every currency loses value when those entrusted with it keep printing more.

David Nzekwu is a public affairs analyst and political commentator.

World.title: Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited Secures Dual Accreditation as System  Integrator and Access Point Provider for Nigeria’s National e-Invoicing  Initiative
World.content:
Company unveils eNvoice.ng to support businesses with smart tax invoicing and seamless compliance under the NRS e-Invoicing regime

Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited has announced its accreditation as both a System Integrator and an Access Point Provider under Nigeria’s National e-Invoicing and Electronic Fiscal System regime.

The milestone positions Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited to support businesses across the full e-Invoicing compliance value chain – from system readiness, ERP integration and invoice data mapping to validation, signing, transmission, status tracking and ongoing compliance support.

The announcement comes as the Nigeria Revenue Service has commenced compliance monitoring for large taxpayers under the National e-Invoicing and Electronic Fiscal System regime. The NRS public notice requires affected large taxpayers to complete onboarding, integration, validation, testing and active invoice transmission to the NRS e-Invoicing platform, while also ensuring that they receive compliant e-invoices with valid Invoice Reference Numbers from suppliers.

Against this background, Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited has unveiled eNvoice, available at www.envoice.ng – a government-accredited e-Invoicing platform built around the brand promise:

Smart Tax Invoicing. Seamless Compliance.

Dual Accreditation: System Integrator and Access Point Provider

As an accredited System Integrator, Vi-M supports businesses in connecting their internal systems, ERP platforms, accounting software and invoicing workflows to the national e-Invoicing framework. This includes readiness assessment, invoice data mapping, API integration, ERP/accounting-system integration, validation support, user training and implementation guidance.

As an accredited Access Point Provider, Vi-M provides a secure pathway for invoice validation, signing, transmission, exchange, status tracking and related compliance workflows within the national e-Invoicing ecosystem.

The dual accreditation enables Vi-M to serve businesses that require end-to-end support as well as businesses that already have internal technology teams but require accredited APP transmission capability.

Introducing eNvoice.ng

eNvoice is designed to make e-Invoicing practical for businesses of different sizes, sectors and levels of digital maturity.

The platform supports:

• large enterprises with ERP systems;

• businesses using accounting software such as Xero, NetSuite, QuickBooks, Sage, Zoho and others;

• businesses requiring API or middleware integration;

• MSMEs requiring a simpler compliance route; and

• businesses without existing accounting software.

For businesses without accounting software, eNvoice provides a lightweight invoicing and compliance workspace that enables them to create invoices, manage customer records, apply relevant tax and classification codes, issue credit notes and debit notes, record partial or full payments, track invoice status, print or email invoices to customers, and transmit compliant e-invoices without first implementing a separate ERP system.

Built-In Compliance Resources and Invoice Controls

eNvoice supports key e-Invoicing and compliance resources, including:

• B2B, B2C and B2G invoice/customer categories;

• NRS-supported invoice types;

• VAT and tax categories;

• payment means;

• product classification guidance using HS codes;

• service classification guidance using ISIC codes;

• quantity and measurement codes;

• currency references;

• credit note and debit note workflows;

• partial and full payment capture;

• invoice printing and email delivery to customers;

• customer and business profile updates; and

• structured invoice history and status tracking.

For high-volume businesses, eNvoice also supports batch invoice processing and bulk upload workflows, enabling larger invoice volumes to be prepared, validated and transmitted more efficiently.

Governance, Security and Operational Visibility

eNvoice is built to support secure and auditable e-Invoicing operations. The platform includes role-based access control, user management, API client management for secure system-to-system integrations, audit logs, customer records, SSO support, MFA capability and controlled access to platform resources.

These features are designed to help businesses manage e-Invoicing compliance in a secure, traceable and operationally practical manner.

Support for SI-Only Providers and Referral Partners

Service providers accredited only as System Integrators can also use eNvoice’s APP services to support their clients seamlessly, without having to build or operate a separate APP infrastructure.

Vi-M is also open to onboarding referral partners, implementation partners, accounting firms, technology consultants, ERP advisers, tax professionals and business advisers supporting clients that require e-Invoicing readiness, integration or compliance support.

Built for Today’s Compliance and Tomorrow’s Expansion

eNvoice is built with a modular architecture that supports multiple implementation paths, including Direct Reporting, System Integrator routes, Access Point Provider transmission and SI + APP workflows.

The platform is also being positioned for future international e-Invoicing expansion, including PEPPOL-readiness and broader cross-border invoicing compliance requirements.

Statement from Vi-M

Speaking on the milestone, Vivian Chigozie-Nmonwu, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited, stated:

“This dual accreditation is a significant milestone for Vi-M and a strong validation of our work at the intersection of tax, technology, regulatory compliance and enterprise systems. eNvoice was built to make e-Invoicing practical, secure and accessible for businesses – whether they operate complex ERP environments or need a simpler invoicing and compliance workspace.”

She added:

“With NRS compliance monitoring now underway, businesses need to move beyond general readiness discussions and confirm their actual

onboarding, integration, validation and transmission capability. Our goal is to support businesses and implementation partners with a platform that combines compliance, usability and technical flexibility.”

About Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited

Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited is a professional services and technology advisory firm focused on tax and regulatory advisory, digital tax systems, enterprise systems integration, governance, risk and assurance, and professional training.

The firm supports businesses with compliance transformation, digital regulatory infrastructure, ERP and accounting systems advisory, tax technology implementation, business process improvement and regulatory implementation support.

For broader Vi-M professional services, visit:

www.vi-m.com

About eNvoice

eNvoice is Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited’s e-Invoicing platform developed to support businesses under Nigeria’s National e-Invoicing and Electronic Fiscal System regime.

The platform enables invoice creation, validation, classification, IRN processing, signing, transmission, invoice status tracking, credit note and debit note processing, payment capture, batch upload, audit visibility and integration with ERP, accounting and business systems.

For e-Invoicing onboarding, implementation support, APP connectivity or product demonstration, visit:

www.envoice.ng

Vi-M Professional Solutions Limited

World.title: 2027: Naval Chief orders election-duty seminars
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

ABUJA — The Chief of Naval Staff, Vice Admiral Idi Abass, has directed naval commands, formations, establishments and bases to organise seminars to educate officers and personnel on their roles and code of conduct during the 2027 general elections.

Commander, Navy Base Abuja, Commodore Oluseyi Oladipo, disclosed this on Monday in his opening remarks at a seminar on “The Role of Armed Forces Personnel in Conducting Free, Fair and Credible Elections” held at the CNS Conference Centre, Naval Base, Abuja.

Oladipo said the seminar was aimed at promoting greater awareness and clarity among Nigerian Navy personnel who would be deployed for electoral duties.

According to him, the initiative was in line with the command philosophy of the Chief of Naval Staff, which seeks to maintain a mission-ready force committed to excellence and service to the nation.

He said the seminar was timely given the 2027 general elections, adding that the Armed Forces of Nigeria would, in line with established constitutional provisions, be expected to support the democratic process by creating conditions for free, fair and credible elections.

Oladipo said that after 27 years of uninterrupted democratic governance, it had become necessary to examine the role of the armed forces in election security within established constitutional and legal frameworks.

He said the seminar would feature a keynote lecture by a lawyer and academic who had served in both the Akwa Ibom State and National Assemblies, followed by an interactive panel discussion.

Oladipo added that the outcome of the seminar would reinforce the Nigerian Navy’s commitment to protecting democracy and complement the Code of Conduct and Rules of Engagement for Armed Forces personnel during elections.

Delivering the keynote lecture, former Speaker of the Akwa Ibom State House of Assembly and former National Assembly member, Hon. Onofiok Luke, urged the Armed Forces to train personnel on civil conduct, human rights and the protection of voters during elections.

Luke said the military must cultivate respect for the democratic process and its sustainability, stressing the need for personnel deployed for election duties to remain apolitical.

“It is necessary for the Army to cultivate an attitude of respect for the democratic process and its sustainability,” he said.

He added that the neutrality of the military must be evident to all political stakeholders and urged personnel to resist attempts by politicians to draw them into partisan activities.

“For no reason should the military be political. Its neutrality must be evident and open to all political stakeholders,” Luke said.

He also noted that military personnel, as citizens, had the right to vote, urging authorities to make adequate arrangements to enable personnel exercise their franchise regardless of their deployment locations.

Luke said this would also help improve public perception of the military.

Addressing concerns over the involvement of the military in election security, he said public apprehension was understandable because of reported incidents involving security personnel during previous elections.

He said the absence of clearly defined roles, regulations and accountability mechanisms had contributed to concerns surrounding military involvement in elections.

“The common claim that the role of the military in elections is ‘secondary’ is vague,” he said.

Luke also cautioned against perceived partisanship among security personnel, saying professionalism and neutrality were essential to maintaining public confidence in the electoral process.

Panelists at the seminar included a Directing Staff of the National Defence College, Commodore I.M. Abbah (retd.); Assistant Commissioner of Police, Operations, FCT Command, ACP Akaniyene Akpan; an instructor at the Command and Staff College, Jaji; and the Assistant Commandant-General of the NSCDC, John Steve Alaba.

World.title: How Browser-Based Trading Is Changing Access to Global CFD Markets
World.content:
Access to the world market has been revolutionized within the last ten years. Traders who used to rely heavily on desktop software installed on their computers can now carry out their operations in a web browser. This development is making the trading of Contracts for Difference (CFD) much more convenient and flexible.

Trading without installation

The use of browser-based trading software eliminates the most common obstacle to market participation – installation. Traders do not need to download any software, configure the device, or rely on a single computer for their trading activities.

Users who trade in different places and use different devices benefit the most from browser-based platforms. The software becomes more accessible to traders who need quick access to charts and quotes.

Faster access when markets move

CFD markets globally can respond swiftly to macroeconomic figures, central bank announcements, earnings news, commodity price fluctuations, and other geopolitical events.

The web-based solution allows traders to respond to these events without the delay of installing complicated software. While this cannot eliminate trading risk, it does increase the convenience of market access.

One platform for multiple CFD markets

For CFD trading, browser-based trading terminals may be helpful, regardless of the asset class the trader uses. Starting with forex and commodities, passing through indices, stocks, and even cryptocurrency, the trader can track multiple markets on a single online platform. It is particularly relevant in cases where traders monitor more than one instrument at a time or develop strategies based on overall market sentiment.

Simplicity for everyday trading

Not all traders require a very complicated trading system for every decision they make. What is required here is simple charts, live quotes, account details, and the ability to execute trades efficiently.

The web interface provides all these essential features through an uncomplicated web platform. New traders can find this feature easy to use, while experienced traders can take advantage of the web terminal to trade from wherever they happen to be.

Flexibility as the new standard

Trading through the browser is part of a broader trend towards multiplatform trading. Traders are beginning to require greater flexibility in how they can access the market, including via desktop, mobile application, or the Web.

However, the objective is not to replace other forms of trading altogether, rather, it is to provide greater flexibility to trade at a client’s convenience. For traders who require market access without an installation process, Web-based trading offers an easy alternative platform.

Browser-based access is becoming part of the trader’s routine

With an increasing number of traders moving across different platforms and seeking to trade faster in the global market, it is quite natural for web-based platforms to form part of the trading experience. JustMarkets is one of the brokers who have built their platform ecosystem with the provision of CFD instruments via platforms suited to various routines, ranging from desktop, mobile and even browser-based platforms.

To the trader, the benefits are obvious: reduced technical hindrances, quick charting and order execution, as well as increased convenience when watching the forex, commodity, index, stock, and crypto CFD markets.

World.title: J.P. Morgan returns Nigeria to bond index after 11 years
World.content:
…$17.47bn FGN debt eligible

…Nigeria gets 7.4% weighting

By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

ABUJA — Nigeria is set to attract fresh foreign capital into its domestic debt market following the decision by global investment banking giant, J.P. Morgan, to return Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) bonds to its bond index under the newly introduced Government Bond Index–Emerging Markets Edge (GBI-EM Edge).

The development is expected to boost demand for Nigerian government securities, deepen liquidity in the bond market and, over time, help drive down domestic borrowing costs as global index-tracking funds adjust their portfolios to accommodate Nigeria’s new 7.40 per cent weighting.

The GBI-EM Edge, managed by J.P. Morgan, one of the world’s widely followed emerging-market bond index providers, tracks local-currency government debt across frontier emerging markets.

Nigeria’s inclusion is particularly significant as it marks the country’s return to a J.P. Morgan benchmark for the first time in more than a decade.

Nigeria exited the GBI-EM Global Diversified Index in 2015 amid foreign exchange liquidity constraints.

The Federal Government said reforms undertaken in recent years, particularly the stabilisation of the naira and clearance of foreign exchange backlogs, had helped address some of the factors that previously constrained Nigeria’s participation.

According to a statement by the Federal Ministry of Finance announcing the development on Monday, Nigeria met key eligibility requirements for inclusion in the new index, particularly in the areas of market liquidity and the size of outstanding bond issues.

The ministry said FGN bonds were actively traded under a Two-Way Quote System, while outstanding volumes across eligible tenors were significantly above the $250 million minimum required for inclusion in the GBI-EM Edge.

With a 7.40 per cent weighting, Nigeria ranks among the highest-weighted of the 26 markets covered by the index and is close to J.P. Morgan’s maximum country weighting of eight per cent.

The index tracks approximately $328 billion worth of local-currency government debt globally.

Nigeria’s allocation translates to roughly $17.47 billion of eligible FGN debt across 16 instruments.

The inclusion is expected to result in additional foreign portfolio inflows as funds tracking the index rebalance their portfolios in line with Nigeria’s new weighting.

The increased demand is also expected to support FGN bond prices and gradually compress yields, thereby reducing the government’s cost of servicing naira-denominated debt.

Beyond FGN bonds, improved liquidity in the government securities market could have wider positive effects across the domestic debt market, including Nigerian Treasury Bills and other fixed-income instruments.

The Federal Government described the development as an independent endorsement of its economic reform programme under President Bola Tinubu.

Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, said the decision reflected growing confidence in Nigeria’s economic management.

According to him, the development would help lower the cost of financing the government’s development priorities.

Oyedele said: “This inclusion is a clear, independent endorsement of the discipline behind President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s reform agenda.

“It reflects the confidence international capital markets now place in Nigeria’s economic management, and it lowers the cost of financing our development priorities.”

He noted that the government remained focused on further reforms needed to secure Nigeria’s full reinstatement in J.P. Morgan’s flagship index.

The latest development is also significant in view of Nigeria’s earlier experience with the GBI-EM.

FGN bonds were first included in the J.P. Morgan GBI-EM in 2012, a move that attracted substantial foreign investment into the domestic securities market.

The earlier inclusion was credited with helping to reduce Nigeria’s cost of debt issuance by about 200 basis points, while also opening the equities and banking sectors to greater foreign capital participation and supporting the country’s external reserves.

The Federal Government said it remained committed to sustaining the reform agenda and deepening investor confidence in Nigeria’s domestic financial market.

The inclusion comes amid efforts by the authorities to strengthen macroeconomic stability, restore investor confidence and reposition Nigeria as a more attractive destination for international capital.

World.title: Canada lists 7 things immigration officers will never demand from immigrants
World.content:
Canada government has warned newcomers and immigrants about common scams involving people pretending to be immigration officials and demanding money or personal information.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) said newcomers should learn how to identify fraudulent calls, emails and messages, particularly those involving threats of deportation or demands for immediate payment.

According to the government, there are seven things IRCC employees will never demand from immigrants.

1. Deposit money into a personal bank account

IRCC employees will never ask an immigrant to deposit immigration fees or other payments into a personal bank account.

Newcomers should be suspicious of anyone claiming to represent the Canadian government who provides a personal bank account for payment.

2. Make an urgent payment

Immigration officials will never rush people into paying fees immediately.

Scammers may create a sense of urgency by claiming that an application will be rejected or an immigration status will be affected unless payment is made immediately.

IRCC advises newcomers to verify such claims through official government channels before making any payment.

3. Pay through gift cards or money transfer services

IRCC employees will never ask people to pay immigration fees using prepaid credit cards, gift cards, Western Union, MoneyGram or similar services.

Government processing fees can be paid through the official payment channels provided by IRCC.

4. Threaten arrest or deportation over unpaid fees

Scammers may pose as immigration officials and threaten victims with arrest, deportation or police action if they do not immediately pay money.

IRCC says its employees will not threaten to arrest or deport people, or send police to arrest them or harm their families, over unpaid fees.

The government specifically warns that threats of deportation over outstanding fees are a scam.

5. Offer special immigration deals

Immigration officials will never offer special deals to people seeking to immigrate to Canada.

Newcomers should be cautious of anyone claiming they can provide a special immigration arrangement or guarantee a favourable outcome.

The Canadian government also warns that no one can guarantee a job, visa or permanent residence in Canada.

6. Promise special treatment for extra payment

IRCC employees will not promise that an immigration application will be approved or receive special attention because an applicant sends additional money or information.

Anyone demanding extra payment in exchange for faster processing or guaranteed approval should therefore be treated with caution.

IRCC employees will not use free email services such as Gmail, Hotmail or Yahoo Mail, or social media platforms, to contact people about immigration matters.

The government also warns that scammers can manipulate caller ID, meaning a phone number that appears to belong to a government agency may not actually be genuine.

Newcomers should therefore verify unexpected calls and messages through official government channels.

Canada warns newcomers about other scams

The government also highlighted other fraud schemes targeting newcomers, including phishing emails and text messages, fake computer virus alerts, fraudulent prizes and contests, and tax scams.

In phishing scams, victims may receive messages containing links to websites designed to steal banking information, passwords or other personal details.

Canada advises people not to click suspicious links or provide personal information if they are unsure who sent the message.

Newcomers should also be wary of messages claiming they have won a prize in a contest they never entered.
