Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. Transcript text may be revised to correct errors or match updates to audio. Audio on npr.org may be edited after its original broadcast or publication. The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.

World.title: Why the timing of Alberta's 2nd referendum (if it happens) is so murky
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Albertans will vote next month on the possibility of a second referendum on separation, but exactly when that referendum — if a majority voted for it — would happen, remains somewhat murky.

The Oct. 19 referendum will include 10 questions, including whether Albertans would like to remain in Confederation, or if they support the province beginning the legal process of holding a binding referendum on separation.

Polls have consistently shown the majority of Albertans would prefer to stay in Canada, but polls aren’t outcomes. Political analysts expect turnout to be a key factor in determining whether a second referendum is necessary.

Elections Alberta said any questions about a future, second referendum must be directed to the provincial government.

“Should Albertans give us that direction in the Fall 2026 referendum, we would begin the legal process under the constitution to hold the binding referendum as soon as possible,” the premier’s press secretary Sam Blackett said in a statement.

Spring? Not spring?

In an audio recording from a UCP town hall in Lethbridge in August, Premier Danielle Smith is heard saying her goal would be to hold a binding referendum in spring 2027, if a majority of Albertans vote for it this fall.

Alberta content creator Lawrence Magee, who runs the account Berta Proud Dad, shared the recording.

In the audio, Smith says holding the vote in the spring would settle the issue before the next provincial election. That election is set for October 2027, though the premier can call a snap election before then.

A mock-up of a ballot with the 10th question in the upcoming October referendum. Elections Alberta gave a preview of the ballots to reporters on Sept. 3. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Smith estimated in the recording a timeline of roughly two-and-a-half months of consultations, before the question would be finalized and submitted to the House of Commons for approval, and a vote scheduled for March or April.

“If this is truly going to [be] a referendum on those precise terms of departure, then there would likely have to be pretty long and pretty deep [consultations] and getting it done in a six-month stretch is extremely ambitious,” University of Alberta associate law professor Gerard Kennedy told CBC News.

But at a news conference on Aug. 26, Smith seemed to backpedal on that proposed timeline, citing the rules in the Citizen Initiative Act that prohibit a referendum from a citizen petition within a year of a general election.

Those remarks had some separatists fuming, including the Alberta Prosperity Project’s Jeff Rath, who rejected the idea the legislation is really any sort of an impediment to holding a binding referendum in 2027.

He suggested Smith is the real hurdle.

“As long as Premier Smith is premier of Alberta, Alberta will never be free,” he told hundreds of supporters outside the legislature late last month.

Jeff Rath speaks at a pro-separation rally outside the Alberta legislature in Edmonton on Aug. 29. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

As to why the act prohibits citizen-initiated referendums in an election year, Kennedy says the reason is likely two-fold: both the burden on Elections Alberta, and the possibility that the issue could be one that comes up naturally in an election campaign.

But couldn’t that change?

“What [Smith] says isn't wrong, but it's not complete,” said Kennedy.

With its majority seat count, he says there is nothing stopping the government from simply changing the legislation.

“It would have to go through the legislative process, but they can do that quickly if they have to,�” Kennedy said.

Plus, he says there’s nothing stopping the premier from calling a vote under the Referendum Act, which, unlike the Citizen Initiative Act, does not stipulate any kind of referendum black-out period before an election.

“Now, I don't think Elections Alberta would be very happy about that, because they are not exactly bored,” Kennedy said.

Under the Referendum Act, a separation vote could even be added as a ballot-box question during a provincial election.

But what makes sense politically for Smith is a separate question.

“If she were to call another referendum, let's say six months after the original referendum, six months ahead of a general election, there I think could be a very considerable political cost to pay,” said political scientist Lori Williams.

“Certainly she'd run into voter fatigue and a considerable backlash from those who object to being asked twice about a question that it's clear the majority of Albertans oppose.”

What needs to happen before a second referendum

In a news conference Sept. 1, Smith said she could not give a clear answer on when a theoretical second referendum might be held, because the court has “put a bit of a monkey wrench” in the situation.

Justice Shaina Leonard quashed a citizen-led petition on separation, ruling the government failed to carry out proper consultations with First Nations.

Smith says the government has not been given parameters as to what those consultations would need to look like.

The government is appealing the court’s decision, as is separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre, who led the petition drive.

It would be helpful, Kennedy said, to have those appeals dealt with first. The appeal court’s ruling — and potentially that of the Supreme Court, should the case go there — could help set the terms for what consultations look like.

Once the province has done consultations, it would need to settle on the wording of the referendum question. Within 30 days of that, the House of Commons would weigh in on the chosen question, as per the federal Clarity Act.

MPs would vote on the question, deciding if it is both clear and would result in clear expression of the will of the province.

Former MP Stephane Dion, who drafted the Clarity Act, is seen receiving a kiss from then-Labour Minister Claudette Bradshaw in the House of Commons on March 15, 2000, at the third and final reading of the bill. (Fred Chartrand/Canadian Press)

Because the Clarity Act was enacted in 2000, following the last Quebec sovereignty referendum, it would be the first time it would be tested.

“We are in uncharted territory. Like, if the province said ‘we don't care what the Clarity Act has to say,' that might be pragmatically unwise, but it's not necessarily doomed to legal failure,” Kennedy said.

However, given the polls that show majority support lies on the remain side, Kennedy doubts that it will be put to the test in this case.

“Do you want what my best prediction is? There's nowhere near a majority vote yes in the Oct. 19 referendum and this is all a moot point.”

World.title: Carney is seeking $1 trillion in investments. What will it take to land major deals at this week's summit?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of deep-pocketed investors have descended on Toronto for the first-of-its-kind Canada Investment Summit.

The summit, which began with a reception on Sunday, aims to bring together global investors with Canadian business leaders in the hopes of catalyzing $1-trillion worth of investments across the country over the next five years.

As a former central banker and head of Brookfield Asset Management, Prime Minister Mark Carney is no stranger to big-name investors. But the stakes are high, as the escalating Canada-U.S. trade war has turned up the pressure to forge new relationships, and prove that Canada is a good place to invest.

So, who is coming to the summit and what does Canada need to do to land new cash for its big projects? Here's what you need to know.

Who's coming?

CBC News previously reported that Carney invited 100 of the world's biggest investors to the summit. The government has kept the final guest list close to its chest, but some big names are reportedly on it.

Larry Fink, chairman of BlackRock Inc. — a U.S.-based investment firm and the world's largest asset manager — and Dilhan Pillay, CEO of the Singapore-based investment firm Temasek, are some of them. Managers of massive sovereign wealth funds including Norway's government pension fund and state-owned firms like the Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. will also be there.

"It's essentially a who's-who on the investment side," said Jeremy Kronick, president and CEO of the C.D. Howe Institute, the economic think-tank, with plenty more banks and money managers from Canada and abroad expected to attend.

WATCH | PM brings in big investors: Carney invites major investors to discuss opportunities in Canada | Duration 3:58 Prime Minister Mark Carney is inviting 100 of the world's biggest investors to a summit in Toronto in September, where he will pitch Canada as a reliable place for investment.

A guest list for Sunday night's reception also named top executives from lots of Canadian companies as attendees in addition to American leaders, including Air Canada, artificial intelligence company Cohere, Enbridge and Alto — which is planning a proposed high-speed rail line that would connect Toronto and Quebec City.

Dozens of Canadian politicians, including a number of premiers, were also in attendance.

What projects are on the table?

Some 167 projects, ranging from a proposed pipeline carrying oil from Alberta to B.C.'s coast to developing satellite technology for Earth observation, are among the investment opportunities on the table, according to a 66-page prospectus obtained by CBC News.

The prospectus groups projects into eight types: 11 conventional energy projects, 31 clean energy ones, 63 in mining and metals, 16 in marine and port infrastructure, 11 others in power and utilities, 10 in digital technology, 19 in advanced manufacturing and six transportation projects.

More than half of them are related to energy and mining, which Kronick says shows where the government's priorities lie.

Some of the most expensive and highest-profile projects on the list include that $35-billion pipeline to B.C., a roughly $79-billion expansion of the Port of Churchill in northern Manitoba and the proposed $28.5-billion Ksi Lisims liquid natural gas terminal on the B.C. coast.

A grain vessel is docked at the Port of Churchill on Aug. 31. Expanding the northern Manitoba port is one of some 167 projects on the table at this week's summit. (Josh Crabb/CBC)

Why do we need it?

The goal is to show Canada off as a "compelling investment destination," as the government puts it — even though that hasn't always been the case.

Kronick says long turnaround times for big projects and uncertainty about whether they will get approved have turned some international investors off of Canadian projects in the past.

A recent report by the CPP Investment Insights Institute — the research arm of the firm which is helping lead the summit — collected responses from 65 global institutional investors about their perceptions around a number of developed countries.

Canada ranked highest in stability and regulatory predictability, and the investors said they saw opportunity in Canada's critical minerals, energy and other resources. But regulatory complexity and permitting timelines were big concerns, especially among those interested in mining and energy projects, according to the report.

Because Canada is considered a small economy, Kronick says more work needs to be done to make it a competitive option compared to other developed nations. And hosting a summit like this — to signal the country is serious about building big things — is a good start.

"I think the change in tone is welcome," Kronick said. "It's been missing in the last number of years."

WATCH | Potential 'supercycle' of investment:

He says business leaders here must show that Canada is serious about the major projects on the table, with the man-power and machinery ready to get them built quickly.

Even if deals don't materialize quickly, Kronick says any that come down the line could boost Canada's productivity and GDP in a big way.

If the government plays its cards right, a report from TD Bank predicts Canada could see an investment "supercycle" that lasts a decade or longer, creating jobs and boosting real output per capita by $12,000 per person.

Why foreign investment?

But for some, the idea of foreign investment raises worries that companies abroad will have too much control over Canadian projects.

Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis, for one, has criticized Carney's investment summit as a plan to "save this country by selling it off."

A protest counter-summit is also planned to coincide with the event. Organizers argue the government will "auction off" public resources in any deals it makes with outside firms.

WATCH | Lewis calls for export taxes: 'We have to use what leverage we have': NDP leader on U.S. trade war escalation | Duration 9:43 NDP Leader Avi Lewis tells Power & Politics that he's calling on the federal government to put export taxes on Canadian energy and critical minerals as the trade war with the U.S. heats up.

And indeed, not all foreign money is created equal, says Walid Hejazi, an economics professor at the Rotman School of Management in Toronto, who focuses on foreign investment.

He says there are always perceived risks with outside investments; that those firms will want to take a heavy hand in controlling the production and strategic decision s of those investments. And public perception only worsens when the investments are in projects that are seen as strategic investments — think critical infrastructure or national security — rather than those that are "simply commercial."

But Hejazi says the government can put terms in place that maintain Canada's sovereignty in any potential deal. There's also no evidence to suggest outside companies are more likely to evade regulations, he says, and Canada has strong laws and institutions to combat that if it were to become an issue.

Plus, he says Canada doesn't have the funds to build all of these big-ticket projects on its own. And especially in the current moment — when Canada's relationship with its largest trading partner is so injured — Hejazi says the need for forging new relationships abroad is obvious.

"We need to broaden our global footprint," he said.

But, "at the same time, we do want Canadians to feel that our sovereignty is not being taken by other countries."

He says if any deals are reached because of the summit, the government will need to be very transparent about the terms of those agreements — explaining why they are beneficial for Canada to prevent that skepticism.

World.title: $5.5M daycare built with provincial funds now derelict, scavenged by thieves and damaged by flooding
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A $5.5-million Winnipeg-area daycare built two years ago with provincial funds sits vacant, derelict and surrounded by weeds after being plundered by scavengers and damaged by flooding.

The non-profit group hoping to operate the daycare and an advocate for not-for-profit daycares are now pleading with the province to open the East St. Paul facility, which has yet to care for a single child.

The 74-space daycare was built in 2024 on behalf of the Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust. It was one of 22 daycares built in Manitoba as part of a project started by the former Progressive Conservative government along with JohnQ Public, a company owned by 11 Manitoba municipalities.

The structure has been vacant since, even though the daycare operator waiting to use the building has 800 kids on its waiting list.

The provincial government has said this is because a change of land ownership has contravened the daycare's operating agreement.

CBC News took a tour of the daycare last week and documented extensive damage to both the interior and exterior of the building.

WATCH | $5.5M daycare built 2 years ago sits empty, vandalized: Vacant daycare built 2 years ago derelict, ransacked by thieves | Duration 3:28 A $5.5-million Winnipeg-area daycare built two years ago with provincial funds has never opened. It now sits derelict and surrounded by weeds after being plundered by scavengers and damaged by flooding.

"It's heartbreaking and frustrating," said Patrick Ryan, the volunteer board chair for Created 4 Me Early Learning Centre, which has been stymied in its efforts to move into the building.

The tour of the daycare revealed broken windows inside the facility, broken glass on the floor and damage to the building's security system.

Two commercial fridges and a dishwasher are missing and presumed stolen. Copper wire has been stripped from inside and outside the building.

Air-conditioning units on the daycare's roof have been partly dismantled, with mechanical parts missing — presumably removed by scavengers — and rainwater has penetrated the building, damaging ceilings. The building went months without power, meaning its sump pump didn't run and about half a metre of water has pooled in the basement.

A flooded crawl space in the daycare. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

Selkirk RCMP investigated the damage but said they did not identify any suspects.

Ryan estimated the damage to the as-yet-unused daycare exceeds $1 million.

"It's frustrating from the perspective of the amount of money that the public has put into the facility to see the building in the state that it is," he said.

His organization hired staff to work at the daycare but had to let them go after making repeated attempts to get the centre open.

Patrick Ryan, the volunteer board chair for Created 4 Me Early Learning Centre, said he's heartbroken the facility still hasn't opened, and has now sustained heavy damage from theft and rainwater. (Travis Golby/CBC)

The executive director of Created 4 Me says the situation has been "very difficult."

"It is very difficult to plan for the unknown, without an opening date being set, or being pushed back," said Laura Van Landeghem.

"It has been emotionally draining."

Provincial funds stopped flowing in 2024

The daycare was built for Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust, an arm's-length entity formed by Manitoba's most populous First Nation to acquire real estate for investment and housing for the benefit of band members, according to its founding documents .

The daycare is built on part of a former golf course east of Highway 59 called The Meadows, purchased by the trust in 2021. The placement of the daycare on land located more than 150 kilometres south of the First Nation's main reserve led some band members to criticize the decision to build in East St. Paul.

In 2024, the Peguis real estate trust sold 75 per cent of a company that controls the Meadows land to a numbered company owned by Andrew Marquess, a former adviser to the trust, according to a purchase and development agreement obtained by CBC News.

Manitoba paid out $3.3 million of the $5.5 million budgeted for the daycare before funding for the project stopped flowing in November 2024, according to the province.

The remains of an air-conditioning unit, scavenged by thieves, on the roof of the still-vacant daycare. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

According to a letter tabled in the Manitoba Legislature the following April, former deputy minister of education and early childhood learning Brian O'Leary said the project may not have followed normal provincial or municipal procurement practices.

In January, Manitoba Education and Early Childhood Learning Minister Tracy Schmidt said the province had an agreement with Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust.

"Our understanding is right now they do not own that land," Schmidt said at the time.

"We need to ensure the long-term viability of this project, so we need to ascertain that the agreement is in compliance. Once we have certainty about the long-term viability of this product, we'll proceed as soon as possible."

Eight months later, Schmidt said the province still has not received documentation from Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust to demonstrate who owns that land.

"Until we receive documentation assuring government who owns the land, we can't proceed," she said earlier this month in an interview in her office.

"Me and my team have been in constant communication with legal counsel, and we are pulling every lever available to us to make sure we can get the centre open as soon as possible."

A crumbling ceiling in the daycare. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

A lawyer for Peguis First Nation Real Estate Trust did not return requests for comment.

Schmidt said she could not provide a timeline for getting the daycare open because the province is not the legal owner of the property.

"If I could walk down there tomorrow … and open it up myself, I would do that, and I think the premier would come with me. We are doing everything that we can."

Delay puzzling: advocate

The delay in getting the East St. Paul daycare open is baffling, said Gerrie Prymak, a retired teacher who now advocates for child care and helped found Little Stars Playhouse daycare in Winnipeg's North End.

Prymak said Little Stars had to enter into an operating agreement with the province before it could open, and questioned why the provincial government can't cut through the bureaucracy in this case.

Daycare advocate Gerrie Prymak urges Premier Wab Kinew to cut through red tape and get the East St. Paul daycare open. (Travis Golby/CBC)

"I don't know why it's taking a year and a half," Prymak said in an interview at Little Stars on Selkirk Avenue.

She urged Premier Wab Kinew to get personally involved.

"[Have] a face-to-face meeting and say, 'Children first.… We've got to get this open,'" she said.

Kinew said Thursday he is "always down to meet."

Prymak said she went to visit the daycare site herself when she heard it still wasn't open.

"When I saw the vandalism, I thought, 'what a waste,'" she said. "Why can't there be some security that they can pay for to take care of this piece of property that we invested so much money for?"

One of the smashed windows within the East St. Paul daycare. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

Prymak also said the province has fallen short of its 2021 promise to create 23,000 daycare spaces by March of this year.

The NDP government said in August it has created or promised to open 12,700 spaces since taking power in 2023.

Schmidt said the province is still working to create more daycare spaces.

"While I understand that every single space counts, and that families are relying on these 74 spaces in East St. Paul to open as soon as possible, Manitobans should rest assured that our government is working as hard as we can to meet that need," she said.

In the meantime, Patrick Ryan is encouraging more action from the province to get Created 4 Me daycare open.

"We're really calling on the provincial government and the Rural Municipality of East St. Paul to step up and do what it takes to get this place open," he said, adding he has had reasonable conversations with all parties involved.

"Everybody has an interest in getting this place opened. Call on everybody to sit down together and figure out a plan to get it open."

World.title: Sydney Sweeney's 'sexualized' sports betting ad slammed by female athletes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. actor Sydney Sweeney is once again facing backlash over an .

This time, she has enraged female athletes around the world with a nude sports gambling ad — and her response.

The Novig sports prediction ad, posted online Sept. 9 and viewed nearly 39 million times by Monday morning, features Sweeney holding various pieces of sports equipment in front of what looks like her otherwise naked body, as bass music plays in the background.

"Think you know sports? Prove it," says the star of Euphoria and The Housemaid at the beginning of the ad as she holds a football in front of each breast.

In other shots, she perches on a basketball net while spinning a ball with only her hair covering her, holds a football in front of her pelvis, lies nude on a bench with a soccer ball resting on her feet and swings a golf club wearing only white underwear.

It set off a backlash from female athletes and Olympians who say the ad sexualizes women in sport and sets them back. The criticism crosses borders and a range of sports, with many posting "Dear Sydney Sweeney" videos on social media in response.

"Dear Sydney Sweeney, this is women in sports," Canadian sprint canoeist Sophia Jensen posted on TikTok on Sunday, alongside a video where the world champion competes on the water and trains in the gym.

"Hey Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Canadian figure skater Madeline Schizas posted on Instagram with a similar video where she competes and trains on and off the ice.

"IDK what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sport looks like," posted U.S. gymnast Gracie Kramer over a similar montage.

British sprinter Amy Hunt got a word in during a post-race interview on Sunday, after she finished fourth in the 200-metre final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

" Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt told BBC Sport, adding "h ard work, blood, sweat, tears."

Sydney Sweeney poses for photographers at the Armani beauty event during the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 3, 2026. (Scott A Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)

Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus, the reigning Olympic champion in the 400-metre freestyle, called the ad "a kick in the face" on Instagram.

"H ow do we live in a world where monetizing a woman's body and sexualizing women's sport is still a thing?" she said, according to Australia's ABC News.

Novig CEO and co-founder Jacob Fortinsky praised the brand campaign for highlighting a platform that's "singularly focused on sports."

"Sydney helped bring that message to life in a way that’s impossible to ignore," Fortinsky said in a press release the same day the ad launched.

In the same press release, Sweeney called the campaign "a fun idea" that "brings that idea to life with confidence, humor and a playful edge."

Not her 1st controversial ad

If this is sounding familiar, Sweeney faced similar backlash last year over an American Eagle  that was criticized for promoting white standards of beauty at best, and eugenics at worst.

In the ad, Sweeney makes a play on words between jeans (the clothing item) and genes (the genetic material).

“Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair colour, personality and even eye colour. My jeans are blue,” Sweeney said in the ad.

Some internet commentators read the ad as having eugenicist undertones. Eugenics is a discredited idea that the human race could be improved by selectively breeding for certain traits.

At the time, the blond-haired, blue-eyed actor stood by the ad and downplayed the reaction, which included support from U.S. President Donald Trump, who called it the "HOTTEST ad out there."

Sweeney appeared to take a more overt approach to the backlash against her new ad, posting a series of photos on Instagram on Sunday that showed magazine covers with male and female athletes posing in little to no clothing.

WATCH | What Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle ad says about marketing: What Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle ad says about the brand's marketing | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 6:07 Morgan Westcott, a marketing professor at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, says the American Eagle ad does not signal a 'shift,' but rather reflects a 'recycled concept' and a clear call to their target market.

This move prompted even more backlash. Canadian alpine skier Cassidy Gray called it "idiotic" and "senseless."

"It's not a joke when your life is actually you being a female athlete, and you being sexualized or not taken seriously and not given the same opportunities, and then you see one of the most famous actresses in the world going and completely wiping away all the work that you have done to be taken seriously," Gray posted in an emotional video on TikTok.

Gray also responded to those who might say it's just a commercial and not meant to be taken so seriously.

"I fear you're just out of touch, because it really is that deep."

Female athletes have historically been marketed in an over-sexualized manner, with a greater focus on t heir appearance than their skills.

This also extends to sports coverage, with women at the Tokyo 2021 Olympics 10 times more likely to be "visually objectified" with a camera angle than men, according to a report from The Representation Project . Researchers defined visual objectification as when a camera panned across an athlete's body or focused on a specific body part in a sexualizing way.

The same study found female athletes were more likely to be infantilized by commentators, often called "young ladies" and "girls."

Another recent study from World Athletics found that female athletes were consistently targeted by online abuse more than their male counterparts at four global sporting events, including the 2024 Paris Olympics.

World.title: They came to Canada for safety. Now they’re suspected of supporting the regime they fled
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Farzin Jafari is facing an impossible choice: wait and hope the Canadian government allows him and his family to remain in Canada, or leave his wife and infant daughter in hopes they can stay if he's deemed inadmissible and forced to return to Iran.

“We are hanging from a rope as a family,” he said. “If I leave that rope, open my hand, and fall… at least my family can stay alive.”

Jafari is one of what one advocacy group says is hundreds of permanent residency applicants who received a Procedural Fairness Letter (PFL) from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada in August.

The letters indicated applicants may be inadmissible to Canada because of their connection to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and would need to prove otherwise. The Canadian government listed the IRGC as a terrorist organization in 2024.

“I am therefore concerned that you served in the IRGC and that you may be inadmissible to Canada per paragraph 34(1)(f) for being a member of an organization … engaging in terrorism,” the letter said.

Jafari said he didn’t have a choice where he served.

“You can't say, ‘I don't want this,’” Jafari said.

I'm not IRGC. I'm a victim of IRGC. - Farzin Jafari

Iran's Revolutionary Guards are a branch of the Iranian military with broad powers that answers directly to the country’s supreme leader. All Iranian men over the age of 18 are required to complete compulsory military service.

Proof of service is required to work or obtain a passport and conscripts have no say in the branch they serve under.

“If you don't participate in that compulsory period, you can't have your basic civil rights,” Jafari said. “They are holding you hostage in the country until you pass this period.”

If a citizen says they don’t want to serve, they risk being jailed by the Iranian government.

WATCH | Former conscript to Iran's Revolutionary Guard may have to leave Canada: Iranian told he may have to leave Canada over past IRGC service | Duration 1:58 An Iranian man is one of hundreds told by the government that he may have to leave over his past mandatory service in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Canada considers a terrorist organization. Farzin Jafari says he had an administrative job in 2011, and has since protested the IRGC publicly.

IRGC deemed a terrorist organization

Jafari completed his mandatory military service in 2011. CBC News has seen his completion card, a document provided by the Iranian military that shows he finished compulsory service.

He described his work as administrative, recording licence plates.

After finishing, he worked privately as a software engineer in Iran before moving to Canada in 2021 to start a family.

His wife had been briefly detained by Iranian morality police and he said they feared for their safety. He has spent much of his free time in Canada protesting the Iranian government and calling for the IRGC’s designation as a terrorist entity.

Jafari said he has attended protests against the Iranian government and the IRGC since coming to Canada in 2021. If he were to return to Iran, he said he could face retribution for criticizing the current regime. (Farzin Jafari)

Jafari and his wife submitted their permanent residency applications in the winter of 2024.

That summer the Canadian government listed the IRGC as a terrorist organization and said the IRGC had provided support to other terror groups including Hezbollah, Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Taliban.

In January 2020, the IRGC shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight PS752 above the skies of Tehran and killed 175 passengers, including 55 Canadian citizens and 30 permanent residents.

Justice Minister Arif Virani said while making the designation on June 19, 2024, the government was concerned about the impact of the listing on those conscripted into the IRGC, but was "careful and measured" in its approach.

"If an individual was conscripted at one point in time and no longer serves with the IRGC, that would affect the analysis," he said at the time.

WATCH | Canada designated Iran's Revolutionary Guard a terrorist group in 2024: Canada designates Iran's Revolutionary Guard a terrorist entity | Duration 2:59 The federal government is declaring Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps a terrorist entity under Canada's Criminal Code after years of pressure. That means police can charge anyone who financially or materially supports the group and banks can freeze its assets.

So when Jafari and his wife received PFLs because of his mandatory service, he was shocked.

“I'm not IRGC. I'm a victim of IRGC,” he said.

Jafari was born in Iran and worked as a software engineer for a private company after completing his mandatory military service. He and his wife came to Canada to start a family in 2021. (Farzin Jafari)

‘Hundreds’ of letters sent

Hundreds of applicants received similar letters on Aug. 6 and 7, according to Nahid Rahmati, a representative of the Unheard Conscripts Advocacy Network.

The group seeks to represent people conscripted to the IRGC and advocate for them within the Canadian immigration system.

Rahmati said she’s never seen anyone receive a PFL and be accepted into Canada.

“I have seen lots of cases that have been rejected,” she said. “They got the PFL and they got rejected.”

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said in a statement it could not confirm the number of letters sent to permanent residency applicants in relation to potential IRGC ties.

CBC News spoke with several recipients of the letters, many of whom declined to speak on the record for fear of retribution from the government of Iran.

Many protesters are afraid to share their identity publicly for fear of retribution from the Iranian government. (Farzin Jafari)

Letters part of ‘normal’ process

In a statement, Canada's immigration and citizenship department said the listing of the guard as a terrorist entity prompts an “assessment of inadmissibility concerns where applications indicate a connection to the IRGC.”

“This is a normal part of applying Canada’s immigration law and does not mean that every person who served in the IRGC is automatically inadmissible."

Conscripts said it is difficult to prove they did not participate in the IRGC after their mandatory service ended. The IRGC does not keep a list of people who left, according to Hossein Raeesi, a criminal and human rights lawyer who practiced in Iran for two decades.

“Someone who served compulsory military service with the IRGC is not considered as a member of the IRGC,” he said.

CBC News asked the Canadian government which documents it would accept as proof that an applicant was not a member of the IRGC beyond mandatory service.

“There is no single prescribed set of documents that applies to every case,” the agency said in a statement.

Conscripts served under duress, lawyer says

Many of the conscripts served under duress, according to Arghavan Gerami, an immigration lawyer based in Ottawa.

Two of her current clients have received PFLs and she worries Canada is expecting them to prove they tried to resist conscription.

Ottawa immigration lawyer Arghavan Gerami has two clients who are currently awaiting an admissibility decision after receiving Procedural Fairness Letters from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. (Francis Deschênes/CBC)

“What are we telling them to do? ‘Say no, stand up to the regime?’” she said. “This is a country that doesn't respect the rule of law. We've seen them kill and shoot civilians and protesters.”

“These people have families and wives. We're asking them to stand up to that regime, say no to something that's mandatory and essentially put themselves in harm's way.”

She added it’s important to deny entry to high-ranking IRGC officials and those who volunteered for service willingly.

“The focus should be [on] individuals that we know are in Canada who are really the key culprits.”

Living in uncertainty

Canada has temporarily paused the removal of inadmissible individuals to Iran due to concerns for civilian safety amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

If Jafari is deemed inadmissible, he and his wife could be removed from Canada when the pause ends — and forced to take their infant daughter to Iran with them.

For now, all Jafari can do is wait.

“It’s a very desperate situation,” he said.

World.title: Reef balls are turning an ocean desert in N.L. into a thriving ecosystem
World.content:
For millennia, seeing the bottom of the ocean floor was reserved for deepsea divers. But that, much like the ocean itself, has changed.

Through an array of cameras, the majesty of the deepsea floor has been brought to life on screens — but so has the polar opposite of a thriving seabed: barren, grey dead zones. It’s a testament to the damage caused to marine ecosystems.

But a team of ocean scientists in Newfoundland and Labrador are turning one ocean dead zone into a thriving marine ecosystem.

“This is really cool because we get to fix a part of the ocean,” Mark Santos, a fisheries technologist with the Marine Institute's Centre for Sustainable Aquatic Resources.

WATCH | ‘Nature will find a way,’ says fisheries technologist: A manufactured reef made of concrete structures brings new life into Placentia Bay | Duration 2:11 A team of Ocean scientists is turning an ocean dead zone into a thriving marine ecosystem. The Fox Harbour area of Placentia Bay was barren a year ago… but now, it's home to fish, lobsters, and more. CBC’s Leila Beaudoin reports.

A year ago, Santos and a team at The Launch, Marine Institute’s coastal state-of-art lab in Holyrood, launched 285 cement reef balls into the bay. The structures are full of nooks and crannies and made from a type of cement that allows for biofouling, a natural process that invites algae growth working with sunbeams to photosynthesize marine snow into life.

The Marine Institute partnered with a major oil company and the government to restore a seafloor zone in Placentia Bay’s Fox Harbour, which is adjacent to a dredging site.

“It was barren,” said Santos, who compared the area to a desert. “It was a mega project in the area, they had to remove some of the sediment in the area and this is a remediation project, we had an opportunity to rebuild.”

These reef balls are built using cement that the sun can penetrate, so that algae can grow on the surface and marine life can move into the nooks and crannies. (Leila Beaudoin/CBC)

The team placed an underwater camera in the area to monitor the balls and watched as the cement became carpeted in algae and slowly, more and more marine life settled into the structures to call them home.

“If you look at the video you’ll see lobsters sticking out of these little slots and their little claws sticking out,” he said.

Through an underwater camera, the artificial marine habitat can be watched through SmartAtlantic.ca.

A reef ball carpeted in algae in Placentia Bay. You can watch the live stream at SmartAtlantic.ca. (SmartAtlantic.ca)

“We actually get to show that to everybody, to say look, we are doing something good. There's a new habitat growing here,” said Bethany Randell, a project engineer with the Marine Institute's Centre for Applied Ocean Technology.

Randell added this is what she got into the ocean science business for, a chance to fix some of the damaged ocean.

“If we just step away for a minute, nature will find a way.”

Since the reef balls were put into place in the bay, Santos said lobsters have migrated there because the layered balls provide an excellent home for the burrowing crustaceans.

The reef balls have a predicted lifespan of 500 years, and while this project has a nine-year span, Santos said he plans to keep the camera down there as long as possible.

“Maybe it would be great to put them in other places too,” added Randell, who has big conservation ideas and started off wanting to be a marine biologist.

Happy to see her ocean saving dreams reflected in this project, like Santos she hopes to keep the balls rolling.

World.title: Bob Mackie, fashion designer and costumer to the stars, dead at 87
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bob Mackie, the fashion designer whose visually provocative Hollywood style defined glamour for the 1970s — including putting Carol Burnett in some of her kookiest getups and Cher in her raciest ones, died Monday. He was 87.

"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," a read statement on his social media accounts.

"His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."

Dubbed the "Designer to the Stars," Mackie won nine Emmy Awards, a Tony Award and was nominated for three Oscars, including one for Barbra Streisand's Funny Lady, in which she wore a sheer batwing gown.

He was inducted into the Academy of Television Arts & Science's Hall of Fame in 2002.

He designed gowns for Madonna, Streisand, Sharon Stone, Diana Ross and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and concert costumes for Pink.

When Marilyn Monroe delivered a breathy, seductive take on Happy Birthday at a fundraiser for President John F. Kennedy and the Democratic National Committee, she did it in a sheer, beaded gown that Mackie dreamed up in a sketch.

Bob Mackie's style influences Miley Cyrus and Taylor Swift today, and can be seen in the styles of Kendall Jenner and Bella Hadid. His archival pieces are worn today by the likes of Anya Taylor-Joy, Cyrus and Zendaya, the latter who wore a Mackie gown to honor Cher at the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony.

Inductee Cher and Zendaya speak onstage during the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame induction ceremony at Rocket Mortgage Fieldhouse in Cleveland on Oct. 19, 2024. (Theo Wargo/Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame)

When Swift wanted to look like a showgirl on the cover of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl, she turned to some Mackie originals.

Sequins and embellishment were natural tools for Mackie — other nicknames for the designer were the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones and the Guru of Glitter. But he had a simple motto: "You don't try to change anybody, you just try to make them look better than ever," he told The Associated Press in 2018.

On Broadway, Mackie dressed the casts of On the Town in 1971 and Moon Over Buffalo in 1995. He also created costumes for Burnett in the revue Putting It Together, Debbie Reynolds in Debbie in 1976, Liza Minnelli in Minnelli on Minnelli in 1999 and, most recently, the cast of The Cher Show, winning his Tony Award.

Nearly half of Canadians (49 per cent) say they would support Canada becoming a member state of the European Union, while another 30 per cent are opposed to the idea and 21 per cent are unsure. World.title: Adam Pankratz: Mark Carney’s elitist quest to turn us into Europeans
World.content:
Article content

While not all of those items may be desirable, some unequivocally are. On the negative side of the ledger would almost certainly be the free flow of workers between Canada and the EU. We have seen this play out in Europe before, notably in the United Kingdom. The simple reality is that more people in Europe (and the world) speak English as a second language than vice-versa. That affects the direction of travel of the workers. On pure linguistic grounds alone, it is nearly certain that Canada, as a primarily English-speaking nation, would be opening its workers up to far more competition from English speaking Europeans, than, say, Greek or German workers would face from Greek or German speaking Canadians. Any politician who avoids the difficulty of that question alone is in for a massive shock when push comes to shove. A “free flow” of people and workers goes both ways and isn’t an unalloyed good for Canadians.
