World.title: Opinion: Mexico is AI’s secret weapon
World.content:
A few days ago, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, published an essay arguing that AI is advancing so fast that we need to slow down — not stop, but ensure safety keeps pace with capability. Within hours, Sam Altman of OpenAI responded: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” Elon Musk followed: “Dario is right.”

When those three agree on something, you pay attention.

Amodei’s warning is specific: “In 6-12 months, a swarm like the one in the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage — and the scale of damage would continue to increase if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”

His proposed solution has three steps: embedded third-party evaluators inside AI companies, democratic coordination among allied countries on safety standards and eventually, global coordination. The phrase “democratic coalition” appears repeatedly in his framework.

That’s where I can actually say something useful.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that “nothing would matter if China wins the AI race.” Amodei agrees. A Chinese lead in AI, he argues, would pose grave danger, economically, but most importantly: militarily, through AI-driven weapons systems and geopolitical dominance. At its core, this is a national security conversation dressed in technology clothing.

And national security conversations have physical requirements. AI runs on hardware: servers, chips, data centers, power, cooling systems, specialized cables, transformers, processing units. It runs on supply chains. It runs on energy. It runs on engineers.

The United States needs all of those things faster than it can build them domestically, and it needs them from partners it can trust.

Which brings me to Mexico.

In the first half of 2026, Mexico’s computer-related exports reached US $82.9 billion, a 172% increase from the same period a year earlier, putting computing equipment ahead of automobiles and auto parts ($74.8 billion) for the first time in thirty years.

Mexico doesn’t export algorithms and code. It is building the physical layer that makes AI possible; the unglamorous, essential plumbing of the AI data center buildout. The United States accounted for 93.9% of those exports, which tells you everything about the strategic nature of this relationship.

This new nearshoring wave is not a buzzword; it is an AI supply-chain strategy embedded in a global security race. BTW: I’ve written about this before.

U.S. data center investment reached $102.2 billion in 2025, growing nearly 30% year over year. Mexico’s export growth tracks that figure almost perfectly — the architecture of an integrated continental co-production system responding to a common demand signal. Folks, this is actually okay! Not just that, it is strategic and necessary.

Amodei calls for cutting off powerful AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment from China and cracking down on smuggling operations. He’s right. But that strategy only works if you have an alternative. Mexico — integrated into North American supply chains, operating under USMCA digital trade rules, with a manufacturing base that pivots fast — is a large part of that alternative.

Now, here’s the number that makes Washington uncomfortable: Mexico’s imports from Taiwan surged 220% in the first half of 2026. Computer equipment imports from Asia into Mexico are booming. Since those components are assembled into goods that cross north into the United States, this shows up, mechanically, as a larger U.S.-Mexico trade deficit.

I can already hear the reaction in certain corners of Washington, D.C.

But this is precisely the kind of number that demands context before it demands a tariff. What is actually happening is that North America — through Mexico’s manufacturing base — is progressively substituting Asian-sourced inputs and redirecting them through a regional production platform that delivers the servers, components, and infrastructure American firms need to build AI data centers faster, cheaper and without the geopolitical risk of direct dependence on Taiwan or China.

A tariff on Mexican electronics would tax precisely the substitution away from China that U.S. policy is trying to achieve. It would be, in effect, a tax on America’s own AI infrastructure — and on America’s own capacity to win this race.

The deficit is not a sign of a broken relationship. It is a sign of an integrated continental production system doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The “democratic coalition” Amodei calls for doesn’t need inventing. It needs to be deepened — starting with the country that shares 2,000 miles of border with the United States, a trade agreement that explicitly covers digital trade, deep supply chain integration, and a talent base that is the envy of the world.

Every day the North American neighborhood spends fighting over tariffs, USMCA renewal mechanics and trade deficits that don’t mean what people think they mean is a day China runs faster on AI infrastructure, critical minerals, energy policy and diplomatic reach.

The question is not whether Mexico is relevant to the AI race. The question is whether the people making policy decisions in Washington are looking at the right numbers and the right strategic angle.

You don’t win a race by slowing down your most integrated and reliable partner.

Pedro Casas Alatriste is the Executive Vice President and CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham). Previously, he has been the Director of Research and Public Policy at the US-Mexico Foundation in Washington, D.C. and the Coordinator of International Affairs at the Business Coordinating Council (CCE). He has also served as a consultant to the Inter-American Development Bank. Follow his Substack here.

World.title: MND Local: Independence Day in Puerto Vallarta and Nayarit
World.content:
It’s Independence Week in Puerto Vallarta and Nayarit, Mexico, and there’s no shortage of ways to celebrate.

From civic ceremonies and charro parades to mariachi, fireworks and the inevitable late-night Grito, the next few days will be about as Mexican as it gets. Even if you’re not planning to attend every event, it’s hard not to get caught up in the atmosphere. Flags appear on balconies and shopfronts, restaurants bring out special menus and the whole region seems to shift into a more festive mood.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Don Capellani (@doncapellani)

Here’s what’s happening around the region this week:

Puerto Vallarta

Puerto Vallarta’s official Fiestas Patrias celebrations run Sept. 13-16, with the Plaza de Armas, Malecón and downtown area serving as the main stages.

Monday, Sept. 14, brought the traditional charro parade at 10 a.m. The parade began on Ignacio L. Vallarta Street, traveled along the Malecón and wrapped up near the Ley store in Cinco Diciembre.

A formal City Council session is scheduled for 8 a.m. Tuesday, Sept. 15, followed by the evening’s celebrations in the Plaza de Armas. DJ Zuar, accompanied by batucada and pre-Hispanic dancers, takes the stage at 6:30 p.m., followed by the Ballet Folklórico Cuauhtémoc and Mariachi Internacional Real de América.

Grupo Caché performs at 9:30 p.m. Then, at 11 p.m., it’s time for the Grito de Independencia from the Municipal Presidency.

Fireworks will follow at 11:30 p.m. over the Malecón, with Banda Vallejo scheduled to close out the night at midnight. That sounds like a long evening, but this is one of those occasions when nobody seems in much of a hurry to go home.

Wednesday, Sept. 16, begins with an 8 a.m. civic ceremony in the Plaza de Armas, followed by the Independence Day civic-military parade at 9 a.m. The parade will follow the same general route as the charro parade.

Bahía de Banderas

Across the river in Nayarit, Bahía de Banderas will have its own Independence celebrations, with the municipal festivities centered in Valle de Banderas.

On Tuesday, Sept. 15, the municipality will hold its Noche Mexicana in the town’s main plaza, including the traditional Grito led by Mayor Israel Santillán.

The evening’s entertainment will include Mariachi Internacional de México, Banda La Taberna “La Más Guapa” and Banda Arkangel R-15.

On Wednesday, Sept. 16, the traditional civic and military parade will take place. Municipal officials are advising residents to check official traffic notices for the parade route and any resulting road closures.

Nayarit

The state government is also preparing for two days of celebrations in Tepic.

The program begins Tuesday, Sept. 15, with the raising of the Mexican flag and Honores a la Bandera at 8 a.m., followed by the lowering of the flag at 6 p.m.

At 7 p.m., the artistic program, “México Vivo, Nayarit Eterno,” begins, featuring the Ballet Nuevo Nayarit, the Traditional Youth Mariachi of the State School of Fine Arts, the State Symphony Band and singer María Dolores, along with Mariachi Nayarit Contemporáneo and Son de Mi Pueblo.

The public celebration gets underway at 9 p.m., with 7,000 free portions of food and drinks planned.

At 11 p.m., Governor Miguel Ángel Navarro Quintero will lead the Grito de Independencia, followed by a musical fireworks display and performances by Banda Ráfaga and norteño group La Session.

The celebrations continue Wednesday with the traditional parade in the morning. At 5 p.m., Marimba Orquesta Águilas de Chiapas will perform in Plaza Benito Juárez, in front of Casa de Gobierno.

So, for the next few days, expect much of the region to be focused on flags, food, music, fireworks and the familiar cry that brings everyone together for at least one night: ¡Viva México!

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Biodiseño MX at the Franz Mayer Museum explores more-than-human design
World.content:
When visitors enter the “Biodiseño MX” exhibition at the Franz Mayer Museum, earthen tones and other elements evoke the feeling of “entering an ecosystem.” Later, the exhibition transforms from its earthy finishes as color and light shift toward white, creating the atmosphere of a laboratory.

The exhibition’s power is reflected not only in this juxtaposition, but can also be seen in the curated design pieces, spanning popular art and practices rooted in ancestral knowledge to technological innovations, such as 3D-printed memorial reefs made from human ashes.

Curated by Taina Campos, “Biodiseño MX” brings together more than 60 creatives who explore design from a more-than-human perspective — in “collaboration with and for nature.”

What is biodesign?

Design is the creative approach to solving a problem. But since the Industrial Revolution, designers have been put at the service of the market, argues Campos. The Mexico-based designer and curator explains that biodesign is a fundamental shift in current design practice from an anthropocentric approach toward a symbiotic worldview, where nature is not only exploited for resources but integrated into the design process.

In interdependence with flora, fauna, microbes and fungi, and drawing from bio-inspiration, design pieces at the exhibition explore a world beyond anthropocentrism.

More-than-human design

Although symbiotic, biodesign is still susceptible to human ideas and needs. Campos acknowledges that, when approaching biodesign from an anthropocentric perspective, the tendency to create objects that cater to human needs persists.

But although a substantial part of the exhibition is centered around objects for human life — like tableware made from eggshells — certain pieces explore a more-than-human design.

The “Memorial Reef” by the U.K.-based company Resting Reef consists of 3D-printed artificial reef structures made from human ashes and calcium carbonate. According to Resting Reef, introducing those phosphorus-rich sculptures to underwater sites is meant to nourish marine communities. This project adds another question to biodesign: How can biodesign move toward regeneration?

The exhibition’s juxtaposition

The exhibition juxtaposes biodesign for functional objects like biofashion with pieces that help restore marine ecosystems or create oxygen.

“Jardín lacustre” by Mariana Paredes and Molecular Lab takes microalgae from Lake Texcoco and feeds them carbon dioxide from Mexico City’s polluted air. Through photosynthesis, these algae produce oxygen, escalating biodesign from a utilitarian need to a question of ecological survival.

The pieces of popular art made by Indigenous peoples of the Global South reflect an understanding that nature is “intrinsic to us,” while contrasting with technological innovation abundant throughout the exhibition.

Design as a revolution

When speaking about Campos’ motivation for biodesign, she mentions that design has an impact on how we understand the world through objects, systems and everyday applications. Biodesign is not only a design practice but another way to see the world.

“For me, biodesign is the language or practice — the material expression of design — that can lead us toward this other pursuit of design,” she explains. “It is no longer only about solving human problems or making beautiful products to sell; it is about generating another understanding of the world.”

She cites Arturo Escobar’s “Designs for the Pluriverse:” “Design designs worlds, and the worlds it designs design us back.”

“Biodiseño MX” is on display at the Franz Mayer Museum until Oct. 25, 2026.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Taste of Mexico: The curious history and myths of chile en nogada
World.content:
September, known as the “mes patrio” or patriotic month, has begun. This is the month when Mexicans commemorate the consummation of our independence, which took place in 1821. During the official celebration on Sept. 15, the president reenacts the way the independence movement began with what we call the “grito” — the cry of independence.

We also celebrate the grito at home, accompanied by family and friends. We dress up to look even more Mexican with sombreros, fake mustaches and braids. We drink tequila, sing Mexican songs, shout “Viva México” and, of course, eat.

Perhaps the most famous seasonal dish, and the one that generates the most intrigue for me, is chile en nogada.



The dish is essentially a stuffed poblano pepper covered in a walnut sauce. The stuffing is a mixture of beef with fruits such as apple, peach, banana and pear, along with almonds, pine nuts, walnuts, onion and garlic. Its flavor profile, combining sweet and salty, is outstanding.

And now, the intriguing part

As a historian, I am fascinated by how official history is shaped, and I find it puzzling that chile en nogada is included in September’s menu as the quintessential Mexican dish.

According to information from an official government page, on Aug. 28, 1821, the Augustinian nuns of the Convent of Santa Mónica in the state of Puebla welcomed the first Emperor of independent Mexico, Agustín de Iturbide, with a newly created dish that represented the colors of the new national flag: green, white and red. This, the tale goes, is how chile en nogada came to be.

The historical records, however, tell a different story: Agustín de Iturbide did travel to Puebla in 1821, but he arrived on Aug. 5. The list of supplies purchased for the emperor’s reception shows that the ingredients needed to make the chile en nogada weren’t acquired, so it is highly unlikely that he ever tried the dish. Nevertheless, he did enjoy a splendid banquet.

The idea that the nuns created the dish for Iturbide is a myth: Historical records indicate that the recipe was already being prepared in the early 1800s. Researcher Lilia Martínez has discovered that nogada is a European sauce with documented origins going back to the 15th century.

It’s important to note that without the Spanish Conquest, this dish would be impossible, since most of the ingredients used in chile en nogada originate in Spain or were brought over in the intercontinental trade of the time. These ingredients include the English walnut, a protein option of pork, beef or chicken, pomegranate, almonds, apples, pears, peaches and bananas.

The poblano pepper is the sole ingredient native to this land — a huge and vital contribution, if I may add.

So why is it considered the quintessential Mexican dish?

“Je ne sais pas,” the French would say. Wouldn’t it make much more sense if we ate a mole madre or a “tlacoyo?” Or maybe we eat it because it’s the conjunction of two great culinary traditions. Regardless of the reason, I can promise you two things: first, it is one of the most delicious dishes in Mexican cuisine you’ll ever try. Second, once I find out when it became the quintessential Mexican dish, I will create a video and write an article about it.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mexico News Daily (@mexiconewsdaily)

Where can you eat it?

Any Mexican restaurant will have its version of chile en nogada. However, in my opinion, the best chiles I’ve had are found in Puebla. If you can’t go there, look for a thick, ivory-white sauce on your plate, and you’ll probably have an amazing chile en nogada.

I considered sharing the recipe, but every family has its own version, and I don’t want to offend anyone by claiming that mine is the ultimate recipe. This recipe is over three centuries old, from a time when people had the luxury of peeling walnuts with their fingernails and taking time to appreciate the landscape, so it requires a lot of time and patience; as in, two whole days. My parents had two comadres who prepared chile en nogada for the entire family, a party of 80 including us. A group of six women had to spend a whole week in the kitchen. We were fortunate, no doubt.



Do you have a good chile en nogada recipe to share with us, or is the one you use a family secret? Do you know where the best chile en nogada can be found? Share in the comments below.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Dairy war between Chiapas, Oaxaca escalates over ‘world’s biggest cheese ball’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

PIJIJIAPAN, Chiapas — Relations between southern regional neighbors in Mexico reached a historic low Thursday following a massive front-line fromage offensive by Chiapas cheesemakers, who ambushed Oaxaca by constructing a 1,611-kilogram ball of quesillo to reclaim their Guinness World Record for the “world’s biggest cheese ball,” escalating a long-simmering border dispute into an all-out dairy arms race.

The offensive in the coastal town of Pijijiapan neutralized Reyes Etla, Oaxaca’s 2024 record of 636.2 kilograms, effectively tripling the tonnage and signaling a strategic shift toward heavy-artillery curd production. Defense analysts confirmed the deployment required 15,500 liters of milk and four hours of continuous tactical winding on a custom-built metal platform designed to prevent structural failure under heat and humidity.

“This is no longer a matter of culinary pride; it is a full-scale declaration of dairy war,” said Chiapas cheesemaker Roberto Morales, addressing reporters near the massive sphere. “For over a year, Chiapas citizens lived under the psychological weight of a superior Oaxacan cheese ball. With this 1.6-metric-ton retaliation, we have fundamentally altered the balance of dairy power in southern Mexico.”

Defense officials in Oaxaca have yet to issue a formal surrender, though intelligence reports indicate high-level emergency meetings are underway in Reyes Etla. Observers spotted local agricultural logistics teams inspecting dairy reserves and evaluating blueprints for a potential 2,000-kilogram counter-ball ahead of the upcoming festival season.

Meanwhile, municipal officers in Pijijiapan face the formidable task of maintaining victory conditions before environmental factors intervene. “While our victory on the culinary battlefield is complete, we are now managing the post-battle logistics,” Morales added. “Specifically, the unraveling, portioning and consumption of 1.6 metric tons of high-density string cheese before ambient humidity forces a tactical retreat.”

World.title: Red threads, witches and upside-down tortillas: Mexican folk wisdom from our grandparents
World.content:
On Aug. 28, Mexico celebrated Grandparents’ Day, an annual tradition since 1983 that recognizes not only our grandparents’ boundless love, experience and wisdom, but also the invaluable contributions they make to Mexican families and communities.

In a country where many parents and caregivers work, grandparents often play a fundamental role in raising children, including picking them up from school, preparing their meals, and keeping them company or supervising them while their parents are away from the home. In fact, according to the University of Colima’s El Comentario, 30% of children in Mexico are cared for by their grandparents.

While capturing the full scope of their impact is nearly impossible, Mexico News Daily did its best, collecting stories from folks across Mexico about the lessons they learned from their grandparents. Some are amusing and quirky, while others are unexpected and confounding.

No matter their essence, though, each word chronicles the everyday wisdom and legacy of those who have left a deep and abiding impression for generations to come.

Pregnancy and babies

If you are pregnant and there is an eclipse, you must wear a safety pin on your belly to protect the baby.

If a pregnant woman has a craving and does not satisfy it, the baby will be born with the face of whatever she avoided eating.

Newborn babies should wear a red bracelet so that a witch will not suck on them.

Alicantes — a type of snake — hypnotize women who have recently given birth to steal their breast milk.

If a baby has a cough, fever or hiccups, the mother must stick a red thread to the baby’s forehead with saliva so it will go away.

If a baby has droopy cheeks, it is because they were made to sit up too early.

If you shave your baby’s head and rub tomato on it, their hair will grow back curly.

If a pregnant woman’s belly is egg-shaped, she will have a boy; if it is round, she will have a girl.

If you are pregnant and go to the beach, your child may be born with blue eyes.

Food

You should not eat watermelon at night because it bloats the stomach and is hard to digest.

If you do not eat what you are craving, you may get a sore on your tongue.

If you get up from the table before you have finished eating, your mouth may become crooked.

If you do not satisfy a craving, you may develop bile.

If you do not plant with enthusiasm, your harvest will not come in.

You must save the best ears of corn from the harvest to attract abundance.

You must rub the ends of a cucumber to remove “the poison:” meaning, its bitterness.

You should not drink plain water on an empty stomach when you are hungover, because it is harmful.

If you eat tortillas upside down, your insides will turn upside down.

Eat pozole with soda or tea, never with fruit-flavored water.

You have to scold or hit fruit trees so that they bear fruit.

To sleep better, drink warm milk before going to bed.

Witches and witchcraft

If you see red balls in the sky, they are witches . If they look close, the witch is far away; but if they look far away, she is close.

Rub an egg over your body to remove negative energy.

If La Llorona’s crying sounds close, it means she is far away; but if it sounds far away, it means she is close. La Llorona is an old legend about a mother who drowned her children in a river and, in sorrow, spends her nights crying for them. She is particularly associated with rivers, lakes and reservoirs.

Weather

If you bury a knife in the ground, you will prevent it from raining.

You should not bathe after an earthquake because the water has been “shaken.”

If you cross your eyes and a gust of air gets into them, they will stay that way forever.

You should not comb your hair, knit or embroider while it is raining, because lightning could strike you.

The first 12 days of the year predict what the weather will be like in each month: these are the famous cabañuelas .

Illnesses

To cure a sore throat, you have to rub roasted tomato on the chest and the soles of your feet.

To cure a cough, you have to iron some pieces of cloth, place them on the back and chest, and sleep with them warm.

Cold enters through the feet; that is why you should not walk barefoot inside the house.

You have to “cool” your eyes — by putting saliva in them — after watching television ; otherwise, you could go blind.

If you feel empachado — with indigestion or a blocked stomach — someone must massage your belly until that person begins to burp; that will relieve the bloating.

If a dog has a cough, you must put a necklace of limes around its neck so it will go away.

Death

If you are lying down, about to fall asleep, and a friend invites you out, you must say no; otherwise, you may encounter death.

If you hear an owl screeching, it means that someone you know will die.

Other beliefs

To cure espanto — a folk illness associated with fright — you must spit mezcal on the face of the person suffering from it while they sleep.

Espanto is cured by drinking a bitter beverage bought at the apothecary.

You should not buy underwear for your partner because it is bad luck: they might leave.

You should not sweep or do housework at night, because negative energy can enter or money can leave.

If you are going on a trip, you must leave a light on to prevent thieves from breaking in.

Stretching at the table is a way of thanking the devil.

You should not cut your hair after eating because it is harmful.

To make visitors leave soon, you must place a broom upside down behind the door.

Tell us in the comments: Did your grandparents have beliefs similar to these? Which ones do you think are true, and which ones are part of Mexican folklore?

María Ruiz is the Director of Digital Marketing at Mexico News Daily. She enjoys photographing her hometown of San Miguel de Allende in her spare time.

World.title: When Mexico bursts into bloom: A wildflower guide
World.content:
Mexico’s wildflowers astounded me … as if Mother Nature had rolled out the red carpet. Traveling through the central highlands in Querétaro and Guanajuato last September, the roadsides, fields and hillsides were covered in colorful blooms. It was a wow moment. Entire mountainsides shone in a patchwork of vibrant yellows, oranges, reds and pinks. Yet, six months earlier, when I passed through, the same mountainsides were dry, arid and sparse.

However, in September, an entirely different ecosystem lay before my eyes. So much so that I asked the driver to stop along the highway beneath the hillside of Mexican sunflowers. The blooms blanketed the landscape in a cheery yellow; he picked some for me after I shared that I was a botanical artist.

When to see the wildflowers

There are two wildflower seasons in Mexico. The first is in spring, from March to May, when arid regions like Baja California and northern deserts bloom after winter rains. These winter rains cause superblooms where desert plants bloom en masse and carpet the landscape.

The second wildflower season is in autumn, from September to November, after the rainy season throughout Mexico. Native plants put on a brilliant flowering display, bursting into bloom.

Of course, wildflower season may start a little earlier, or end a little later depending on the weather. Having been in Queretàro and Guanajuato in September for the last two years during the autumn wildflower season, I can tell you September is a great time to visit states in Central Mexico.

What flowers can you expect to see?

Cosmos, marigold, Mexican sunflowers, globe mallows, morning glory, salvias, mirasol and many more. From tiny butter daisy flowers blanketing the ground at your feet to the huge blooming shrubs of Mexican sunflowers looking you in the eye. There is a wide variety, from light happy yellows to deep striking purples.

Some flowers were a surprise to me. Like the soft baby pink hues of globe mallows. Not a plant that I had seen before. So, seeing a big patch was quite the sight. Another surprise was massive patches of happy pink cosmos. A popular garden plant, grown for its flowers, it was delightful to find out it is native to Mexico.

Seeing the stunning beauty of wildflowers transform the landscape, I knew there had to be symbolic meanings attached to these flowers.

My top 5

Someone asked me what my favorite flower was. It’s almost impossible to choose, but these five left the biggest impression. Especially the white poppy.

Chicalote, or Mexican white prickly poppy

The Chicalote, a native white prickly poppy, won my heart. Its delicate papery petals shining under the sun were so dreamy and elegant that I painted one. The delicate white petals symbolize tranquility, peaceful dreams and quiet rest.

These white prickly poppy flowers stand for endurance and resilience, peace and sleep.

Because the spiny plant thrives in dry, harsh and disturbed soils where other plants fail, to many it represents the ability to survive tough conditions through deep inner strength.

Mirasol, or cosmos

In a show-stopping display of vibrant pinks, cosmos put on quite a show. Huge patches waved to us along the roadside. Swaying on long feathery stalks as we passed. Another beautiful member of the daisy family, cosmos represents balance, peace and tranquility.

Also, cosmos is believed to act as a bridge between life and the afterlife, linking the physical world with the spiritual realm.

Girasol, or Mexican sunflower

Cherry sunflowers were by far the most common. Entire fields and mountainsides radiated in cheery yellow everywhere I went. This member of the daisy family represents faith, loyalty, and adoration.

Some Indigenous populations associated the flower’s bright face with solar deities. Aztec and Mexica people treated the plant as sacred. Dried sunflower seeds were left as offerings at major ceremonial sites like the Templo Mayor in Mexico City.

Mexican passionflower

Walking the streets of Queretàro, Mexican Passionflowers were abundantly climbing up trees or along old gates. This one was growing outside a church, which I found fitting, as they symbolize the Passion of Christ and the crucifixion.

The 10 petals and sepals represent the faithful apostles, while the corona filaments (seen as the purple inner ring) represent the crown of thorns. Inside, the three stigmas represent the nails, and the five anthers represent Christ’s wounds.

Copper globemallow

New to me, this member of the hibiscus family had me stopping for a closer look. The soft baby pink petals are as delightful as the velvety feel of its leaves. Flourishing in dry, harsh desert heat, the flower symbolizes endurance and resilience. Also standing as powerful emblems of hope, gentle comfort and vitality.

The best way to see them

Take a drive. These flowers line highways and laneways, lowlands and mountain ranges. So, by driving, you will see the greatest variety. I loved them all so much I made a quick sketchbook page with the most abundant. I hope you enjoy them as much as I have over the last couple of years.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel Woodhouse is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

World.title: What Is Documented About De la Espriella and the Gilinski Group
World.content:
COLOMBIA · MEDIA AND POLITICS

Key Facts — What is reported Links between President Abelardo De la Espriella’s campaign and the Gilinski business group.

— Who reported it La Silla Vacía, a Colombian investigative outlet.

— The central item A campaign loan of 17,500 million pesos, about US$4.4 million, from Gilinski-controlled GNB Sudameris.

— The media element Semana, owned by the Gilinskis, ran 133 campaign videos without labelling them as electoral material.

— The response The campaign refused the outlet’s questions. Semana and the president’s lawyer demanded a rectification.

— What is not established Any finding by a court or electoral authority. Nothing has been adjudicated.

A bank loan, a media group and a cabinet appointment sit in the same reporting. Each element is documented, contested, and none of it has been before a court.

What Is Documented About De la Espriella and the Gilinski Group

Colombian reporting has set out several links between President Abelardo De la Espriella’s campaign and the Gilinski business group. The president’s side disputes the framing.

What La Silla Vacía Reported

The outlet published an investigation into the president’s business and political circle during the campaign and after it.

Its central financial item is a loan to the runoff campaign of 17,500 million pesos, roughly US$4.4 million. The lender is GNB Sudameris, a bank controlled by the Gilinski group.

Campaign lending by banks is lawful in Colombia and is regulated rather than prohibited. The question the reporting raises is one of proximity, not legality.

The outlet also reported that the Gilinskis attended the inauguration on 7 August as guests.

The Media Strand

Semana is one of Colombia’s largest news magazines and is owned by the Gilinski family.

La Silla Vacía reported that Semana ran 133 of the campaign’s videos in full, without labelling them as electoral propaganda.

Labelling matters under Colombian electoral rules because it determines whether coverage counts as campaign spending or as journalism.

This is the element with the clearest public-interest bite. It concerns disclosure to readers rather than a private commercial arrangement.

The Appointment

Sandra Suárez was appointed director of the Department for Social Prosperity, the agency that runs Colombia’s main cash transfer programmes.

She had previously advised Semana and sat on its board alongside Gabriel Gilinski.

Moving from a media board to a senior public post is not unlawful and is not unusual in Colombia.

It is reported here because it sits in the same circle as the other items, not because any impropriety has been established.

A rectification demand is a recognised instrument in Colombian media law.

What the President’s Side Says

The campaign declined to answer La Silla Vacía’s written questions. It described them as captious and tendentious.

Semana and the president’s lawyer subsequently sent the outlet a formal rectification demand.

A rectification demand is a recognised instrument in Colombian media law. It obliges an outlet to consider correcting material it published.

That demand is part of the record and belongs in any account of this reporting. Readers should know the material is contested.

What We Are Not Reporting, and Why

Several claims circulating alongside this material do not meet a publishable standard, and we are naming them rather than repeating them.

One outlet has alleged a coordinated media operation to manufacture the president’s standing. It is unbylined, offers no data and carries no response from anyone named.

A figure of 2,100 million pesos in Gilinski and Semana campaign money is also circulating. That money financed a different candidate, Vicky Dávila.

A claim that De la Espriella acted as the Gilinskis’ lawyer in the Nutresa and Sura takeover does not hold. El Tiempo’s own reporting on that deal names different firms.

There is also no allegation on record involving the Santo Domingo group. Its chairman joined a reconstruction summit in Quibdó in September, which is cooperation rather than a claim.

The Gilinski group is a major force in Colombian banking, food and media.

Why Any of This Matters to Outsiders

Colombia elected a president with a business and legal career rather than a political one. Mapping his commercial relationships is ordinary scrutiny.

The Gilinski group is a major force in Colombian banking, food and media. Where it overlaps with a presidency, the overlap is a matter of public interest.

For foreign investors, the practical question is regulatory independence. A banking group close to an administration is a governance question, not a scandal on its own.

None of this is a finding of wrongdoing. It is a map of relationships that readers are entitled to see.

What Is Not Known

No electoral authority or court has examined the campaign loan. No proceeding has been reported.

The Gilinski group has not issued a public response to the reporting beyond the rectification demand sent through Semana.

Whether the outlet will amend its material is not known. The rectification process had not concluded at the time of writing.

More: Colombia news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the reported campaign loan?

17,500 million pesos, about US$4.4 million, from GNB Sudameris to the runoff campaign, as reported by La Silla Vacía.

Is campaign lending by banks legal in Colombia?

Yes. It is regulated rather than prohibited, and no authority has examined this loan.

What is the Semana element?

The magazine, owned by the Gilinskis, ran 133 campaign videos without labelling them as electoral propaganda.

Has the president responded?

His campaign refused the outlet’s questions, and Semana and his lawyer sent a formal rectification demand.

Is the Santo Domingo group implicated?

No. No allegation involving that group exists in this reporting.

Has anything been adjudicated?

No. No court or electoral authority has made any finding.

Sources: La Silla Vacía, El Tiempo, Semana, Portafolio, El Espectador.

World.title: Chile Denies Argentina’s Claim of Joint Patrols in the Magellan Strait
World.content:
CHILE · ARGENTINA

Key Facts — What happened Argentina’s defence minister said the two navies run combined patrols in the Strait of Magellan.

— The response Chile’s defence minister denied it the same week.

— Chile’s position The strait is guarded and controlled exclusively by the Chilean navy.

— What does exist A combined Antarctic naval patrol, and a joint exercise in the Beagle Channel area.

— The legal basis The boundary treaties of 1881 and 1984.

— The unresolved item An Argentine decree of 2021 describing the strait as a shared space remains in force.

One minister described joint patrols and the other said they do not exist. Both were describing real naval cooperation, and only one of them was describing the strait.

Chile Denies Argentina’s Claim of Joint Patrols in the Magellan Strait

Argentina’s defence minister said on television that the two navies patrol the Strait of Magellan together. Chile’s defence minister said that is not the case.

The Exchange

On 11 September, Argentine Defence Minister Carlos Presti said there is combined patrolling between the Argentine and Chilean navies in the strait.

Chile’s Defence Minister Fernando Barros rejected that directly.

The waters, he said, are guarded and controlled exclusively by the Chilean navy.

He added that combined activity is confined to two specific arrangements, neither of which covers the strait.

What the Two Navies Do Together

The first is the combined Antarctic naval patrol, in which both navies cover search and rescue in Antarctic waters each season.

The second is an exercise conducted in the Beagle Channel area.

Both are long-standing, and both are examples of successful cooperation between the two countries.

Neither takes place in the Strait of Magellan. That is the whole substance of the disagreement.

Why the Strait Is Sensitive

The Strait of Magellan lies entirely within Chilean territory, under the boundary treaty of 1881 and the 1984 peace and friendship treaty.

Chile’s foreign ministry describes its sovereignty there as indisputable. Argentina has not formally contested it.

The strait is one of two natural passages between the Atlantic and the Pacific at the southern tip of the continent. Its value is strategic rather than commercial.

It is also the physical expression of a border settlement that took a century to complete.

The strait lies entirely within Chilean territory under two treaties.

How the Row Started

On 23 August, the head of Argentina’s air force described Magallanes, the south and the Drake Passage as matters of sovereignty.

Chile’s foreign ministry responded by citing the two treaties.

On 3 September, presidents Javier Milei and José Antonio Kast met in Santiago. Their joint declaration affirmed Chilean sovereignty over the whole strait.

The following day Argentina’s foreign minister described the country as bicontinental and bioceanic, and the friction resumed.

The Decree Nobody Has Signed Away

An Argentine decree from 2021 describes the strait as a shared space for exploration, study and control.

It has not been repealed. Chilean officials say an amended text has been awaiting the Argentine president’s signature since March.

That unsigned amendment is the practical core of the dispute. Everything else is commentary on it.

Chile’s lower house has voted to summon the foreign minister to appear on 28 September.

Nothing operational has changed. The disagreement is diplomatic.

Mendoza Is a Different Story

Some coverage has attached the province of Mendoza to this dispute. There is no Chile-Mendoza incident.

Mendoza is exposed to the relationship through infrastructure rather than friction. The Cristo Redentor pass carries around 1,300 trucks a day.

The GasAndes pipeline also runs through the province. Governor Alfredo Cornejo has an agenda for the bilateral committee in October.

That agenda covers pass upgrades and tunnel projects. It is trade business, not a sovereignty argument.

What Is Not Known

Argentina has not clarified or withdrawn the minister’s remark. No correction has been issued.

It is not known when or whether the amended decree will be signed.

For shipping and for residents of the far south, nothing operational has changed. The disagreement is diplomatic, and the strait is being policed as it was before.

More: Chile news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Argentina’s defence minister say?

That the Argentine and Chilean navies conduct combined patrols in the Strait of Magellan.

How did Chile respond?

Defence Minister Fernando Barros said the strait is guarded and controlled exclusively by the Chilean navy.

Do the navies cooperate at all?

Yes. They run a combined Antarctic naval patrol and an exercise in the Beagle Channel area.

Who has sovereignty over the strait?

Chile, under the boundary treaty of 1881 and the 1984 peace and friendship treaty.

What is the 2021 decree?

An Argentine decree describing the strait as a shared space. It has not been repealed.

Is Mendoza involved?

No. Mendoza’s interest is in road and pipeline links, not in the sovereignty argument.

Sources: Ministerio de Defensa de Chile, Emol, La Política Online, Mendoza Today.

World.title: Trump’s Venezuela Oil Claim, Measured Against the Production Data
World.content:
VENEZUELA · OIL

Key Facts — What was said President Trump linked a possible exit from Iran to keeping oil, comparing it to Venezuela.

— Where Speaking to reporters in Ireland on 13 September 2026.

— The claim attached to it That American revenue from Venezuelan oil has paid for the war many times over.

— What Venezuela produces 1.145 million barrels a day in August, on OPEC secondary-source estimates.

— What the US imports 630,000 barrels a day in June 2026, the latest monthly figure from the Energy Information Administration.

— The arithmetic At those volumes the trade is worth low tens of billions a year at most.

The quote is real and the figures around it are checkable. Putting the two side by side is what the claim has mostly been spared.

Trump’s Venezuela Oil Claim, Measured Against the Production Data

President Donald Trump spoke to reporters in Ireland on Sunday. The United States might stay in Iran and keep the oil, he said, the way it has with Venezuela.

What He Actually Said

The remarks were made to reporters in Ireland on 13 September 2026, while he was attending the Irish Open.

His words were that the country would ultimately get out of Iran. Unless, he added, it decides to stay and keep the oil like Venezuela.

He added that American revenue from Venezuelan oil has paid for the war many times over.

He said he expects the Iran conflict to end this year, possibly after the November midterm elections. Petrol prices would then fall sharply, he added.

What Venezuela Actually Produces

OPEC publishes two figures for Venezuela each month, and they differ.

Secondary-source estimates put August 2026 output at 1.145 million barrels a day. That figure appeared in the monthly report published around 10 September.

The other figure is what Venezuela itself reports. In April, direct communication gave 1.136 million barrels a day against 1.031 million from secondary sources.

The secondary-source series is the one to use, and it should be named as such. Quoting a producing country’s own number as its production is a standard error.

What the United States Imports

The Energy Information Administration publishes monthly and weekly series. The latest monthly figure is June 2026, at 630,000 barrels a day.

The trajectory this year has been steep. January was 200,000 barrels a day and February 231,000. March reached 373,000, April 429,000 and May 471,000.

The weekly series peaked in early August at 743,000 barrels a day and had eased to 599,000 by 4 September.

For contrast, the series bottomed at 7,000 barrels a day in July 2025. The change over fourteen months is the substance of this story.

US imports ran at 630,000 barrels a day in June 2026.

Does the Money Add Up?

This is where the claim separates from the data.

Take roughly 600,000 barrels a day at prevailing crude prices. The annual import value runs to the order of low tens of billions of dollars.

That is a gross trade value, not a government revenue. The United States government does not receive the proceeds of commercial crude imports.

No published arrangement describes a transfer of Venezuelan oil revenue to the American state. There is no disclosed agreement text to examine.

The claim that this paid for a war many times over is an assertion. No figure in the public record supports it.

Why the Comparison Is Being Made

The framing links two separate situations: a military engagement with Iran and a commercial and sanctions relationship with Venezuela.

What the two have in common is that both involve oil and both are contested domestically in the United States.

What they do not share is a legal structure. No published mechanism exists by which the United States keeps Venezuelan oil, in the sense the phrase implies.

Import volumes rose from almost nothing to 630,000 barrels a day. That is a licensing and sanctions story rather than a seizure.

Production near 1.1 million barrels a day is far below historical capacity.

What This Means for the Region

For Venezuela, restored export volumes are the single most consequential economic development in years.

For Caribbean and Latin American refiners, Venezuelan heavy crude returning to the market changes freight patterns and discounts.

For anyone modelling Venezuelan output, the constraint remains upstream. Production near 1.1 million barrels a day is far below the country’s historical capacity.

What Is Not Known

The terms of any arrangement have not been published. No text, licence schedule or revenue mechanism is in the public record.

Neither the White House nor the Treasury has published figures supporting the payment claim.

July and August monthly import data had not been released at the time of writing. The weekly series suggests volumes eased through late August.

More: Venezuela news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Trump say about Venezuela?

That the United States might stay in Iran and keep the oil, as it has with Venezuela. He spoke in Ireland on 13 September 2026.

How much oil does Venezuela produce?

About 1.145 million barrels a day in August 2026, on OPEC secondary-source estimates.

How much does the US import?

630,000 barrels a day in June 2026, the latest monthly figure from the Energy Information Administration.

Has that changed recently?

Sharply. The series bottomed at 7,000 barrels a day in July 2025.

Did Venezuelan oil pay for a war?

No figure in the public record supports that. Commercial import value does not accrue to the US government.

Is there a published agreement?

No text, licence schedule or revenue mechanism has been disclosed.

Sources: OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report, US Energy Information Administration, The Hill, Jerusalem Post.

World.title: What the 1982 Files Show About Chile’s Help to Britain
World.content:
CHILE · HISTORY

Key Facts — What is new A book by two Chilean journalists, launched in Santiago at the end of August 2026.

— What is not new The documents. They are British files, declassified through the normal process.

— The authors Daniel Avendaño and Mauricio Palma, who worked the British archives from 2019.

— The key document A British defence paper of 1 May 1982 ranking options for Chilean involvement.

— What it describes Use of Chilean airfields and airspace, a radar installed at Balmaceda, and British aircraft in Chilean markings.

— The correction These are not Chilean documents and they are not newly declassified.

Chilean help to Britain in 1982 has been known in outline for decades. What the new book adds is the paperwork, and the paperwork is British.

What the 1982 Files Show About Chile’s Help to Britain

A new Chilean book draws on British archive documents from 1982. They show how far London considered taking Chilean cooperation during the South Atlantic war.

What the Book Is

El Pacto Perfecto was launched in Santiago in the week of 31 August 2026.

Its authors are the Chilean journalists Daniel Avendaño and Mauricio Palma. They began working in the British archives in 2019.

The book draws on files released by the United Kingdom National Archives through ordinary declassification.

That distinction is worth stating plainly. The research is new. The documents have been available to researchers.

The Central Document

The most striking item is a British defence ministry paper dated 1 May 1982, running to fifteen pages.

It was marked secret and restricted to British eyes. It ranks military options by degree of Chilean involvement.

Option fourteen covers active Chilean participation. Option fifteen goes further, to deeper military cooperation and a possible alliance.

A separate chiefs of staff paper of 2 April 1982 addresses the use of Chilean airfields.

What Chile Actually Provided

The files describe the use of airfields including Easter Island, Concepción, Punta Arenas and San Félix.

They also cover Chilean airspace for British reconnaissance flights.

A Marconi radar was installed at Balmaceda. British aircraft were repainted in Chilean air force markings.

In return, Chile received favours connected to intelligence on Argentina. The relationship ran in both directions.

The files describe use of Chilean airfields and airspace.

Why This Still Matters in 2026

The South Atlantic dispute is live again. Argentina escalated its sovereignty claim in early September after remarks from Washington on British backing.

Chile and Argentina have also been trading statements over the Strait of Magellan. Historical memory is part of how those arguments are conducted.

For Chile, the 1982 cooperation took place under the Pinochet government, which complicates domestic discussion of it.

For Argentina, it is a grievance with documentary support. Publishing the files in Spanish puts that support within reach of a general readership.

Punta Arenas is among the airfields named in the British files.

How to Cite It Correctly

Three errors are circulating and each is easy to avoid.

The documents are British, not Chilean. They come from the United Kingdom National Archives.

They are not newly declassified. Declassification happened through the normal thirty-year process, and researchers have used these collections before.

The aggregating outlets that first carried the story in Spanish are not the source. Credit belongs to the authors and the archive.

The Argentine Reading

In Argentina the material lands on well-prepared ground. Chilean assistance to Britain has been an article of national memory since the war itself.

What was missing was the paper. Testimony and inference carried the claim, and documents settle arguments that testimony cannot.

The current diplomatic temperature gives the release additional weight. Buenos Aires and Santiago have been exchanging statements over sovereignty and naval patrols.

None of that changes what the files say. It changes how loudly they are quoted.

What Is Not Known

No Chilean government response to the book has been reported. Nor has any British one.

The files record options considered and assistance given. They do not establish how far option fifteen was ever pursued.

It is also not known whether further material remains withheld. Archive releases are staged, and some 1982 defence files remain closed.

More: Chile news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new book?

El Pacto Perfecto, by Chilean journalists Daniel Avendaño and Mauricio Palma, launched in Santiago in late August 2026.

Are the documents Chilean?

No. They are British files from the United Kingdom National Archives.

Are they newly declassified?

No. They were released through the normal declassification process and researched from 2019.

What do they show?

Use of Chilean airfields and airspace, a radar at Balmaceda, and British aircraft repainted in Chilean markings.

What is the key document?

A British defence paper of 1 May 1982 ranking options, including active Chilean participation and a possible alliance.

Was Chilean help already known?

In outline, yes, for decades. The book supplies the documentary detail.

Sources: The National Archives (UK), El Pacto Perfecto, Infobae, La Nación.

World.title: Video Places Pataz Massacre Suspect Drinking Inside a Colombian Prison
World.content:
PERU · JUSTICE

Key Facts — What surfaced Video of a prisoner drinking and toasting inside a maximum-security prison in Colombia.

— Who Miguel Antonio Rodríguez Díaz, known as Cuchillo, a former Peruvian soldier.

— What he is accused of Being the intellectual author of the Pataz massacre, in which 13 mine security workers died.

— Where he is El Pedregal prison in Antioquia, Colombia, awaiting extradition to Peru.

— What the video shows At least two mobile phones visible alongside him.

— The concern That he continues to direct his organisation from inside.

A man awaiting extradition for thirteen murders appears on film toasting with other inmates. Two mobile phones are visible in the same frame.

Video Places Pataz Massacre Suspect Drinking Inside a Colombian Prison

Peruvian television has published video of the main suspect in the Pataz massacre. It shows him drinking inside the Colombian prison where he awaits extradition.

What the Video Shows

The footage was broadcast by the Peruvian programme Panorama and reported by Infobae Perú on 14 September 2026.

It shows Miguel Antonio Rodríguez Díaz drinking and toasting with other inmates.

At least two mobile phones are visible. Phones inside a maximum-security facility are prohibited, and they are the mechanism by which imprisoned leaders keep operating.

The Peruvian security analyst Pedro Yaranga described it as a breach of control. He urged that the extradition proceedings be accelerated.

The Case Behind It

The Pataz massacre took place in late April 2025 in Peru’s La Libertad region.

Thirteen mine security workers were killed. The attack was filmed and the footage circulated, which is how it functioned as intimidation.

Pataz is a gold-mining district where informal and illegal mining operate alongside formal concessions. Control of access to the shafts is what the violence is about.

Rodríguez Díaz is a former Peruvian military officer. Prosecutors allege he was the intellectual author rather than a participant.

Why He Is in Colombia

He was arrested in Medellín on 15 May 2025.

Peru obtained 36 months of preventive detention in May 2025. He has been held at El Pedregal prison in Antioquia since.

Extradition to Peru is pending and has not been completed. That is the delay the analyst was pointing at.

The case is therefore Peruvian in substance and Colombian in location. That combination is why it falls between the two countries’ news cycles.

He was arrested in Medellín in May 2025 and held in Antioquia.

The Name Confusion Worth Avoiding

There was an earlier and entirely different figure known by the same alias in Colombia.

Pedro Oliverio Guerrero Castillo, a paramilitary and trafficking leader who used the alias Cuchillo, was killed in 2010.

He has no connection to this case. Colombian archive material about him surfaces readily in searches on the alias.

The person in the video is Peruvian, and his case concerns Peru.

A maximum-security designation describes the building, not the regime inside it.

What It Says About Prison Control

Directing a criminal organisation from prison is a documented pattern across the region, not a Colombian peculiarity.

It depends on two things: communications and the ability to move money. A visible mobile phone addresses the first.

A maximum-security designation describes the building rather than the regime inside it. The distinction is the whole problem.

For Peru, the operational consequence is direct. Witness protection and the security of the Pataz proceedings depend on the accused being cut off.

The Extradition Question

Extradition between Peru and Colombia runs through the courts of the requested country and then a government decision.

Preventive detention gives a defined window, and 36 months is the period Peru obtained in May 2025. Roughly a third of it has passed.

Delay in these cases is usually procedural rather than political. Documentation, translation and appeals all add months.

The video changes the political temperature rather than the legal timetable. That is the pressure the Peruvian analyst was applying.

What Is Not Known

Neither the Colombian prison service nor the Colombian government had responded publicly at the time of writing.

The date on which the footage was recorded has not been established. Nor has its provenance been explained.

No extradition date has been published. It is also not known whether any internal investigation has been opened at El Pedregal.

More: Peru news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is in the video?

Miguel Antonio Rodríguez Díaz, a former Peruvian soldier known as Cuchillo, held in Colombia awaiting extradition.

What is he accused of?

Being the intellectual author of the Pataz massacre of late April 2025, in which 13 mine security workers were killed.

Where is he held?

El Pedregal prison in Antioquia, Colombia, after his arrest in Medellín on 15 May 2025.

What does the video show?

Him drinking and toasting with other inmates, with at least two mobile phones visible.

Has he been extradited?

No. Extradition to Peru is pending.

Is this the Colombian trafficker of the same alias?

No. That man was killed in 2010 and has no connection to this case.

Sources: Panorama, Infobae Perú, Diario Correo.

World.title: Peru’s Hotel Pipeline Is US$495 Million and 21 Projects
World.content:
PERU · TOURISM

Key Facts — The pipeline US$495 million across 21 hotel projects over the next two years.

— Who says so The Sociedad Hoteles del Perú, the hotel industry association.

— The brands Ritz-Carlton, Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, Pullman, Meliá, Conrad, Novotel, Casa Andina, Inkaterra and Aranwa.

— The build rate Five to six hotels a year, against ten or eleven before the pandemic.

— A second, different figure US$347 million across 43 projects, from the state promotion agency.

— Why they differ One is a committed pipeline. The other is a portfolio being marketed to investors.

Two hotel investment figures for Peru are circulating and they measure different things. Adding them together would double-count projects that have not been financed.

Peru’s Hotel Pipeline Is US$495 Million and 21 Projects

Peru’s hotel association has put the country’s development pipeline at US$495 million across 21 projects over two years.

What Is Being Built

The association published the figure in late August 2026. It covers the period to 2028.

The brand list is unusually broad for a market Peru’s size. It runs from luxury to select service.

At the top end are Ritz-Carlton, Conrad and Pullman. The Ritz-Carlton arrives through a conversion of the JW Marriott in Miraflores rather than a new build.

Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, Meliá and Novotel cover the middle. Casa Andina, Inkaterra and Aranwa are Peruvian operators.

The Number That Tells the Real Story

The build rate is the more revealing figure. Peru is opening five to six hotels a year.

Before the pandemic it was opening ten or eleven. The pipeline is therefore recovering rather than expanding.

A US$495 million pipeline sounds substantial in isolation. Set against a halved construction rate, it reads as catching up.

The Other Figure and Why It Is Different

The state promotion agency published a separate number in March 2026: US$347 million across 43 projects.

Those projects span Lima, Arequipa, Cusco, Piura and Tumbes. It is a promotional portfolio, offered to prospective investors.

That is not the same as committed capital. Some of those projects will proceed, some will not, and some overlap with the association’s list.

The two figures cannot be added. A combined total of US$842 million would be a number nobody has claimed.

Peru is opening five to six hotels a year, against ten or eleven before the pandemic.

What This Says About Peruvian Tourism

Peru’s tourism economy is concentrated on Cusco and Machu Picchu, with Lima as the gateway.

It has been through a difficult few years, with political instability, protests and access restrictions at the main sites.

International brands committing to conversions rather than new builds is a cautious form of confidence. It puts a flag in the market with less capital at risk.

The regional spread of the promotional portfolio points the other way, toward the north coast and Arequipa.

International brands are committing through conversions rather than new builds.

What a Traveller or Investor Should Take From It

For travellers, the practical effect is more upper-tier rooms in Lima over the next two years.

For investors, the association’s figure is the firmer of the two. It comes from operators rather than from a promotion agency.

Neither figure tells you occupancy or rate. Those are what determine whether the pipeline gets built out.

How Peru Compares in the Region

Peru’s pipeline is modest next to Mexico or Brazil, and that is a function of market size rather than appetite.

What distinguishes it is the mix. A single market drawing Ritz-Carlton, Conrad and Moxy at the same time is unusual at this scale.

The Peruvian operators on the list matter as much as the international names. Casa Andina, Inkaterra and Aranwa are domestic groups with established regional positions.

That balance is a sign of a market being developed rather than simply entered. Foreign brands and local operators are expanding at the same time.

What Is Not Known

Neither release gives a project-by-project breakdown with financing status. Completion dates are not published.

No occupancy or average rate data accompanied either figure.

It is also not known how much of the promotional portfolio overlaps with the committed pipeline. Until that is published, treat the two as separate readings of the same market.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is being invested in Peruvian hotels?

US$495 million across 21 projects over two years, on the hotel association’s figures.

Which brands are coming?

Ritz-Carlton, Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, Pullman, Meliá, Conrad and Novotel, alongside Casa Andina, Inkaterra and Aranwa.

How fast is Peru building hotels?

Five to six a year, against ten or eleven before the pandemic.

What is the US$347 million figure?

A separate promotional portfolio of 43 projects published by the state promotion agency in March 2026.

Can the two figures be added?

No. One is committed pipeline, the other is projects being marketed to investors.

Where are the projects?

Mainly Lima, with the promotional portfolio also covering Arequipa, Cusco, Piura and Tumbes.

Sources: Sociedad Hoteles del Perú, PROMPERÚ, El Comercio.

World.title: Panama’s Draft Budget Cuts the Gorgas Institute by US$5.8 Million
World.content:
PANAMA · PUBLIC HEALTH

Key Facts — What is proposed A cut of US$5.8 million to the Gorgas Memorial Institute in Panama’s 2027 draft budget.

— What Gorgas is Panama’s public biomedical and public health research institute, and its national reference laboratory.

— The detail that stands out The line for electricity and utilities is set at zero.

— For scale The institute had about US$39.4 million in 2025.

— The status It is a draft. The National Assembly has not passed the budget.

— Not alone The social development ministry loses US$46.8 million in the same draft.

A research institute with a zero line for electricity is not a normal budget entry. The National Assembly has not voted, which is why this is worth reading now.

Panama’s Draft Budget Cuts the Gorgas Institute by US$5.8 Million

Panama’s draft 2027 budget removes US$5.8 million from the Gorgas Memorial Institute, the country’s main biomedical research body.

What the Institute Does

The Instituto Conmemorativo Gorgas de Estudios de la Salud is Panama’s public health research institute.

Its work covers infectious disease, vector-borne disease and epidemiological surveillance. It also operates the national reference laboratory.

That laboratory role is the part with immediate consequences. Reference laboratories confirm diagnoses that ordinary hospital labs cannot.

The institute is directed by Nicanor Obaldía the third. It carries the name of William Gorgas, the American physician who worked on disease control during canal construction.

The Numbers in the Draft

The 2027 draft national budget totals US$35.1 billion.

Within it, the Gorgas institute loses US$5.8 million against its previous allocation.

For scale, the institute had about US$39.4 million in 2025, split between US$23.7 million of investment and US$15.7 million of operations.

The line covering electricity and utilities is set at zero in the draft. That is the entry that has drawn attention.

It Is Not the Only Cut

The social development ministry takes the largest reduction, from US$238.6 million to US$191.8 million.

The foreign ministry loses US$7.6 million. The National Assembly itself loses US$1.7 million, and the housing ministry US$1.3 million.

That pattern matters for interpretation. This is a general tightening rather than a decision aimed at one institute.

It sits alongside the fiscal consolidation the finance ministry has been reporting, with the deficit down to 2.78% of output through July.

A draft budget is a proposal. The Assembly debates it, amends it and votes.

Why This Is Worth Watching Early

A draft budget is a proposal. The National Assembly debates it, amends it and votes.

Public attention at the draft stage is usually what changes individual lines. Once passed, a budget is difficult to reopen.

Panama has been through this before with the same institute. A previous budget cycle also proposed a reduction, under a different director.

That earlier episode is a separate story from three years ago. It is circulating in search results and should not be cited as current.

Private laboratories still refer confirmatory testing to the national system.

What It Means for Residents and Visitors

Most people never interact with a reference laboratory directly. They rely on it through the hospital system.

Panama is a tropical country with dengue, and a transit hub with high cross-border movement. Surveillance capacity is not an abstraction here.

Foreign residents using private healthcare are affected as much as anyone. Private laboratories still refer confirmatory testing to the national system.

How Panama’s Budget Process Works

The executive drafts the national budget and sends it to the National Assembly. Committee review comes first, then debate and a vote.

Individual institutional lines can be amended during that passage. Ministries and agencies routinely lobby for restoration at this stage.

The budget must be approved before the fiscal year begins. That timetable gives affected bodies a defined window to make their case.

For anyone tracking Panamanian public spending, the draft is the document to read. The passed budget tells you what was decided, not what was proposed.

What Is Not Known

The institute has not published a response to the draft figures. No statement from the health ministry has been reported.

It is not known whether the zero utilities line is an error, a reallocation to another budget head, or a decision.

Nor is it known how the Assembly will treat the line. Until the budget passes, nothing has been cut.

More: Panama news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the Gorgas institute losing?

US$5.8 million in the 2027 draft budget. The budget has not yet been passed.

What does the institute do?

Biomedical and public health research, disease surveillance, and Panama’s national reference laboratory.

What is unusual in the draft?

The line for electricity and utilities is set at zero.

How big is its budget?

It had about US$39.4 million in 2025, split between investment and operations.

Are other bodies being cut?

Yes. The social development ministry loses US$46.8 million, and the foreign ministry US$7.6 million.

Has the cut taken effect?

No. It is a draft before the National Assembly.

Sources: La Prensa Panamá, Instituto Conmemorativo Gorgas, Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas.

World.title: Panama’s 4.4% Growth Number Is a Forecast, Not a Measurement
World.content:
PANAMA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Finance Minister Felipe Chapman gave Panama’s fiscal and growth figures at an investor forum.

— The growth figure 4.4% for 2026. It is an ECLAC projection, not a measured outcome.

— The measured figure First-quarter output grew 4.8%, published by the statistics institute on 16 June.

— The deficit 2,642 million balboas through July, equal to 2.78% of output.

— The comparison That is down from 3.27% in the same period of 2025.

— The currency point The balboa is pegged one to one with the US dollar, which circulates as legal tender.

The 4.4% figure now attached to Panama is a forecast quoted by a minister, not a statistic. The measured number and the fiscal number are both better than the forecast suggests.

Panama’s 4.4% Growth Number Is a Forecast, Not a Measurement
