Panama’s finance minister set out growth and deficit figures at an investor forum last week. One of the two numbers being repeated is a projection.

What Was Actually Released

Economy and Finance Minister Felipe Chapman spoke at the Latinex investor forum. The ministry issued its release on 11 September 2026.

Wire coverage picked it up on 14 September, which is why the figures read as new.

The deficit number is the ministry’s own. Through July 2026 the non-financial public sector deficit was 2,642 million balboas, equivalent to US$2.64 billion.

That equals 2.78% of output, against 3.27% in the same period of 2025. The improvement is real and it is measured.

Where the 4.4% Comes From

The growth figure is different in kind. It is a projection by the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean.

The commission revised Panama up from 4.0% to 4.4% for 2026, and projects 4.6% for 2027.

A minister quoting a forecast at an investor event is entirely normal. Reporting that forecast as national accounts data is not.

The distinction matters because projections for Panama have moved repeatedly, and because the measured data tells a slightly different story.

First-quarter output grew 4.8%, on the statistics institute’s measurement.

What the Measured Data Shows

The statistics institute published first-quarter 2026 growth of 4.8% on 16 June 2026.

No second-quarter national accounts release was available at the time of writing.

The monthly activity indicator ran at 8.23% year on year in June and 5.19% in May. Those are volatile monthly readings rather than quarterly output.

Taken together, the measured evidence is of growth at or above the projection so far this year.

Why Panama Is Read Differently From Its Neighbours

Panama uses the United States dollar as circulating currency, alongside the balboa at par. There is no exchange rate risk of the kind that dominates Argentine or Bolivian analysis.

That removes one variable and sharpens another. Without a currency to devalue, fiscal discipline carries the whole adjustment burden.

It also means Panamanian interest rates track external conditions rather than a domestic central bank. Panama has no monetary authority issuing its own currency.

For an investor, the deficit path is therefore the number to watch. It is the main lever the state actually controls.

Without a currency to devalue, fiscal discipline carries the adjustment burden.

The Fiscal Question Behind the Numbers

Panama lost its investment-grade rating from one agency in 2024, and the others have kept it under scrutiny.

The deficit falling from 3.27% to 2.78% of output is the kind of movement the agencies look for. It is seven months of data, not a year.

The 2027 draft budget, still before the National Assembly, is the next test. It totals US$35.1 billion.

What Is Not Known

Second-quarter national accounts have not been published. The full-year outcome against the 4.4% projection cannot be assessed yet.

The ministry has not published a month-by-month deficit breakdown alongside the headline figure.

For readers tracking Panama, one rule avoids most of the confusion. Ask which institution produced a number and whether it describes the past or the future.

More: Panama news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Panama grow 4.4%?

Not as a measured figure. 4.4% is an ECLAC projection for 2026 quoted by the finance minister.

What is the measured growth figure?

First-quarter 2026 output grew 4.8%, published by the statistics institute on 16 June 2026.

What is the deficit?

2,642 million balboas, about US$2.64 billion, through July 2026, equal to 2.78% of output.

Is that an improvement?

Yes. The same period of 2025 recorded 3.27%.

Where were the figures given?

By Finance Minister Felipe Chapman at the Latinex investor forum, in a ministry release of 11 September 2026.

Does Panama use the dollar?

Yes. The US dollar circulates as legal tender alongside the balboa, which is pegged at par.

Sources: Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas, Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo, CEPAL, La Prensa Panamá.

World.title: A Record Quiet Atlantic Does Not Mean a Calm Costa Rica
World.content:
If you have been watching the hurricane season to decide whether this is a good month to be in Costa Rica, the headline number is genuinely remarkable, and easy to read the wrong way. As of yesterday, not a single hurricane had formed anywhere in the Atlantic all year. That is the latest the area has ever gone without one since satellites began tracking storms reliably in 1966.

The previous record was September 11, shared by Gustav in 2002 and Humberto in 2013. Five tropical storms have formed this season. None of them reached hurricane strength. Edouard came closest on September 1. It was still gaining strength when it moved ashore near the Texas-Louisiana line, roughly 22 km/h (14 mph) short of hurricane force and coming ashore cut it off from the warm water it needed.

The reason is El Niño, and the mechanism is simpler than it sounds. El Niño speeds up the winds high in the atmosphere blowing from the west, while near the surface the trade winds keep coming from the east. A storm needs its column stacked more or less straight up to organize and intensify. When the top gets pushed one way and the bottom the other, the whole thing pulls apart before it can get going.

Rodrigo Castillo, a researcher at the Centro de Investigaciones Geofísicas at the Universidad de Costa Rica, explained that with El Niño strengthening, above-average wind shear over the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic is what you would expect. NOAA’s updated outlook for the 2026 season anticipated exactly that across the main development region for August, September and October.

Phil Klotzbach, the hurricane researcher at Colorado State University, has described the shear in that region, the corridor running from Africa to the Caribbean where most Atlantic storms are born, as reaching record levels. Tropical Storm Dolly, the only system to form there all year, was torn apart within a day. Klotzbach has 2026 tracking as the least active Atlantic season since 1950.

A thick layer of dry Saharan dust drifting across the ocean over the past week has made development harder still. Daniel Poleo, a meteorologist at the Instituto Meteorológico Nacional, said this is the lowest tropical cyclone activity at this stage of a season since the satellite era began, and that no tropical cyclone formation is expected in the Atlantic, the Caribbean or the Gulf over the following seven days.

Here is the part that matters if you are actually in the country. A quiet Atlantic does not make your week drier, and it does not make it safer. Costa Rica sits south of the corridor where Atlantic hurricanes normally travel. The rain that floods roads here, swells rivers and cancels plans come from something else: tropical waves crossing the country every few days, and the band of convergence that parks over the region through the wet season. Neither of those shows up in a hurricane count.

You saw both this weekend as tropical wave No. 43 crossed Saturday and today the IMN reported the atmosphere remained unstable, with storms forming off Limón and afternoon downpours across the Pacific. On Saturday around midday, a sudden surge of water swept six people downstream at a Guanacaste waterfall, killing an adult woman. No named storm was anywhere near Costa Rica.

That is the practical lesson and that is to treat the hurricane forecast as background, not as a safety check. What puts people in danger here is a river rising fast while the sky directly overhead still looks clear, water that fell an hour earlier and kilometers upstream, arriving all at once. The record also does not mean the season is finished.

More than half the activity in a typical Atlantic year normally arrives after September 10, and conditions can shift. One further record is within reach: reanalysis of the 1941 season places its first hurricane on September 21, and AccuWeather meteorologist Jesse Ferrell noted that if nothing forms before that date, 2026 surpasses that mark as well.

The Pacific side of the region is telling a very different story. The eastern Pacific has produced 13 named storms, five hurricanes and three major hurricanes, close to a full normal season’s output while the Atlantic sits empty. El Niño is expected to reach its peak strength in November or December, which suggests the conditions suppressing Atlantic development will hold through what remains of the season.

World.title: Alexander Zverev and Elena Rybakina Win 2026 US Open Titles
World.content:
Alexander Zverev and Elena Rybakina left New York as US Open champions after a championship weekend that produced two first-time winners at Flushing Meadows and ended an American bid to reclaim the men’s title. Zverev defeated American Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 on Sunday at Arthur Ashe Stadium, completing a remarkable Grand Slam season for the German.

One day earlier, Rybakina beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 to win the women’s championship. For Zverev, the victory carried extra significance. Six years after surrendering a two-set lead to Dominic Thiem in the 2020 US Open final, the 29-year-old returned to the same stage and finished the job.

The title is Zverev’s second Grand Slam championship, following his breakthrough victory at the French Open in June. Germany had gone three decades without a men’s Grand Slam singles champion before Zverev won Roland Garros, and he has now collected two major titles in three months.

Zverev took control of Sunday’s final immediately, breaking Shelton in the opening game and using his powerful serve and backhand to keep the American from settling into the match. He won the second-set tiebreak 7-2 to move within one set of the championship. Shelton refused to disappear. The 23-year-old broke late in the third set and won it 7-5, briefly bringing a strongly pro-American crowd back into the match.

But Zverev responded quickly. A 25-shot rally helped him secure an early break in the fourth set, and he never surrendered the advantage. The ending was unusual: Zverev initially failed to realize that Shelton’s final return had gone long and walked toward the baseline before the umpire’s announcement confirmed he had finally won the US Open.

(Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP)

The defeat ended a memorable tournament for Shelton, who reached his first Grand Slam final after one of the biggest victories of his career. In the quarterfinals, Shelton eliminated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set match that finished at 3:33 a.m., the latest finish in US Open history. He then came from a set down to defeat fellow American Frances Tiafoe in the semifinals.

Shelton became the first Black American man to reach the US Open singles final since Arthur Ashe in 1972. His loss, however, means the wait continues for an American men’s Grand Slam singles champion. Andy Roddick remains the last to do it, winning the US Open in 2003.

The women’s final produced its own change at the top. Rybakina ended Sabalenka’s attempt to win a third consecutive US Open title, using the controlled power that has made their rivalry one of the strongest matchups in women’s tennis. The Kazakhstan player broke for a 3-2 lead in the opening set and held on to take it 6-4. Sabalenka responded in the second, finding her range late to force a deciding set.

Rybakina then pulled away. She built a 5-2 advantage in the third and closed out the championship, ending Sabalenka’s 20-match winning streak at the US Open. It was Rybakina’s third Grand Slam title and her first in New York. She won Wimbledon in 2022 and defeated Sabalenka in the Australian Open final earlier this year.

With victories in Melbourne and New York, Rybakina became only the third woman this century to win both hard-court Grand Slam tournaments in the same season. She also reached the world No. 1 ranking. The championship was particularly notable because an ankle injury had raised doubts about Rybakina’s fitness before the tournament began. Instead, she made it through seven matches and defeated Coco Gauff in the semifinals before overcoming Sabalenka in the final.

Both singles champions earned a record $5.5 million winner’s prize. The results closed a US Open in which the established order was repeatedly challenged. Shelton knocked out defending champion Alcaraz, Rybakina ended Sabalenka’s two-year reign in New York, and Zverev finally erased the memory of his painful 2020 defeat.

This time, both championship trophies went to players who had never before lifted one at Flushing Meadows.

World.title: Cartago Merchants Demand Legal Basis for Independence Day Business Closures
World.content:
The Cámara de Comercio, Industria, Turismo y Servicios de Cartago has demanded that the Municipalidad de Cartago withdraw an order requiring businesses around the Palacio Municipal to close tomorrow and that it publish the documents justifying the decision.

The order reached business owners on Friday as a circular from the municipality’s Departamento de Patentes, three days before the celebrations marking the 205th anniversary of Costa Rican independence. Establishments that fail to comply face administrative sanctions and, in the municipality’s terms, possible closure of the premises.

Mario Redondo, mayor of Cartago, confirmed that the closure originated as a request from the Ministerio de Seguridad Pública. He said he had asked the ministry to reconsider it.

According to Redondo, authorities grounded the order in security incidents recorded in the area over recent months, the large crowds expected for the civic act, and threats directed at President Laura Fernández. The president and other Executive Branch officials are scheduled to attend the reception of the Independence Torch outside the municipal building from 6 p.m. Monday.

The terms of the order have shifted since it was issued. As first communicated, the closure covered establishments within a 200-metre (660-foot) radius of the Palacio Municipal, an area merchants describe as 18 city blocks, with general commerce ceasing at midday and food service at 3 p.m. The restriction was to hold until the civic act concluded, at around 9 p.m.

Following the criticism, Redondo announced an agreement reached with Seguridad Pública under which businesses may operate normally until 4 p.m. and the affected perimeter is reduced to 100 metres (330 feet). He presented the change as a balance between security requirements and local economic activity, saying the objective was to provide security without disrupting merchants’ operations.

The chamber says the additional four hours do not resolve its objection. In a statement issued on September 12, the organisation demanded that the order be left without effect and that the municipality disclose the record behind it.

If the closure was requested or ordered by the Ministerio de Seguridad Pública or another institution, the chamber wants the corresponding oficio made public. If it was a municipal decision, it is asking for the administrative act, the technical report, the legal criterion, the security studies, and the identity of the authority that drew the perimeter.

The organisation has focused in particular on the role of the Departamento de Patentes. It argues that the department’s powers to inspect and shut down businesses over licensing matters do not necessarily extend to ordering a preventive, blanket closure of establishments that hold valid patentes and have committed no infractions. It has asked the municipality to identify the specific rule granting that authority.

The chamber also argues that security is not built by closing businesses or emptying streets, and that premises left open, with staff, customers, lighting and foot traffic, help keep public space active. It called it contradictory to summon people into the city centre while simultaneously ordering the closure of the businesses that would serve them.

According to the records the organization holds, no general measure of this kind has been applied in Cartago during Independence celebrations in previous years, and it has asked the municipality to explain what new and exceptional circumstances justify it now. Merchants say it is the first commercial closure of its type in the city for these dates.

The chamber further objected to the timing and to inconsistencies in the terms, pointing to the 200-meter perimeter cited initially against the 100 meters announced later by the mayor, and to a lack of clarity over when businesses may reopen. Notification arriving on Friday, it said, left little room to reorganize staff, deliveries, suppliers and operations.

The Ministerio de Seguridad Pública has said that it reinforced its preventive and operational protocols because of disputes between organised crime structures and the execution of Operación Cacería.

Two Cartago legislators from Partido Liberación Nacional, Salvador Padilla and Janice Sandí, questioned the decision before the agreement was announced. Padilla said that a visit by the national government, with security grounds cited for closing businesses, was not sufficient reason to act on one of the most important dates in the province’s calendar. Sandí said a presidential visit could never become an excuse to paralyse a city, and that security is guaranteed without sacrificing people’s work.

A separate municipal instruction attached to the original perimeter set waste collection for businesses within 200 meters between 11:30 a.m. and midday on Monday, after which garbage may not be left on public roads. The chamber said it will accompany affected merchants in defense of their rights, their employment and local economic activity.

World.title: Woman’s Body Found After River Surge Near Rincón de la Vieja
World.content:
The body of a woman swept away by a sudden river surge in Guanacaste was recovered Sunday morning, ending a search that had run since midday Saturday at the Oropéndola waterfall in Curubandé de Liberia.

The Costa Rican Red Cross said rescuers located the body of an adult woman in a pool below the falls after search teams resumed work at first light. She was the only person still unaccounted for after the surge caught a group of visitors the previous day.

The emergency reached the Red Cross at 12:16 p.m. on Saturday, September 12. Responders confirmed that six people were swept into the current and that five of them got themselves out of the water and reached safety. Early reports had suggested as many as 10 people were involved, a figure the Red Cross later revised down to six.

Crews worked for several hours Saturday before suspending the search around 7 p.m. Adrián Gómez, regional operations coordinator for the Red Cross, said that day’s effort had produced no results. Teams returned early Sunday and found the woman a short time later.

Once the body was located, rescuers assembled specialized swiftwater and vertical rope equipment to lift it from the pool and move it to firm ground. Agents from the Judicial Investigation Agency were expected to take charge of the scene for the formal recovery and for identification procedures. Authorities had not released the woman’s name or nationality.

The Guanacaste Conservation Area clarified that the surge happened outside the boundaries of Rincón de la Vieja National Park, in the Guachipelín sector of Curubandé. The 25-meter (82-foot) Oropéndola waterfall sits on private land belonging to Hacienda Guachipelín, directly beside the national park entrance, and visitors reach it through the hotel rather than through the park itself. The distinction matters for anyone planning a trip, because the two sites have separate access points, separate admission and separate operators.

What swept the group away is what Costa Ricans call a cabeza de agua, a sudden rise in the level and force of a river or stream. It happens when heavy rain falls upstream and pushes a wall of water downstream, often reaching people who are standing in bright sunshine several kilometers below. Water level and current strength can change within seconds, which makes waterfalls, swimming holes and river crossings some of the most dangerous places to be during the rainy season.

The incident comes during a stretch of unsettled weather, with tropical waves and high atmospheric moisture producing heavy rainfall across much of the country. The area around Rincón de la Vieja has also drawn attention recently because of volcanic activity at the summit.

There is no indication that Saturday’s surge was linked to the volcano. Authorities have previously warned communities near Rincón de la Vieja about lahars, which are fast-moving flows of water, mud, rock and volcanic material that travel down river channels after eruptions or heavy rain. That hazard is separate from an ordinary rainy-season surge unless authorities establish a connection, and none has been established here.

If you are visiting rivers or waterfalls in the coming weeks, the most useful habit is to watch the water rather than the sky above you. Rain falling on a mountain you cannot see is what puts the surge in motion. Get out immediately if the water starts rising, turns muddy or begins carrying branches and debris, and do not wait to see whether it settles.

Costa Rica records deaths from cabezas de agua nearly every rainy season, most often at popular swimming spots where the water looks calm and the danger is entirely upstream.

BREAKING: Two bodies found inside home in Santa Elena, Cayo

World.title: Prime Minister congratulates student-athletes at CODICADER
World.content:
Prime Minister congratulates student-athletes at CODICADER

By Zoila Palma: On September 13, 2026, Prime Minister John Briceno joined the nation in congratulating all student-athletes representing Belize at CODICADER in Honduras.

“We especially want to recognize Jordi Escalante forhis receiving the silver award in his sport – Javelin – at Codicader. He is a member of our OW Central BYM and a camp volunteer for our constituency summer programme,” the Prime Minister said.

Belizeans join the PM in congratulating Jordi and all medalists.

“We’re proud of all of you,” the PM said.

World.title: National Day of Prayer ceremonies hosted in Benque Viejo del Carmen
World.content:
National Day of Prayer ceremonies hosted in Benque Viejo del Carmen

By Zoila Palma: On Sunday, September 13, 2026, community members gathered at Our Lady of Mount Carmel church in Benque Viejo del Carmen for the National Day of Prayer, bringing together Belizeans in solemn devotion during the September celebrations.

The prayer service was hosted by the Benque Viejo House of Culture and held at the historic Our Lady of Mount Carmel Church.

The service was attended by prominent government officials, including Governor-General Dame Froyla Tzalam and Prime Minister John Briceño, who joined the congregation in collective prayer for the nation.

The National Day of Prayer provided an opportunity for people from across the community to pause from the Independence celebrations and reflect on Belize’s future, while reaffirming the importance of faith, unity and peace as the country marks another year of independence.

World.title: Smart Belize named Overall Business Excellence Award Winner at Expo 2026
World.content:
Smart Belize named Overall Business Excellence Award Winner at Expo 2026

By Zoila Palma: Smart Belize has been named the Overall Business Excellence Award Winner at the BCCI Expo 2026, marking the company’s second time receiving the prestigious recognition.

The Expo was held over the weekend in Belize City.

Smart said the achievement reflects the passion, dedication and commitment of its entire team as it continues working to raise the standard of service in Belize.

Smart Belize congratulated its employees and expressed pride in the recognition, reaffirming its commitment to serving customers and bringing people together across the country.

World.title: Belmopan night market to kick off Independence celebrations on September 20
World.content:
Belmopan night market to kick off Independence celebrations on September 20

By Zoila Palma: The Belmopan City Council is inviting residents and visitors to the September edition of its Night Market, which will be held on September 20 at the Governor General’s Field as part of celebrations marking Belize’s 45th anniversary of Independence.

The event will run from 5:00 p.m. until midnight and will feature an evening of music, food, shopping, entertainment and Belizean culture.

The council is encouraging families and members of the community to come out and enjoy the festivities while supporting local vendors and businesses.

The Night Market will also lead into the official Independence celebrations, including the Flag Raising Ceremony and Gun Salute.

The council says the event will provide an opportunity for residents and visitors to celebrate Belize’s national identity while enjoying locally produced food, crafts, products and entertainment.

Vendor registration available here.

World.title: New National Symbols coin series to enter circulation September 18
World.content:
New National Symbols coin series to enter circulation September 18

By Zoila Palma: The Central Bank of Belize has announced that the new National Symbols Coin Series will officially enter circulation on Friday, September 18, 2026, celebrating Belize’s rich natural heritage and national identity.

The coins were minted by the Royal Canadian Mint and complement the National Heroes banknote series introduced in 2025.

The new coins will be distributed through normal cash transactions at commercial banks, credit unions, and businesses across the country.

The Central Bank said the new series will circulate alongside the existing coins featuring the late Queen Elizabeth II, which will remain valid legal tender.

Members of the public are therefore not required to deposit or exchange their existing coins, as both series will circulate concurrently.

As part of the launch, the Central Bank will also issue a limited-edition painted 50-cent collector’s coin featuring the Mahogany Tree.

The commemorative coin will not enter general circulation and will instead be sold exclusively as a numismatic item beginning September 18. It will be available either individually or as part of a complete National Symbols Coin Series collector’s set.

World.title: Opposition Leader calls bus contractors’ situation “unacceptable”
World.content:
Opposition Leader calls bus contractors’ situation “unacceptable”

By Zoila Palma: Bus contractors in Southern and Western Belize have gone on strike this morning following delays in payments by the Ministry of Finance.

Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton says that this situation is unacceptable.

“School bus drivers contracted by the Ministry of Education have reportedly gone unpaid for three weeks.

These drivers provide an essential public service by transporting our children safely to and from school. Yet they have been forced to strike simply to receive money they have already earned,” Panton said.

Panton said that the bus contractors have families to support, fuel to purchase, vehicles to maintain and bills to pay.

“Neither Bus Operators or students and their families should be placed in such an unnecessary predicament. The math is not mathing.

Belize @45, let us get it together,” Panton stated.

21st Belize City bash to bring Independence Day celebrations to Digi Park

Entertainment will include performances by Supa G, T.R. Shine, Newani Martinez & Friends, TLC Band, Wappag G, Echo Middleton, Kenny Gladden & The New Creation Band, C. Wills, Terry Di Brukdown Gyal, Nello Player and The Red Band. The event will also feature food and refreshments, games and live entertainment throughout the afternoon.

The Belize City Bash forms part of the country’s Belize @ 45 Independence celebrations and is being supported by the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH).

With free admission and a full lineup of entertainment, the 21st Belize City Bash is expected to provide residents with an opportunity to come together and celebrate Belizean music, culture and community.

World.title: Sigh of relief
World.content:
ARCHIBALD... had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines, remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses

THE Chinese business community is breathing a sigh of relief after the fatal shooting of Dewar Archibald — who police sources say was part of an organised criminal network operating across several parishes — during a reported gun battle with cops in St Andrew early Sunday morning.

According to a highly placed source, Archibald, otherwise called Max, was a thorn in the side of several Chinese individuals as he preyed on their businesses and homes.

“He and his cronies were on their way to hit the home of a Chinese man in the Corporate Area when they were intercepted by the police Sunday,” the Jamaica Observer source said.

Police reported that Archibald, whom they described as a “high-risk criminal target linked to two murders and a series of major robberies and break-ins across Jamaica”, was among three people fatally shot during an operation by members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Specialised Operations Branch along Red Hills Road about 1:45 am.

According to the police, the Specialised Operations team was on patrol in the Red Hills area when information was received that a group of armed men travelling in two vehicles — a red Honda HR-V and a white Toyota Probox — was allegedly preparing to carry out criminal activity in the St Andrew North Police Division.

A preliminary police report said the cops attempted to intercept the vehicles but the drivers did not stop. The Probox eluded the police.

“Police subsequently intercepted the Honda HR-V in the vicinity of Knightsdale Drive. Occupants of the vehicle reportedly opened fire at members of the police team, who then discharged their service weapons,” the police said.

Three people, one of them a woman, were subsequently found with gunshot wounds. The two men were identified as Archibald, 44 years old of Mountain View, Lincoln, Manchester; and Damian Byfield, 39 years old of Fraser’s Content, St Catherine. Police sources said the woman, who was unidentified at press time, was of brown complexion, approximately 5 feet seven inches tall, with braided hair, and was clad in a black dress.

Two firearms along with ammunition were recovered, the police said.

Police said Archibald was a member of the Speculation Gang and had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines (ATMs), remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses.

According to police sources, the woman is critical to the criminals’ modus operandi as “they use her as a lookout or a distraction”.

Archibald has also been implicated in two murders committed within the past nine months — Chevardo Messam at Galleon Beach in Crawford district, St Elizabeth, on December 21, 2025; and Kemar Brown, otherwise called Mars, in Bristol, Alexandria, St Ann, on January 9, 2026.

A woman was shot and injured during the second incident.

Police also reported that Archibald had been linked to a shooting during an attempted theft of an ATM in Drax Hall, St Ann, in April.

Additionally, investigations had further implicated him in a series of robberies and break-ins in Linstead, St Catherine, in February and June; Kingston in April; and Croft’s Hill, Clarendon, in May.

World.title: Ministry targets book list abuse
World.content:
There have been mounting complaints annually about lengthy and expensive book lists.

JAMAICA’S education authorities are moving to rein in controversial school book lists after a special review found that some lists issued to parents do not match those approved by the ministry.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon says an electronic system is being developed to prevent such discrepancies, amid mounting complaints annually about lengthy and expensive book lists.

The issue has dominated the news over the past few weeks, resulting in the ministry indicating that it would review schools’ textbook lists to ensure that only essential, high-quality texts are required, given agitation about escalating back-to-school costs.

Following on those indications Morris-Dixon, in a recent interview with the Jamaica Observer, said the measures contemplated will address not just the expense but also waste.

“Sometimes the books are not used. I have seen it too where you look through the book at the end of the year and you are like ‘Wait a minute, I spent all this money on this book and it was not being used’, and so I sympathise with parents,” Morris-Dixon said.

“I spoke to the ministry team, they put together a team to relook the book lists — because book lists have to be approved by the ministry — and we have seen some instances where the book list that the parent gets is not necessarily looking like what we have approved, so we are actually putting in place an electronic system that the schools will have to upload their book lists to. We will go through it and we will make the necessary adjustments,” Morris-Dixon disclosed.

She said the ministry is also mulling whether it could further absorb more of the costs which parents now bear.

“We are also looking at whether or not it is possible — we already spend about a billion dollars on books — to add some more books in terms of the [government-provided book] programme to support students, but obviously that’s another financial expense,” the education minister told the Observer.

Noting that the ministry, at present, provides textbooks for core subjects for grades four to six students in primary schools, Morris-Dixon said the intent is to explore whether or not it “could add to the number of books that are already provided”.

“So we are exploring it, and we are looking at all different methods that we can use, but what we are thinking is: The approval process for the book list, it’s important that we tighten that up and change the process so that we in the ministry review it prior to it getting to the parents, and we can look to see whether it’s an unnecessary burden, and also looking at the extent to which we could probably give more books to the schools,” she explained.

Recently, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness addressed the issue, saying that he had received complaints from parents.

“Many parents have said, ‘Prime Minister, why am I being asked to purchase so many books that my child who is in the grade below… when I purchased them last year… didn’t use at all? When I see the book list for this year, it’s a totally different book list and I can’t use those books again,’ ” Holness said during the Office of the Prime Minister and Office of the Cabinet Primary Exit Profile Awards Ceremony.

“Then there are other parents who said to me, ‘Prime Minister, I have family who live overseas and nobody’s using books. All the books are on tablets and computers; they’re all e-books.’ So there has to be a consideration of a more economical approach without losing the value of books,” he added.

The prime minister emphasised that books remain an essential part of the learning process and stressed that the Government is not seeking to diminish their importance in education.

The education minister, in the meantime, told the Observer that the use of the electronic books sourced by the Government in 2022 has also been contemplated in the search for solutions, but said this measure would need more thought.

“We do have e-books but what we found, we did some work and the e-books are not being used, and so we know probably the students don’t have the devices to use it, and we also want to limit device use in schools, so it’s a delicate balance. We know the e-books could solve one problem, but you may create other problems, so we are obviously trying to be very balanced in the way we move forward,” Morris-Dixon told the Observer.

World.title: Gun law credited with decrease in murders, says Chuck
World.content:
CHUCK... the mandatory minimum sentence is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck signalled Sunday that while legislators are set to review the mandatory minimum sentences under the 2022 Firearms Act, a repeal is unlikely as security forces and other key stakeholders are crediting the law for the sharp decline in murders and shootings in recent times.

According to the Serious Crimes Report published by the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), up to July this year Jamaica recorded 275 murders, 23 per cent less than the 335 reported during the same period in 2025. It said overall, Category One crimes declined by 15 per cent, with 322 fewer major crimes reported than last year.

According to the JCF, the reduction in murders formed part of a broader decline in serious crimes, with shootings falling by 27 per cent, robberies by 25 per cent, while both rapes and break-ins declined by 10 per cent over the comparative period.

In January this year the country reported its lowest monthly murder figure since national crime data collection began in 2001 with 33 homicides, representing a 55 per cent reduction when compared to January 2025 which recorded 74 murders.

“I am aware that in the Firearms Act you have mandatory [minimum] sentences. It is a matter that is being examined but I can tell you that ,from where I sit, the security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings. It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck told members of the judiciary attending the 2026 Assize Church Service at East Queen Street Baptist Church.

The Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

However, members of the bench have telegraphed that the provision is problematic. In 2024, Appeal Court President Marva McDonald Bishop revealed that there would be a full court sitting soon to hammer out issues with aspects of the new Act which, she said, have been proving a pain to lawyers and judges alike.

“The Firearms Act is giving problems to prosecutors, it’s giving problems to trial judges, and surely at the Court of Appeal. We might have seen other cases where the court might seem inconsistent in its approach, and we have taken the decision that we have to take steps to put the court in a position where we can declare conclusively what the position of the court is on a particular area of the law so to avoid confusion,” the Appeal Court president said in presiding over a special sitting of the court marking the opening of the Michaelmas Term — her first since being appointed in July that year.

Additionally, concerns have been that the mandatory minimum provisions in the Act counteract the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act (plea bargaining legislation), with many accused opting to head to trial rather than plead guilty at their first appearance.

On Sunday, the justice minister’s remarks about the provision came in the course of his comments about the deluge of criminal matters awaiting trial before the island’s circuit courts.

Said Chuck: “Probably one of the main criticisms of our justice system is not access to justice but the inordinate and unnecessary delays in the delivery of justice. In truth, there are non-contentious matters which really should be dealt with in weeks rather than months and years, and it’s a major complaint which we need to address. And then… there are trials that must be heard and must be determined… we cannot try all cases, it’s just impossible, and so over the next many months I will be, literally, not only advocating but on a missionary zeal to urge persons in dispute to really settle matters by mediation.

World.title: Double impact for I-Octane
World.content:
I-Octane.

Recording artiste I-Octane is maintaining his musical momentum with two female-focused singles, Balance Pan Yuh Hand and Whine Up, which are gaining traction in different markets.

Balance Pan Yuh Hand, produced by long-time collaborator Seanizzle, was released on July 22, while Whine Up, produced by Costa Rican producer DJ Kendo, followed on August 12.

The entertainer, whose given name is Byiome Muir, told the Jamaica Observer his relationship with Seanizzle dates back to the early stages of his career, making their latest collaboration a natural one.

“Seanizzle is my brother and a producer I’ve always worked with from day one. He called me and said he had a song that he wanted us to work on, so he linked me in New York City with the idea and we completed it together right on the spot,” he shared.

Balance Pan Yuh Hand has been reportedly generating encouraging feedback from listeners and is also making an impact in the dancehall space. However, he believes there is still considerable room for the song to grow.

“I love the feedback it’s getting from the fans, plus the impact in the dance. We still have a far way to go in terms of promotion, but we’re doing it stage by stage with this song because it’s a big song, so we have to stay consistent,” he said.

Meanwhile, Whine Up has been expanding I-Octane’s reach in the Latin American market, reaching #1 on the Shazam Costa Rica charts. According to the artiste, the song has also been gaining traction in other Spanish-speaking countries.

The track has also found an audience online, particularly on TikTok, where numerous women have been using the sound in their videos.

“This achievement is great because it’s a great look when you have a big song in different markets worldwide. Plus, it extends the I-Octane brand globally,” he said.

Consistency has remained a major part of I-Octane’s strategy as the way audiences consume music continues to evolve.

“We live in a time now where people’s attention spans are very short, so most of the time you have to stay consistent within the algorithms,” he explained.

He described the year so far as a positive one but said his focus remains on finishing even stronger.

“It’s a very good start, but we’re working so we can end it great. We have a lot of new projects coming soon, plus more shows,” he said.

Among those projects are a new album, additional singles, and a new branding line, which the artiste said he is particularly excited about.

On the performance front, I-Octane’s team is currently putting together a winter European tour, which he described as his next major move.

World.title: ‘Dellmar’ remembered as loyal, considerate bespoke photojournalist
World.content:
The urn with the cremains of Headley “Dellmar” Samuels rests at the front of East Queen Street Baptist Church, downtown Kingston, beside a large photo of the celebrated photojournalist on the job, accompanied by his signature floppy hat, during the thanksgiving service for his life last Saturday.

Family, friends, and colleagues paid glowing tributes to celebrated photojournalist Hadley “Dellmar” Samuels on Saturday, bringing to a close a colourful and exceptional career that saw him travel the world capturing events through his lens for posterity.

Among the tributes paid to Samuels, who passed on August 1, 2026 at age 84, was former Prime Minister PJ Patterson who described his late friend as a bespoke photojournalist.

“His active engagement in the Jamaica Progressive League ignited the spark of nationalist fervour which impelled him to return home and contribute through the mastery of the camera to the wave of our cultural evolution and the quest to fashion an egalitarian society,” Patterson said in his tribute, read by veteran journalist and broadcaster Fae Ellington.

He said that “the photo archives of the People’s National Party contain a catalogue of historic photographs taken by Comrade Dellmar as his inimitable contribution to the political mission in which he passionately believed”.

Noting that Samuels covered 175 Test cricket matches and seven International Cricket Council World Cups, Patterson said that Samuels’ logic was impeccable that “if the West Indies had the greatest cricket team in the world, we should also have the finest photographers to record this triumphant dominance wherever they performed”.

Patterson also remembered Samuels as outspoken, gregarious, convivial, loyal, generous and considerate to his special circle of genuine friends.

Additionally, Patterson noted that Samuels’ contribution to journalism was recognised in 2000 by the Government, which vested him with the Order of Distinction.

Also paying tribute were journalist Audley Boyd, a current news editor at

The Gleaner, who recalled his many interactions on the job with Samuels, and Antigua and Barbuda journalist Colin James. Samuels’ three children — Carey, Karyn, and Kornell — shared memories of their dad, while former Government minister and veteran PNP member Colin Campbell, who was friends with Samuels for more than 50 years, delivered the eulogy. The thanksgiving service for Samuels’ life was held at East Queen Street Baptist Church, downtown Kingston.

World.title: PNP staging public session of 88th annual conference in Westmoreland
World.content:
People’s National Party (PNP) President Mark Golding gathers with recipients of the party’s education grants at PNP headquartes on Old Hope Road in St Andrew last Saturday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

THE People’s National Party (PNP) will stage its 88th annual conference over three days this weekend, in two venues, at opposite ends of the island — a move that appears to be a first in the party’s history.

“Instead of the normal public session at the [National] Arena we decided to go to western Jamaica where the effects of [Hurricane] Melissa are still very serious and just to show solidarity with the people there, PNP President Mark Golding told the Jamaica Observer on Saturday after an education grants award ceremony at the party’s Old Hope Road headquarters in St Andrew.

“We’ll be doing a few social things during the course of the day and then we’ll culminate with a rally in Sav-la-Mar. So it’s really just to show solidarity and gratitude to the people of Westmoreland in their struggle to get through this terrible hurricane and the aftermath,” added Golding, who said the move to stage the public session outside the Corporate Area is a first, as far as he is aware.

General Secretary Dayton Campbell explained that the private session of the conference will be held over two days at Jamaica Conference Centre, downtown Kingston, after which the public session is scheduled for Independence Park, Westmoreland, on Sunday.

“We start at 12:00 am on Friday, September 18 and 10:00 am on Saturday, September 19 at the conference centre… then on Sunday we’re going to the west, because we felt it important to go to the western end of the island — based on the damage to the west by Melissa — to show solidarity with the persons. And so we’ll be having a church service in the morning at Negril New Testament Church of God, after that we’re going into the communities,” Campbell said.

He shared that the party has two projects — one at Race Course and the other in Mount Airy where it will be handing over a house to a beneficiary.

“After that we go to the public session of the conference for a rally at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar that will start at about 3:00 pm. We’ll also be doing some other things during the presentation to highlight what is going on in western Jamaica, you know the damage from the hurricane,” Campbell said.

Category 5 Melissa unleashed extensive damage to Westmoreland and other parishes in western Jamaica on October 28 last year.

Both Campbell and Golding pointed out that many hurricane victims have not yet recovered from the effects of the storm.

Noting that in his Westmoreland Eastern constituency 40 per cent of the houses are still covered by tarpaulin, while schools, health centres and roads remain badly damaged, Campbell said “There is a lot of work still to be done.”

He said the party will use the public session to highlight the difficulties being faced by Jamaicans in the west, as well as the challenges being faced by the education and health sectors, in addition to the “significant pressure” on the economy.

Both men said they expect “a good crowd” at the public session, with Campbell pointing out that the conference is coming a year after the September 3, 2025 General Election which the party lost to the Jamaica Labour Party.

“I think we will have a good conference. It’s year one after the elections and so, normally, in year one you’re sort of building back the vibe, but we expect that we’ll have a good conference,” the general secretary said.

— Garfield Robinson

World.title: ULTIMATE BLOW
World.content:
Jamaica’s Ackelia Smith competes in the women’s triple jump final during the World Athletics Ultimate Championship at Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre, in Budapest, Hungary, on Sunday. (Photo: AFP)

JAMAICANS had a lukewarm finish to the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary, failing to get into the top three in six finals they contested on Sunday.

Sanique Walker, in the women’s 400m hurdles, and Ashanti Moore, in the women’s 200m, both achieved personal best times.

Walker, the Commonwealth Games champion, was fifth in 53.61 seconds, making her the eighth-best Jamaican ever.

Rushell Clayton was eighth in 54.32 as American Jasmine Jones was a surprise winner, running a season’s best 52.45 to beat Slovakia’s Emma Zapletalova (52.68). World leader Anna Cockrell of the United States placed third in 53.09 seconds.

Moore, who had run a lifetime best 22.30 to finish second in her semi-final, clocked 22.34 (-0.6m/s) for fifth in the final. Her time in the semis shaved one-hundredth off her previous best 22.31 set at that venue a year ago.

American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden completed the sprint double, running a mouth-watering, world-leading, personal best 21.47 to win in a sweep for the United States.

Gabrielle Thomas was second with 21.77 and Kayla White (21.93) was third.

Lavanya Williams, a finalist in the women’s 100m on Saturday, finished sixth in her women’s 200m semis in 23.10 (0.7m/s) and failed to advance.

Bryan Levell was sixth in the men’s 200m final in 20.07 (-0.1m/s), after he ran 20.08 (-0.2m/s) for third in his semi-final. National champion Christopher Taylor was sixth with 20.36 and failed to reach the final.

Kenneth Bednarek of the USA completed the men’s sprint double, winning the 200m final with a world-leading and personal best 19.52. He defeated Botswana’s Letsile Tebogo, who ran a season’s best 19.76. Courtney Lindsey of the USA clocked a season’s best 19.79 to finish third.

Romaine Beckford was fifth in the men’s high jump with 2.26m as Italy’s Gianmarco Tamberi won with a world-leading 2.37m. Tamberi topped American JuVaughn Harrison (2.30m) and Mexico’s Erick Portillo (2.26m).

Ackelia Smith was fifth in the women’s triple jump with 14.23m (0.3m/s), as Senegal’s Saly Sarr got her biggest win with 15.06m (0.3m/s) to hold off the Cuban pair of Davisleydi Velazco, who registered 14.04m (0.5m/s), and Leyanis Perez Hernandez, who leapt 14.90m (0.7m/s).

Jamaica’s mixed 4x400m relay team of Zandrion Barnes, Shana Kay Anderson, Assinie Wilson and Stacey Ann Williams finished sixth with a time of 3:11.46.

The United States completed the sweep of relay titles when they won with 3:08.32, ahead of Great Britain (3:09.40) and the Netherlands (3:09.57).

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Renee Watkis on security, leadership, and service
World.content:
SECURITY is often understood through cameras, access controls, guards and gates. For Renee Watkis, however, the deeper lessons are about people behaviour, leadership, judgement and service.

Those ideas sit at the centre of Beyond the Gate: Human Behaviour, Leadership, and the Future of Security, which examines how behaviour, leadership, and organisational culture influence whether security systems work as intended.

Her second book, Standing at the Gate: A Woman’s Journey in Security, Leadership, and Service turns the focus inward, exploring the experiences that shaped the woman behind the professional journey.

Together, the books tell two connected stories: one about the profession and the other about the woman growing within it.

Growing up, Watkis’s family could not afford to send her to university, and at 16 she entered the workforce. She remained with her first employer for 19 years, learning through experience long before university became an option.

Years later, after the death of her stepfather, her younger brother was preparing to enter university. Watkis decided to help finance his education. Not long afterwards, her son was also preparing to enter university.

She was supporting two young men through higher education while still without a degree herself. Then came a realisation: “If I can send two people to university, then I can send myself too.”

At 42, Watkis began pursuing her first degree. By then, she had already spent approximately 11 years in the security industry. University gave her the theory behind much of what she had learned through practice.

Throughout the four-year programme, she took what she was learning back into the workplace, strengthening processes, reconsidering procedures and sharing knowledge with her team.

For Watkis, education was never simply something to place on a résumé. It was something to use.

Her career took another turn when she was offered an operations management position with a security company.

The role broadened her understanding of the industry and allowed her to strengthen policies, processes and organisational structure.

She also became involved in training security officers preparing for their Private Security Regulation Authority licensing requirements and quickly recognised that people learned differently.

A definition in a manual could be correct, but that did not always mean the person hearing it understood how to apply it. “You have to meet people where they are”, became part of her approach.

Realistic scenarios and practical examples often helped people understand security concepts more clearly. That lesson became part of

Beyond the Gate: a policy may be well written and a procedure technically sound, but if the people expected to follow them do not understand them, weaknesses can remain.

After completing her first degree, Watkis moved directly into a Master’s degree in Human Resource Management.

Her studies strengthened the connection between behaviour, communication, leadership and change management.

She had learned that introducing a new process did not automatically mean people would accept or follow it. They needed to understand why change was necessary and how it related to their work.

These experiences helped shape Beyond the Gate. The book explores why human behaviour deserves greater attention in security, how leadership influences security culture and why technology alone cannot solve every problem.

A camera may record an incident, but someone must recognise its significance. Technology can assist with detection and analysis, but people still have to decide what happens next.

While Beyond the Gate reflects what Watkis learned about the profession, Standing at the Gate reflects what those years taught her about herself.

The book reaches back to life before the qualifications and titles, beginning work at 16, supporting family, entering university at 42, and helping others develop. It speaks to women whose lives have not followed the timetable they once imagined.

Watkis believes representation matters, but contribution matters too. Women should have opportunities not only to enter professional spaces, but to develop expertise, influence decisions and lead.

The objective is not simply to be noticed because you are the only woman in the room. It is to be respected because of what you bring to it.

For Watkis, the gate is more than a title connecting two books. In security, a gate represents access, protection and control. In life, it can represent a decision.

Beyond the Gate asks security professionals to look beyond equipment and consider the people, behaviour and leadership behind the system. Standing at the Gate asks women to consider the experiences, barriers and possibilities that shape their own journeys.

One examines the profession. The other examines the woman becoming more fully herself within it. You do not have to know everything before you begin. You do not have to hold the highest title before your contribution has value. And you do not have to wait until every doubt disappears before moving forward.

Sometimes the most important decision is simply to walk through the gate.

World.title: Unions move to back political cash reforms after Farage’s £72M haul
World.content:
Farage — who is already facing investigations into his right-wing populist party’s funding sources — announced over the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, had donated £36 million each.

Each of those donations was record-breaking in British politics, which currently sets no upper limit on what U.K.-based individuals can hand to a party. Together, they have reignited a row about Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s position on funding. He has so far held off on imposing a cap on domestic donations to political parties.

Nigel Farage addresses delegates during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 5, 2026. | Anthony Devlin/Getty Images

Both officials quoted above said the Trades Union Congress — which is this week hosting its annual conference in Brighton — is expected to issue a joint statement setting out an updated position on political financing, which could be released as soon as Tuesday. But the talks are politically delicate and the unions have not yet reached agreement.

One of the two senior officials said unions are likely to back a cap that applies to wealthy U.K.-based individuals and to trade unions, but — crucially — would be calculated in different ways for these two types of donor.

That would mean that while wealthy individuals and unions would both be subject to donations caps, the rules would apply differently for each group.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told union members Monday: “We will defend our democracy and society from any foreign dictator or fascist oligarch who seeks to divide our country and buy our politics — but we will never undermine the rights of working people to organize collectively and democratically.”
