World.title: Nationalist chiefs sign pact to make Burnham ‘the last UK prime minister’
World.content:
But all three agreed that Trump’s sentiments reinforced their own sense that the time was right for independence referendums in Scotland and Ireland, and a push for greater devolution of powers from Westminster to the Welsh Assembly.

“Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people,” the three parties said in a joint statement.

They met in Cardiff to acknowledge the fact that all three devolved administrations in the U.K. are now led by nationalists for the first time following May’s electoral trouncing by Plaid Cymru of Burnham’s Labour, long the party of government in Wales.

Sweeney, Scotland’s leader since 2024, is seeking a second independence referendum following the failed 2014 vote. Burnham, who holds the levers on permitting such a ballot, has ruled it out.

“I think he [Burnham] will be the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, because the people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum, will take that choice,” Sweeney said, citing recent polling trends.

World.title: Record number of Brits have unfavorable view of Nigel Farage
World.content:
Newly-installed Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham continues to be viewed favorably by 46% of Brits — the same figure as last month — though the proportion who view him unfavorably has risen six points to 39% in the last month.

YouGov sampled 2,099 adults in Great Britain between Sept. 9 and 10.

The findings come at a difficult time for Reform UK.

Farage’s party — which stormed ahead in local elections earlier this year in a grim night for the governing Labour Party — is now under investigation by parliamentary authorities over an undeclared £5 million gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Two of Farage’s aides — Dan Jukes and policy chief James Orr — stood down earlier this month pending an investigation into an undercover donations sting.

But the outfit has just been buoyed by a record £72m cash injection from two financiers. It has promised to use the funding — which has triggered a row over political financing in the U.K. — to beef up its policy and campaigning operations.

World.title: Eurocrat salaries, staff numbers face cuts in next long-term budget
World.content:
The Irish presidency, which is steering the budget talks, wrote that “reductions could be made, with many [countries] questioning the justification of the proposed increase in staff levels” at a time when they’re making domestic personnel cuts.

The Commission proposed hiring an extra 2,500 officials over the next seven years, fueling discontent from nine countries led by Austria.

In the Commission's proposal, which was drawn up in July 2025, administrative costs will be worth €118 billion from 2028 to 2034, which is around 6% of the overall budget.

However, Ireland is facing strong resistance to cutting other areas of the budget. The Irish presidency wrote in the document that most capitals oppose reductions in agricultural spending and regional payouts, which it described as countries' “most important priority.”

Ireland hinted that the overall budget might face cuts as countries opposed increasing their national contributions and challenged new EU-wide taxes to finance the budget.

“These factors point to a need to reflect on our level of ambition for expenditure increases,” the Irish wrote.

During a meeting on Wednesday, Dublin will sound out the EU’s 27 ambassadors on which budget items they want to downsize.

"Are there any other elements in terms of changes to the Negotiating Box [the working document that guides budget talks] that would be helpful in formulating your views regarding the expenditure level?" it wrote.

World.title: Europe hesitates as Russian attacks escalate
World.content:
“We have all the response options ... some of them will be public, some are not,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told POLITICO on Monday. “I'm saying to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and everyone who wants to listen, if you continue doing this, we will not only have our response options .... we will also continue the support in Ukraine.”

Marie Agnes Strack-Zimmermann in the European Parliament an institution of the European Union in Brussels on 16th of July 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

The calls for action underscore growing anxiety around the increasing frequency of sabotage, cyberattacks and other actions that fall below the threshold of conventional war across Europe. Over the weekend, a Russian drone hit a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border shortly after top Western security officials passed through, while Bulgarian authorities launched investigations into two explosions at weapons storage sites in the country.

“The pressure is mounting in view of the events on the Polish border,” said a fourth, senior NATO diplomat. But for now, the strategy is “keep calm and carry on and … continue our support for Ukraine.”

The most serious incidents pinned on Russia — including an attempted attack on Leipzig airport last month — have so far been thwarted. But European officials are increasingly grappling with the prospect they may soon face a successful attack with casualties, and the backlash that brings.

“The secret services have done a good job” so far, said one senior European defense official. But “we have been lucky — there have been no big incidents … if we do not act, then things might get much worse.”

“We are too shy — definitely,” said German lawmaker Marie Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s defense committee. “Vladimir Putin never stops, he’s always coming closer … we have to show we’re willing to fight back.”

World.title: Von der Leyen to skip Carney speech in EU Parliament
World.content:
Mark Carney speaks with Ursula von der Leyen prior to a working session at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Thibault Camus via AFP/Getty Images

Canadian prime minister will watch Commission president’s speech but she won’t be there when he speaks.

STRASBOURG — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will not attend Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s address to the European Parliament on Thursday.

Carney will speak to lawmakers on Thursday at 11.30 a.m. as he seeks closer ties with the EU amid deteriorating relations with Washington. He is expected to set out his wishlist for Brussels ahead of a Canada-EU summit in October. The address comes a day after he will attend von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union speech.

During Carney's speech, the Commission will instead be represented by Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič — one of von der Leyen’s most trusted lieutenants — the executive's chief spokesperson Paula Pinho confirmed.

The Commission president won't be in Strasbourg on Thursday as she has to return to Brussels due to "prior commitments," Pinho said. One of those prior commitments is a press conference on the child online safety initiative.

The Commission is represented by one of its 27 members during all Parliament keynote addresses and debates. On Thursdays during Strasbourg sessions, the majority of the College usually returns to Brussels, with a small group of commissioners remaining in France for the final plenary debates.

World.title: European firms unprepared for China shock as EU tries to cut reliance on Beijing
World.content:
“It makes it just very clear that companies know that they can feel the pain of geopolitics disrupting their everyday business operations,” study co-author Jacob Gunter of the Mercator Institute for China Studies told POLITICO. “They have such a clear example, but haven’t done much with that.”

“To not see more action on that is quite worrying to me,” he added.

The same vulnerability runs through companies’ exposure to China. Just 24% of those questioned plan to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers, while roughly one-third are considering strategic stockpiles of critical raw materials. And yet China’s export controls, including on rare earths, have already exposed those dependencies.

“It is, to me, quite shocking that we’re not seeing more stockpiling or diversifying of suppliers for the things that are already identifiable as part of ongoing trade and technology conflicts,” Gunter said.

Nearly one-third of respondents reported negative effects from U.S.-China trade and tech restrictions; among firms operating in China, the share was around half.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to meet later this month, with suspended Chinese export controls likely back on the agenda.

World.title: Germany to order soldiers to Lithuania amid volunteer shortage
World.content:
The German military is having to rely on compulsory assignments to fill positions in a German brigade stationed in Lithuania.

 

The move is said to be necessary because of difficulties filling planned voluntary positions, which has left a shortage of specialists.

According to information obtained by Bild, the first soldiers could be ordered to serve there from the end of September, with up to 1,000 Bundeswehr personnel potentially in line to be affected.

By the end of 2027, the 45th Panzer Brigade is expected to grow to around 4,800 German soldiers and be stationed permanently in Lithuania, on NATO's eastern flank.

The brigade’s main base will be Rūdninkai, around 30 kilometres from Belarus.

Bild was the first to report on the planned compulsory assignments, and the Ministry of Defence has since confirmed the measures. Almost 80% of the posts are currently filled by volunteers.

“According to current forecasts and in view of the continued influx of volunteer applications, the proportion of compulsory appointments is expected to be in the mid three-figure range,” it said in a press release.

“Maintaining the Bundeswehr’s operational readiness is the top priority and is the decisive criterion in all measures," it continued. "In all decisions to be taken, the personal interests of service personnel will be taken into account as far as possible."

Germany's Ministry of Defence plans to brief the representatives on the Defence Committee on Monday about next steps.

For those affected, a compulsory posting means additional notice. They also have the opportunity to challenge the decision in court.

Lieutenant Colonel Kaufmann, Corporal Rogi and Staff Sergeant Kevin in Sennelager, 13.05.2026 Franziska Müller / Euronews

Euronews accompanied two soldiers from Panzer Battalion 203 during the "Freedom Shield" exercise last June. Their battalion is to be redeployed to NATO’s eastern flank by the end of 2027.

In an interview with Euronews, the battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Oliver Kaufmann, said that Panzer Battalion 203 has "actually a very high proportion of volunteers."

"I can speak for my battalion, and the majority of soldiers are willing to go to Lithuania voluntarily, and that is exactly what I want: I want soldiers by my side who are convinced of the mission and who, as part of the Panzer Battalion 203 team, take on this responsible task," said Kaufmann.

Among the forces already stationed in Lithuania, the staffing rate is about 92%. These forces include, in particular, the multinational battlegroup that has been stationed there since 2017.

Panzer Battalion 203 and Panzergrenadier Battalion 122 are not due to be moved to Lithuania until 2027. According to the investigation, around 40% of the personnel required for those units are still missing.

World.title: Succession row kicks off in Uganda after amateur goalkeeper says no to throne
World.content:
A non-league goalkeeper from south-east London turned down the throne of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom last week, setting off a succession battle that erupted into open confrontation prior to King Oyo's funeral on Saturday.

 

George Desmond Kamurasi, 36, captain and goalkeeper of SE Dons — a club competing at the ninth tier of English football in Crayford — had been selected by a 21-member royal succession committee as the preferred candidate to succeed his cousin, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV.

Fifteen of the 18 members who took part in the vote backed him. He said no, citing other responsibilities, committee member Fr Charles Oyo told ESPN.

In Tooro tradition, refusing the throne after being formally selected is considered a disgrace. Kamurasi has not commented publicly on his decision.

Reports in Ugandan media said he was reluctant to leave London — he has family relations in England and was due to play an FA Vase qualifying round the same weekend as Oyo's funeral.

The committee then turned to Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at Uganda's public broadcaster UBC, who was announced as successor earlier this week. That decision has since been rejected by the late king's immediate family.

'Let us grieve'

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ascended to the throne at the age of three and reigned over the Tooro Kingdom for 31 years, died recently at the age of 34 while receiving cancer treatment in the US.

Guinness World Records had recognised him as the world's youngest reigning monarch.

Several thousand people gathered on Saturday in Uganda to pay final respects to the monarch, with President Yoweri Museveni urging unity.

"Once the matter of the new king of the Batoro is settled, we will be happy to work with him, just as we did with His Highness Oyo," he said in a statement read out during Saturday's ceremony at Saint John's Cathedral in the city of Fort Portal in western Uganda.

"I call on the Batoro to use peaceful and lawful means to resolve this issue and to favour unity over division."

The dispute fractured the royal family, with the late king's mother charging that she and other members of the royal family had been put under effective house arrest.

The king's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, accused "evil vultures" of conspiring against her and Queen Mother Best Kemigisa.

She produced a will, which she said the king drafted in 2022, designating "a biological son" as heir without naming him.

This came as a surprise to many in the Tooro elite, who had never heard of the son and did not include his name in the succession vote.

The Babiito royal committee, which traditionally presides over and determines matters relating to royal lineages, succession, and family affairs, defended its choice on Saturday.

"We have done everything in observance of the culture and traditions of Tooro. We must all preserve peace and serenity," the head of the committee, Omusuuga Charles Karumasi, said.

The Queen Mother said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death.

“I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said in a statement. “Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo.”

'One of those deaths one never heals from'

Uganda is a republic but officially recognises four traditional kingdoms, banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country. They were restored in 1993.

The kingdoms serve mostly as cultural institutions with no formal political power, but the monarchs can command considerable support and loyalty.

King Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest monarch, a much-beloved figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela.

The late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi befriended the Tooro royals as if they were part of his extended family. He made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for years before his death in October 2011.

“This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, said in a eulogy posted on social platform X.

“Not Oyo, not that likeable young man, not at 34. That’s what makes it so painful.”

"He had a gift to make people laugh," his sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said at the burial ceremony.

"He always knew how to brighten my day," she said.

World.title: Butter late than never: Paris gets its first boutique entirely dedicated to butter
World.content:
“If you have extraordinary bread and extraordinary butter, it's hard to beat bread and butter.”

 

How right French chef and author Jacques Pépin was when he said those enduring words. And a boutique in Paris is further proving him right. About the butter part, at least.

Billed as the French capital’s first shop entirely dedicated to butter, Le Butter Shop opened its doors last month and offers 30 varieties of France’s favourite fat - from small family producers in Brittany, the Loire Valley and northern France, with varieties including flavoured kinds like shallot, pepper, seaweed, wild garlic and lemon with green pepper.

France eats around 8 kilograms of butter per person a year, according to the agriculture ministry, so it was about damn time.

Customers can taste by the spoonful before buying anything from a 10-gram pat to a kilogram block. And if the aforementioned varieties didn’t appeal, there are sweet ones too, including vanilla, raspberry, strawberry and chocolate.

“Most people don’t expect to like a raspberry butter or to like chocolate butter,” said owner Erwan Leo. “And when they try it, this is where they’re just like, ‘Oh wow, OK.'”

Owner of Le Butter Shop, Erwan Leo, in his shop devoted entirely to butter in Paris, France AP Photo

Leo, who also runs a wine-tasting business, said butter should be used like wine, to make a meal better. “The goal isn’t to get drunk,” he cautions, adding that tasting butter works like tasting wine.

“You have to grab your spoon, you put it on your palate, on your tongue, it has to melt a little bit, and then the flavours are going to start coming one by one.”

Leo adds that the secret to savoring fatty butter is to be like Parisians: Walk a lot, and practice moderation.

“We don’t go beyond four tartines a day,” he said.

“The Italians choose olive oil, we choose butter. We learn how to master it.”

Leo’s producers churn from selected cows and higher-fat milk; an extra 2 or 3 percentage points, he said, “really makes a huge difference.”

An employee gives information to a customer at Le Butter Shop, the first shop devoted entirely to butter in Paris, France AP Photo

The tiny shop has drawn crowds through social media and now has a staff of four.

“From day one, it’s been crazy,” Leo said. “Most people come in with wanting to try one or two butters, they end up trying 25 butters because they’re just so curious.”

Next up: a croissant-flavored butter, and perhaps violet.

“This is limitless,” Leo said.

If you’re not thinking “butter me up”, we don’t know how to help you.

Le Butter Shop is located at 5 Rue Bouchut in Paris, a stone’s throw away from the Champ de Mars and the Eiffel Tower.

World.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia agree to halt strikes on energy targets
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to pause strikes on energy targets as he sought to shift the blame for rising fuel prices from the Iran war to the war in Ukraine.

 

"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account.

"The World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran," he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has suggested that no deal has been officially confirmed but that Ukraine had "proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure."

"If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes," he added.

While both conflicts have produced significant global energy shocks, experts have pointed to the war in the Middle East as having caused considerably larger disruption to the global oil supply.

Oil prices have soared since the start of the conflict in late February, when the US and Israel carried out strikes on Iran.

Iranian forces effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz - one of the world's most crucial oil and gas transit chokepoints - in response to the attacks, sending energy markets into chaos.

The Strait, which usually carries around a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade, has remained a key sticking point in negotiations between Washington and Tehran, and attacks on vessels navigating the passage are ongoing.

Trump's announcement comes after he called on Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure during a trip to Ireland over the weekend.

Speaking to reporters, Trump said: "Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia."

"Let him go after targets, but not diesel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel," he continued.

Ukraine has ramped up its attacks on Russian energy facilities in recent months as part of Zelenskyy's "long-range sanctions," which aim to grind down the Russian economy and hamper the Kremlin's war machine.

For its part, Russia has launched repeated attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure since it launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022, as Moscow has sought to force Kyiv into submission - particularly over winter periods.

Gas prices are displayed in front of a gas station, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Carlsbad, Calif. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The spike in oil prices has brought rising fuel costs to Americans ahead of November's key midterm elections, which will determine the makeup of Congress for the final two years of Trump's term.

In a post on X on Monday, California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, hit out at US Energy Secretary Chris Wright over rising costs.

"Everyone knew Trump’s Iran war would disrupt the Strait of Hormuz and skyrocket costs," he wrote. "So why did Energy @SecretaryWright do nothing to protect us?"

"Americans are owed answers about what the Trump Admin knew and why they failed to shield us from these predictable consequences," he added.

World.title: French-Slovak veto deepens EU deadlock on Russia sanctions renewal
World.content:
The deadlock on the renewal of EU sanctions on Russia deepened on Monday after France and Slovakia, in a rare joint effort that has baffled Brussels, continued to demand the removal of Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov from the blacklist.

 

Faced with an expiration date that loomed dangerously close, ambassadors agreed, as a last resort, to extend the sanctions for just one week until 22 September to give themselves more time to find a solution that has so far proven stubbornly elusive.

"Consultations will continue, and further discussions are expected to be held in due course," a spokesperson for Ireland's EU Council presidency said.

"Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia's war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefitting from it. This is a priority for the Presidency."

Diplomats are still trying to figure out why France has suddenly joined Slovakia's yearslong campaign to spare Usmanov from the sanctions list, which covers almost 3,000 individuals and entities accused of propping up Russia's war on Ukraine.

France has only argued a "national security" reason, without any details.

According to an EU diplomat, the French delegation did not elaborate further on their position during the discussion on Monday.

Usmanov was added to the backlist in the early days of the full-scale invasion over his "close ties" with Russian President Vladimir Putin and his stakes in "key sectors" of the Russian economy, according to the EU Council.

Usmanov has denied this.

Slovakia has long called for Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, another high-profile oligarch, to be deleted from the sanctions list. Until now, other member states have been unwilling to grant the request, which they consider to be politically motivated.

Earlier this year, a media investigation published a two-page letter allegedly sent by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico asking for help to end what Erdoğan called "the unfair practice" involving Usmanov.

"Your support in removing him from the EU sanctions list and restoring his violated rights would be extremely valuable," Erdoğan wrote in the letter dated 2 March 2026.

The document mentioned Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan as countries that also backed Usmanov's removal.

"We have a separate issue related to national security, and we would like to respond positively to our international partners who are approaching us regarding Mr Usmanov," a French diplomat told Euronews.

It is unclear if the French position has anything to do with the behind-the-scenes lobbying. What is clear, however, is that it has added an unexpected dimension to the Slovak veto and made it considerably harder to find an agreement by unanimity.

Member states are trying to renew the individual sanctions by 12 months to align them with the economic sanctions, which EU leaders extended by one year in June.

Amid the stalled negotiations, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a rebuke.

"Usmanov and Fridman are exactly the kind of Russian business figures who need to find the courage to take concrete steps against the war," Zelenskyy said.

"This is exactly the kind of Russian economy that should not be given additional opportunities while the Ukrainian economy is suffering from Russian terror and Putin's refusal to stop the war."

World.title: Fuel price protests spread across Syria as parliament summons energy minister
World.content:
Protests against fuel price increases spread across Syria for a second consecutive day on Monday, with demonstrators blocking roads and oil tanker routes in several provinces and calling for the dismissal of Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir, as parliament summoned him to appear before a hearing on Thursday.

 

More than 50 members of Syria's People's Assembly signed a request on Sunday demanding the energy committee question al-Bashir over the price hikes and their impact on living conditions.

The assembly confirmed on Monday that the hearing had been set for Thursday at noon local time (11 am CEST).

Fuel prices rose by 25% to 40% after Syria's standing committee for the pricing of petroleum products issued a new temporary price list that took effect at midnight on Sunday.

The price of a litre of 95-octane petrol rose from 152 to 195 new Syrian pounds, 90-octane from 147 to 185 pounds, and diesel from 125 to 175 pounds — an increase of 40%. A household gas cylinder rose from 1,470 to 1,600 pounds.

100 Syrian pounds is about 1 eurocent, but the average net monthly salary in Syria varies widely by sector and can amount to just €50 to €60, according to publicly available figures.

The government of interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa has increased the minimum wage by 550% in March, as part of a broader recovery plan for the Middle Eastern country whose years-long civil war devastated most of its economy and resulted in the deaths of more than 580,000 people, with another 13.5 million displaced.

Protests were reported in Hasakah, Deir ez-Zor, Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Daraa. In Hasakah and Deir ez-Zor, demonstrators blocked roads used by crude oil tankers and cut the al-Suway'iya bridge crossing between Syria and Iraq near al-Bukamal.

In the city of al-Shahil, residents blocked the road leading to the al-Omar oilfield, preventing tankers from passing.

In Raqqa, truck and haulage drivers staged a sit-in outside a grain storage centre, with the road to the silos remaining blocked on Monday.

In Idlib province, protesters blocked the M5 motorway near Maaret al-Numan, while video circulating online showed a night-time demonstration in the city of Idlib with crowds demanding al-Bashir's removal.

Local sources reported that a young man in Hasakah province attempted to set himself on fire in protest at the price increases and worsening living conditions before bystanders intervened. Video of a separate incident showed another man threatening to burn his car. Euronews could not independently confirm these reports.

Al-Bashir said on Saturday the price rise was needed to bridge a gap between the cost of importing petroleum products and their domestic selling prices.

Syria produces approximately 102,000 barrels of oil per day against domestic demand of around 325,000 barrels, leaving it heavily dependent on imports, he said.

Major maintenance work at the Baniyas refinery in the southern Tartus governorate has further reduced domestic refining capacity, requiring additional imports of finished petroleum products.

The ministry said it would review prices as global market conditions change and the refinery returns to full capacity. Oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel in recent days amid disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz linked to the Iran war and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Ukraine’s prosecutor general suspended after leaving country amid corruption scandal
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suspended Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Monday, hours after it emerged that he had left the country after resigning amid a major corruption probe that had reached his own office.

 

Kravchenko crossed the border overnight, according to Ukrainian media citing law-enforcement sources.

Kravchenko also released a video saying he had signed a notice of suspicion against Semen Kryvonos, director of Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU).

Kravchenko alleged that Kryvonos had forged official documents to obtain an unlawful benefit.

Kryvonos rejected the allegation and told reporters later on Monday that he had neither seen the notice nor been formally served with one.

NABU and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) described Kravchenko’s actions as part of what they called a “systematic attack” on Ukraine’s independent anti-corruption institutions.

Zelenskyy intervened later on Monday, signing a decree suspending Kravchenko and asking parliament to dismiss him.

“This prosecutor general has only one path ahead: dismissal from office,” Zelenskyy said, urging lawmakers to act without delay.

The relevant parliamentary committee has backed the request, with lawmakers expected to vote on Kravchenko’s dismissal on Tuesday.

Kravchenko submitted his resignation on 7 September after NABU and SAPO uncovered an alleged criminal organisation involving officials in the Prosecutor General’s Office.

Investigators allege that members of the group regularly received bribes from fraudulent call centres in return for not interfering with their activities, and laundered millions in criminal proceeds.

Investigators searched Kravchenko’s office as part of the probe. NABU also released recordings referring to a person described as the “boss,” whose patronymic and former position as head of Ukraine's State Tax Service correspond to Kravchenko.

Kravchenko has not been charged or named as a suspect and denies any involvement.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Donald Trump dismisses concerns about dangers of AI
World.content:
The president called efforts to slow the development of artificial intelligence a "sick conspiracy," claiming they only serve China. Market leaders have warned of the dangers of the pace of the technology's development.

US President Donald Trump has called concerns that artificial intelligence is progressing too quickly a "SICK conspiracy."

Trump's statement followed calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman for more governmental regulation of AI. In recent months, several incidents have highlighted the risk that AI agents could go rogue.

What Trump said about AI 'guardrails'

"The only control or ‘guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump posted on his Truth Social account.

Anthropic is the developer of the popular AI model Claude Image: IMAGO/ZUMA Press

Trump added that his administration has already prevented Anthropic from "doing bad, or potentially bad" things with the technology.

The Pentagon previously tried to brand Anthropic's models a security risk and posed a temporary ban on one of its more advanced models.

"There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China," Trump wrote.

Anthropic boss Amodei warned against uncontrolled global AI development over the weekend saying that there's a risk of AI-led agents taking over the entire internet within six to 12 months. Microsoft published its own code of conduct to ensure human control over AI.

This led to AI stocks falling worldwide, including those of chip maker Nvidia (3.5%) and Elon Musk's SpaceX (1.7%).

World.title: Yemen's Houthis attack Saudis, seize crucial Red Sea islands
World.content:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have tightened their grip on a key shipping route, capturing two strategic Red Sea islands. The closure of another global transport route is the latest ripple effect of the US war with Iran.

Iranian-backed Houthi rebels on Monday announced they had captured Greater and Lesser Hanish Island in the southern Red Sea.

The move bolsters the group's ability to choke traffic in another key global maritime shipping route as the ripple-effect of the war in Iran grows.

The strategic advance comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces try to regain territory recently lost near the Bab el-Mandab Strait, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran has held closed since US President Donald Trump began bombing the Islamic Republic on February 28.

The closure of the Hormuz Strait, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the US began hostilities, has led to a global economic and energy emergency, driving up prices around the world and forcing petro-monarchy Saudi Arabia to move its oil exports through Bab el-Mandab.

But the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and last week seized strategic Mayun Island and the Red Sea port of Mokha, cutting off the alternative route.

The capture of Greater and Lesser Hanish now puts even more pressure on Saudi shipments and thus global oil supplies and prices.

Beyond putting the squeeze on Saudi Arabia — the Houthis' proxy enemy for backing the internationally recognized government in the Yemen's reignited civil war — it could also provide Iran added leverage in defending itself against the US.

Houthis seize Red Sea chokepoint: What can Saudi Arabia do? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthi offensive continues to escalate as Iran war expands

The Houthis pressed on with their offensive Monday, launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets.

A spokesman for the group said the strikes had caused "significant damage" and had come in response to "more than 300 [Saudi] airstrikes in [Yemen over] the past five days."

Despite being a longtime backer of the Houthis as part of its anti-Israel "axis of resistance," Tehran has denied any involvement in Yemen's revived civil war.

"Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs," said Tehran's Foreign Ministry on Monday, with spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters the Houthis are "entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests."

Yemen's civil war — dormant for four years until the conflict in Iran broke out — began in 2014, when Houthi rebels seized large parts of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, and forced the government to flee to Aden in the south.

In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition aiding the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.

Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Concerning situation for US and its Saudi, Gulf State allies

On Monday, Admiral Brad Cooper of US Central Command (CENTCOM) was in Jeddah to discuss "the latest developments in the region" with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

US news site Axios reports that Cooper has been in the kingdom since Thursday, dealing with urgent coordination meetings as the situation in the Red Sea escalates.

US media outlets reported last week that President Trump had rejected a request by the crown prince for the US to directly intervene.

Despite turning down the request to unleash US firepower, Trump reportedly agreed to provide intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.

Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran blames Saudi Arabia for stalling Hormuz talks

Iran on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of delaying talks aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Baghaei called a meeting set to take place in Oman, a "real opportunity" to restore security in the region and added that an agreement between Iran and Oman on opening the passage had been finalized and would be announced later.

Saudi Arabia reportedly has concerns over the lasting implications of a deal for the Strait of Hormuz and how it might negatively impact Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.

Tehran says Riyadh is using Yemen as a "pretext" to delay talks on how the Strait will be governed now that the status quo has been upended by the US.

Currently, the only secure routes allowing Saudi Arabia to deliver its oil to Asian markets are via the Suez Canal or around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope.

On Monday, China's Foreign Ministry called attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure "unacceptable," saying Beijing is "deeply concerned" about further escalation.
