World.title: Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks
World.content:
New trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US could begin in October, according to Kyiv and Moscow. Few expect a breakthrough, but Ukraine is seeking a partial de-escalation to help it get through the winter.

Ukraine and Russia have signaled their readiness to resume trilateral talks under US mediation.

"We're preparing. For October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president's office.

Similar signals came from Moscow: "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner aimed to revive trilateral talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, visiting Moscow and Kyiv in the first week of September.

The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.

Territory remains a difficult subject

Vladimir Putin still demands more territory than Russia currently controls, Kushner confirmed on September 12, speaking online at the YES security conference in Kyiv.

"President Putin [has] laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that," the US envoy said.

The Ukrainian government has indicated it is willing to freeze the fighting along the current frontline in exchange for security guarantees. Such a step could be supported by 60% of Ukrainians, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted in summer 2026. A similar majority of respondents rejected giving up territory that Russia hasn't been able to conquer. 33% said Ukraine should give up territory that Putin demands.

Russia's air superiority is a problem for Ukraine

Few expect a breakthrough anytime soon.

"For there to be a negotiated end to the war, there has to be parity. Right now, there's a stalemate on the front lines and not much is changing there, but in the air war, unfortunately, Russia currently has a significant advantage," Volodymyr Fesenko, a Kyiv-based political scientist, told DW.

Ukraine is running low on interceptors for Russian ballistic missiles. Russia has also stepped up attacks with new jet-powered drones, which fly faster than older gasoline-powered models and are harder to intercept.

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russian airstrikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine's economy, including warehouses, energy facilities, gas stations and railway infrastructure.

The Kremlin has accused Ukraine of opening a "Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and fuel and energy facilities with deep strikes since the summer. Ukraine says the attacks are intended to force Russia to the negotiating table.

Ukraine is worrying about the winter

Ukraine's supporters say Kyiv's strategy is working.

"The escalation ... is not a problem. It's a sign of success," said Jonathan Powell, the United Kingdom's National Security Adviser, speaking at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on September 11. "Of course [Putin] doesn't go straight to negotiations, he tries to escalate in the ways that he can."

The West must "keep its foot on the gas" to make Putin negotiate in earnest, Powell said.

Such optimism contrasts with concerns in Ukraine about the upcoming winter. In 2025, Russian attacks on energy infrastructure caused extended blackouts and left people without heating in freezing temperatures.

"We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country," said Ukraine's Economy Minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko.

Zelenskyy calls for partial de-escalation

Russia rejected the idea of a ceasefire during the upcoming talks. Ukraine is now calling for a de-escalation of attacks on energy infrastructure and the unblocking of grain exports via the Black Sea instead.

"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So, energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told DW in an interview aired on September 12.

Zelenskyy backs Putin meeting at Miami G20: 'Results matter' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Political scientist Fesenko says an agreement on grain exports could prove the easier task: "In the Black Sea, both Ukraine and Russia are facing major problems. Grain exports have been blocked; ports have been shut down and therefore both sides have a stake in the matter."

An energy truce, however, remains elusive, as Ukraine's vulnerability in the winter gives Putin leverage he would not give up easily, Fesenko said.

At the same time, the US is increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy facilities.

"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Donald Trump said on Sunday, September 13. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world."

Kremlin rejected Zelenskyy-Putin meeting

The Kremlin has already rejected another of Zelenskyy's proposals: a meeting between the Ukrainian and Russian leaders in December on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Miami.

"Putin doesn't want to negotiate with Zelenskyy. It's been obvious since last year that he wants to reach an agreement with Trump," said Fesenko. "If Trump insists, Putin may agree to a meeting between the three leaders. But he has no intention of negotiating with Zelenskyy."

If negotiations start in October as expected, negotiating teams rather than the leaders themselves will conduct them. But Ukraine insists that only the presidents can decide the territorial issue.

"The territorial question remains a pressing one... Complex issues such as this are only resolved at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said during the US envoys' visit to Kyiv.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Women's Basketball World Cup: Can Germany harness a boom?
World.content:
Germany thrilled fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup. But even if this sparked a boom in the women's game, the infrastructure simply isn't ready for it.

The world's best players showcased their sport at the Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin, which wrapped up on September 13.

Germany, led by Leonie Fiebich and Nyara, improved with every game throughout the preliminary and intermediate round of the 10-day tournament. In the quarterfinals, Germany beat European champions Belgium, delivering what was arguably their best-ever performance.

The final weekend though, revealed the team still isn't quite ready to compete with the world's elite over a full 40 minutes. Germany lost to France in the semifinals before losing to Spain in the match for third place. Despite their disappointment, the Germans still saw the tournament as a huge success.

"We simply aren't good enough yet," said Fiebich after the Spain match.

"We played the tournament with a lot of euphoria and beat the European champions, Belgium. But it's hard to keep overperforming. Still, we will get better."

The World Cup marked a climax of the positive development seen in German women's basketball in recent years. In 2024, the team qualified for the Olympic Games for the first time, where the women also won a surprising gold in the 3x3 basketball. At the 2025 EuroBasket, Germany's women finished fifth. The next women's EuroBasket is next year and if Germany qualify, they should be medal contenders.

"I think it's important to harness the pain the players are feeling right now," Germany head coach Olaf Lange said.

"Because in our day-to-day work over the coming months and years, we need to improve individually. That requires a lot of motivation, and this pain acts as fuel for improvement."

The support from Germany fans could hardly have been greater. A total of around 230,000 tickets were sold for the World Cup and although visiting fans were present, the crowds were made up primarily of Germans.

Only three play for German clubs

While the national team is just a few steps away from establishing itself among the world's elite, Germany's top women's basketball league (DBBL) lags well behind the international competition.

Most players from the World Cup squad play abroad. Fiebich, Nyara Sabally and her sister Satou, who missed the tournament due to injury, as well as Luisa Geiselsöder and Frieda Bühner, play in the WNBA. Team captain Marie Gülich is moving to a club in Australia after the World Cup, having previously played in Taiwan. Emily Bessoir, Lina Sontag, and Alexis Peterson-Smalls play in Spain. Clara Bielefeld currently plays US college basketball.

Frieda Bühner and the other Germany players enjoyed the attention of the Berlin fans Image: Tonhäuser/BEAUTIFUL SPORTS/picture alliance

Only three Germany players; Alexandra Wilke, Emma Eichmeyer, and Britta Daub, play for DBBL clubs, although both Eichmeyer and Daub have previously played abroad.

In Germany, they simply can't earn a living from playing basketball. Wilke, for example, works as a teacher at a secondary school.

DBBL level 'semi-professional'

Lange, who was a coach in the league from 1995 to 2002, describes it as "semi-professional," and says it has gone downhill since he left.

"Back then, the top clubs had better structures than they do today—and we are in 2026. That says it all. Things are really going backwards," he lamented during his post-tournament press conference.

Olaf Lange's day job is as an assistant coach of the WNBA's Toronto Tempo Image: Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press/ZUMA/picture alliance

"I have to ensure that our top players go abroad. As long as nothing changes in the league, it will be difficult to sustain this success."

Professionalization efforts

Changes are needed to ensure the national team's continued success. Ireti Amojo took over as DBBL president in March. The former Germany player is a TV pundit and podcaster and has also worked in management of the women's program of top men's club ALBA Berlin. She has introduced several measures aimed to professionalize conditions at DBBL clubs.

"We aim to hire full-time youth development coaches. We also want to increase arena capacities," Amojo told daily newspaper TAZ prior to the World Cup.

"Currently, some venues hold a maximum of 600 spectators, and if interest grows – as it is now – we will need larger arenas."

DBBL President Ireti Amojo is seeking to professionalize the league Image: Alexander Trienitz/nordphoto/picture alliance

'Too late to capitalize on a World Cup boom'

However, the top division is not the whole story; even if the Women's Basketball World Cup were to trigger a surge of young girls taking up the game in Germany, most clubs would be ill-prepared to handle them. This is partly due to a shortage of coaches, but also because there is a lack of basketball facilities, making court time scarce.

"We should have started five years ago so that we could say now: 'We are capitalizing on the momentum of the World Cup and ensuring that all these kids who have become basketball fans can play the sport in clubs across Germany,'" Amojo told Magenta Sport after the World Cup final.

"We are too late. We lack the structures to harness this interest and provide all the children fascinated by basketball with the opportunity, under perfect training conditions, to develop into the next Leonie Fiebich or Nyara Sabally."

Still, Amojo thinks the World Cup may just prove to be a much-needed spark for future development.

"It was the kind of proof we all needed, because people are quick to dismiss it, claiming that no one in Germany is interested in women's basketball. Now we've seen that people in Germany are interested in women's basketball," she said.

"We already have a few levers we want to use to work on the structures. And this certainly shouldn't be the end of things."

This article was originally written in German.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: IPO 'for the people' is out of reach for many in Nigeria
World.content:
Dangote seeks $1.6 billion from investors to finance a $14.3 billion expansion and thus double the oil refinery's capacity. The offer could give millions of Nigerians a stake in the company. But who can truly afford it?

The industrialist Aliko Dangote is turning to Nigerians to help finance the next growth phase of his oil refinery: The richest man in Africa announced that he is seeking to attract about $1.6 billion (€1.4 billion) by going public.

This initial public offering of Dangote Industries is intended to help support a $14.3 billion expansion, which would more than double the refinery's production capacity. In absolute numbers, it would increase capacity from 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 1.4 million bpd.

It would also include new petrochemical and refining units designed to reduce Nigeria's reliance on imports of some petrochemical products while also allowing the plant to produce different grades of diesel.

This plan would make the refinery one of the largest single-site refining complexes in the world.

Dangote's ambitious plans also include the launch of a processing plant in Kenya to extend his reach from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, which is planned to be launched in partnership with governments in eastern Africa.

He might be the richest man in Africa, but it appears that Dangote is banking on public support to expand his operations Image: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto/picture alliance

African success story

Since it began operations in 2024, the Dangote Petroleum Refinery has started to reshape Nigeria's fuel market, and has become one of the few businesses in the world to benefit from the ongoing supply disruptions caused by the war in Iran.

The refinery has become an important supplier of petrol and other fuels domestically and abroad; in fact, it made Nigeria a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time after reaching its full capacity in early 2026.

The refinery reported making an after-tax profit of $1.82 ​billion in the first half ​of 2026, following ⁠a $476 million loss for all of 2025.

Things appear to be on the up-and-up for Dangote — so, why is the company seeking public investment now?

Why go public?

Ayodele Oni, an energy analyst and partner with the Bloomfield Law Practice in Lagos, told DW that the public offering could be a "game changer," as it alters the role of who could stand to benefit from Dangote's expansion drive.

Oni said equity invested by potentially millions of Nigerian and international shareholders would shield the corporation from having to rely solely on expensive dollar debt "with permanent Naira capital, which matches a business now earning heavily in Naira."

This could also unlock additional long-term investment as any "listed company answers to ... its shareholders every quarter."



"That transparency is precisely what long-term lenders and international partners want to see before the next billion is committed," Oni said.

He said this would turn into a sustainable model for Dangote, as the approach would be designed to permanently "lower its cost of capital for every future phase."

Why Nigeria's largest refinery is importing US oil To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For 'the people'

Oni summarized the potential of the deal by referring to it as a restructuring of both who bears the risk — and who stands to share with the reward, with "the people" being the greatest beneficiaries of the IPO, at least to his mind.

Opening up the ownership of the refinery business to ordinary Nigerians does not automatically mean that many can afford it, however.

The pricing of the initial offering is indeed priced at an affordable 525 Naira (€0.34/$0.39) a piece for each of the 4.1 billion ordinary shares, and a minimum of just 10 shares.

At the signing ceremony in Lagos, Dangote said the company was trying to "make sure that the majority of … our drivers, our cook, our servants, our managers, everybody will have an opportunity to have a stake in the refinery."

Nigeria cost-of-living protests turn violent To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Deep inequality, deeper pockets

In a country where almost two-thirds of the population is struggling with extreme poverty, according to Nigeria's National Bureau of Statistics, that figure can translate into 10% of the minimum wage — for people who are fortunate enough to have a job.

Entry-level employees and workers who perform menial tasks at Dangote are fortunate enough to earn almost four times the minimum wage in Nigeria, according to media reports — though this still translates to only about $150 a month in a country that has been witnessing steep inflation, especially in petrol prices. For most, seeing any personal benefit by investing in Nigeria's oil remains a pipe dream.

Charles Asiegbu, a policy and economic analyst who has worked as a consultant for various Nigerian organizations, told DW that Dangote's description of the offer as "for the people" could still qualify as a "psychological masterstroke" for those who can afford to invest.

Asiegbu said broader ownership could bring a large number of Nigerians into one consolidated platform, changing how they view the refinery.

"With millions as shareholders, it would shift from a private enterprise to a national asset in the public consciousness," Asiegbu said.

Dangote's current success is linked to the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz — but what happens when the Middle East returns to normal? Image: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

IPO excites investors

Nigerians who can afford to invest in Dangote appear to quickly be adopting that mindset.

Olamilekan Oladehinde, a Nigerian retail investor, told DW that he is "excited" to partake in the launch and buy shares. He said Dangote was now much more than just a private enterprise: It has become a key national asset that addresses direct social problems in Nigeria — including fuel shortages.

"They're trying to expand, and that's something I am very proud and happy to identify with," Oladehinde said. "The fact that it's also owned by a Nigerian makes me more than happy, and that's why I will be buying a stake in the company," he said about the richest man in Africa.

Risks and opportunities

Oladehinde said he had no concerns about investing in Dangote — despite the fact that various market experts have cautioned investors to be mindful of potential risks, especially because refining is a cyclical business.

Oni said Dangote was riding a wave during the current situation across the Middle East; however, fortunes could change — especially when the tensions around the Strait of Hormuz eventually ease. A return to steep competition in oil prices from those Middle Eastern countries could then saturate markets.

Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dangote's strengths were a mitigating factor, Oni said: "The Middle East disruption showed that a refinery on [Nigeria's] Atlantic coast can supply Europe and the Americas faster than the Gulf can — and, at 700,000 bpd, the plant has already proven the model, so the expansion is about scale on an existing site, which is the cheapest capacity anyone can build."

Oladehinde said this was exactly the outlook that he will be betting on. "I believe the time has come for us," he said. "We can't lose this the momentum."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Germany news: Merz urges CDU discipline as pressure grows
World.content:
09/14/2026 September 14, 2026 Germany and Hungary seek reset after political change

Johann Wadephul said Hungary's new government had launched a number of important reforms in a short amount of time Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

Germany and Hungary have "an enormous amount of catching up to do" in their diplomatic relations, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said.

The politician is visiting Hungary as the first German foreign minister to do so in almost seven years.

"Hungary and Germany are opening a new chapter together," Wadephul said before his departure.

He said the political change in Hungary offered an opportunity to rebuild relations "at great speed" on a foundation of mutual trust and reliability.

Hungary's new government had launched important reforms within a short period, he said, adding that a return to the rule of law and implementation of EU requirements were good news both for Europe and for Hungarians.

The nationalist Fidesz party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban was voted out of office in April. Orban had faced years of criticism from the EU over concerns about democracy and the rule of law.

Since May, conservative Prime Minister Peter Magyar has led a new pro-European government.

Wadephul said predictable rules and the rule of law were important not only for public confidence but also for companies considering investment.

"If fair and reliable competitive conditions once again apply to companies from all EU member states, Hungary's economy will benefit considerably," he said.

German companies already account for around 250,000 jobs in Hungary, according to Wadephul.

A delegation of German business representatives is accompanying him to Budapest to discuss what further steps are needed.

World.title: Ukraine: AfD questions German aid, Berlin remains committed
World.content:
Emboldened by its win in Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany wants the government to change its Ukraine and Russia policies. Berlin is staying the course, but support is fading — especially in the east.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is standing firm on military aid for Ukraine in its war with Russia.

"We support Ukraine, and we will continue to support her, because she is also defending our freedom," Merz said on September 9 during a debate in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament.

He was reacting to Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, who had urged him to "finally start pushing for peace talks, like the US is doing."

US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would make far-reaching concessions to Russia at such negotiations; critics in Germany have described that as dictated peace.

On the topic of high energy prices in Germany, Weidel said, "We need cheap natural gas from Russia. That is what we will work toward."

She insinuated that the Ukrainian government was responsible for blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany in September 2022. "They continue to reward the suspected masterminds of the attack in Kyiv with billion-dollar payments at the expense of Germany." A Ukrainian sabotage team is suspected to be behind the attack.

Merz and Weidel clash in parliament after AfD election win To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How pro-Russia the AfD is, despite its invasion of Ukraine, was shown clearly by its lawmaker Jürgen Koegel during the debate. He spoke of "valued President Vladimir Putin," who posed no threat of war to NATO.

East-west division in Germany over Ukraine aid

The AfD's position on the war in Ukraine is nothing new. However, since winning the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 by a large margin, gaining almost 44% of the vote, it has expressed it even more vehemently.

Combining the votes for the AfD, the socialist Left Party and the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), about 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that either oppose support for Ukraine or are skeptical of it.

According to one survey, citizens' concerns about peace in Europe influenced their votes. Those surveyed named this topic as their second-most important, after "social security" and far ahead of "immigration" or "environment and climate."

In addition, there is the result of an ARD Deutschlandtrend survey conducted shortly before the election. It showed an east-west divide on the question of military support for Ukraine. About 39% of western Germans (from the area which was West Germany prior to reunification) thought military assistance went too far, while it was 54% for eastern Germans — that is, people who live in the area which used to be the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR/DDR).

"The course that the German federal government is taking on Ukraine does not have majority support in the east," Johannes Varwick, a political scientist at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, told DW.

"I would not describe that as 'pro-Russia'; it comes from the desire to focus more on diplomacy rather than delivering ever more weapons to fuel a war which Ukraine cannot win."

Fear in Germany of Russian threats

On September 2, the German government blamed Russia for a failed attack with an armed drone in early August at Leipzig airport, a key hub for military aid to Ukraine.

Putin spoke of a "grave error," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov even called the accusation the "start of a real war." The exchange of verbal blows marked a new level of escalation in an already tense relationship.

According to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, most Germans (56%) see themselves currently either strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia. But it also showed that eastern Germans and AfD voters feel less threatened by Russia. The election results in Saxony-Anhalt also seem to reflect this.

Political scientist Sven Leunig from the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in the state of Thuringia has his own take on the reaction of eastern Germans, especially after the Leipzig incident.

"It is less a fundamental rejection of support for Ukraine, more a reaction based on fear," Leunig said. "They want to keep out of the conflict, so as not to be drawn further into it. That of course strengthens parties like the AfD, BSW and Left, who accommodate these sentiments."

Support for Ukraine is also coming under pressure for another reason. According to the AfD and BSW, the money Ukraine receives could be better spent on Germany's stretched social services. AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio, for example, accused the German government of cutting social benefits and raising taxes "to keep on giving billions to foreign countries," to finance "foreign wars" such as in Ukraine.

Germany seeks extradition of Nord Stream 2 bombing suspect To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Support for Ukraine is crumbling, but slowly

Chancellor Merz still believes he has political and public backing for his course. During the Bundestag debate, this was his response to the AfD's suggestion of resuming energy deliveries from Russia and ending German support for Ukraine: "This path that you depict is not supported by the majority in the German parliament and it is also not supported by the majority of the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. We will defend our freedom, also in the future."

But support for Ukraine, as shown in ARD Deutschlandtrend surveys over the years, is becoming less favored by the public. The share of people who think military support goes too far is growing, slowly but steadily, and is now 42%.

Leunig thinks the German government is not yet under pressure to reconsider its Ukraine policy: it still has "clear support" for the current course. "Plus, the threat coming from Russia is also becoming widely recognized. Of course, if public support weakens in the long-term, the government will have to react to that."

Is Ukraine 'another Afghanistan'?

His colleague Johannes Varwick, on the other hand, advises a course correction now, but not so much due to the mood in Germany: "Yes, we should stand with Ukraine, but standing by Ukraine does not mean fueling a futile war of attrition without a viable political strategy. That runs Ukraine into the ground, even if it is portrayed as 'pro-Ukraine'."

Critics have drawn parallels to Western intervention in Afghanistan, which after 20 years, billions of dollars spent and about 3500 western soldiers killed, ended with the Taliban retaking power.

But Leunig sees it differently. "I think both cases are not identical. In Afghanistan there was a direct military intervention by Western countries with ground and air forces. In Ukraine, the support is supplying weapons. But the public fear that the war will drag on for a long time, in this there is of course a parallel to Afghanistan, and that in the end Ukraine might still have to give up."

So far, however, there is no sign that the German government is rethinking its position. During a recent (September 10) visit from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, "Germany will stay the course during this time," despite the domestic debate.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: The Crusades: How a medieval Holy War still shapes politics
World.content:
In 1095, the Catholic Church launched the Crusades: wars that left millions dead and whose legacy still shapes political and ideological conflicts.

"The present moment is much like the 11th century. ... We don't want to fight, but, like our fellow Christians a thousand years ago, we must." Those are the words of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in his 2020 book, "American Crusade: Our Fight to Stay Free."

Hegseth has repeatedly used the biblical language and symbolism of the Crusades to frame both domestic and foreign policy, from the current war in Iran to the "fight" against the "scourge of leftism."

Nearly 1,000 years have passed since the November day in 1095 when Pope Urban II delivered the fiery speech that would ignite centuries of warfare and change the course of history.

But Hegseth is only the latest in a long line of politicians and extremists to reference the Crusades — from the Ku Klux Klan to US President George W. Bush and Osama bin Laden.

Why do the Crusades remain such a powerful source of inspiration for contemporary leaders?

Princes and peasants promised eternal salvation

The history of the Crusades is long and complex. But it can be summarized as an extraordinary example of how religion can become a powerful tool for political goals, helping leaders to unite people, justify wars and mobilize support on a massive scale.

In the mid-11th century, Muslim Seljuk Turks conquered vast swaths of territory in the Middle East. In the early 1070s, they took control of Jerusalem, the most important holy site in Christendom. Rumors spread that pilgrims and Christians living in the region were being persecuted, and holy sites desecrated.

At the Council of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II used the words that would become the battle cry of the Crusaders: 'Deus vult!' ('God wills it!') Image: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/IMAGO

The papacy in Rome at the time was locked in a bitter power struggle with Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV over who really held the reins of power in Western Christendom. When Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos appealed to Pope Urban II for help to defend against the Seljuks in 1095, it presented the papacy with an opportunity to demonstrate its power by bypassing Henry to rally Europe's nobility for nothing less than Holy War.

Urban believed that a major Christian cause would strengthen his authority by uniting Western Europe toward a common external enemy.

War was the status quo in medieval Europe, which had been hit by a series of droughts, famines and plagues. Belief in the "end times" was widespread.

In this context, Urban's call for a Holy War to "liberate the Church of God" was persuasive: He demonized Muslims and promised Crusaders complete forgiveness for all past sins — as well as eternal salvation.

"If you think about what a Crusade is, it's asking people to go into the unknown, thousands of miles into an unknown land," said Jonathan Phillips, an expert on crusading history at Royal Holloway University in London. Their chances of dying were about 35% to 40%, he said. So they had "to be driven by something. Religion has to come at the top," he added.

Crusaders murdered thousands of Jews, whom they believed to be "enemies of Christ," during the Rhineland Massacres in 1096 Image: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/IMAGO

Urban's call to Holy War was taken up by men and women from every level of society, from "princes to peasants," Phillips said. A "tabby cat army," as he describes it, composed of peasants, low-ranking knights and nobles, and led by preachers, set out for the Holy Land in 1096.

This would later become known as the People's Crusade, which claimed its first victims in the Rhineland, where Jewish communities were massacred in one of medieval Europe's earliest outbreaks of antisemitism.

A better-organized army of European upper nobility was eventually assembled in Constantinople between November 1096 and April 1097.

Unprecedented bloodshed

The Holy Land, located between what is today Turkey, Syria and Egypt, was a polyglot society divided among Sunni Seljuk Turkish warlords and the Shi'a Fatimid Caliphate.

Godfrey of Bouillon, a Frankish knight, led the siege of Jerusalem in 1099 Image: Ken Welsh/UIG/IMAGO

It took some time for locals to understand that this wasn't just another raid, said Mohamad El-Merheb, an expert on the premodern Islamic Eastern Mediterranean at SOAS University of London: "It takes maybe at least a decade for some people to see it as an ideological project to convert and take the Holy Land."

"Some of the cities are well defended, some are not. But it is all in the context of very fragmented political power," El-Merheb said.

The Crusaders had what El-Merheb describes as a series of swift conquests in important cities such as Edessa and Antioch. Despite these early victories, life fighting a Holy War was grueling. The majority returned home, or died of disease, hunger or sheer exhaustion.

When they captured Jerusalem in 1099, Crusaders massacred thousands of Muslims and Jews because they couldn't tell them apart.

The Crusades remain a fixture in the popular imagination through symbols, stories and films such as 'The Crusades' (1935), a historical drama directed by Cecil B. DeMille Image: Everett Collection/IMAGO

Many historians consider the fall of the city of Acre to Mamluk warriors in 1291 to be the end of the Crusades in the Holy Land.

Later crusades were also called, however, including to block the advance of Ottoman Turks in Eastern Europe in 14th century. "Reconquista" Christian military campaigns aimed to retake the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule into the late 15th century.

The Crusades meet the culture wars

The legacy of the Crusades remains a powerful and polarizing cultural touchstone. In both the East and the West, the historical memory of these medieval holy wars is frequently repurposed to frame modern identities, politics and conflicts.

In 2001, US President George W. Bush caused uproar when he described the so-called "War on Terror" as a "crusade," a term already used by Osama bin Laden to frame US-led wars as religious wars intended to destroy Islam.

Saladin, depicted here receiving the English Bishop of Salisbury in 1192, successfully united fractured Muslim territories from Egypt to Mesopotamia Image: GRANGER Historical Picture Archive/IMAGO

In his propaganda to legitimize his global jihad, bin Laden also invoked the legacy of Saladin, a legendary Kurdish commander revered to this day as the hero who recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

"As of the 19th century, Saladin specifically becomes a symbol of fighting Western colonialism and imperialism," said El-Merheb. "Throughout the 20th century, a lot of Islamist groups also start referring to the Western powers as Crusaders, so this becomes part of political nationalism on the state level and also on a more popular level in films, for example. This is happening in the West now in the opposite way."

Crusader symbolism has long been used by far-right movements in the United States and Europe to promote narratives of civilizational conflict. The Latin phrase "deus vult," or "God wills it," has been used by figures including far-right mass murderer Anders Breivik and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, while France's far-right party Reconquête draws its name from the Reconquista campaigns. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth famously has "deus vult" tattooed on his arm and a Crusader cross on his chest.

In "American Crusade," Hegseth calls the Crusades a "defensive" and "existential" war to defend Europe against Islamic expansion Image: Sra Madelyn Keech/DoD/ZUMA/IMAGO

But El-Merheb believes that such references often reduce the Crusades to a simple clash between Christianity and Islam, "which really was never simply the case."

This framing, he said, ignores "how the Crusades were from the start very antisemitic projects, or violent projects against other Christian communities in Europe such as the Cathars in France, against Byzantium and the Islamic world and ignores the many cross-religious alliances between Muslims and Crusaders."

Along the way, he said, these politicians are also forgetting how violent and destructive these historical campaigns were.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: El maestro que hizo de Iberoamérica y Europa una casa común
World.content:
Tras ocho años al frente de la Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI), el educador español Mariano Jabonero deja este diciembre una institución convertida en una red de cooperación “muy americana”, con 23 países integrantes, más de 600 proyectos anuales, millones de beneficiarios y reconocida con el Premio Princesa de Asturias. Su última batalla es también una idea política: América Latina no es la periferia de Occidente, sino una de sus partes esenciales

Habla

En El Salvador, país que por entonces lloraba las 80.000 almas que se había tragado su guerra civil, se le acercó un día un campesino:

—Gracias por enseñarme a usar el ordenador.

Mariano Jabonero (San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Madrid, 1953), que llevaba desde 1984 asistiendo al Gobierno en tareas de cooperación con Latinoamérica, había recibido el encargo de capitanear un proyecto de cooperación con apoyo español en el plan de paz y reconstrucción institucional allí. Extrañado, miró al hombre que tenía a su frente y le respondió:

—Disculpe, pero no hemos entregado ordenadores.

—Este es mi portátil —indicó el campesino, sacando del bolsillo un bolígrafo— Ahora sé escribir y contar. Ya no volverán a engañarme.

La anécdota es de 1992, pero la moraleja sigue igual de vigente: “En los países con alta alfabetización, los ingresos per cápita se duplican. Es el primer paso para una sociedad libre”, explica Jabonero, sentado en la sala de reuniones de la sede de la Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI) de Madrid, ahora que se despide, tras ocho años, de su cargo de secretario general. Lo que sigue es el balance de lo logrado en ese período por parte de quien, antes que ninguna otra cosa, se reclama “maestro”. Resuena con gravedad el sustantivo cuando lo pronuncia, acarrea su voz el orgullo del verdadero sentimiento de pertenencia. Porque en cuarenta años no ha cambiado su convencimiento de que es en el aula, entre pupitres y pizarras, donde se construye ciudadanía; de que el diálogo y la democracia se aprenden.

Un repaso a la labor de ocho años Acción siempre sobre el terreno La Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI) es la mayor red multilateral de cooperación en la región, con 23 Estados miembro. En la imagen, una actividad de la Noche Iberoamericana de l@s Investigador@s, celebrada en Montevideo (Uruguay) en 2023



Fotos: Cedidas por OEI Trabajando por el futuro Uno de sus principales ámbitos de actuación es la educación, entendida también como la formación que dará futuro y empleo a los beneficiarios de estos programas. En la imagen, una alumna de la Escuela Taller de Asunción (Paraguay), impulsada por la OEI en colaboración con la Agencia Española de Cooperación Internacional para el Desarrollo (AECID) Más científicas iberoamericanas La igualdad de oportunidades y la inclusión de la mujer en el ámbito de la investigación y la ciencia es uno de los grandes retos regionales en Iberoamérica, y como tal tratan de afrontarlo los proyectos de la OEI. En la fotografía, un instante del programa Mujeres en ciencia celebrada en 2023 en Montevideo (Uruguay) Energía limpia (y justa) La sostenibilidad y la suficiencia energética son un desafío de presente y futuro, como señala Jabonero. Con financiación europea, la OEI desarrolló el proyecto Energytran para impulsar una transición justa y limpia entre Europa y América Latina. La imagen corresponde a una instalación de placas fotovoltaicas en Ciudad de México, en 2024 COP30 (Brasil) Uno de los grandes hitos recientes fue la organización por parte de la OEI, en colaboración con el Gobierno de Brasil, de la COP30, la cumbre anual de Naciones Unidas sobre el cambio climático, celebrada en noviembre de 2025 en Belém (Brasil), en la que se adoptaron 56 decisiones consensuadas, incluida una hoja de ruta para el abandono del uso de los combustibles fósiles. Reunió a más de 300.000 asistentes: el mayor proyecto organizado en la Amazonia Alfabetización, la base Los tres ejes principales de actuación de los proyectos de la OEI son la educación, la ciencia y la cultura. Pero, para todos, el primer paso fue el lograr que Iberoamérica sea una región con un 98% de alfabetización. En Honduras (en la imagen), la OEI contribuyó a la declaración del país como “Territorio libre de analfabetismo” en 2025 Un balance inmaculado Durante los último ocho años, el periodo durante el que el pedagogo Mariano Jabonero ha estado al frente de la secretaría general de la OEI, la institución ha puesto en marcha 2.500 proyectos en los 23 países integrantes, que han impactado en la vida de un total de 22 millones de personas. “Nuestro equipo está formado por excelentes profesionales, actuamos con transparencia y autonomía. Tenemos un enorme arraigo y, sobre todo, logramos que la cooperación suceda, lo que hace que todos los países y beneficiarios confíen en nosotros”, explica Jabonero

Este diciembre deja Jabonero una OEI que, alejada del papel asistencial y burocrático que pudo tener en sus comienzos (se creó en 1949), se ha convertido en un bien público regional de utilidad indiscutida, que, bajo su gestión, ha impulsado más de 600 proyectos anuales en educación, ciencia, cultura y educación en derechos humanos y democracia para más de 22 millones de beneficiarios, una organización de gestión transparente (“podemos rastrear en directo adónde ha ido el dinero de una factura pagada en Honduras”) que trabaja sobre el terreno en los 23 países que la integran; una OEI, remarca Jabonero, “muy americana, pero sin injerencia ni un solo dólar de EE UU”. “Al principio la financiación procedía sobre todo de España. Ahora el porcentaje de aporte español es mínimo. Hemos logrado que se entienda como un invento de la región y para la región”.

Un profesor filósofo forjado en la Transición

Jabonero nació en un pueblo del suroeste de Madrid y su juventud es la de quien, frente a los estertores represivos y violentos de la dictadura de Franco, anhelaba “la llegada de un régimen de libertades y tolerancia”. Fue su conciencia social la que, en un tiempo tan efervescente, lo condujo hacia los estudios de Filosofía y Ciencias de la Educación.

Estudiantes de un centro educativo cubano participan en la Noche Iberoamericana de l@s Investigador@s. OEI

“Recuerdo la publicación del primer número de EL PAÍS, en mayo de 1976. Lo compré en un quiosco en Campamento [barrio del distrito La Latina de Madrid donde se asentaban cuarteles de militares y guardias civiles]. Mi primer destino como maestro fue allí cerca, en un colegio público de Aluche”. Para entonces, Jabonero ya había viajado a Francia, y a su regreso la mitad de la carga clandestina de su mochila eran libros aquí prohibidos: “La poesía española censurada o a pensadores como Paulo Freire los leí en panfletos ciclostilados”.

Repite una cita célebre, atribuida a uno de los padres de esta Europa nuestra, Jean Monnet: “Si tuviera que volver a empezar [a construir la Unión Europea, se refiere], empezaría por la cultura”. Pedagogía, educación y sociología son para Jabonero caras del mismo cubo. A finales de los años 70, obtuvo, frente a 850 candidatos, una de las 18 plazas a inspector de Educación, momento en que descubrió lo que realmente entrañaba el derecho a la educación, la enorme responsabilidad sobre sus hombros: “el sistema, las políticas públicas, tienen que lograr que el alumnado pueda sentarse en el aula y aprender lengua o matemáticas en condiciones óptimas; y eso incluye desde la rehabilitación de escuelas rurales que no tenían ni baños ni agua corriente en aquel tiempo hasta la garantía de que esos niños y niñas hubieran podido desayunar en casa antes de venir al colegio”.

En Madrid, la OEI ha impulsado varias ediciones del Festival 'Celebremos Iberoamérica' (CIB Fest), con miles de asistentes en la capital española. OEI

No podemos perder de vista el valor de la Educación como elemento corrector de las desigualdades de cuna, esa fe democrática que hoy Jabonero observa a su alrededor “tristemente cansada, agotada”, expresa, tomando las palabras del filósofo germano-coreano Byung-Chul Han. Los siguientes pasos, como en un destino inexorable, fueron los que modelaron al pedagogo indispensable que Jabonero es hoy: pasó por el Ministerio de Educación, llegaron El Salvador, Argentina, Colombia y la cooperación —la literatura del bum fue su llave hacia eso que a Martín Caparrós le gusta llamar Ñamérica—, dio clase en la Complutense, trabajó para Unesco, dirigió la Fundación Santillana, ejerció de consultor para gobiernos de todo el continente… hasta que en 2018 y por unanimidad fue elegido, durante dos mandatos, secretario general de la OEI.

Sentirse en casa: por qué Iberoamérica es Occidente

Cola de un cine. En París o en Berlín. Si, entre el tumulto de voces, Jabonero oye la suave cadencia del colombiano o el marcado deje del español caribeño dice que no puede evitar girarse y trabar conversación. “He vivido en muchos países de Iberoamérica y siempre me he sentido en casa”. Le apena la concepción errada que todavía, dice, se tiene en España de los vecinos del otro lado del Atlántico: “Respecto de la tierra de dictaduras, guerras y pobreza que pervive en cierto imaginario, el cambio ha sido brutal: 98% de alfabetización, es la zona donde más ha crecido la matriculación en estudios superiores, 33 millones de estudiantes, en el 70% de los casos de familias donde los progenitores no pasaron por la universidad”.

El Museo de Arte de Río de Janeiro (MAR), está gestionado por la OEI desde 2022. Thales Leite (OEI)

Todavía pesan la inequidad o sus economías, demasiado dependientes de la venta de materias primas: “El litio boliviano está en manos de empresas chinas; el cobre se produce en Chile y Perú, pero se cotiza en Estados Unidos; las flores ecuatorianas se venden en Ámsterdam”. Pero están, cuenta, “a un salto de constituirse en verdaderas sociedades de conocimiento, como lo son las más competitivas”.

Entre los hablantes de español y portugués —esta última, la lengua cuyo uso más crece en África— sumamos 850 millones de personas en el mundo. Se trata de un potencial incontestable, que motiva el alegato que quiere lanzar “sin caer en demasiada retórica”: por lengua, por historia, por derecho, por cultura, por religión “América Latina no es la periferia de Occidente, sino una parte más de su núcleo”.

Reputación y futuro

¿Qué méritos motivan un galardón como el Princesa de Asturias de Cooperación Internacional de 2024 o el premio Anna Frank del pasado marzo? ¿Cómo navega la OEI para que gobiernos de todos los colores la valoren por igual en sus 77 años de acción? “Hemos sabido estar a la altura de las circunstancias”, responde Jabonero. Y enumera algunos ejemplos de por qué sus proyectos de cooperación han generado un inmensurable impacto en la zona: fue, por ejemplo, un costarricense becado por la OEI para doctorarse en la Universidad de Sevilla quien redactó la Ley de Cuidados de su país.

En 2024, la OEI fue reconocida con el Premio Princesa de Asturias a la Cooperación Internacional. En el centro de la imagen, su secretario general Mariano Jabonero. Yeray Menendez

Durante la pandemia, unos 180 millones de estudiantes latinoamericanos quedaron excluidos de las aulas y aproximadamente la mitad no tenía una conexión a internet suficiente. La OEI produjo entonces cientos de contenidos digitales, ayudó a los sistemas educativos nacionales a mantener la actividad y concedió miles de becas para formar a profesores universitarios que hasta entonces trabajaban casi exclusivamente con cuaderno y tiza. En una de las escenas más insólitas de aquel periodo, programas educativos de televisión mexicanos llegaron a emitirse en Guinea Ecuatorial.

Si la democracia se tambalea, hará falta más democracia y más consenso. Eso defiende a capa y espada Jabonero para un futuro en el que identifica varios desafíos que no admiten complacencia: la transición digital —una tecnología al servicio de todos—, la transición verde —nuevas y sostenibles fuentes de energía que no subyuguen a los habitantes del Sur Global— y, sobre todo, una transición justa, sin perdedores, imposible si no se recupera esa vieja e inquebrantable fe en la Educación. Cómo no va a creer en su poder este maestro que vio cómo un campesino podía cambiar su mundo con un boli.

World.title: Skoda, la fuente de beneficios de Volkswagen que terminó por comer el terreno a Seat
World.content:
La nueva hoja de ruta anunciada este mes por el grupo Volkswagen, en pleno plan de ajuste para asegurar su competitividad frente a los fabricantes chinos, busca aumentar sensiblemente la rentabilidad por cada vehículo que vende. Para lograrlo, el gigante alemán puede tomar como ejemplo a una marca que se ha alzado como la gran excepción del grupo: Skoda. La firma de origen checo lleva tres ejercicios consecutivos (entre 2023 y 2025) batiendo récords de beneficios operativos y ganando terreno en el espacio generalista. Por el contrario, Seat, históricamente vinculada al mismo perfil de cliente, corre el riesgo de desaparecer, ya que el fabricante no asegura su continuidad más allá de 2030 por los costes que acarrea electrificarla y la necesidad de reducir la venta de coches de combustión por la regulación europea.

De poco le sirve a Volkswagen ser la segunda mayor automovilística del mundo en matriculaciones (solo por detrás de Toyota) y la que más factura, si en la cuenta de beneficios ni siquiera entra en el podio mundial del sector. “Nuestro margen operativo sigue siendo demasiado bajo y subraya la necesidad de actuar”, había alertado en julio el director financiero del grupo, Arno Antlitz, en la presentación de los resultados semestrales.

Dicho margen fue del 3,8% por cada coche matriculado, contando todas las marcas del grupo, y el objetivo es llevarlo hasta el 9% para 2030. Una hoja de ruta que Skoda ya casi cumple. De hecho, la firma va camino de volver a batirse a sí misma este año tras unos resultados semestrales en los que sus ganancias han subido un 6,3% entre enero y junio, hasta los 1.366 millones. Esto se traduce en un margen operativo del 8,5%, casi en línea con la meta que se ha puesto el grupo para 2030 y más del doble del porcentaje registrado entre enero y junio por todo el consorcio alemán.

Belén Trincado Aznar

Skoda supera así en beneficios a todas las marcas de la compañía, algunas incluso contabilizándose de forma conjunta, como sucede con las llamadas “progressive brands”, una denominación que engloba a Audi, Lamborghini, Bentley y Ducati. Entre todas, registraron un beneficio operativo en el semestre de 1.122 millones. Porsche, tradicionalmente considerada como la niña bonita del grupo, también ganó menos que Skoda, con un beneficio operativo en el semestre de 1.208 millones. Volkswagen, marca que da nombre al grupo, ganó 995 millones en su división de turismos y 275 millones con sus furgonetas. Seat y Cupra suman apenas 122 millones entre ambas, a pesar de haberse quitado de encima la cruz de los aranceles al Cupra Tavascan que viene de China. En este contexto, solo Skoda supone el 23% de todo el beneficio operativo del grupo Volkswagen.

“Incluso en un entorno volátil, mantenemos un modelo de negocio resiliente gracias a factores como los costes operativos en la República Checa, estructuras ágiles, disciplina operativa y una búsqueda continua de la eficiencia. Formar parte del grupo Volkswagen nos aporta tecnología y escala, lo que impulsa aún más nuestras operaciones. En conjunto, estos factores contribuyeron a un sólido crecimiento de las entregas, los ingresos y la rentabilidad durante el primer semestre”, responde el consejero delegado de Skoda, Klaus Zellmer, a preguntas de CincoDías.

Aunque el directivo evita hacer comentarios sobre la posibilidad de que el grupo deje de hacer modelos de la marca dentro de la estrategia del gigante de reducir su oferta, viendo el rendimiento de Skoda parece difícil que esto vaya a suceder. Un modelo de éxito que, en paralelo, escenifica los problemas de Seat. “El consorcio considera que el espacio generalista de gama media y media baja del grupo ya lo ocupan Volkswagen y Skoda, que son ya la primera y la segunda marca del continente. Para un grupo que está eliminando la mitad de sus modelos por solapamiento, una tercera marca generalista europea es exactamente el tipo de redundancia que su nuevo plan intenta eliminar”, argumenta Francesc Rufas, docente de EAE Business School,

El investigador apunta a que Skoda está soportando mejor la competencia con las marcas chinas en el vehículo eléctrico, con el Elroq como el segundo eléctrico más vendido de Europa el año pasado, gracias a su posicionamiento en un segmento más bajo que Volkswagen y Porsche. “Hemos hecho evolucionar la marca manteniéndonos firmemente arraigados a nuestros orígenes. Skoda es sinónimo de una excelente relación calidad-precio: lo que se paga por un Skoda ofrece un gran valor a cambio”, defiende Zellmer.

El coste laboral, clave en Skoda

Rufas incide en que la estructura de costes de la marca es un aspecto clave: “En 2025, la hora trabajada en la industria manufacturera alemana costó 49,50 euros, mientras que la de Chequia, donde produce Skoda, fue de 20,20 euros. Producir en Alemania cuesta 2,45 veces más. Eso explica buena parte del diferencial de margen frente a Volkswagen Turismos”. Otro punto a resaltar es la reducción de su estructura, ya que Skoda está en un proceso de recorte de su plantilla del 15% hasta 2028. “Además, Skoda apenas está en EE UU, por lo que la crisis arancelaria que ha afectado principalmente a Porsche y Volkswagen parece no haberle pasado factura”.

Más allá del golpe arancelario, la principal causa de este difícil momento que ha llevado a Volkswagen a recortar 100.000 puestos de trabajo, sumando los anuncios realizados desde finales desde 2024, es la competencia con las marcas chinas, tanto en el propio mercado chino como fuera de él. A esto se suma la costosa conversión al vehículo eléctrico y la construcción de una cadena de valor que China ya tiene desarrollada. En las cuentas semestrales de Volkswagen, por ejemplo, se observa un resultado operativo negativo de 473 millones de euros para la división de baterías. Cariad, su negocio de software, es una losa aún más grande, con unas pérdidas operativas de 855 millones en apenas seis meses.

La marca checa se encuentra inmersa en aumentar la oferta de eléctricos, con modelos como el Epiq, que es uno de los cuatro eléctricos que parten desde aproximadamente los 25.000 euros que el grupo Volkswagen hace en España. El Epiq sale de la planta de Landaben (Pamplona), al igual que el Id. Cross, mientras que el ID. Polo y el Cupra Raval se están haciendo en Martorell (Barcelona). “El lanzamiento de los nuevos modelos Epiq y Peaq es un claro ejemplo de esta estrategia en acción. Ambos duplican nuestra gama de vehículos totalmente eléctricos, manteniendo al mismo tiempo la identidad inconfundible de Skoda”, añade Zellmer.

World.title: La última frontera nazarí: ruta por los castillos y torres vigías de los guardianes de Boabdil
World.content:
Las localidades de Montefrío, Moclín e Íllora convocan a un turismo de historia, naturaleza y tranquilidad en el oeste de la provincia de Granada

Mirar hoy al horizonte desde los castillos de Íllora, Montefrío y Moclín, en Granada, permite ver las llanuras y sierras que divisaban los centinelas nazaríes hace más de cinco siglos. En esas fortalezas y en las torres vigías que jalonan el camino hacia la ciudad de Granada descansaba buena parte de la supervivencia de la dinastía nazarí frente a las tropas castellanas. Y lo ocurrido allí en junio de 1486 hizo comprender a los reyes nazaríes que su época estaba a punto de concluir. Ese mes de aquel año cayó su penúltima línea defensiva —la última era la Alhambra misma— en manos de los Reyes Católicos. A cuatro leguas de la ciudadela capitalina, poco más de 20 kilómetros en línea recta, el 8 de junio de hace 540 años el castillo árabe de Íllora pasaba a manos de las tropas castellanas. Días después, las fortalezas musulmanas de Moclín y Montefrío caían del mismo lado. El camino entre esta última frontera y la capital del reino nazarí quedaba prácticamente expedito. Por delante, la sierra y la Vega de Granada. Seis años después, Boabdil, el último rey nazarí, entregaría las llaves de la Alhambra para poner rumbo a la Alpujarra.

Ese legado de construcciones defensivas musulmanas sigue en pie, con más o menos fortuna, al oeste de la provincia andaluza, en el Poniente granadino. Y, más de cinco siglos después, permite disfrutar de un turismo de historia, naturaleza y, por añadidura, de calma. Son sitios tranquilos, sin prisa y con poco turismo que merecen una visita. Si el tiempo apremia, la zona puede visitarse en una jornada; pero si a este turismo patrimonial le añadimos un poco de actividad y deporte, el viaje puede alargarse un par de días o más con paseos entre castillos, olivos, montañas y una interesante trama de torres vigías que, gracias a sus fogatas y al humo, hacían llegar la señal de peligro a la torre destino, la Torre de la Vela, en la Alhambra, donde residían los reyes nazaríes.

La jornada de visita a estos tres pueblos puede arrancar perfectamente en Montefrío, la localidad más lejana de la capital, a 50 minutos en coche. El viajero se adentra, como sin querer, en un territorio de miles de olivos hasta alcanzar la primera parada, el mirador de National Geographic. Esta revista declaró en 2021 Montefrío como “uno de los 10 pueblos con las mejores vistas del mundo”. Sea top 10 o no, la panorámica desde el mirador muestra el pueblo, un gran peñón coronado por la iglesia que se construyó sobre el antiguo castillo árabe. Una imagen para recordar.

Terminado el deleite de las fotos y las vistas, toca ir al centro del pueblo y estacionar en alguno de los aparcamientos públicos que facilitan el trámite de encontrar sitio. Como la visita que planteamos es de rampas y cuestas, lo más sensato es empezar con un desayuno en alguno de los bares del centro. El castillo está sobre un peñón, recordemos, y hay que subir. Esa subida está bien indicada, siguiendo siempre las señales de “Fortaleza árabe / Iglesia de la villa”.

Uno de los miradores para observar el paisaje de Montefrío y su entorno. Margouilla ( GETTY IMAGES )

Del castillo apenas quedan unas pocas señales y lo que se yergue en la cima de la peña es una iglesia, la de Santa María, que los Reyes Católicos ordenaron levantar sobre los restos del antiguo castillo nazarí para mostrar que el poder había cambiado de manos. Diseñada por Diego de Siloé, la iglesia era, además de un mirador al nuevo territorio conquistado, un lugar para que, quien mirara, supiera quién gobernaba. El recinto alberga un centro de interpretación de aquella última frontera de hace 500 años, interesante para el inicio de la jornada.

De vuelta al centro de Montefrío, encontraremos un templo único en España. La iglesia de la Encarnación está inspirada en el Panteón de Agripa (Roma), tiene planta circular y una cúpula de 30 metros de diámetro y 15 de altura. Su construcción data de finales del siglo XVIII y principios del XIX. Merece la pena una visita, aunque el horario es solo matinal (de 10.00 a 13.30).

La iglesia de la Encarnación, en Montefrío. Oliver Hoffmann ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Un desvío para amantes de la arqueología

De camino al próximo castillo, a cinco kilómetros de Montefrío, hay una parada que puede alargar el viaje de los amantes de la arqueología. Es el Paraje Arqueológico de las Peñas de los Gitanos, uno de los yacimientos prehistóricos andaluces más destacados, que estuvo ocupado desde el V milenio a.C. hasta época romana. Han aparecido hasta cuatro agrupaciones de sepulcros, una de ellas con 50 estructuras. Una parte de la visita es gratuita pero otra, la necrópolis megalítica, requiere reserva y pago. En el entorno puede visitarse la torre vigía de los Anillos, bien conservada y de fácil acceso.

El Paraje Arqueológico de las Peñas de los Gitanos. Universal History Archive / GETTY IMAGES

A media hora de Montefrío está Moclín, donde encontramos el segundo castillo de esta ruta histórico-patrimonial. Este pequeño pueblo acoge “una de las mejores piezas defensivas de la época nazarí, y el único [castillo] que conserva el cinturón de murallas al completo”, según el Instituto Andaluz de Patrimonio Histórico. El castillo requiere aún un importante trabajo de restauración después de ser destruido en la Guerra Civil, pero la muralla está en buen estado. Sobre otro imponente peñón, dominando la localidad y buena parte del territorio circundante, esta fortaleza del siglo XIII permitía la vigilancia de un enorme territorio. Desde allí, por ejemplo, se ve con total claridad la Fortaleza de la Mota, en Alcalá La Real (Jaén), a 20 kilómetros de distancia. Los fines de semana, el recinto permanece abierto para la visita (de 11.00 a 17.00), pero lo más seguro es garantizar esa visita con el Ayuntamiento de la localidad. También aquí, como en Montefrío, la primera vista desde abajo es una iglesia construida en el interior del recinto amurallado.

Vista aérea de las murallas y el castillo de Moclín. Tomka ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Pero 30.000 años antes de que ese castillo estuviera habitado, ya ocurrían cosas relevantes en la zona. En la cueva de Malalmuerzo habitaron grupos de Homo sapiens durante miles de años. Entre ellos hubo comunidades que encontraron refugio allí durante la última glaciación europea, hace entre 23.000 y 19.000 años. No es visitable, pero los muy interesados, que han de estar familiarizados con la espeleología y no tener miedo a las estrecheces, pueden consultar en el Ayuntamiento si es posible hacer una incursión en ella.

Ya al aire libre y para los caminantes, Moclín cuenta con la conocida Ruta del Gollizno —un gollizno es una estrechura de un paraje—. Comienza en el pueblo y, con ocho kilómetros de distancia en una ruta circular, es un agradable paseo por la sierra del entorno. La ruta permite ver hasta cuatro de las torres vigías, algo que permite también la Ruta de las Atalayas, de la misma longitud pero algo más complicada. Un paseo más largo que nos haría pasar por Moclín es el del Camino Mozárabe de Santiago, pero esa es otra historia.

Una pasarela en la Ruta del Gollizno. Joseph Creamer ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Visitados Moclín y Montefrío, la siguiente parada es Íllora, a 15 kilómetros. Su castillo —restaurado recientemente— ofrece una imagen imponente y guarda algunas sorpresas, más allá de sus impresionantes vistas. Como los otros dos, se sitúa sobre un gran peñón y todavía esconde algún secreto a los historiadores. Por ejemplo, la importancia de la fortaleza y su relación con el agua. Como explica Juan José Peña Agea, su magnífico guía, estas construcciones tenían habitualmente uno o dos aljibes, pero este tiene cinco, uno de ellos con capacidad muy superior a la habitual y, por suerte, visitable. Mientras, solo se puede elucubrar que, si el agua era poder, Íllora tuvo un papel relevante entonces.

Si el visitante busca empaparse de historia, en Íllora encontrará aliados excepcionales para comprender el territorio. La Asociación La Pileta agrupa a vecinos expertos en el patrimonio local, siempre dispuestos a organizar actividades sobre el terreno. Quienes prefieran explorar la zona haciendo deporte, a pie o sobre dos ruedas, pueden apoyarse en el activo Club Gallipatos de Parapanda.

Vista de la localidad granadina y el castillo de Íllora. Charles Stirling ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Y para comer, qué mejor que poner un broche gastronómico a la ruta. En Alomartes, pedanía de Íllora a cinco kilómetros, está el restaurante Camino de la huerta, un lugar donde las chacinas de Joselito se mezclan con las del vecino pueblo de Brácana; donde los garbanzos vienen acompañados de un carabinero con todo el sentido y donde, en época de trufas, hay que ir a las jornadas que dedica a este producto. También es interesante probar el aceite del olivo autóctono, el lucio, una variedad llegada hace siglos desde el norte de África y de la que existen ejemplares con centenares de años. Un cierre gastronómico para una jornada entre castillos, murallas y torres vigías.

Turismo de pantalla como experimento

¿Cómo conseguir que alguien viaje a un castillo, una torre vigía o una muralla de la que nunca ha oído hablar? Un grupo de investigadores y artistas de la Universidad de Granada, dirigidos por la investigadora de la Facultad de Bellas Artes Ana García López, ha decidido intentarlo a través de las pantallas. Su proyecto, La voz de las Torres, desarrollado en el marco de la iniciativa europea HERIT ADAPT, parte de una idea sencilla: despertar, a través de una serie, el interés por unos lugares que muchos potenciales visitantes aún no conocen.

De esta iniciativa ha surgido una docuserie de cinco episodios de unos 20 minutos que combina recreación histórica y elementos de ficción para narrar los acontecimientos que rodearon la caída de las fortalezas de Montefrío, Moclín e Íllora y el avance de las tropas castellanas hacia Granada. Mediante herramientas de inteligencia artificial, la serie pone rostro, voz y contexto a algunos de los episodios que marcaron los últimos años del reino nazarí.

El proyecto se completa con una guía digital y con espacios de visionado previstos en las distintas localidades. La intención es que quienes descubran estas historias a través de la serie sientan después la curiosidad de recorrer el territorio real: subir a los castillos, caminar entre torres vigías y contemplar desde sus murallas el mismo horizonte que observaban los centinelas nazaríes hace más de 500 años.

World.title: Public broadcasters to be merged into four “houses” from 2029
World.content:
The cabinet has published its plan to reform the Dutch public broadcasting system, which will replace the current 11 broadcasting organisations with four “broadcasting houses” from 2029.

News broadcaster NOS and educational broadcaster NTR will also merge under the NOS name, and no new broadcasters will be allowed to join the system, media minister Rianne Letschert told parliament on Friday, NOS reported.

The plan was first drawn up last year and was included in the coalition agreement and is open to public consultation.

Current system

There are currently 11 public broadcasting organisations under the umbrella of public broadcasting body NPO: AVROTROS, BNNVARA, EO, Human, KRO-NCRV, Max, Ongehoord Nederland (ON), PowNed, VPRO, WNL and Zwart.

Each has its own political, religious or social focus and together they make programmes for three national television channels and five radio stations.

To join, a group must sign up at least 50,000 paying members, which earns it a provisional licence for five years. To keep a permanent place it needs 100,000 members.

A broadcaster can lose its licence if the media regulator sanctions it twice in five years, if it no longer meets the legal requirements, or if the NPO says it refuses to cooperate with the others. These are the three grounds Letschert used last week when she said she would withdraw the licence of far-right broadcaster ON.

Under the new plan, the membership requirement is scrapped and broadcasters will no longer be able to join the system or be thrown out, although the regulator will still be able to act against wrongdoing.

Four houses

Which broadcasters go into which house has not been decided yet, but the broadcasters have already said who they want to work with: KRO-NCRV, Max and WNL; EO, VPRO and Human; AVROTROS and PowNed; and BNNVARA and Zwart.

Zwart, set up by rapper Akwasi to bring more diversity to television, has been broadcasting on a provisional licence since 2022 but still has to win a permanent one before it can join a house.

The houses can keep their old names or choose new ones, and will have more say over their own programming as the NPO’s coordinating role shrinks.

Letschert said the current system has too many boards and too much internal competition. “With less administrative bustle and more shared responsibility, the public broadcaster can focus on making good programmes, strong journalism and digital innovation,” she said.

The media regulator, the Commissariaat voor de Media, has criticised the plan, saying it gives broadcasters too few clear rules and relies too much on self-regulation.

The draft law goes next to the Council of State (Raad van State), the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, and then to parliament and the senate. The cabinet wants the new system to start in 2029.

World.title: FNV union demands 5.5% pay rises to tackle high inflation
World.content:
Trade unions are demanding pay rises of up 5.5% in next year’s pay round to offset the impact of high inflation.

The FNV, the Netherlands’ largest labour union, published its demands on Monday as part of the regular build-up to the opening of parliament and Budget Day this week.

The FNV says it will press for a 5.5% increase in basic pay during collective bargaining negotiations and a flat payment of €80 a month for all workers to give an extra boost to low earners.

Inflation is currently 3.3%, having risen in August, according to the government statistics agency CBS.

“We see that inflation is rising and is still well above the average while productivity is rising, companies are making big profits and the labour market remains tight,” Jacqie van Stigt, the union’s interim collective bargaining co-ordinator said.

The CNV, another of the major unions, said last week it would be seeking pay rises of between 3% and 5.5% next year as well as an increase in the travel allowance to 25 cents per kilometre, after the government raised the maximum tax-free amount from July 1.

AI concerns

The FNV also said it wanted to draw up stricter rules to ensure employees were consulted on the use of AI in the workplace.

The union is concerned that using machine-generated text is leading to more pressure on workers and giving companies an excuse to cut jobs.

The FNV also announced that cleaning staff have begun a week-long strike to protest against the pay deal struck between employers and the CNV union, which 80% of FNV members have rejected.

Staff at Schiphol airport and railway stations will take part in the strike. The union wants the employers to go back to the table and discuss their demands, which include not cutting pay for sick employees and paying hotel cleaners equal rates.

“We will continue until the pay negotiations are reopened and our cleaners are actually listened to,” said union spokeswoman Carolien Lambers.
