World.title: EU Moves to Curb Airbnb-Style Rentals to Boost Long-Term Housing
World.content:
The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.

The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.



“Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. “Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans.”

“The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify ‘areas under housing stress’ using a common methodology,” a Commission press release explains.

Housing in Europe is getting worse

The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.

Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can’t afford to buy or rent, but also aren’t eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU’s total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.

“Airbnb shares the Commission’s ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities,” the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission’s announcement.

The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.

World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: Hungarian police officer admits beating defenceless man, breaking several bones
World.content:
A police officer in Gyöngyös, Hungary, has received a suspended prison sentence after admitting that he and a colleague beat a defenceless man, breaking his jaw, nose and facial bones. The second officer denies the charges and will face further proceedings in January.

Officer admits to assault in court

A police officer from Gyöngyös has been sentenced to one and a half years in prison, suspended for three years, after admitting that he and another officer assaulted a defenceless man in January 2024.

The officer was convicted at a preparatory hearing before the Military Council of the Budapest-Capital Regional Court. He admitted all the charges against him, allowing the court to issue a final verdict. He was also demoted.

The second officer accused of taking part in the assault continues to deny the charges, meaning his trial will continue in January. The victim is represented by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, which said the case involved an especially serious abuse of power.

If you missed it: Former school guard jailed in Hungary for sexually abusing two vulnerable minors

Police officers allegedly took man to outskirts of Gyöngyös

According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, the victim, identified as “András”, is a homeless man living in the Duránda area of Gyöngyös. In January 2024, he was warming himself in the entrance of a bank when the two officers approached him for an identity check. His documents were in order, and no proceedings were launched against him.

The officers then offered to drive him home in their patrol car. Instead, they took him to the outskirts of the town and stopped near a forest.

One of the officers restrained the man while the other punched him in the face. The officer who had initially restrained him then also hit and kicked him in the thigh. The officers pushed him to the ground and allegedly threatened to call a hunter to have wild boars eat him.

The assault continued for several minutes and only stopped when another vehicle approached on the road. The man then managed to escape and return home.

Victim suffered multiple fractures

His mother saw his injuries and called an ambulance. At the hospital, doctors diagnosed him with fractures to his jaw, nose and facial bones, as well as concussion. A criminal investigation was subsequently launched. The two officers initially denied the allegations during the investigation.

However, one of them later admitted the charges in court. He reportedly said that the day of the hearing was also his final day as a police officer. The second defendant continues to maintain his innocence, with his case scheduled to continue in January.

Ivóna Bieber, a lawyer for the Hungarian Helsinki Committee representing the victim, said that around 90% of complaints concerning assaults allegedly committed by police officers do not even result in charges being brought. She nevertheless praised the prosecutors’ work in this case and said the court had delivered a fair judgment, taking into account the officer’s full confession and remorse.

World.title: Russian gas deliveries to Hungary suddenly halved after diplomat expulsions: here’s the reason
World.content:
Gas imports from Russia via the southern route fell to around half their usual level just one day after Hungary expelled ten Russian embassy staff; however, the timing appears to have been coincidental.

Russian gas deliveries suddenly plunge

The amount of natural gas entering Hungary from the south fell sharply last week, reaching levels not seen for years, according to Hungarian economic news outlet G7.

Between Wednesday and Friday, just 11.6 million cubic metres of gas per day entered Hungary via the southern route from Serbia. Since only Russian gas enters Hungary from Serbia, the drop effectively meant that Russian gas deliveries through this route were cut by roughly half.

The timing immediately attracted attention. The decline came just one day after Hungary’s Foreign Ministry expelled ten employees of the Russian embassy, which raised the question: maybe Moscow had responded by reducing gas supplies?

However, the available evidence suggests that the two events were not connected.

A technical restriction was already planned

The southern route has become highly important for Hungary’s gas supply in recent years. Most Russian gas imports now arrive through the TurkStream pipeline, which runs under the Black Sea before passing through Bulgaria and Serbia.

The pipeline has generally operated close to full capacity for around three years, apart from scheduled maintenance periods.

But according to G7, Hungary’s gas network operator, FGSZ, had already included a restriction for this period in its annual maintenance schedule. The document shows that the relevant cross-border capacity would operate at 50 per cent.

In other words, the sharp decline appears to have been the result of a planned technical restriction rather than a political response from Russia.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Russian senator had warned of gas consequences

The possibility of Russian retaliation was particularly notable because a Russian senator had warned about potential consequences following the expulsions.

According to reporting by Világgazdaság, the senator said the diplomatic move could have “unpleasant consequences” for Budapest, including a reduction or even a complete halt to Russian gas deliveries through the TurkStream pipeline.

The timing of the subsequent drop in deliveries therefore fuelled speculation about a possible connection.

However, industry sources and experts contacted by G7 were initially unable to identify a clear explanation for the sudden fall. Most ultimately considered technical or commercial factors more likely, with the planned technical restriction providing the apparent answer.

Have you heard? Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels

Gas flows have since recovered

The reduced imports did not last. Although the southern route was still not operating at full capacity over the weekend, gas flows have since largely returned to their usual levels. G7 noted that total Russian gas imports for last week amounted to around 122 million cubic metres, making it the lowest weekly figure in almost three years, excluding scheduled maintenance-related shutdowns.

Hungary’s state-owned MVM buys Russian gas from Gazprom under a long-term agreement, while traders have also purchased billions of cubic metres of Russian gas on the spot market in recent years because of its competitive price.

It is therefore possible that short-term commercial purchases were particularly affected by the temporary capacity restriction. However, because Russian gas currently enters Hungary through this southern route, the reduction would have affected at least some of the gas purchased by MVM as well.

All in all, the available evidence points to an unfortunate coincidence rather than a Russian response to Hungary’s diplomatic move.

World.title: PM Magyar says former PM Orbán could face prison over threats against new asset recovery office staff
World.content:
Hungary’s prime minister accused former PM Viktor Orbán of threatening prosecutors, police officers and investigators who may work for the newly established National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office.

Magyar: “This is violence against an official”

Speaking in Parliament, Péter Magyar criticised Viktor Orbán over remarks the former prime minister made about employees of Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office.

Magyar said Orbán had “specifically threatened Hungarian prosecutors, customs officers, police officers and investigators”, accusing members of the former governing party of remaining silent about the remarks. According to Magyar, Orbán’s statements could amount to the criminal offence of violence against a public official under Hungary’s Criminal Code.

He cited provisions under which anyone who uses violence or threats to obstruct an official carrying out a lawful procedure, or to force them to take action, can face between one and five years in prison.

“What Orbán did is violence against a public official under the Criminal Code,” Magyar said.

He also pointed out that, as a former prime minister, Orbán no longer has parliamentary immunity.

What did Orbán say?

The dispute follows an interview Orbán gave to Hír TV after his closed-door speech in Kötcse at the weekend. In the interview, Orbán referred to the newly established asset recovery office as an “ÁVH-type institution”, 444.hu writes. The ÁVH was Hungary’s communist-era state security organisation.

Orbán warned that if his political side returned to power, people who worked for the office, took part in its procedures or made decisions there would face accountability.

He also said the names of every employee involved would be made public, along with details of their work and the procedures in which they had participated.

Orbán argued that those responsible would have to face financial and legal consequences once, in his words, the rule of law was restored.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Magyar calls for solidarity with officials

Magyar said the remarks were particularly serious because the people being targeted were public servants who would be carrying out lawful procedures. He called on Tisza MPs to express their solidarity with the affected officials and to defend them against what he described as threats.

The confrontation comes as the new Hungarian government prepares to use the asset recovery office to investigate cases involving suspected corruption and recover public assets “lost” during the 16 years of the previous Orbán era.

Orbán also attacks the Tisza government

In the same interview, Orbán criticised the government led by Magyar, arguing that it was handing Hungary’s economy back to Brussels and pursuing policies that would make the country less sovereign. The former prime minister also attacked the planned introduction of the euro, calling it the “biggest scam” and claiming that the stated 2030 target was merely a cover for future austerity measures.

Orbán further argued that the political right could only have a chance of returning to power if it remained united, and said his priority over the next six months would be to reorganise Fidesz rather than focus on Tisza.

World.title: German foreign minister visits Hungary; Budapest and Berlin agree on major new cooperation plans, announce visit
World.content:
Hungary and Germany have agreed on closer political, economic and diplomatic cooperation, while Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s November visit to Berlin is already being prepared.

Budapest and Berlin seek to strengthen ties

Hungary and Germany are preparing to open a new chapter in their bilateral relations, Hungarian Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán said following talks with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Budapest.

The two sides agreed on a series of measures aimed at strengthening political dialogue, economic cooperation and people-to-people ties. Orbán said the meeting had also begun preparations for Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s visit to Berlin on 9–10 November.

The timing has historical significance: the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, one of the defining events of the end of the Cold War.

In a joint statement, the two countries said they wanted to renew their partnership and open a new, trust-based chapter in Hungarian-German relations, nearly 35 years after the signing of their friendship treaty in 1992.

If you missed it: FM Anita Orbán reports progress on minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine

Economic and energy cooperation in focus

Hungary and Germany said they intend to further develop and broaden their economic ties, including beyond the automotive industry, where German companies have a major presence in Hungary.

The two governments also stressed the importance of strengthening the European single market and creating an attractive, innovation-friendly and reliable investment environment.

They agreed that Europe needs to preserve and develop the foundations of a competitive industrial sector so that the continent can remain competitive globally.

Energy security was another key area of cooperation. Hungary and Germany called for greater European coordination to protect the region’s energy security.

The countries also said they face significant migration pressure and share the goal of stopping illegal migration and strengthening the protection of the EU’s external borders.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Closer cooperation between foreign ministries

The two countries agreed on a number of concrete measures to deepen cooperation. These include strengthening the Hungarian-German Forum, which brings together political and civil society representatives. The next forum, scheduled to take place in Berlin in autumn 2026, is being presented as a concrete sign of a new beginning in bilateral relations.

Hungary and Germany will also establish regular professional consultations between their foreign ministries on bilateral relations and European policy, as well as on geo-economic and defence industry issues where relevant.

The ministries plan to increase exchanges on strategic planning and communication, including cooperation on the challenges posed by disinformation. A regular dialogue between Hungarian and German think tanks will also be established.

The two sides additionally agreed to expand exchanges between young diplomats and connect training programmes preparing participants for diplomatic service. The countries also plan to increase the exchange of diplomats between their foreign ministries.

Cooperation in education and culture

Budapest and Berlin also intend to maintain close cooperation with Andrássy University Budapest, youth exchange organisations and other partners in culture, language and education. The two sides will examine the possibility of organising a Hungarian-German Year of Culture in 2028.

The joint statement also highlights the role of science, education, culture, civil society and youth exchanges in strengthening mutual understanding between the two countries.

Germany’s large Hungarian diaspora and Hungary’s German minority will continue to receive particular attention, with the two governments also stressing the importance of the future and accessibility of German-language education in Hungary.

Shared positions on European and international issues

The joint statement says Hungary and Germany want to work together for a strong, secure, free and competitive Europe as EU member states and NATO allies.

On Ukraine, both countries reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and backed the European Council’s June 2026 conclusions calling for an immediate ceasefire and a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.

They also said they would increase efforts to promote peace and security in the Middle East and South-West Asia, while supporting Israel’s right to self-defence.

On the Western Balkans, Budapest and Berlin said they share an interest in peace, stability, successful EU integration and economic development, and pledged to support candidate countries on their path towards EU membership.

The statement also refers to the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 revolution and uprising, saying it reinforces the two countries’ commitment to European values, including human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and the protection of human rights.

World.title: Road collapses under bus carrying dozens of passengers in Budapest
World.content:
The asphalt gave way beneath a bus in Budapest’s 15th district on Monday morning after water washed away part of the road. Six people, including four children, were taken to hospital.

Road collapsed beneath packed bus

A section of road collapsed beneath a BKK bus carrying around 30–40 passengers in Budapest’s 15th district on Monday morning. The incident happened on Sződliget Street in Rákospalota after water washed away the road surface, according to Hungary’s disaster management authority.

Firefighters and ambulances were called to the scene, while the affected section of the road was closed to traffic. The National Ambulance Service later told Hungarian News Agency MTI that six people were taken to hospital from the scene.

Four children and one adult were transported with minor injuries, while another woman suffered a head injury. She was in a stable condition when taken to hospital.

A photo of the asphalt can be seen here.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Several bus routes diverted

The incident has caused significant disruption to public transport in the area. According to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), buses 96, 124, 225, 296 and 296A are currently operating on diverted routes.

As a result, the services are not currently stopping at Géza fejedelem Square, Sződliget Street or Fő Road.

The affected section of Sződliget Street remains closed while authorities deal with the damage caused by the collapsed road.

World.title: Flydubai resumes Budapest flights as airline expands network to more than 125 destinations!
World.content:
Flydubai has resumed its direct Budapest–Dubai flights as the airline restores most of its network and expands to more than 125 destinations across 56 countries. The service is currently operating three times a week, with daily flights planned from late October.

Budapest flights resumed at the end of July

The Dubai-based carrier restarted its direct flights between Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport (BUD) and Dubai International Airport (DXB) on 31 July 2026.

The Budapest route currently operates three times a week on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. From 25 October, flydubai plans to increase the frequency to a daily service.

The airline operates the route with Boeing 737 aircraft. The service also forms part of flydubai’s partnership with Emirates, giving passengers access to a much wider combined network via Dubai.

According to flydubai, passengers travelling on connecting Emirates flights can benefit from a single booking and checked baggage transferred through to their final destination.

Flydubai network grows to more than 125 destinations

The Budapest service comes as flydubai continues to rebuild and expand its international network. In a press release issued on 14 September, the airline said it had restored operations to 85% of its network and now serves more than 125 destinations in 56 countries, with an average of 2,200 flights per week.

In recent months, flydubai has resumed or launched services to several destinations, including Aleppo, Benghazi and Bangkok. The airline has also increased its Bangkok service to three daily non-stop flights, citing strong demand.

Flydubai is due to add another destination on 23 September, when it launches flights to Pokhara in Nepal, its second destination in the country after Kathmandu.

The carrier said it expects travel demand to remain strong during the upcoming winter season, with Dubai continuing to attract visitors while passengers use the city as a hub for travel elsewhere.

Flydubai’s Boeing 737 MAX 9 in Greece. Photo: depositphotos.com

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Budapest offers connections to destinations beyond Dubai

Flydubai said back in July that the Budapest route also strengthens connections between Hungary and the United Arab Emirates while giving Hungarian travellers easier access to destinations in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

The airline has previously highlighted destinations such as the Maldives, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Kenya as examples of places that can be reached through Dubai.

The wider Emirates and flydubai network now offers access to more than 214 unique destinations in over 100 countries, with more than 4,600 possible connections through Dubai.

“Despite the challenging operating environment, we have remained focused on restoring our network safely and efficiently, adding capacity where we see demand while opening new markets,” flydubai Chief Executive Officer Ghaith Al Ghaith said.

He added that the airline was encouraged by strong customer demand during the summer and remained positioned to further restore its network in the coming months.

Read more travel news: Good news for passengers: Wizz Air restarts popular flights to multiple destinations from Budapest

Daily Budapest service coming in October

For Hungarian travellers, the most important change will come in late October, when the Budapest–Dubai route is scheduled to become a daily service. Flydubai said it is continuing to add capacity to its year-round routes as more aircraft become available. The airline currently operates an average of 2,200 weekly flights and aims to increase this frequency further.

World.title: The fast and easy-to-use qualified electronic signature your lawyer will approve
World.content:
Digital administration is becoming increasingly popular. However, those seeking to achieve high-level digital trust in full compliance with legal requirements have so far had to use several systems in parallel. One provider identifies them and issues their qualified electronic signatures, another platform enables user-friendly contract management, while their customers are identified through an external service provider. The renewed Netlock is now putting an end to this fragmented approach. Led by András Somkuti, former President of Docler Holding, and Bálint Lévai, owner of the BioTechUSA Group, Netlock’s new service integrates essential digital trust functions into a single, closed ecosystem, serving not only individuals but also large enterprises such as banks, insurers and media companies, as well as players in the SME sector.

Collaborative content

Netlock Democratizes Digital Contracting

Netlock’s 2026 story does not begin from scratch. As one of Europe’s first qualified trust service providers, the company has been offering qualified electronic signature services for 25 years. These services comply with the strictest EU regulations and, from several legal perspectives, provide greater security than a standard electronic signature. The newly launched Netlock provides digital identity, KYC services, and qualified electronic signatures in an easy-to-use, authentic and secure environment. Its range of functions is going to be expanded with contract lifecycle management, known as CLM, as well as content authentication and advanced cryptographic solutions. Together, these capabilities may provide a significant competitive advantage in any sector.

“With the two decades of expertise, we merged the best of our business-supporting services into a single, closed platform using one unified credit system. As a result, Netlock has become a comprehensive service provider capable of guiding our clients through the entire lifecycle of a contract, from preparation, approval and signing to tracking and archiving. We do all this while ensuring that our system is easy to use, authentic and secure at the same time. It can even support international copyright disputes by verifying the origin of media files, making it possible to prove that a given piece of content has existed in unchanged form since authentication and to identify who it is linked to,” said András Somkuti.

Media attestation in a convenient way

As AI-generated media becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic content, Netlock shifts the focus from detecting what is fake to proving what is trusted, authorised, and legally defensible. By combining C2PA content provenance with qualified electronic signatures, timestamps, electronic seals, verified identities, and embedded rights documentation, Netlock creates a cryptographically secure and legally meaningful trust layer that travels with the content itself. Organisations can certify origin and authorship, bind agreements and permissions directly to specific media files, preserve provenance throughout distribution and monetisation, and produce verifiable evidence in disputes or audits. Advanced fingerprinting can also reconnect altered or redistributed content to its original certified record even when metadata has been removed. Designed to support scalable rights management, compliance, and emerging requirements such as the EU AI Act, Netlock transforms digital content into a trusted, verifiable asset backed by human accountability and legal infrastructure.

Digital Identity in 1 Minute

Until now, the wide adoption of paperless contracting has been hindered by several overlapping challenges. Previously, no contracting party could be certain whether their partner had an electronic signature or whether they were able to use it properly. If they did not, obtaining a trusted signature usually involved a slow and costly identification process. In addition, document management systems and trust service providers typically operated on two separate platforms, and integrating them could have created an inconvenient user experience in everyday use. Furthermore, electronic signature and document management systems were usually priced on a per-user basis, which could make the process disproportionately expensive for partners who only sign documents occasionally. Together, these factors have led users in two main directions: either they have used electronic signatures that have long been available on the market but are not qualified from a legal standpoint, or they have reverted to “old-school” paper-based contracting.

“We have applied UX/UI solutions that allow anyone to use Netlock intuitively in everyday situations, regardless of their level of digital competence. Obtaining the right to use a qualified electronic signature, from identification to issuing the first trusted signature, takes no more than one minute. With this new service, users can begin digital administration not only quickly, but also on a reliable, authentic and legally robust foundation,” added András Somkuti.

Unique Business Model With Transaction-Based Pricing

Unlike the industry standard, Netlock’s business model is not user-based but transaction-based. This means a company does not need to maintain unnecessary monthly subscriptions for colleagues who merely sign only once or twice. Instead, they need to pay only after transactions. The platform also allows one party to “sponsor” the other party’s signing cost, meaning any external partner can be included in the signing process without requiring expensive licenses for those who sign only rarely.

“A business that is able to centralize trust functions in a single system can significantly reduce trust-related risks and losses arising from administrative errors. Clients using Netlock can more easily enter the world of fully digital contracting without having to compromise between usability and a reliable trust framework. European regulation is also moving in this direction: the future of digital administration will be built on more unified, secure and better-controlled trust services,” said Bálint Lévai.

Simple Electronic Signature Platform vs. Qualified Trust Service Provider

The ecosystem provided by Netlock is based on the company’s status as a Qualified Trust Service Provider, or QTSP. Qualified trust service providers are organizations that are officially audited and registered by international authorities. “The fundamental difference compared to a simple platform is that, in this case, it is not merely software recording that someone has participated in a process. Instead, a legally accountable and regulated organization ensures that the signer really is who they claim to be, that the time of signing is authentic, and that the document has remained unchanged. As a result, the Netlock signed documents can also be interpreted in court or administrative proceedings,” added András Somkuti.

“In the case of financing documents or multinational contracts, the stakes are high, and the question is always the same: if something becomes disputed, how can be proved that the signature was valid? Through a qualified trust service provider, this is never a matter of retrospective reconstruction. Fast signing is now available from many providers, but far fewer are capable of ensuring that behind the signature there is a regulated and audited trust framework. We have entered the market at the right time, and there is enormous international interest in Netlock, particularly from the financial, enterprise and legal sectors. Our mission is to establish the fundamental conditions of trust in the digital world for everyone,” said Bálint Lévai.

World.title: Behind the scenes: Tisza Party rocked by internal clash just months before Hungary’s election?
World.content:
A small group of senior Tisza figures reportedly challenged Péter Magyar’s leadership style and campaign strategy just five months before the 2026 election, with some fearing the conflict could derail the party’s campaign.

A confrontation inside Tisza

According to an investigation by Hungarian news outlet 444, a small group of Tisza figures confronted then-opposition leader Péter Magyar and campaign chief Péter Tóth in November 2025 over the party’s campaign strategy and Magyar’s leadership style.

The group reportedly objected to what they considered an increasingly centralised and authoritarian approach to running the party. They also believed the campaign strategy was flawed and felt their opinions were being ignored.

The meeting took place roughly 150 days before the election, according to people familiar with the events who spoke to 444 on condition of anonymity.

Among those associated with the critical group were Márk Radnai, Ervin Nagy, Kriszta Bódis, Tamás Tóth, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, Ágnes Forsthoffer, event organiser Miklós Zelcsényi and businessman Henrik Hanzel.

Péter Magyar Ágnes Forsthoffer. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes

Dispute over Tisza’s campaign strategy

The tensions reportedly centred partly on a roughly 120-page campaign strategy prepared by Péter Tóth and a small team in October 2025. The document was reportedly produced in strict secrecy, with only one copy printed and fewer than ten members of the party’s leadership given access to it.

Tóth wanted to create a disciplined, highly centralised and fast-moving organisation for the most intense phase of the election campaign. The party’s internal structures were reorganised accordingly, including arrangements designed to give the central campaign team greater control over individual candidates.

Some Tisza figures reportedly felt uncomfortable with this approach and considered Tóth’s growing influence within the party disproportionate.

They also objected to Magyar’s leadership style, which sources described as dominant and strict. However, people close to Magyar also argued that these characteristics had helped him and the organisation withstand the enormous pressure of the election campaign.

Péter Magyar and Márk Radnai. Photo: Facebook/Radnai Márk

‘It could have destroyed the whole community’

The November meeting reportedly left both Magyar and Tóth deeply affected. According to 444, three sources claimed that Magyar became uncertain about whether he should continue his political career after the confrontation and had to be persuaded that night to carry on.

There were also fears that the dispute could become public and provide ammunition for Fidesz during the election campaign.

One source reportedly described the situation in stark terms, saying that if the story had “exploded”, it could have damaged both the political community and the election campaign. The group’s critics, however, rejected the suggestion that they had been attempting a coup against Magyar.

One source from the critical camp said they believed the party was heading in the wrong direction and felt they could not remain silent. They reportedly offered to prepare an alternative campaign strategy and suggested that an independent group of experts could decide which of the two approaches should be adopted.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Tisza leadership backs Tóth

The day after the confrontation, Tisza held an internal meeting attended by around 50–80 people. Magyar reportedly gave his full backing to campaign chief Péter Tóth, while the overwhelming majority of those present sided with the party leadership.

Miklós Zelcsényi, one of the figures associated with the critical group, reportedly clashed with Magyar during the meeting before leaving and subsequently stepping back from party work. Radnai also attended the meeting and later spoke privately with Magyar.

Although the confrontation did not turn into a public political crisis at the time, 444 reports that the disagreement was not simply forgotten. Some people involved reportedly continued to regard it as a serious breach of trust.

If you missed it: PM Magyar promises major family allowance hike and new constitution: here are the deadlines

Magyar says he still fully trusts Radnai

Magyar was asked about the 444 investigation during his Monday morning interview on Kossuth Radio. The prime minister rejected the idea that the dispute had permanently damaged relations within Tisza and explicitly expressed his continued confidence in Márk Radnai.

“I have complete trust in Márk Radnai,” Magyar said.

He described Tisza as an “entirely unprecedented” political community that had been built up within weeks and months. According to Magyar, disagreements are natural in a new political movement bringing together people from many different backgrounds.

“We discussed these conflicts,” he said, arguing that Tisza does not operate according to a system in which one leader makes a decision and anyone who disagrees is simply expelled.

“The trust in everyone who is in our community today remains unbroken,” Magyar added.

Some former critics now hold senior positions

The 444 investigation also examined what happened to members of the group after Tisza came to power following the April 2026 election. The outlet said it could not establish that those involved in the dispute were systematically excluded from senior government or political positions.

For example, Ágnes Forsthoffer is now House Speaker, while Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi became a minister.

At the same time, several figures who supported Magyar and Tóth during the November confrontation now occupy influential positions in the government and parliamentary group. Gábor Pósfai became interior minister, Márton Melléthei-Barna became deputy parliamentary group leader, and Andrea Bujdosó became parliamentary group leader.

444 contacted Magyar, Radnai, Tóth, Zelcsényi and Hanzel for comment. None agreed to speak to the outlet. Nagy, Bódis, Tamás Tóth, Ruszin-Szendi and Forsthoffer did not respond to the newspaper’s requests.

World.title: BIRN Launches ‘Trial Stories’ Page for Hashim Thaci Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Illustration: Tijana Dupanovic/BIRN.

Ahead of the verdict in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against for former senior Kosovo Liberation Army officials at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday, BIRN has launched a special focus page dedicated to the trial and its impact.

The page compiles BIRN’s reporting on the trial since it started in April 2023 – analysis articles as well as news reports from Kosovo and The Hague.

“BIRN is one of the few media outlets that has followed the prosecution of Hashim Thaci and his co-defendants in genuine depth from the beginning, reporting on the latest developments but also examining their potential implications,” said BIRN’s deputy regional director Gentiana Murati.

“The verdict is an event of major significance for Kosovo and the region and BIRN will continue to analyse its consequences as they develop, not only on the day of the judgment,” she added.

Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers are calling for 45-year prison sentences for the four defendants – Kosovo’s ex-President Hashim Thaci and fellow former guerrilla leaders Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi.

They are accused of having command responsibility for a campaign of persecution by KLA fighters during and just after the 1998-99 war, which allegedly included murders, torture, forced disappearances and unlawful detentions.

The defendants have denied the charges and their lawyers are seeking acquittals.

The case has sparked anger in Kosovo, where it is seen as an attempt to vilify the KLA’s war for liberation from Serbian oppression. Supporters of the defendants have staged a series of demonstrations and are expected to rally in The Hague for the verdict.

World.title: Turkey Rounds Up 2,447 People in Operation Targeting Crime Gangs
World.content:
Turkish Police and Gendarmerie launched a major operation called “The Streets Are Safe” on Monday, detaining 2,447 people to coincide with the first morning of the new school year in 78 provinces across the country.

“Our streets will not be left to criminal organisations. Our children and young people will not become the human resources of criminal organisations,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said in a statement, defining the detainees as members of “new generation of street gangs”.

The operation targeted criminal groups allegedly involved in offences ranging from drug trafficking, robbery and arms dealing to blackmail, money laundering and illegal betting.

Gurlek said the campaign was intended not only to detain suspects but also to dismantle the criminal groups’ finances, networks, logistical capabilities and ability to recruit new members.

He highlighted the alleged recruitment of young people through social media, accusing criminal groups of seeking to portray involvement in crime as a source of “power and status”.

“We are resolutely continuing our fight against street gangs that threaten the peace of our people, the security of our cities and the future of our children,” the minister added.

In a separate development on Sunday, Turkish police authorities detained members of the LGBTQ+ rights organisation Kaos GL and raided activists’ homes as well as bars and nightclubs in separate operations across 15 provinces, targeting 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses.

Kaos GL said at least 10 of its members were detained. Separately, courts blocked access to websites and social media accounts belonging to a number of LGBTQ+ organisations, activists and rights defenders, including Kaos GL, Lambdaistanbul, Pembe Hayat and UniKuir.

World.title: North Macedonia to Tweak Investment-for-Citizenship Rules, But EU Concerns Remain
World.content:
The European Union has criticised proposed changes to North Macedonia’s Law on Citizenship, saying they fail to go far enough in abolishing a ‘golden passport’ scheme that critics say is widely abused.

In June, the government in Skopje proposed amendments that it said would tighten citizenship rules and satisfy EU concerns over its ‘golden passport’ scheme.

The proposal scraps a threshold of 400,000 euros in investment in exchange for citizenship, as well as a requirement that the person hires 10 people.

However, authorities will still be able to issue citizenship to individuals deemed of special interest to North Macedonia, whether that interest be, for example, economic, cultural, or sporting, as many other countries around the world do, including in the EU.

World.title: In Kosovo’s Guerrilla Heartlands, Impending Trial Verdict Stirs Anger, Fierce Loyalty
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Milazim Thaci survived unscathed, hidden beneath the bodies of those who could not escape the bullets.

On March 28, 1999, four days into a NATO air war to drive Serbian forces from Kosovo, he was among a group of 33 men led away for execution in the Drenica Valley, the heartland of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA.

He recalled the Serbian policemen and soldiers taunting them: “Where’s Thaci? Where’s NATO?”

By ‘Thaci’ they meant Hashim Thaci, one of the KLA’s top leaders. Milazim knew him better as his younger cousin, a shy, lanky boy always respectful of his elders. “He was a boy of few words,” Milazim told BIRN in his home in Buroje, a village in the Skenderaj/Srbica district.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Elections Will Test PM Radev’s Grip on Power
World.content:
Following a seemingly endless series of elections and short-lived administrations in Bulgaria from 2021 to 2026, former Bulgarian President Rumen Radev won in a landslide victory in April, successfully formed a government and became prime minister.

But now the country is bracing for presidential elections on October 25. If Radev’s former Vice President Iliana Iotova wins, the prime minister and his Progressive Bulgaria party will secure major political power.

Iotova’s potential win might also have geopolitical stakes for Ukraine and Europe. In a campaign event in Sofia on September 8 she said that “the war in Ukraine cannot be solved through military means” and that “more weapons and wasted billions bring more victims and are pitting Orthodox nations against each other”. This is in tune with Radev’s softer approach to the Kremlin.

The centre-right party GERB – which was the dominant power in Bulgaria from 2008 to 2025 and is now in second place – has surprisingly abstained from nominating a candidate for president. This may be a sign of the party being in free-fall after losing to Radev in April or at least a tactical retreat.

However, several GERB members ended up in Iotova's initiative committee, the list of people endorsing an independent candidate. The committee also included pro-Russia voices, previously socialist-affiliated politicians and various figures in sports and entertainment.

Expectations are building around three of the candidates: the acting President Iliana Iotova, the pro-EU and opposition-minded former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, and the former interim agriculture minister Ivan Hristanov.

All are running as independents, though each is supported, more or less directly, by different parties. This is part of a trend – individual personalities are being foregrounded rather than party members with political baggage.

“We’re about to see a campaign dominated by battling social media narratives, rallying cries adapted for different audiences and quite a lot of populist promises,” said Ivaylo Madzharov from Active Politics, a youth-led organisation popular on Instagram and TikTok for its explainers on Bulgarian politics.

Madzharov sees Iotova as a clear favourite in the election, although, he said, surprises are possible.

World.title: Kosovo Ex-President Thaci’s Defence Seeks Acquittal in Obstruction of Justice Trial
World.content:
The defence teams of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and four others co-accused of obstruction of justice in Thaci’s war crimes trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague have called for their acquittal, accusing the prosecution of charging them based on conversations that did not result in any witness-tampering or intimidation.

The prosecution claims that that during visits at the Detention Centre in The Hague, where Thaci is being held, he told the other four defendants – Hajredin Kuci, Fadil Fazliu, Isni Kilaj and Bashkim Smakaj – to instruct certain witnesses in his war-crimes trial about what to say in court.

But Sophie Menegon, Thaci’s lawyer, told the court during closing statements on Thursday that Thaci was “on trial for having a conversation in the Detention Unit [where he is being held pending the verdict in his war crimes trial]. There is no allegation of a bribe, compulsion, or threat against witnesses.”

She added: “There is no allegation of actual interference with witnesses …There isn’t any victim in this case …The prosecution asks you to send Mr Thaci to prison for six years over conversations inside a detention unit that resulted in zero real-world impact.”

The claims are based on recordings of the visits as well as physical evidence found also at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 – less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci – allegedly printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Smakaj’s lawyer, Jonathan Elystan Rees, in his closing statements on Friday, called for the acquittal of all the defendants.

“You should find Mr Smakaj and all the other defendants not guilty, whether individually or collectively,” he said, because Smakaj’s actions did not obstruct or have an impact on the course of justice.

Smakaj “cannot be convicted on the allegation that he intentionally aided in disobeying court orders, because he was completely unaware of the court’s orders”, Rees said.

He added: “There is no evidence from the prosecution, nor any legal obligation, requiring my client to be aware of the operational guidelines and functioning procedures of the detention centres.”

The lawyer for Isni Kilaj, Ian Edwards, told the court on Friday that Kilaj did not take any action after visiting Thaci at the Detention Centre in The Hague, saying he “neither called nor met with any witnesses”, so showing a lack of intent to obstruct justice.

“Everything else is mud that the prosecution is throwing at Mr Kilaj, hoping that some of it will tarnish his reputation,” he added.

David Young, lawyer for Fadil Fazliu, highlighted that his client was not even questioned by the prosecution.

“We can infer that the prosecution adopted a strategic approach of not interviewing them, of not questioning these individuals regarding the allegations. Is this the right way to initiate investigations or bring charges? I believe not. I state clearly that it is not,” Young told the court.

Alexander Admiral, lawyer for Hajredin Kuci, told the court that his client had been charged based on a wrongful translation of a message he sent to one of the witnesses in Thaci’s war-crimes trial, former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA fighter Rrustem Mustafa.

According to Admiral, the message had been misinterpreted as passing a note from a third individual when the rightful translation revealed that Kuci was passing his support to Mustafa and was basically “a man calming an old friend”.

During the prosecution’s closing statements on Thursday, it was claimed that Thaci tried to influence Mustafa and another former KLA, fighter, Bislim Zyrapi, both of whom were testifying in his war-crimes case.

The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Hit by Fresh Dispute Over Deputy Speakers
World.content:
Kosovo parliament session on September 11, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s parliament failed to find a way out of a fresh crisis on Friday when MPs reconvened in two attempts to elect new deputy speakers.

The legislature derived from the June 7 snap partliamentary elections has not yet been inaugurated because the ruling Vetevendosje party refuses to support proposed candidates from two opposition parties, Vlora Citaku, from the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Kujtim Shala, from the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Under the constitutional rules, parliament cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and all five deputies are elected.

Albulena Haxhiu from Vetevendosje was elected speaker on Wednesday, Ardian Gola, from the same party, was installed as deputy on Friday.

When Citaku of the PDK received only 44 of a minimum of 61 votes on Friday, her party colleagues left the session and accused Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje of blocking the inauguration of parliament.

“As of today, the PDK has no reason to participate in parliamentary sessions and we will take the case to the Constitutional Court,” Bedri Hamza, the PDK leader, said as soon as speaker Albulena Haxhiu interrupted the session.

In the June elections, Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the chamber, well ahead of the next-placed PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats.

Vetevendosje claims it can call on 62 MPs to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved, as parliament needs to elect a new president of Kosovo within two months of its inauguration. Failure to do so would trigger another election, the fourth within less than two years.

As the post-election blockage enters its second month, Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed on August 31 to nominate Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as Kosovo’s president. But, days later, six LDK MPs refused to support his candidacy, making the necessary quorum impossible.

For a president to be elected, a candidate must win at least 80 votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, they need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

Arberie Nagavci, head of Vetevendosje’s parliamentary group, said its MPs would not support any candidate for deputy speaker who is against the deal on the new president. Both Citaku and Shala have announced their opposition to Sejdiu’s candidacy.

“Of course, the MPs who are in favour of the Vetevendosje-LDK agreement [on the president] have the support of our 53 MPs,” Nagavci said after the interruption of the session.

Parliament will resume work on Sunday.

World.title: Hajduk Jump Past Dinamo to Top of the SuperSport HNL
World.content:
Hajduk beat Slaven Belupo 1-0 at Poljud in round seven of the SuperSport HNL, with Brazilian forward Dalisson netting the only goal in the 22nd minute. The win was Gonzalo Garcia’s side’s fifth league victory in a row, and it sends them to the top of the table. Hajduk now sit a point clear of Osijek, and three points above both Dinamo and Varaždin, who have a game in hand.

Hajduk set the tempo from the first whistle, with Bamba a constant threat down the right. The hosts thought they’d broken the deadlock in the 15th minute when Hrgović fired home after a quick break and Šego turned the ball into the net, but the effort was ruled out for offside.

The breakthrough eventually came in the 22nd minute, and it came from the same source: Bamba again got to the byline and whipped in a cross from the right, and this time Dalisson rose highest to plant a precise header past Sentić and put Hajduk 1-0 up. It was the Brazilian’s fourth goal in just 15 appearances for the club since arriving on loan from Córdoba in the summer, alongside four assists. It underlined just how well he’s settled in at Poljud.

The tempo dropped considerably after the break. Hajduk were happy to control possession while Slaven struggled to fashion anything in reply. In the 70th minute Dalisson turned provider, squaring for Carlos Martín, who blazed over from a promising position. The game’s defining moment came in the 79th minute, when Filip Mažar was shown a second yellow card for a foul on Dalisson and had to leave the field. With a man advantage for the final stretch, Hajduk saw out the win without any further alarms.

Osijek stunned Dinamo 4-2 in seven-goal thriller

On Saturday, Osijek beat Dinamo 4-2 at Opus Arena in round seven’s other big clash. The hosts were excellent in the first half, racing into a 2-0 lead through Armando León before extending it to 300 with a goal from Luka Vrbančić — only to be made to sweat for the win late on.

Osijek opened the scoring in the 12th minute when Domagoj Bukvić whipped in a cross from the right and León rose highest in the box to head past Dominik Kotarski. The second goal followed in the 34th minute: Dinamo failed to make the most of a chance of their own, and Osijek broke swiftly the other way — after a shot from Ljatifi was saved by Kotarski, León was on hand to bundle the rebound home for 2-0.

Dinamo had a handful of half-chances in the first half without seriously testing Marko Malenica, coming closest through a Miha Zajc free-kick and an Arber Hoxha header from a cross. Mario Kovačević made a triple substitution at the break, but the changes didn’t immediately shift the picture. Osijek kept pushing and made it 3-0 in the 60th minute, when former Dinamo man Luka Vrbančić raced onto a ball in behind after a quick counter and calmly slotted past Kotarski.

Dinamo hit back just a minute later — after a scramble in the box, the ball fell to Zajc, who pulled one back to make it 3-1.

Dinamo pushed hard for a way back into the game in the closing stages. Frane Topić came closest in the 81st minute, heading against a great save from Malenica after a Kačavenda cross. Then, in the 90th minute, Malenica brought down Galešić inside the box, and the referee pointed to the spot. Smail Prevljak converted in the 92nd minute to make it 3-2 and set up a frantic finish.

But Osijek held their nerve, and in the 96th minute they put the result beyond doubt. A major mix-up in the Dinamo defence left Domagoj Bukvić with an empty net to finish into, sealing a 4-2 win. It was a statement victory for Osijek, proof they can go toe-to-toe with the league’s best — and Dinamo’s first league defeat of the season.

World.title: Porsche Made €820 Million on Rimac, €250 Million to go to Pensions
World.content:
September the 14th, 2026 – A consortium led by HOF Capital has officially taken over the stake held by Porsche in the Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac.

The consortium, headed by HOF Capital (with BlueFive Capital as the largest investor), has completed the acquisition of Porsche’s shares in Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac in recent days. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the value of the transaction, fully financed by the consortium’s own funds, is approximately €1 billion. The deal has now been closed, and Rimac Group remains the majority owner of Bugatti Rimac with a 55% stake.

where will this enormous sum go?

Mate Rimac will be supported by a new management team in the new period. Christophe Piochon will step down as President of the Management Board of Bugatti Automobiles and Chief Operating Officer (COO) of Bugatti Rimac. Mate Rimac takes over as President of the Management Board of Bugatti Automobiles, while Marko Brkljačić, former Chief Operating Officer (COO) at Rimac Technology, will join the leadership of Bugatti Rimac as Chief Operating Officer (COO). It is interesting to examine the details of the deal itself, the second-largest M&A transaction in Croatian history, after Barr’s takeover of Pliva back in 2006. From Porsche’s perspective, it was an excellent deal. They once invested €180 million in Rimac and have now realised €1 billion. In other words, Rimac generated €820 million for Porsche. It should be borne in mind that Bugatti had always been unprofitable until last year, when it achieved €200 million in EBITDA.

supervisory boards

To maintain control over its investment, HOF Capital holds three seats on the supervisory boards of both Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac. It is also curious to see how Porsche will use the money it has earned. According to announcements by Dr Jochen Breckner, Member of the Porsche Executive Board responsible for Finance and IT, €250 million will go into the company’s pension fund — specifically for the pensions of Porsche employees. Taking into account the cash inflow and the further funding of pension obligations, the net cash flow margin of Porsche’s automotive segment for the full year 2026 is expected to rise to 5.5–7.5% (previous forecast: 3–5%). Porsche will now focus on its core business.

This is a diplomatic way of saying that the company now has other priorities, including improving profitability and directing resources towards its own product range. Such a move was, in any case, expected after Porsche’s operating profit fell by as much as 93% last year. On the other hand, for Rimac this deal is confirmation of the value he has created, because it is worth remembering that this was Porsche’s first investment in history. They invested the largest amount of capital in Rimac Group, and Rimac was the only one that ultimately integrated components into their cars. Not only that, all of Porsche’s other similar partnerships ended fairly badly. Those projects either no longer exist or are barely surviving, so they are unlikely to bring any tangible benefits. Hisham Elhaddad, co-founder and managing partner of HOF Capital, appeared on Bloomberg News to discuss the completed acquisition of Porsche’s stakes in Bugatti Rimac and Rimac Group by HOF Capital. With this move, HOF has become the largest shareholder in Rimac Group alongside Mate Rimac, and Hisham has joined the supervisory boards of both Bugatti Rimac and Rimac Group.

“We entered Rimac Group back in 2022, but as a small investor with only a one-per-cent stake. So we have been following this story for five years, and especially since Mate Rimac became CEO, when we saw a major positive turnaround. After all, last year was a record year in Bugatti’s 117-year history. We have now completed a transaction worth more than €1 billion and our stake has jumped to 23.5% in Rimac Group and 45% in Bugatti Rimac,” says Elhaddad. 55 percent of the stake in Bugatti Rimac will be held by Rimac, with the remainder by HOF Capital.

a sense of optimism

He added that the investment in Rimac actually fits well with their investment strategy, which over the past ten years has brought a series of investments in the tech sector. “We’ve invested in SpaceX and in Anthropic. We see an explosion of projects in the AI segment on the market. We believe that in the next five to ten years AI will be widely adopted. Value will lie in uniqueness and exclusivity, and there really is no better company than Bugatti where we can see that. Bugatti has survived both world wars, and even this recent crisis. If you want your Bugatti model, you have to wait four or five years. We are excited about the partnership with Mate Rimac and his exceptional team and want to increase the value of this iconic brand. For HOF, this deal is a natural step from our roots in venture capital towards leading complex transactions that cover the entire capital structure,” Elhaddad concluded.

In order to have good control over its investment, HOF Capital now holds three seats on the supervisory boards of Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac. Hisham Elhaddad has joined the supervisory boards of Rimac Group and Bugatti Rimac, while Josh Klaczek, a partner at HOF Capital, joins the supervisory board of Rimac Group as the second representative of the firm.

World.title: Will Restrictions on Croatian Short-Term Rentals Solve Housing Crisis?
World.content:
September the 14th, 2026 – The Association of Family Hosts say that more restrictions on Croatian short-term rentals absolutely won’t solve the ongoing housing crisis, and certainly not without solid evidence.

In response to the recently presented proposal for a European Regulation on affordable housing, the Croatian Association “Save the Small Family Hosts” (SMOi) has issued a sharp appeal to the public and the Government of the Republic of Croatia. Morski reports that the aforementioned association has warned of the risk of shifting blame for the housing crisis onto citizens engaged in family tourism and stress that any restrictions are being introduced without concrete data and analysis of the actual impact. Association president Vedran Tomić emphasises that they support housing affordability, but states that a structural problem cannot be solved by restricting the constitutional right to the legal use of one’s own property.

european data leaves many scratching their heads…

In cooperation with the European Holiday Home Association (EHHA), the SMOi association recalls that the European system for collecting data on short-term rentals is not yet fully operational and that the first comparable data will only be available in 2028. Introducing bans before then is considered decisions based on assumptions rather than facts, while the numbers themselves clearly refute the current accusations. While short-term rentals account for only about 1.2 percent of the EU housing stock, and in Croatia even less than one percent, at the same time around 40 percent of Croatia’s housing stock is completely out of residential use.

In addition, while the number of beds offered by family hosts in Croatia has been stable for years, ranging between 650,000 and 670,000, non-commercial accommodation in the form of holiday houses and apartments has experienced explosive growth, from 355,000 in 2016 to more than 700,000 in 2025. That abolished apartments do not automatically become available housing is also proven by the example of Barcelona, where despite the freezing of rental licences, rents per square metre rose by as much as 72 percent.

damage to the local economy and to family budgets

The association emphasises that family accommodation is not a business empire, but a key source of income for topping up the household budget and maintaining family heritage. Shutting it down directly harms the wider local economy, affecting craftsmen, builders, restaurateurs and shops. As a warning example they cite the French Basque Country, where after the introduction of bans and the withdrawal of around 6,000 apartments, only 5 percent of the properties returned to year-round rental, with a projected loss of 230 million euros and the endangerment of more than 4,000 jobs.

an appeal to the croatian government: try focusing on some actual problems

SMOi is not seeking complete deregulation, but clear and fair rules that must be temporary, locally targeted and based on cause-and-effect evidence. Instead of a witch hunt, they call on the Croatian Government to direct housing policy towards encouraging new housing construction and activating empty properties, while clearly distinguishing family accommodation from non-commercial and speculative capital, and protecting domestic hosts in European negotiations.

“Before introducing bans, it’s necessary to quantify how many specific apartments will actually be returned to the market, because if that cannot be proven, then the housing crisis is not being solved, instead, people are being harmed and corporate investors in resorts are being directly favoured,” concluded Hana Matić, vice-president of the association.

World.title: New Rental Rules in Croatia Coming in 2027
World.content:
September the 14th, 2026 – New rental rules are set to come into force in Croatia as of January the 1st, 2027. It would provide protections for both tenants and landlords.

The Croatian Government is currently busy preparing a new Law on the Rental of Apartments that aims to more clearly regulate relations between tenants and landlords, limit arbitrary rent increases, and speed up eviction procedures when a contract is not respected. The new law is expected to enter into force on the 1st of January 2027. Index reports that one of the main reasons for adopting the new law is the strong growth in the number of long-term rental contracts. According to current data, their number has risen from 100,000 to 240,000 in the last six years, that’s almost two and a half times.

rent can only be increased once per year

One of the more important novelties is the restriction on rent increases. Under the proposal, rent could be raised only once a year, and the increase could not exceed the rate of growth in residential property prices. It has been stated that this rate currently stands between 14 and 15 percent this year. The goal, it was explained, is to give tenants greater legal certainty and prevent situations in which the rental price is changed arbitrarily or without clear rules.

notaries will be needed for rental contracts

The new law also envisages the mandatory conclusion of contracts before a notary public. This way, both parties would be more clearly informed of their rights and obligations, and the contracts would also contain enforceable clauses. This should enable faster action in the event of a breach of contract, without lengthy court proceedings. State Secretary Željko Uhlir said that if eviction becomes necessary, it would proceed according to clearly prescribed deadlines and steps. First there would be a warning, and if that produced no result, an enforcement procedure based on the solemnised contract would follow.

the landlord bears the cost

According to the state secretary, the cost of solemnising any rental contract would be borne solely by the landlord. Uhlir said such a procedure would have multiple benefits: the notary would familiarise both parties with the provisions of the contract, the security of both the tenant and the landlord would increase, and the contract would be directly linked to the Tax Administration.

easier eviction procedures for contract violations

The new law should at the same time increase security for apartment owners. One of the problems landlords often highlight is the length of the procedure for evicting a tenant who does not respect the contract. According to Uhlir, the new law introduces clear deadlines and procedures, and the contract would be enforceable without the need for prior court proceedings. This should significantly speed up eviction in cases where the legal conditions for it exist.

cracking down on the rental black market

A major problem remains unregistered long-term rentals. It has been stated that the Croatian Government wants to increase the number of legally registered contracts and link the rental system with the Tax Administration. Uhlir said that the introduction of the real-estate tax has already prompted some owners who were on the black market to legalise their rentals. He also noted that from 2024 to 2025 the number of rental contracts increased by 75,000.

The report also stressed that a greater supply of apartments for rent cannot be achieved without protecting property owners. Experts have clearly warned that an owner who fears they will not be able to regain the property within the agreed time or under the agreed conditions will either factor that risk into the price or withdraw the apartment from the market altogether. The new law should soon enter the regular parliamentary procedure and is planned to enter into force on the 1st of January, 2027.

World.title: Brač Resident on the Fire: “I’m 80, I’ve Never Experienced Anything Like This”
World.content:
September the 14th, 2026 – One Brač resident has spoken out about the fire that has so far burned an area larger than Rijeka on the island, claiming to never have experienced anything like it in his life.

Zorislav Bonačić Sargo, a local chronicler of Milna and the western part of the island of Brač, and the first mayor of the Municipality of Milna, says he does not remember a fire like this. “I’m 80 years old, and I’ve never experienced anything like this. So this situation with a fire site like this, which has already been going on for several days, is difficult. The changes in the wind that happened during the night, that was unprecedented,” he said for Croatian Radio.

Index reports that Zorislav Bonačić Sargo has long been a well-known name in Milna. He is also known as a chronicler of local history and heritage; he has published a book dedicated to Milna, its dialect, maritime and shipbuilding tradition, and the everyday life of the place. Damjan Tomašić, owner of apartments in Osibova Bay, added that the firefighters did an outstanding job. “The biggest problem of all is the disorder in the state, where people should by law be cleaning their plots. That’s why this is happening to us,” he said.

hundreds evacuated by sea

As a reminder, the fire on Brač broke out in the area of Ložišća on Thursday and over the past few days repeatedly spread under the influence of strong winds. Last night was particularly difficult, when the fire approached houses and bays in the Milna area, including Duboka, Lučice and Osibova. Some residents and tourists were then moved to safer locations. People were also evacuated by sea, with the help of boats from the Harbour Master’s Office, maritime police, Coast Guard, Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS), tourist boats and private vessels. Some people were accommodated in Milna and other reception locations.

During the worst night, firefighters defended buildings and stopped the spread of the fire toward inhabited areas. Hundreds of firefighters with dozens of vehicles were on the ground, assisted by Canadair water bombers and other firefighting aircraft. Canadairs have remained present because of open flames, but the situation is calmer.

World.title: Croats more Generous Than Most Europeans: 68% Have Donated Money
World.content:
September the 13th, 2026 – Croats seem to generally be more generous than most Europeans as a new survey reveals that as much as 68% of them have donated money to various charitable causes.

Research shows that the decision to donate is influenced not only by the financial resources a person has at their disposal, but also by a sense of belonging to the community, personal values and trust in the organisations that receive donations. Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni that Croatia is actually among the leaders in the share of income that citizens give for donations.

Croatian citizens set aside more for others than most Europeans. According to a new report by the Charities Aid Foundation (CAF), 68% of Croatian citizens donated money during 2025, whether to charitable organisations, directly to people in need or for religious purposes.

a culture of solidarity

Domestic donors most often provide direct help to people in need, while donations to organisations are mainly directed towards local and national civil society organisations, states the National Foundation for Civil Society Development, according to CAF data. Research shows that the decision to donate is influenced not only by the financial resources a person has at their disposal, but also by a sense of belonging to the community, personal values and trust in the organisations that receive donations. Countries in which citizens feel a stronger connection with their local communities also record a significantly higher level of giving. Social connectedness is important for the development of philanthropy. The share of income that residents of Croatia set aside through various forms of financial assistance places our country in second place among European Union members, behind Romania, where that share is 0.9 percent, and ahead of Ireland with 0.7 percent. Domestic organisations that we asked for comment are not surprised by such a level of generosity.

“Croatia’s high position did not completely surprise us. In Croatia there is a strong culture of solidarity and helping, especially when it comes to concrete people and needs. Over the past 10 years we have recorded greater visibility and diversity of philanthropic activities and citizens’ readiness to help. It is important to further develop this culture of giving towards longer-term forms of philanthropy,” said Smiljana Rađa, Managing Director of the European Foundation for Philanthropy and Social Development.

From Croatian Caritas they said that, although they currently do not have consolidated statistical data with which they could give a precise answer to the question about donation trends, they confirm the tendency towards mutual help. “From our everyday experience we can confirm that the solidarity of Croatian citizens and companies is extremely great, especially in moments of crisis, which coincides with the positive trends cited by CAF,” they told us from Croatian Caritas.

donations directly to those in need

Of the 0.8 percent of citizens’ income that is on average set aside for various forms of giving, as much as 0.4 percent goes directly to people in need, while 0.2 percent goes to charitable organisations and the same amount for religious purposes. In other words, Croatian citizens on average direct twice as large a part of their income directly to individuals than to organisations.

“This shows that in Croatia there is strong direct solidarity; citizens often want to help a concrete person or family. At the same time, there is room for greater trust in civil society organisations, which can turn donations into long-term and systematic support for a larger number of people,” said Rađa.

between 10 and 19 euros

Research by the National Foundation for Civil Society Development from 2024 also showed what typical Croatian donating looks like. According to the research on citizens’ donating habits in Croatia, as many as 67 percent of citizens would rather donate to local than to international organisations, while the most common donation amount is between 10 and 19 euros. Donating is at the same time strongly connected with concrete circumstances. Around 53 percent of citizens say that crisis situations prompt them to donate, while 46.3 percent with higher personal incomes would donate more. Total donations in the three largest economies of the European Union, Germany, France and Italy, in 2025 on average amounted to only 0.4 percent of income. Europeans on average donated 0.6 percent of their income, compared to the global average of one percent.
