World.title: Kashagan Expansion Could Reshape Kazakhstan’s Oil Export Needs, Experts Say
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan may face new oil infrastructure requirements in the next decade if plans to increase production at the Kashagan field significantly move forward, even as the country seeks to more than double domestic refining capacity by 2040. Experts say the timing of production growth, refinery projects and export infrastructure will be crucial.

The draft 2027-2029 national budget assumes oil production of 96 million tons in 2027, an oil price of $70 per barrel and an exchange rate of 480 tenge per US dollar. Oil-sector revenues to the National Fund are projected at 3.78 trillion tenge (US$8.5 billion).

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan plans to raise annual refining capacity from around 18 million tons to nearly 40 million tons by 2040.

Kashagan is the wildcard

Oil and gas expert Abzal Narymbetov does not expect Kazakhstan to produce more crude than it can transport and export immediately. However, expanding refining capacity will take years given the scale of investment required.

“Any large capital-intensive project that requires a technological process, such as building a new refinery, is quite complex. It will require time, capital, money and resources,” Narymbetov told The Astana Times.

The longer-term picture could change if Kazakhstan significantly increases production at Kashagan, according to Nurlan Zhumagulov, executive director of the Energy Monitor Fund.

“If Kazakhstan finally manages to implement Phase 2 [second-stage expansion of oil production] at Kashagan, then a new oil pipeline will be needed,” Zhumagulov said in comments to The Astana Times.

He said one potential option could involve transporting additional crude from Atyrau towards the Mangystau Region and then across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, by subsea pipeline or tankers. He estimated that such a route could potentially handle up to 37 million tons annually.

Refining cannot simply replace exports

Expanding domestic refining will give Kazakhstan more flexibility, but it cannot simply substitute for crude exports. Narymbetov said directing more crude to the domestic market could mean losing export revenues while still supporting domestic fuel prices.

“If we direct it to the domestic market, we will lose, first, export revenue, and second, we will subsidize the domestic market. So it is a double loss,” he said.

The issue also has a consumer dimension. Zhumagulov said that if refining reaches 40 million tons, fuel prices would eventually need to become market-based, but household incomes would need to rise accordingly.

“The question is whether people will be ready to pay world prices for petroleum products. That is a separate issue, because higher wages and incomes would be needed first,” he said.

The infrastructure race

Kazakhstan’s challenge is therefore not simply how much oil it can produce, but whether it will have enough economically viable options to process or export it when production changes.

The 96 million tons projected for 2027 is a near-term planning assumption. The bigger uncertainty lies beyond it: if Kashagan production expands while new refineries and alternative export routes are still being developed, infrastructure could become a constraint.

For Kazakhstan, the key will be ensuring that production growth, refining investment and export capacity develop in the right sequence.

World.title: Tokayev Honors South Korean Figures as Kazakhstan-Korea Ties Deepen
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Sept. 14 presented the Order of Dostyk (Friendship), second degree, to five prominent South Korean state and public figures for their contribution to strengthening Kazakhstan-Korea relations, as cooperation between the two countries continues to expand into practical areas including employment, trade, investment and technology.

The awards ceremony was held in Seoul during Tokayev’s state visit to South Korea. Addressing participants, Tokayev emphasized the longstanding friendship between the Kazakh and Korean peoples and described South Korea as a strategic partner of Kazakhstan, Akorda reported.

“Despite the fact that our countries are separated by significant distances, we are brought closer by mutual respect and common interests,” Tokayev said, highlighting South Korea’s economic achievements and international standing.

He noted that the two countries adopted a Declaration on Enhanced Strategic Partnership five years ago and have continued to strengthen political dialogue and cooperation across multiple sectors, including mechanical engineering, energy, metallurgy and advanced technologies.

Employment links add new dimension to cooperation

Recent developments are also creating new opportunities for people-to-people cooperation. Kazakhstan was officially included in South Korea’s Employment Permit System (EPS) in August, becoming the 18th participating country. The first recruitment of Kazakh workers under the system is expected to begin in 2028 following the completion of the necessary procedures.

Dmitry Lee, an entrepreneur living in South Korea, said the development of legal employment opportunities illustrates how bilateral relations are increasingly translating into practical opportunities for citizens.

“Kazakhstan and South Korea continue to develop bilateral relations. One of the most recent significant developments is the expansion of opportunities for Kazakhstan citizens to work legally in South Korea. This is one of the agreements that really demonstrates in practice how relations between Kazakhstan and South Korea are developing,” Lee told The Astana Times.

He also pointed to the broader cultural ties between the two countries, saying that Kazakhstan and South Korea share mutual respect that extends beyond economic cooperation.

Korean community strengthens people-to-people links

Tokayev likewise highlighted the contribution of South Korean companies operating in Kazakhstan and the growing cultural and humanitarian ties between the two countries.

Particular attention was given to Kazakhstan’s Korean community, which numbers more than 100,000 people. Tokayev said the Koryo-saram community plays an important role in the country’s economic and social development and helps strengthen national unity and solidarity.

He noted that Korean cultural centers operate in Kazakhstan, while the Korean Academic Theatre in Almaty remains popular with audiences. Korean-language media, including a newspaper and a dedicated radio program, are also produced in the country.

“The strengthening of friendship between Kazakhstan and Korea meets the common interests of our two peoples,” Tokayev said, describing the awards as a sign of Kazakhstan’s respect and recognition.

Professor Song Young-hoon of Hankuk University of Foreign Studies has taught the Kazakh language for more than 20 years, helping introduce the Korean public to Kazakhstan and its culture. He thanked President Tokayev for the award and expressed appreciation for the recognition of his contribution to strengthening ties between the two countries.

“I have come to believe that Kazakhstan is the most developed country in Central Asia. Through recent reforms, the country has been making important steps forward in its development. I believe that the upcoming summit will further strengthen relations between Kazakhstan and South Korea and open up broader opportunities for cooperation in the future,” he said in the Kazakh language.

World.title: Oil Transport via Kazakhstan-China Pipeline Rises to 13.1 Million Tons
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan transported 13.121 million tons of oil through the Kazakhstan-China Pipeline in January-August, up 2% year-on-year, underscoring the route’s role in Kazakhstan’s oil transportation network and exports to China.

Oil freight turnover along the route reached 11.879 billion ton-kilometers, increasing 3% compared with the same period last year, according to KazTransOil.

The Kazakhstan-China pipeline system remains one of Kazakhstan’s key oil export routes, connecting the country’s oil-producing regions with the Chinese market and supporting the diversification of its export infrastructure.

Broader pipeline network

Overall, KazTransOil transported 30.639 million tons of oil through its main pipeline system in January-August, up 4% year-on-year.

Oil transportation through the MunaiTas Northwest Pipeline Company LLP system reached 4.302 million tons, up 10% year-on-year, while freight turnover increased 8% to 1.784 billion ton-kilometers.

The Batumi Oil Terminal group handled 1.251 million tons of oil, petroleum products and gas, up 3% compared with the same period of 2025.

Expanding Caspian route

The figures come as Kazakhstan continues to diversify its oil transportation and export routes, including efforts to increase shipments via the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan.

In an exclusive interview with Trend, Kuanysh Keskinbayev, Deputy General Director for Commercial Affairs at KMG Kashagan B.V., said Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan were working to optimize oil supply chains and increase transit volumes.

“We have a general agreement under which we operate. Under this agreement, we are constantly working to increase transit volumes. However, frankly speaking, the most important issue is the economics of the route. Because it’s a very long, multimodal route, we are currently actively working to resolve this issue,” Keskinbayev said.

Nearly 250,000 tons of oil from Kashagan and approximately 1.5 million tons from Tengiz are shipped via Azerbaijan annually, according to Keskinbayev.

Oil prices

The increase in transportation comes amid higher global oil prices. On Monday, Brent crude futures rose 2.69% to $107.42 per barrel, while WTI gained 2.73% to $102.78. Urals crude increased 8.31% to $103.70 per barrel.

World.title: Moving to Kazakhstan? Kazakhstan Introduces Kazakh Language Test Requirement
World.content:
ASTANA – People seeking kandas (ethnic Kazakhs returning to their historical homeland) status or permanent residence in Kazakhstan must take an online KAZTEST as part of a new pilot system assessing applicants’ potential for integration and permanent residence.

The pilot project came into effect on Feb. 16, introducing a new procedure that combines a Kazakh language test, a migrant questionnaire and an interview. The system applies to ethnic Kazakhs seeking kandas status as well as foreign nationals and stateless persons planning to reside permanently in Kazakhstan.

The KAZTEST component assesses practical knowledge of the Kazakh language rather than advanced academic proficiency. According to the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of the Population, the test focuses on understanding Kazakh in everyday situations and on whether applicants can comprehend spoken and written information needed for daily life and adaptation.

What does the test include?

The online test includes 60 multiple-choice questions in two sections: listening (20 questions, 20 minutes) and reading (40 questions, 50 minutes).

The total testing time is one hour and 10 minutes. Applicants must achieve at least 70% in each section to receive a certificate. Results are issued within three working days after the test and completion of the proctoring review.

The test is conducted under an online proctoring system. Candidates are therefore expected to have a functioning camera and microphone and a stable internet connection. Mobile phones, headphones, smartwatches, other electronic devices and study materials are prohibited during the test.

If a candidate does not reach the required score, the procedure allows two additional attempts within 30 calendar days of the last attempt.

Preparation is available

Applicants can prepare through adaptation and integration centers, where they can receive consultations, learn about the test format and complete practice tasks.

The aim is to help applicants understand the assessment structure in advance rather than approach it as an academic language exam.

The introduction of the KAZTEST requirement has prompted mixed reactions. Some kandas and observers have raised concerns that the test could be difficult for applicants who speak Kazakh but have limited reading skills, particularly those who have studied the language using a different alphabet.

In May, Murat Abenov, a former deputy of the Mazhilis, Kazakhstan’s lower house of the former Parliament, said he had received several complaints from kandas and noted that some ethnic Kazakhs returning to Kazakhstan do not know the Cyrillic alphabet.

At the same time, supporters of the requirement note that basic knowledge of the Kazakh language is a reasonable condition for people planning to live permanently in Kazakhstan. The ministry said the assessment aims to determine whether applicants have sufficient practical Kazakh-language skills for everyday communication and integration. Similar language requirements are also used internationally in procedures for permanent residence or citizenship.

Part of a broader migration assessment

KAZTEST is only the first stage of the broader assessment. After completing the language test, applicants proceed to a questionnaire covering personal, educational and professional information, followed by verification procedures and an interview.

For kandas, the new procedure is part of a wider pilot system for determining an applicant’s eligibility for kandas status. The rules also require those receiving kandas status to relocate to government-designated settlement regions.

The pilot is currently scheduled to remain in force through Dec. 31, meaning the procedure could still be adjusted based on implementation experience.

World.title: Why Reading Matters in Age of AI? Kazakhstan’s PISA Results Offer Answer
World.content:
ASTANA — The latest PISA 2025 results reveal a tension likely to grow more important in the years ahead: how can a country prepare young people for an economy shaped by AI without allowing technology to displace the foundational skills that make knowledge useful in the first place? For Kazakhstan, the question is particularly relevant. The country has made significant progress in digital readiness, but those advances have not yet translated into the level of reading, mathematics, science and problem-solving performance that Kazakhstan needs.

The country scored 385 points in reading in PISA 2025, compared with an OECD average of 461. Its mathematics score was 414, against 463 for the OECD, while science stood at 420 versus 482. In the new computational problem-solving assessment, Kazakhstan scored 449 compared with an OECD average of 500. Mathematics declined by 12 points from the 2022 assessment, while reading remained broadly unchanged. The results are based on 22,680 students from 643 schools, representing around 324,600 15-year-olds nationwide.

The mathematics results are difficult to overlook. Kazakhstan remains far behind the strongest-performing education systems, with B-S-J-Z (China) at 612 points, Singapore at 563, Macao at 549, Chinese Taipei at 546 and Japan at 525. At the same time, Kazakhstan is part of a broader international trend: mathematics performance has declined across many education systems. Across the OECD, the average mathematics score fell by nine points between 2022 and 2025, while the decline over the longer 2015–2025 period was 22 points

The PISA paradox

Reading, however, raises a different and perhaps deeper question because it concerns the very capacity students need in order to make sense of all those other sources of information.

Andreas Schleicher, OECD Director for Education and Skills and head of the PISA program, describes the latest findings on AI and education as “somewhat sobering,” noting that the students who perform best academically tend, as a rule, to use AI less often.

“Reading has always been the foundation of all other skills, so this is particularly important. What worries me most is the decline in those reading skills that are becoming increasingly important in the age of AI: the ability to compare information from different sources, distinguish facts from opinions and navigate ambiguous information,” he said.

That distinction matters. Reading is not simply the ability to understand the words on a page. It is the ability to follow an argument, recognize its assumptions, weigh evidence and decide whether one interpretation is more convincing than another. Those are precisely the kinds of tasks that become more, not less, important when people are surrounded by an enormous volume of machine-generated information.

Schleicher says the problem is not only that reading habits are changing, but that the quality of engagement with information may be changing as well.

“Young people have started to read faster, but at the same time less accurately. Of course, this cannot be called a healthy trend. Perhaps new technologies place fewer demands on young people in terms of critical thinking, making sense of information, comparing it and critically evaluating it. They increasingly become consumers of already prepared knowledge. Unfortunately, these changes in behavior are also reflected in learning outcomes,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s results illustrate why this matters. Only 36% of Kazakh students reached at least Level 2 proficiency in reading, compared with 69% across the OECD. At the higher end, almost no students in Kazakhstan reached Level 5 or above, compared with 6% across the OECD. Reading remained broadly unchanged from 2022, but stability at a comparatively low level is not necessarily reassuring, particularly when the skill itself underpins performance across other subjects.

At the same time, Kazakhstan does not fit a simple narrative of technological backwardness. Forty-seven percent of Kazakh students report using AI chatbots at least weekly to support their learning, close to the OECD average of 45.5%. More than 80% say they have learned at school how to assess AI-generated information, compared with 62.6% across the OECD, while around 85% attend schools with subject-specific guidelines on using digital devices. This combination of relatively strong digital preparedness and weaker foundational performance is one of the most interesting features of Kazakhstan’s PISA results.

Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, notes that the country should not read the results simply as a verdict of failure.

“These numbers matter. In an age when access to generative AI is becoming almost universal, the central educational question is no longer whether students can use AI. It is whether they can question it, verify it and use it without surrendering their own judgement,” Raza said.

His assessment of reading, however, is more pointed. According to him, digital competence cannot compensate for weak comprehension.

“AI literacy without strong foundational literacy risks becoming technological fluency without intellectual depth,” he said.

That may be the central paradox for education in the AI era. A generation can become increasingly comfortable with technology while becoming less comfortable with the slower, more demanding process of understanding something for itself.

When AI makes answers easy

The consequences extend beyond the classroom. A student who cannot follow a complicated argument will have difficulty evaluating an AI-generated explanation. A future engineer who cannot distinguish evidence from assertion may struggle to assess technical information. A policymaker who relies entirely on summaries becomes increasingly dependent on whoever produced the summary. And a citizen who cannot compare competing accounts becomes more vulnerable to simplified narratives and manipulation.

This is why reading should not be treated merely as a cultural preference, something desirable for educated people but secondary to the supposedly more practical skills of the digital economy. The PISA results suggest almost the opposite: reading is becoming a form of intellectual infrastructure.

Raza emphasizes that the answer is not to retreat from technological transformation.

“This should not lead Kazakhstan to slow its digital transformation. It suggests the opposite, the country now needs to deepen it. The next phase should move from measuring access and adoption towards measuring what technology actually contributes to learning. AI should increasingly be used to strengthen reasoning, feedback, inquiry and personalized support rather than simply to generate answers. Teacher development should focus not only on how to operate new tools, but on designing learning tasks in which students must explain, defend, verify and improve what AI produces,” he notes.

That is a more useful way of thinking about the role of technology in education. The question is not whether schools should use AI, because reality has already largely settled that debate. The question is whether the technology helps students become more capable thinkers, or simply makes it easier for them to avoid thinking.

Schleicher makes the same point through a much simpler analogy: “it is impossible to become physically strong simply by watching sports training.”

“To become stronger, you have to exercise yourself. In the same way, students do not become smarter simply by consuming ready-made content. They become smarter when they make their own effort,” he said.

Some of the effort removed by technology is precisely the effort through which learning occurs: reading a difficult passage twice, staying with an unfamiliar argument, discovering that two sources contradict each other, trying to formulate a response without assistance, or realizing that an apparently convincing answer does not withstand closer examination. This is also where reading and mathematics become part of the same conversation.

Gazis Abishev, a political analyst, commenting on the PISA results, focuses on Kazakhstan’s 414-point mathematics score and the 12-point decline from 2022 as a serious warning. He acknowledges the broader international context, including the effects of the pandemic and the increasing presence of mobile phones and neural networks, as well as Kazakhstan’s relatively large rural population.

“Of course, on average mathematics has declined in many countries. Children were affected by the pandemic lockdown, plus the active penetration of mobile phones and neural networks. Kazakhstan also has a larger rural population. It is easier to educate children in urban lyceums in Singapore. But nevertheless, a gap of one and a half hundred points is a fairly serious problem,” Abishev wrote on his Telegram channel.

He gave a blunt prescription: “Mathematics, mathematics, mathematics. More mathematics at all levels.” But he also calls for “the cult of reading”: accessible books, the promotion of literature, debates, essay competitions and a stronger intellectual culture.

The two recommendations are not as far apart as they may appear. Both math and reading depend on sustained attention, and both are increasingly challenged by an information environment built around speed, convenience and constant novelty.

The cost of losing attention

That is why the renewed discussion about reading in Kazakhstan matters beyond the education sector. In May 2026, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree on measures to develop a reading culture and form a “reading nation,” making the development of reading culture and the formation of a reading nation a priority of state policy in culture, education and innovation. The document also calls for new library formats, wider access to books and a national concept to promote reading culture in the age of AI.

There is something timely about that agenda. Reading is being elevated as a national priority precisely as technology makes it easier to generate, summarize and redistribute written information. In that environment, the scarce resource may no longer be access to text but the ability to stay with it long enough to understand it.

This does not mean Kazakhstan should choose books over technology, or classrooms over digital tools. Its own PISA results point to a more demanding conclusion: the country needs both, but it must ensure that technological progress strengthens rather than substitutes for foundational learning.

“At the same time, reading and mathematical reasoning should remain at the centre of the reform agenda. These are not skills from a pre-digital age. They are the foundations that allow students to navigate an AI-rich one,” said Raza.

That may be the clearest way to read the PISA results. Kazakhstan does not need to retreat from the digital future. It needs to make sure that the children entering that future have enough intellectual depth to navigate it.

A reading nation is not simply a nation of people who read more books. It is a society that has developed the habit of paying attention to an argument long enough to understand it, to evidence long enough to test it, and to another person’s point of view long enough to consider that it might contain something the first answer did not.

In an age when machines can increasingly process information for us, attention may be one of the most valuable human advantages left.

World.title: Elena Rybakina’s Historic Rise to World No. 1 Culminates in US Open Triumph
World.content:
ASTANA – Elena Rybakina has officially become the new World No. 1 in women’s singles, making history as the first Kazakh tennis player to top the WTA rankings, and has crowned the milestone with victory at the U.S. Open.

Rybakina defeated Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the U.S. Open final on Sept. 13 in New York.

The victory secured Rybakina’s third Grand Slam singles title. She won her first major at Wimbledon in 2022 and claimed the Australian Open title earlier this year.

Following the tournament, Rybakina moved from second to first place in the WTA rankings with 9,901 points, ahead of Sabalenka with 7,875 and U.S. Jessica Pegula with 7,265 points.

Her rise to the top was confirmed after her semifinal victory over China’s Zheng Qinwen, which guaranteed her the No. 1 ranking regardless of the final result. Rybakina subsequently capped her historic campaign by lifting the U.S. Open trophy.

At 27, Rybakina became the 30th woman in WTA history to reach the world No. 1 position.

President of the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation Bulat Utemuratov congratulated Rybakina on her achievement, calling it “a tremendous victory for Elena and a historic day for Kazakhstan’s tennis.”

World.title: South Korea Meets Central Asia: What is at Stake at Seoul Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and the leaders of all five Central Asian states will meet in Seoul on Sept. 16 for their first summit, seeking to turn nearly two decades of ministerial dialogue into a leader-level partnership focused on critical minerals, energy and resilient supply chains.

Lee has described Central Asia as a region of considerable growth potential, reported his press office. His office said the summit would establish a leader-level multilateral framework, diversify South Korea’s supply chains and give new momentum to its New Northern Policy, which seeks to deepen ties across Eurasia.

The summit’s significance, however, will hinge on whether the six governments can translate those ambitions into commercially viable projects with buyers, financing, transport routes and institutions responsible for implementation.

The Korea–Central Asia Cooperation Forum was launched in 2007, followed by the establishment of a permanent secretariat in Seoul in 2017. The Sept. 16 meeting marks the first time the dialogue will be elevated to the leaders’ level. Tokayev arrived in Seoul on Sept. 14 and is expected to meet Lee ahead of the multilateral gathering.

One region, five different partnerships

Nargiza Murataliyeva, an associate professor at the American University of Central Asia in Bishkek, said the mechanism has demonstrated its value in trade, official development assistance and environmental cooperation.

“Previous meetings, however, were largely sector-specific and practical in scope,” she told The Astana Times.

“The shift from ministerial meetings to full-fledged leaders’ summits, along with the dialogue’s alignment with the K-Silk Road initiative, marks an effort to move beyond individual projects toward a more systematic geoeconomic partnership,” said the professor.

The regional format, however, brings together five countries with different economic relationships with South Korea.

Mehmet Fatih Oztarsu, a professor at Joongbu University and deputy director of the Seoul Institute of Global Affairs, said South Korea has gradually moved away from treating Central Asia as a single economic space since the forum was established in 2007. Although the regional format provides an institutional umbrella, Seoul has increasingly tailored its bilateral ties to the different strengths and opportunities each country offers.

“This is why I would be careful about speaking of a single Korean strategy for Central Asia. Korea is actually developing several different relationships under the same regional framework,” Oztarsu told The Astana Times.

Kazakhstan has emerged as South Korea’s leading resource and energy partner in Central Asia, the expert said. He estimated that South Korean imports of Kazakh mineral fuels could reach nearly $1 billion.

The relationship is now expanding into new areas, including lithium exploration and potential nuclear energy cooperation.

“Uzbekistan is a very different story. Its significance does not come mainly from what Korea imports from it. The relationship is built around industrial cooperation, technology transfer and local production. More than 700 Korean companies operate there, and projects such as the Ustyurt Gas Chemical Complex created a level of industrial integration that Korea has not achieved elsewhere in the region,” said Oztarsu.

The Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan have gained strategic importance as demand for critical minerals has grown, the expert said. Tajikistan holds significant antimony reserves, while the Kyrgyz Republic offers rare earth potential and substantial hydropower capacity. Turkmenistan, by contrast, remains primarily a market for South Korean engineering and petrochemical companies.

“This differentiation is actually one of the strengths of Korea’s regional policy. Seoul does not need to offer the same model to every country. It can provide mining technology in one case, industrial processing in another, and digital infrastructure or education elsewhere,” said Oztarsu.

“Therefore, what makes this interesting is that Korea does not necessarily need to compete with Russia or China everywhere and in the same way. Its strength is specialization,” he added.

Moving beyond raw material exports

Across these relationships, Central Asian governments share a common objective: attracting Korean capital without remaining merely suppliers of raw materials or markets for finished products.

“Kazakhstan should use the summit to strengthen its capacity to produce and export higher-value goods. The most substantial outcomes would connect Korean investment with production in Kazakhstan and give local enterprises a realistic route into supply chains,” Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, told The Astana Times.

He pointed to the KIA plant in Kostanai in northern Kazakhstan as an example.

“According to the Kazakh government’s June 2026 report, the plant represents an investment of $310 million and employed around 800 people at that time. The next task is to develop suppliers around such enterprises and connect technical education with their production needs. This is how an individual investment can generate wider industrial activity,” Kurmashev explained.

Bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and the South Korea reached $3.17 billion in 2025, up 1.3% from $3.13 billion in 2024, according to government figures. Trade between the two countries was $1.3 billion from January through June, while Kazakhstan’s exports to South Korea increased by 17.2%.

Since 2005, gross investments from South Korea to Kazakhstan have surpassed $12 billion, according to figures from the National Bank.

In an August interview with The Astana Times, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea Jung Ki-Hong said critical minerals would be featured prominently in talks in Seoul .

In this area, Kazakhstan also wants foreign investment to support domestic processing rather than extraction alone. Kurmashev said the country will benefit from “partnerships that include commercially viable processing and access to Korean buyers.”

“A long-term purchase contract can give a processing project a stronger basis for financing, provided that the plant can meet the buyer’s requirements at a competitive cost. The location of a deposit alone does not establish the case for building a factory,” he said.

Transport cooperation goes hand in hand and should support these production decisions. “A manufacturer needs to know whether it can receive components and deliver finished goods reliably. An agreement that reduces uncertainty on an existing route could therefore have immediate economic value,” said Kurmashev.

“For Kazakhstan, the strategic gain would be a broader choice of technologies and export markets. That would give its policy of diversifying external partnerships a stronger economic foundation,” he added.

Energy security

Energy has emerged as a common thread in South Korea’s engagement across Central Asia. The region’s resources increasingly complement Seoul’s search for secure and diversified energy supplies.

“The energy relationship is becoming more interesting because Central Asian governments increasingly want something beyond selling resources. Ten or fifteen years ago, discussions were often dominated by oil, gas and uranium. Today, the more important question is what can actually be built around those resources,” Oztarsu said.

“It [Kazakhstan] is already important for South Korea’s uranium and energy security but Astana is also looking for technology, investment and processing capacity. The lithium cooperation now being developed is important for exactly this reason. Kazakhstan does not want to remain only an exporter of raw materials. It wants a larger part of the value chain to stay inside the country,” said Oztarsu.

Uzbekistan has moved furthest toward this model, the expert said, pointing to the Ustyurt Gas Chemical Complex located in Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan, where domestic gas is processed into polyethylene and polypropylene rather than exported as a raw commodity.

The project illustrates the potential value of Korean engagement: South Korea provides engineering expertise and industrial technology, while its partner gains production capacity, jobs and a foothold in higher-value industries.

The incentives for deeper energy cooperation run in both directions, but ambitions are constrained by geography and infrastructure.

“The recent closure of the Strait of Hormuz showed how vulnerable South Korea remains to disruptions in its traditional energy routes. Even a disruption in one strategic chokepoint was enough to push Korea into an energy crisis lasting for months and intensified the search for alternative markets and supply routes,” said Oztarsu.

While Central Asia could help South Korea diversify away from vulnerable maritime supply routes, realizing that potential would require major infrastructure investment and navigating a region whose export corridors remain shaped by geography, geopolitics and dependence on neighboring powers.

“This is also why I increasingly see energy, critical minerals and connectivity as one single strategic discussion. Central Asia can become a serious alternative for Korea, but geological potential alone is not enough. The real opportunity begins when resources can be processed locally and moved reliably to international markets,” Oztarsu said.

Why a regional summit is needed

Solid bilateral ties alone cannot resolve many of the cross-border obstacles facing Korean-backed projects in Central Asia.

Kurmashev said a Korean-backed plant in Kazakhstan might rely on Uzbek components or sell to customers elsewhere in Central Asia. Its viability could therefore depend on common customs procedures, mutually recognized documents and transport rules that no bilateral agreement between Seoul and Astana could establish on its own.

“The summit can bring the relevant governments into one discussion and give their agencies a mandate to work through the obstacle,” he explained.

The expert said greater predictability across neighboring markets could make investments commercially viable for South Korean companies when no single national market offers sufficient scale. Kazakhstan could become a production base serving regional demand, while neighboring countries could secure supplier contracts and access to processing facilities.

Beyond minerals: technology and skills

The partnership also extends to technology and human capital. Oztarsu expected digital cooperation to follow the same differentiated model as energy and industry. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are better positioned for advanced AI applications, he said, while the other countries may initially benefit more from digital infrastructure, training and public-sector technology.

Murataliyeva also pointed to labor migration as an essential component of South Korea’s relations with Central Asia. Its Employment Permit System allows workers from designated countries to take jobs in South Korea through a government-managed process.

Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan participate in the program. South Korea designated Kazakhstan as the system’s 18th labor-sending country on Aug. 14, with the first Kazakh workers expected to arrive in 2028. The relevant agreement is expected to be signed in Seoul.

For the Kyrgyz Republic, Murataliyeva said there were growing expectations that labor cooperation could evolve from the movement of workers into a channel for transferring technology and expertise. “Joint IT hubs and training centers could enable returning specialists to contribute to the development of Kyrgyzstan’s digital economy,” she added.

From declarations to delivery

The summit alone may not automatically elevate relations to a strategic level. “It is still premature, however, to expect the summit alone to automatically elevate relations to a strategic level. Without joint investment funds and stronger mechanisms for economic cooperation, high-level declarations risk amounting to little more than political symbolism,” Murataliyeva said.

The forum’s permanent secretariat gives the participants an institution capable of monitoring progress after the leaders leave Seoul. But Kurmashev said each proposed project should have an identifiable buyer or user, a responsible institution, a preparation schedule and a transparent account of the financing still required.

“Responsibility for implementation needs to be clear from the moment leaders endorse a proposal. The summit can set priorities and resolve political obstacles. Ministries, regulators and companies must then carry out the decisions within their respective powers,” Kurmashev said.

“A signed memorandum should not be counted as money already invested,” he added.

For Oztarsu, the next stage may entail matching South Korean capabilities with each country’s needs, not just announcing a single policy for Central Asia.

World.title: Tokayev Advances Kazakhstan’s Partnerships with India, US at BRICS Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev held a series of high-level meetings on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12-13, focusing on expanding Kazakhstan’s cooperation with India, the United States, the UAE and Ethiopia.

Kazakhstan-India relations

During a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Tokayev congratulated him on successfully organizing the BRICS Summit and highlighted India’s growing role in the global economy and its achievements in science and technology, Akorda reported.

“Under your wise and strong leadership, India is confidently advancing towards progress and sustainable development,” Tokayev said.

He noted that around 600 Indian-invested companies operate in Kazakhstan and nearly 150,000 Indian citizens visited the country last year. The officials discussed cooperation in energy, digitalization, education and tourism, with particular attention to cooperation between Astana Hub and Hyderabad’s technology ecosystem.

Modi thanked Tokayev for participating in the BRICS Summit and stressed the importance he attaches to friendly and trust-based relations with Kazakhstan. The two leaders also discussed prospects for a free trade agreement between India and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Tokayev, noting Kazakhstan’s chairmanship of the EAEU, reaffirmed the country’s readiness to facilitate the negotiations and invited Modi to pay a state visit to Kazakhstan.

Strengthening Kazakhstan-U.S. partnership

Tokayev also met with U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor, who conveyed a personal message from President Donald Trump congratulating Kazakhstan ahead of the 35th anniversary of its independence. Tokayev reaffirmed his invitation to Trump to visit Kazakhstan and stressed the importance of achieving tangible results in the Enhanced Strategic Partnership.

“We prefer not fine words, but tangible results and practical steps to advance our mutual cooperation,” Tokayev said, noting that his participation in the upcoming G20 Summit in December in Miami would provide an opportunity to discuss the bilateral agenda.

For his part, Gor noted that close and trust-based contacts between the leaders had brought Kazakhstan-U.S. relations to an unprecedentedly high level. The officials also discussed priority areas of cooperation, notably artificial intelligence and digitalization.

Expanding partnerships beyond BRICS

On the sidelines of the summit, Tokayev also met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheik Khaled bin Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. With the Crown Prince, he reviewed major investment projects in energy, transport and logistics, information technology and agriculture, while with the Ethiopian Prime Minister he discussed expanding trade and investment ties, including the possible establishment of a hub in Kazakhstan for Ethiopian tea, coffee and floral products. Tokayev invited both leaders to visit Kazakhstan.

Speaking at the BRICS Plus plenary session on Sept. 13, Tokayev called for deeper practical cooperation with BRICS countries in trade, logistics, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and water security, highlighting the format’s potential to open new markets, attract investment and strengthen technological and transport connectivity.

World.title: ‘Helping Baku justify ethnic cleansing’: Yerevan views on diplomats’ trip to Karabakh
World.content:
Views from Yerevan on diplomats’ visit to Nagorno-Karabakh

In Armenia, the visit to Nagorno-Karabakh by diplomats accredited to Azerbaijan has caused a strong reaction and remains the subject of intense discussion. According to Azerbaijani media reports, 150 people representing 58 countries and nine international organisations took part in the trip.

They included Magdalena Grono, the European Union’s special representative for the South Caucasus. She is also expected to arrive in Yerevan today.

The diplomats visited the territory that the entire Armenian population left in 2023. They also visited historical and cultural monuments. Hikmet Hajiyev, an aide to Azerbaijan’s president on foreign policy, accompanied them.

He showed the diplomats the Armenian monasteries of Gandzasar and Dadivank. Hajiyev said they form “an integral part of the ancient Albanian Christian heritage”.

“Such statements do not contribute to peace, nor can they be helpful in that context. Moreover, they are groundless,” Armenian parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan said earlier today.

Video footage of the diplomats’ visit shows Hajiyev displaying “samples of ancient manuscripts” with an ironic smile as he flips through blank pages. The diplomats present responded with laughter.

The footage sparked outrage in Armenia. Local experts also expressed bewilderment. Do officials in Baku really not know that, under standard international practice, people usually keep original ancient books in archives and secure storage facilities, rather than in churches?

They also ask whether it is really unclear that Armenians would not have left ancient manuscripts in monasteries they were abandoning.

Armenian analysts criticised the Azerbaijani authorities for organising an event that “distorted historical facts”. They also criticised the diplomats present for failing to respond appropriately.

Edmon Marukyan, head of the Enlightened Armenia party, even called for “a diplomatic note to be sent to all international structures”.

“I consider it unacceptable that diplomats representing various international organisations and states visit Artsakh, where no Armenians remain as a result of ethnic cleansing, while the representatives of its military and political leadership remain held hostage in Azerbaijani prisons.

“Instead of raising these issues, they listen attentively to Hajiyev’s disinformation and laugh at his cheap jokes,” he wrote.

Armenian political scientists say Armenian society’s trust in the European Union has grown significantly in recent years.

At the same time, they stress that such events “cast doubt not only on Europe’s reputation but also on the trust needed to build a lasting peace”. Historian and publicist Karen Harutyunyan made this point in an open letter to Magdalena Grono.

Grono’s post on “diverging views” between Yerevan and Baku

Magdalena Grono, the EU’s special representative for the South Caucasus, wrote on X:

“Deep divergences in views and narratives remain — for example, regarding the origins of certain sites. Azerbaijan and Armenia need to resolve these issues to overcome this aspect of past conflicts as part of broader reconciliation efforts.”

Grono did not specify which “sites” she was referring to. Most likely, she meant the Gandzasar and Dadivank monasteries, which Baku describes as monuments of Caucasian Albania.

Historian and publicist Karen Harutyunyan described the EU special representative’s post as “puzzling”. He said the issue was not simply a difference in viewpoints, but a distinction between “scientific research and disinformation spread as part of state propaganda”.

“If you are genuinely interested in the history of Caucasian Albania, you can consult the works of internationally recognised experts rather than Armenian or Azerbaijani authors,” he noted.

Statement by the Bridge of Peace initiative

Armenian participants in the Bridge of Peace initiative, through which representatives of civil society in Armenia and Azerbaijan work to normalise relations between the two countries, expressed concern over the latest developments.

They stressed that, at a stage of “significant progress” in the Armenian-Azerbaijani peace process, when both societies are expected to move towards a new quality and culture of relations, public statements take on critical importance:

“Recent developments deepen mistrust and provide new arguments to those who claim that dialogue is a pointless exercise and efforts to achieve peace are futile.”

According to the five Armenian founding members of the initiative, building peace requires sincere dialogue, careful attention to each other’s concerns and conscious efforts to avoid actions that could reopen old wounds or intensify hostility.

“We call on all actors in the peace process to act with an awareness of the responsibility of the present moment and refrain from rhetoric and actions that could be perceived as destructive,” the statement said.

Comments

Azerbaijan expert Tatevik Hayrapetyan stressed:

“The fact that Azerbaijani officials falsify history and seek to erase the traces of centuries of Armenian presence in Artsakh/Nagorno-Karabakh does not surprise me. I know the state-sponsored anti-Armenian policy too well to be surprised by it each time.

“However, my question is addressed to those very ‘diplomats’ — especially representatives of Western countries who laugh at the falsification of historical facts and help an authoritarian regime justify an aggressive war and ethnic cleansing.

“What message are you sending to the world and to other dictatorships? What are you telling them? That it is acceptable to start a war, carry out the ethnic cleansing of an entire region’s population, and then falsify indisputable facts?

“Is this how you see the world order? You should reflect on why you chose a career in diplomacy in the first place. This is not merely a political issue; it is a problem of civilisational scale. Sooner or later, the consequences of your policies will turn against you.”

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan noted:

“It has been a long time since I saw anything so shameful and indecent. And the problem lies not only in the visit itself, but also in the way its participants behaved.

“The undisguised rejoicing and ‘dancing’ against the backdrop of destroyed neighbourhoods, churches and cemeteries looked grotesque and shocking. Even from a pragmatic perspective, however, this visit and the behaviour it displayed are examples of catastrophically poor diplomacy.

“First, if the stated goal is to establish peace, exploiting the trauma and feelings of displaced people and rubbing salt into the wounds of society as a whole will hardly help achieve it.

“This applies above all to those diplomats who intend to play the role of mediators.

“Moreover, the visit dealt a serious blow to the reputation of the countries and organisations involved in the eyes of Armenian society. The reaction on social media already makes this clear.”

Historian and publicist Karen Harutyunyan wrote in an open letter titled “Reconciliation cannot be built on deception”: wrote

“The reconciliation process cannot begin by presenting documented historical heritage and its political denial as equally valid views. […] However, the problem extends beyond history.

“You walked through places where their former inhabitants no longer live. Three years ago, around this same time, many Karabakh Armenians had to exhume the remains of their sons, who had been buried only recently, and transport them to Armenia. Many still have no home, no job and no confidence in the future. Nineteen Armenian hostages remain in Baku’s prisons. Their only ‘crime’ is that they are Armenian and fought for their people’s right to self-determination.

“Visiting places that symbolise military victory, remaining silent about the consequences of forced displacement and failing to publicly respond to attempts to rewrite the history of Armenian cultural heritage do not contribute to peace. On the contrary, such actions only deepen the sense of injustice and humiliation.

I am not saying that the EU should not engage with Azerbaijan or work towards peace. However, such engagement must rest on clear moral principles.

“Reconciliation cannot be built on the assumption that displaced people should forget their homes and that their churches should receive a new identity. It rests on truth, respect for the dignity of victims and accountability.

“Armenia is currently weakened and unable to fully guarantee its own security. But the continued humiliation of the Armenian people and disregard for their suffering cannot lead to peace. These actions only compound the injustice and further undermine the prospects for reconciliation. I am confident that Europe can and must choose the right path.”

By the time of publication, Magdalena Grono had arrived in Yerevan and immediately headed to the Matenadaran repository of ancient manuscripts.

Grono is shown ancient manuscripts kept at the Matenadaran.

Matenadaran director Ara Khzmalyan also addressed the books with blank pages that Hikmet Hajiyev displayed.

He stated: “There are no blank pages in our manuscripts.”

Khzmalyan explained that the original manuscripts had never been kept at Gandzasar because the monastery lacked the facilities needed to ensure their safety and proper storage.

“Only copies of the manuscripts were displayed at Gandzasar. The original of each one is kept at the Matenadaran. The Matenadaran is ready to show them to any diplomat who has even one per cent doubt about their authenticity,” Ara Khzmalyan stressed.

Views from Yerevan on diplomats’ visit to Nagorno-Karabakh

World.title: Copyright complaints as a tool to pressure Azerbaijan’s independent media
World.content:
Blocking media accounts in Azerbaijan

Published by Meydan TV

Following a series of account blocks targeting independent Azerbaijani media outlets at the end of August, the story has taken on an international dimension. In early September, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and the Exiled Media Network (NEMO) publicly condemned attacks on the social media pages of Azerbaijani newsrooms. They urged platforms to examine possible abuses of copyright-protection mechanisms.

The issue concerns a series of copyright complaints that led Meta to block the Instagram accounts of Abzas Media and Toplum TV. Earlier, pages belonging to Azadlıq Qəzeti and Azərbaycan Saatı had been blocked in a similar way. Meydan TV and HamamTimes have also reported receiving comparable complaints.

Independent newsrooms consider the incidents part of a coordinated campaign. They see them as a continuation of the pressure Azerbaijani media have faced following journalists’ arrests, website blocks and the forced relocation of some editorial operations outside the country.

Four complaints in a matter of days

On 25 August, Meta blocked the Instagram pages of Abzas Media and Toplum TV following complaints of copyright infringement.

Abzas Media director Gunel Safarova told Meydan TV that the newsroom received four such complaints between 22 and 25 August.

One concerned a video originally published by the newspaper Azadlıq. Another involved a video based on an interview published on Musavat.com. A third concerned material from HamamTimes. The fourth complaint targeted a short video about flooding in Goychay in 2022, which Abzas Media had taken from social media.

According to Safarova, Abzas Media credited the sources when it published the material. However, she said, the complaints did not come from those sources.

The newsroom was particularly struck by the information provided by the complainants. Safarova said several complaints had been submitted under different names but used the same email address, registered to Farid Guliyev.

In addition, the complainants cited as links to the alleged original material the publications of the same media outlets that Abzas Media had credited as its sources — Azadlıq, Musavat.com and HamamTimes.

HamamTimes separately told Meydan TV that it had not submitted any complaints to Meta against Abzas Media over its use of the outlet’s material.

These circumstances led the newsroom to suspect that the complaints may have come from one person or a group of connected individuals.

Abzas Media sought assistance from the digital rights organisation Access Now and requested a review of Meta’s decision.

Similar complaint against Toplum TV

Toplum TV faced a similar situation.

The outlet’s editor, Parvana Gurbanli, told Meydan TV that someone had filed a copyright complaint against a video about a landslide in Baku’s Khatai district on 3 August. Several cars were buried under the soil.

According to Gurbanli, the video came from the official YouTube channel of the state-funded public broadcaster İctimai TV, and Toplum TV had credited the source in its post.

However, the complainant claimed that the material had come from his personal profile. Following the complaint, Instagram also blocked Toplum TV’s account.

Like Abzas Media, the Toplum TV newsroom suggested that the incident was not an ordinary copyright dispute but a targeted action against an independent media outlet.

Other media outlets also targeted by blocks

Abzas Media and Toplum TV were not the only Azerbaijani media outlets to face such restrictions.

The Facebook and Instagram pages of the newspaper Azadlıq were also blocked following copyright infringement complaints. The outlet’s editor-in-chief, Rahim Hajiyev, told Meydan TV that the platform cited copyright complaints as the reason for the block.

The Instagram account of Azərbaycan Saatı was also blocked in a similar way. Meydan TV and HamamTimes have received comparable complaints about their material at different times.

For newsrooms that continue operating abroad after facing persecution in Azerbaijan, social media are among the main channels for distributing information inside the country.

In recent years, employees of Abzas Media, Toplum TV and Meydan TV have been arrested and prosecuted in Azerbaijan. The journalists and their newsrooms reject the charges and link the criminal cases to their professional activities. Some outlets continued operating from abroad after their staff members were arrested.

Eight newsrooms issue a joint statement

On 28 August, eight independent Azerbaijani media outlets — Abzas Media, Meydan TV, Toplum TV, Azadlıq Qəzeti, HamamTimes, Azərbaycan Saatı, Qəzetçi and Mikroskop Media — published a joint statement.

They described the series of copyright complaints as a possible coordinated campaign against independent media.

According to the newsrooms, the complaints targeted material published at different times, unrelated to one another and obtained from different sources. Media representatives said the complainants had provided no evidence that they held the copyright to the disputed material.

The newsrooms also reported that some complaints came from the same person and identical email addresses. In other cases, the names differed, but the email addresses, information contained in the complaints and the submission process were the same.

The signatories linked the incidents to a broader campaign of pressure against the independent press, which has intensified in Azerbaijan since late 2023.

During this period, authorities arrested and prosecuted journalists from several independent outlets. Some media effectively ceased operating inside the country, while others moved abroad. The websites of several independent media outlets also remain blocked in Azerbaijan.

The newsrooms believe that, following journalists’ arrests, website blocks and the forced relocation of their operations abroad, social media have become the latest target of pressure. They are among the few remaining ways to deliver material directly to audiences in Azerbaijan.

How Meta’s system is being used

According to the joint statement, the problem is partly linked to how platforms handle copyright infringement complaints.

The newsrooms claim that, after receiving such complaints, platforms’ automated systems may remove individual posts. A build-up of complaints can also lead to an entire account being disabled.

As a result, a complaint may concern a specific video or post, but its consequences can affect the media outlet’s entire page and the newsroom’s access to its audience.

The eight media outlets called on Meta and other social platforms not to assess such cases in isolation. Instead, they urged the platforms to examine possible links between complaints, including matching email addresses and complainant details, whether the complainants actually hold the relevant copyrights, and possible systematic abuse of the copyright complaint mechanism.

They also called for the affected accounts to be unblocked.

International organisations respond

On 2 September, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and the Network of Exiled Media Outlets (NEMO) condemned the incidents.

CPJ highlighted the blocking of accounts belonging to Abzas Media, Toplum TV and Azadlıq. It linked the blocks to the broader problem of copyright-protection systems being abused against independent media.

The organisation also pointed to similar cases previously recorded in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Georgia, where copyright complaints had been used against journalistic material.

NEMO, meanwhile, said platforms must prevent their moderation systems from being used to restrict the work of media outlets operating in exile.

The organisation stressed that social platforms are particularly important for newsrooms forced to work outside their countries. They allow journalists to maintain access to audiences at home.

Blocking media accounts in Azerbaijan

World.title: Another head of Georgia’s State Security Service resigns: what does it mean?
World.content:
Georgia’s State Security Service chief Geladze resigns

Another head of Georgia’s State Security Service has resigned. On 14 September, Gela (Geka) Geladze announced on Facebook that he was stepping down.

Parliament approved his candidacy on 28 April 2026 for a six-year term, but he headed the State Security Service for less than five months.

The media and opposition link these personnel changes to the ongoing developments that began with Mamuka Mdinaradze’s sudden withdrawal from politics, although no one in the government has confirmed such a connection.

Geladze is described as a close friend of former Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze, whom he replaced in the post. Mdinaradze, who was considered one of the leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party, also headed the State Security Service for a short time before becoming deputy prime minister. He resigned and left politics altogether at the end of August.

“Following consultations with the political team, I will continue my work in another agency, where I will continue to serve the interests of our country and society with full responsibility,” Geladze wrote, without specifying where he would work next.

In his statement, Geladze thanked the “political team”, singling out Bidzina Ivanishvili, the honorary chairman and founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party, and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

It remains unknown who will replace him as head of the State Security Service..

Frequent changes in the State Security Service leadership

Parliament approved Gela Geladze as head of the State Security Service on 28 April 2026. Before that, he served as interior minister. His candidacy received the support of 85 MPs, while 12 voted against.

Over the past year and a half, he has become the fourth head of the security service to leave the post ahead of schedule.

Grigol Liluashvili left his position as head of the State Security Service on 2 April 2025. He is currently in custody on bribery charges, which he denies.

His successor, Gela Geladze, headed the law enforcement agency until 14 September.

Significantly, two prominent members of the ruling team at the Finance Ministry also left their posts just two days before Geladze’s resignation: Revenue Service head Mikheil Maghlakelidze and Investigative Service head Levan Kharabadze.

According to official information, Maghlakelidze resigned at his own request. No reason has been given for Kharabadze’s resignation.

Georgia’s State Security Service chief Geladze resigns

World.title: Iran envoy: Georgia not the only destination for Iranians
World.content:
Iranian envoy to Georgia makes pointed remarks

Iranian Ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Moujani has responded to a statement by Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency saying the country would fully comply with sanctions against Iranian airlines imposed by the United States. The ambassador said Georgia had been one possible destination for Iranians, but was not the only one.

On 8 September, the United States imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines. Six of them — Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Qeshm Air, Fly Kish Airlines, Taban Airlines and AVA Airlines — also operate flights between Georgia and Iran. “As the expanded sanctions list announced by the US State Department includes airlines that currently operate flights between Georgia and Iran, the Georgian side, as in other cases, will act in full compliance with the international sanctions regime,” the Civil Aviation Agency said.

In turn, the Iranian embassy published a map of the Black Sea region showing only half of Georgia. When the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty asked the Iranian ambassador whether the map was intended to convey a political message, he replied:

“Sometimes a diplomat can say nothing, write nothing and simply share a picture… Water knows no borders; the Caucasus and Iran need a common, interconnected future.”

Map published by Iranian ambassador to Georgia

What Iran’s ambassador said

Seyed Ali Moujani said Iranian tour operators had contacted the embassy’s consular section in recent days with questions about whether tourist trips to Georgia would continue.

“Georgia has undoubtedly been one of the important Black Sea tourist destinations for Iranians,” Moujani wrote, noting that the country had attracted many Iranian tourists in recent years.

He also said Iran respected Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s independent decisions.

“Georgia’s recent decision to introduce certain restrictions in connection with Western sanctions is one that we must respect as the country’s choice. However, respecting the choices of others does not mean disregarding our own right to choose,” the Iranian ambassador wrote.

Moujani said Iranian tourists, like citizens of other countries, considered a range of factors when choosing a holiday destination, including safety, convenience, cost, mutual respect and dignity.

The ambassador also noted that tourism generated mutual economic benefits.

“The arrival of tourists does not simply mean travellers entering a country. Hotels, restaurants, transport providers, shops, tour guides, craftspeople, public services and dozens of other sectors of the economy all benefit,” Moujani wrote.

He said travellers had also historically played an important role in building links between cultures and peoples, and sometimes in creating new opportunities for cooperation and development.

“If a new situation has emerged today, we should not view it solely as a restriction; every restriction can become an opportunity to find new paths,” the ambassador said.

Seyed Ali Moujani said there were other coastal destinations in the Black Sea region besides Georgia that could serve as alternatives for Iranian tourists.

“There are other destinations — other countries worth visiting, other cultures worth discovering and other peoples worth engaging with,” Moujani wrote.

The ambassador described Iran’s respect and friendship for Georgia and the Georgian people as unwavering, but stressed that Iran and the Iranian people’s right to choose also deserved respect.

World.title: Second chance: South Ossetia revives efforts to promote Ossetian amid leadership change
World.content:
South Ossetian Education and Science Minister Aslan Lolayev has announced plans to open a specialist class offering advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

Lolayev said the class would accommodate more than 30 pupils, but did not specify which school it would be based at or which year group it would be for.

“The authorities plan to open another three such classes in the next academic year — two in Tskhinvali and one in one of the districts,” Lolayev added.

He said the authorities hoped the introduction of classes offering advanced Ossetian-language study would “become one of the stages in developing a national Ossetian school system and expanding the use of the native language in education”.

Russian and Ossetian are South Ossetia’s official languages, but administrative work and education are conducted only in Russian. Russian is dominant overall, and is also the language predominantly used by the local population in everyday life.

However, Zarema Ts, a schoolteacher from Tskhinvali, says there is demand among young people for greater promotion of the Ossetian language. She believes the younger generation should therefore be encouraged to study the Ossetian language and literature, as well as Ossetian history and ethnography.

“There should be more opportunities, clubs and classes for studying Ossetian, not only within the education system but also outside educational institutions. For example, why not organise Ossetian-language classes for visitors and Russian specialists working here?”

North Ossetian experience not fully embraced

Zarema says, however, that proficiency in Ossetian is considerably higher in South Ossetia than in North Ossetia. Statistics appear to support her claim: in North Ossetia, which is part of the Russian Federation, the situation surrounding the Ossetian language has been recognised as critical, prompting the local authorities to take serious steps to preserve it.

The Alan Gymnasium, a multilingual Ossetian-Russian boarding school, has been operating in Vladikavkaz for nine years, with most subjects taught primarily in Ossetian. The school was established at the initiative of then North Ossetian leader Vyacheslav Bitarov, who continues to provide it with financial support.

South Ossetian officials, however, have been slow to adopt this model.

In early 2026, Aslan Lolayev was preparing to present a project for a national school in Tskhinvali modelled on the Alan Gymnasium. Reports said the project had already been agreed with the relevant Russian authorities and only needed to be implemented.

Lolayev was subsequently dismissed as education minister, and acting minister Rimma Pliyeva said the North Ossetian gymnasium model was unsuitable for South Ossetia. She argued that South Ossetia’s education system was already “perfectly fulfilling its role in teaching the Ossetian language”.

Second chance

Several months later, however, there was another twist: South Ossetian President Alan Gagloyev resigned early and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov took over as acting president.

Kambolov reinstated former Education Minister Aslan Lolayev, giving him another opportunity to implement at least part of his programme to expand advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

How successful the initiative will prove remains unclear, with South Ossetian experts so far reluctant to make predictions.

Three years ago, in September 2023, Aslan Lolayev raised concerns about a shortage of Ossetian-language textbooks.

“These textbooks cannot be purchased commercially because they were published under a state procurement programme. All copies were distributed to educational institutions. Moreover, the textbooks were published in 2019 and, if handled with care, have a lifespan of five years. After that, they need to be replaced,” he said at the time.

Lolayev added that the republication of the textbooks was included in a three-year programme that was due to be submitted to parliament and the government for consideration.

“I hope it will receive support and that we will be able to resolve this issue,” Lolayev said in 2023. There have been no reports of new textbooks since then.

South Ossetia is due to hold a presidential election on 18 September. Whether the change of leadership and the arrival of a new team, which includes Aslan Lolayev, will alter the situation remains to be seen, although there are hopes within society that it will.

Madina Valiyeva, a finalist in the Team of the Future personnel programme, for example, says that if she is appointed to an official post, one of her goals will be to establish a South Ossetian version of the Alan Gymnasium.

“There is a very apt saying: ‘No language, no nation.’ We must preserve our native language and pass it on to future generations. That is the future of our people,” Valiyeva said.

World.title: Abkhaz president voices blacksmith in cartoon
World.content:
Abkhaz President Badra Gunba has voiced a character in the animated film Nart Sasrykva, dedicated to a hero of the Abkhaz epic. Gunba provided the voice of one of the film’s characters, the blacksmith Ainar.

Work on the 36-minute animated film, which has taken five years to complete, is nearing its end, with its official premiere due in a month. Director Astamur Kvitsinia adapted the heroic epic, which has several versions, into a format designed to be engaging and accessible to children.

It is unclear why the president became involved in voicing the film. One possible explanation is the longstanding friendship between Badra Gunba and Astamur Kvitsinia, dating back to Gunba’s time as Abkhazia’s culture minister from 2011 to 2014.

Astamur Kvitsinia is widely regarded as the father of Abkhaz animation and has created more than a dozen animated films based on Abkhaz fairy tales and myths.

Versions of the Nart epic, about warrior brothers who battle giants, are found among many peoples of the Caucasus. Most scholars date the epic to the 8th-7th centuries BC.

Each people’s version has its own distinctive features and reflects its particular worldview. In the Abkhaz version, the Narts are a family of 100 brothers and their only sister. Sasrykva, the youngest of the brothers, is the epic’s main hero.

World.title: “Injustice prevails under oligarch Ivanishvili” — video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Opinion: ‘Arresting a person in Georgia over their views on a 34-year-old war is a legal absurdity’
World.content:
Opinion on Giorgi Baramidze’s arrest

“Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity,” said Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, commenting on the arrest of Georgian opposition leader and former defence minister Giorgi Baramidze.

On 11 September, Giorgi Baramidze was arrested on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. His arrest followed an interview on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners because they were “shot”.

Tamta Mikeladze: “Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity.

The prosecutor’s argument that the statement damaged Georgia’s international standing and image, offended the honour of war veterans and so on has no basis in criminal law. If specific individuals believed Baramidze had defamed them, they could have taken him to court in a civil case.

Claims that the statement could be used in international legal proceedings are also unfounded. There are no international legal proceedings concerning the war in Abkhazia, and Baramidze was not a decision-maker at the time. His words therefore could not carry the kind of weight that would affect any legal consequences.

Arresting someone for expressing an opinion – even if that opinion is unfounded, foolish, offensive or unacceptable – is therefore an unimaginable departure from the rule of law.”

Mikeladze also examines the alleged offence in detail and points to a mismatch between the charge and the statement, arguing that no remarks of this kind can legally constitute sabotage.
