World.title: Azerbaijan’s parliament chief addresses NAM Youth Organization (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Speaker of the Parliament o Azerbaijan Sahiba Gafarova has delivered a speech as a guest of honour during the event “The Role of Youth in Parliamentary Co-operation” at the Headquarters of the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Organisation (NAMYO) on September 14.

This was announced by the Press and Public Relations Department of Milli Majlis (Parliament of Azerbaijan).

According to the statement, the Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament first acquainted herself with the arrangements in place at the Headquarters.

In her following address to the youth, Gafarova talked about Azerbaijan’s important contribution to the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) during the four-year chairmanship of this organisation. It was remarked that the Azerbaijani chairmanship had coincided with a period of grave global challenges, especially COVID-19. Led by President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijan played an important role in demonstrating solidarity within the NAM and displaying its practical operation capabilities in the pandemic spell.

She mentioned Azerbaijan’s initiatives to hold an online summit of the NAM on COVID-19 and a Special session of the UN General Assembly on COVID-19. At the same time, Azerbaijan helped ensure an equal access to the vaccines and helped those countries which needed help.

The parliament speaker also said that the Azerbaijani chairmanship had been focused especially on strengthening the international role and institutional growth of the NAM. The emergence of the Non-Aligned Movement Youth Network and Parliamentary Network at the initiative of President Ilham Aliyev was one of the important areas of the institutional development. The NAM Youth Network was transformed to a Youth Organisation pursuant to the 2019 resolution.

According to the Speaker of Parliament, NAMYO and Parliamentary Network (NAMPN) perform different but complementary functions. One of them provides an international youth platform whereas the other unites the NAM Member States’ Parliaments. Furthermore, Gafarova stressed that those two institutions had expanded the institutional foundations of the NAM and made its operations closer to parliaments, youth and society. Those entities are amongst the more important and long-term outcomes of the period of Azerbaijani chairmanship.

Touching upon the establishment of the NAMPN in her address, she pointed out that, established on the sidelines of the 143rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union in Madrid in 2021, the Parliamentary Network chaired by the Parliament of Azerbaijan has formed its structure, broadened international co-operation and held five conferences in various countries in the elapsed period. The Parliamentary Network introduced the important parliamentary dimension to the activities of the NAM and makes it possible to underpin the obligations assumed internationally within national parliaments, which is done through legislation and budget and parliamentary control.

The speaker also addressed youth’s involvement in political and public processes and accentuated the importance of them being represented in various facets of life more actively. Besides, Gafarova highlighted the significance of quality education, professional skills, decent employment and access to digital opportunities for youth development as well as on their engagement in discussions about AI, data protection and digital economy.

She emphasized in the conclusion of her address that the NAMYO and the NAMPN, the important legacy of the Azerbaijani chairmanship, are the active bodies serving the future of the Non-Aligned Movement.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Türkiye discuss co-op in media and communications (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Cooperation in the fields of media and communications has been discussed between Azerbaijan and Türkiye.

This was reflected in a statement published by the Media and Broadcasting Council of Azerbaijan following the meeting between the Council Chairman, Ahmad Ismayilov, and a delegation led by Deputy Head of the Public Relations Department of the Presidential Administration of Türkiye, Ferhat Pirinççi, held on September 14.

According to the statement, at the meeting, Ahmad Ismayilov emphasized the importance of existing cooperation between the two countries in the mentioned fields.

The importance of cooperation in areas such as expanding the mutual exchange of experience and strengthening joint efforts to combat disinformation within the modern information environment was highlighted.

Meanwhile, Ferhat Pirinççi spoke about the new opportunities created by digital transformation in the media and communication sectors. Emphasis was placed on the effective application of new media tools, the development of modern communication approaches, and the expansion of professional ties and joint initiatives among media representatives from both countries.

During the meeting, views were exchanged regarding opportunities for a coordinated approach to modern information challenges and other matters of mutual interest," the statement added.

The Media and Broadcasting Council was established by a corresponding decree of the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev. According to the decree, the Council is the legal successor to the Council on Audiovisual Mass Media of the Republic of Azerbaijan; its rights, obligations, and assets have been transferred to the Council. The Media and Broadcasting Council has a staff of 108 people.

In addition, the state legal entity “Media Development Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan” was dissolved. Its rights, obligations, and assets were transferred to the Council. In accordance with the amendments made to the Law “On the Media,” the Media and Broadcasting Council is considered the authorized state body in the field of media and television and radio broadcasting in Azerbaijan.

World.title: Putin’s border drone strikes show ‘desperation’, NATO chief says
World.content:
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has said Russian drone strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border show Moscow's growing desperation.

A Russian strike on the Ukraine-Poland border on Sunday just missed a train carrying diplomats, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt.

Russian strike on Ukraine-Poland border A Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after European diplomats, including former prime ministers of the UK and Sweden, had used the same line.

Speaking at NATO's political headquarters in Brussels on Monday, Mr Rutte said the strikes would only drive the military alliance to increase its support for Kyiv.

The strikes "close to NATO territory" show Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror," he said.

"Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine."

Mr Rutte pledged to increase support for Ukraine and bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defences along its long eastern border with Russia.

" He [Putin] thinks that he can stop us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. "

Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said on Monday that the drone attacks near Poland's border were "clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine".

"We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared," she said.

Kaja Kallas is the European Union foreign policy chief. (AP: Mindaugas Kulbis)

Poland pledges increased security

Sunday's strikes near the Polish border are the latest in a string of incidents that officials say point to a deliberate pattern of escalation by Putin, as Moscow tests NATO's response while pressing its offensive in Ukraine.

Mr Rutte's comments came as Poland pledged increased security along its border with Ukraine after a wave of Russian drone strikes near the frontier, including two that landed within kilometres of Polish territory.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned after a governmental security briefing in Warsaw on Sunday that Moscow appears poised to intensify its campaign against Ukraine's borders with European countries.

Donald Tusk warned Moscow appears poised to intensify its campaign against Ukraine's borders. (AP: Omar Havana)

Ukraine is under mounting pressure from Russia's intensifying air campaign that uses ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defences.

"These coming weeks and months will be a time of very intensified actions on the Russian side, and unfortunately we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory," he said,

Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Monday in a post on X that the army recovered what was believed to be a Russian military drone from the Baltic Sea near the coastal village of Jaroslawiec.

Mr Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Polish army recovered what was believed to be a Russian drone from the Baltic Sea. (Supplied: X)

Polish officials said intelligence reports, including a CIA briefing last week, suggested Russia was likely to attack border points and intensify sabotage actions inside European countries as part of its efforts to discourage partners from supporting Ukraine.

Mr Tusk said he would consult NATO allies on preparing a potential joint response.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski underscored the alliance's military edge in a social media post — saying that in the event of Russian aggression against NATO, European NATO air forces without US participation would be capable of destroying half of Russia's oil refineries faster than Ukraine.

Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk described Sunday's drone strikes as a serious escalation from Russia.

He told broadcaster TVN24 on Monday that any spillover into European countries could take the form of sabotage or a sharp intensification of hybrid warfare "on a scale that we have not seen before".

Kremlin says Russia will continue strikes throughout Ukraine

Dmitry Peskov said Russian forces we operating across the entire country of Ukraine and would continue to do so. (Reuters: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik)

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, asked on Monday about the strike on the train near the Polish border, said Russian forces were operating "across the entire territory of Ukraine and continues to do so — and will continue to do so".

Mr Peskov noted the potential role of Global South nations in a settlement, saying "any country can use its influence on the Kyiv regime to encourage it to show greater flexibility".

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi each expressed willingness to help broker a settlement during recent meetings with Mr Putin, who briefed them on the situation in Ukraine, Mr Peskov said.

Mr Peskov also addressed US President Donald Trump's call for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel facilities, saying "any call on the Kyiv regime to stop strikes on civilian economic infrastructure can only be welcomed".

Mr Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage.

He spoke after diesel prices in the US hit a record on Friday, soaring past an average of $US6 ($8.40) per gallon.

AP

World.title: Joyce dismisses threats of 'tanked economy' from negative migration rates
World.content:
One Nation is "not afraid" to drive migration to negative levels, with its Treasury spokesman saying he will follow the will of the people, not warnings from economists in deciding how deeply to cut migration rates.

Business and the university sector have warned One Nation's proposal to cut migration by about 750,000 places over three years would devastate the economy.

Speaking on ABC National Forum, Mr Joyce said voter concerns on migration had to be respected.

"The will of the Australian people is so pronounced, this has to be dealt with, we will deal with it," Mr Joyce said.

One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce said voters were tired of public policy being determined by economists. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Political commentator George Megalogenis said no government had ever purposefully caused a net outflow of migrants, adding migration had been negative only four times in Australia's history: twice during the depressions of the 1890s and 1930s, and twice during the deployment of soldiers during the first and second world wars.

"If you're going to take ... 766,000 people out of the Australian economy and society for three years, you have tanked the economy in a way that is on the scale of the depression of the 1890s and 1930s," Mr Megalogenis said.

Net overseas migration has been falling from its peak in mid-2023, when international borders reopened after the COVID-19 pandemic.

While the surge of migrant arrivals has slowed to pre-COVID rates, the number of migrants departing has also remained flat, leading to migration rates still above the government's long-term forecasts and above the pace of housing construction.

Joyce: People 'tired' of economists

The National Forum heard views on migration amid a raging debate on the issue — while Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all taken a position to cut migration rates, the details of which visa categories should be cut often prompts fierce reactions from sectors where there are sometimes already workforce shortages.

Earlier today, One Nation announced its plan to heavily restrict the number of international students allowed to study in Australia and blocking skilled workers from bringing family to Australia.

Net migration would be net negative for three years — meaning more people leaving the country than arriving — until an ongoing cap of 130,000 places a year took effect.

Migration is more complicated than this one number It's one thing to set a net migration target, but working out how to achieve that is a conversation political leaders have been less keen to have.

Mr Joyce defended One Nation's proposal, but dismissed questions about the economic impact it could have.

"The issue of what it is going to cost I think is contentious, but I have no concern about following the will of the Australian people," Mr Joyce said.

"I think the Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with public policy, to go to the Parliamentary Budget Office, and, to be quite frank, I have been around this game for a while and I have never seen a forward estimates in any budgetary paper be even close to the mark."

Mr Joyce said he was not worried about what the Parliamentary Budget Office or another office might conclude about One Nation's migration policy "because they're not elected, I am".

He noted that the party's policy did not touch demand-driven visa programs, like the Pacific worker program which many farmers rely on, or visas for skilled workers themselves — just those that would allow them to bring family.

750k visas cut under One Nation plan One Nation unveils its plan to slash immigration by 750,000 places over three years, with major cuts targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants.

Earlier, the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) warned that pursuing a pre-determined migration target was a mistake.

"If you are basing the outcome on a set of arbitrary numbers and an arbitrary target, which is not achievable without across-the-board cuts in a whole range of categories, then you are going to do long-term damage to the Australian economy," ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar said.

Speaking on National Forum, former deputy prime minister and Nationals MP John Anderson said Australia had only avoided recession because of high migration rates.

But he said that voters were being drawn away from the major parties by a concern about migration.

"A balanced, reasonable, immigration rate is good economically," Mr Anderson told National Forum.

"It's good socially, whilst we agree 'the law of the land' really does apply, but we need to realise how badly broken [the migration system] is."

"We are here because One Nation has captured the initiative, because vast numbers of Australians think the system is now not working for them."

Labor and Coalition yet to settle migration policy

Both Labor and the Coalition have announced their own intentions to cut migration as One Nation's popularity has surged.

The federal government has a target to reach a net migration rate of 225,000 a year by 2028, but is yet to detail new policy intended to bring down migration from the current rate of about 300,000 a year.

Labor's planned changes to migration were postponed several weeks ago, and continue to be debated by cabinet.

The Coalition, meanwhile, has signalled its intention to tie Australia's migration program to housing construction rates to ensure that migration does not outpace housing supply — though it has not yet detailed that proposal.

Frontbencher Andrew Hastie said cutting migration would require "trade offs", which was why his party was still working through its position.

"We are committed to this, to getting it right, though — that is the difference between us and One Nation," Mr Hastie said.

Mr Hastie said he agreed with One Nation's proposal to reduce temporary graduate visas, as was "stopping the visa hopping", but he said it was unclear how One Nation intended to do that.

Loading...

Nyadol Nyuon: Migration debate a proxy for race

While much of the debate has focused on what level to cut migration by, and population pressures on housing and infrastructure, there has also been a question around who should be allowed to migrate to Australia.

One Nation has proposed banning some migrants by preventing travel from countries where the Department of Foreign Affairs has issued a "do not travel" advisory due to terrorism or other security risks.

And the Coalition has proposed tightening the test for prospective migrants to make compliance with a statement of Australian values a binding visa condition, and delay access to social security supports for non-citizens.

Human rights advocate and lawyer Nyadol Nyuon said trying to pin criminality on certain communities was the kind of thing dividing Australians.

Ms Nyuon said the migration debate was often used as a placeholder for conversations around race.

"I don't have to look a particular way to love this country, but whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," Ms Nyuon said.

Loading...

Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly said she feared losing the Australia she grew up in.

"I grew up playing cricket in a street with kids from Greece and Yugoslavia at the time, Italian, Chinese, and nobody cared. Nobody cared what language your mum spoke," Ms Aly said.

"Nobody cared that my skin got darker as the sun was over us. Nobody cared about any of that. And that's the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we're losing."

World.title: Local government inspector launches probe into City of Perth
World.content:
Dysfunction at the City of Perth is set to be investigated further, with the local government watchdog launching an inquiry into the problem-plagued council.

Local Government Inspector Tony Brown said the inquiry would yield the "best result" for residents and ratepayers, adding that it would would take about three months and cost about $120,000.

"There are fractured working relationships and ongoing governance issues at the city," Mr Brown said.

"So this is not a two-year process that happened before that cost $7.2 million. This will be a short and effective way of providing a good outcome for the City of Perth community."

Mr Brown's office said it had received 25 complaints involving elected members since the start of this year.

Action needed

In January, the ABC revealed a damning report that found the relationship between council and management was in "crisis".

That report followed Mr Brown's appointment of former Kwinana mayor Carol Adams as a monitor to oversee the council and encourage "greater accountability and appropriate decision-making".

What's going wrong inside the City of Perth? It's been labelled "dysfunctional" and "diabolical". What does the lord mayor have to say about the embattled City of Perth?

Mr Brown said he had presented the city with the monitor's findings, as well as 12 actions that "focus on the council working together better and their governance processes".

He did not elaborate on the actions, or the monitor's findings.

Working together

The inquiry would be the first held by the inspector under a new regime that places councils under significantly more scrutiny than in the past.

The final report of that inquiry can recommend the council, or individual members, be suspended or dismissed, but it would be up to the local government minister to make that decision.

Tony Brown says the City of Perth must set an example for governance. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Brown said the council had advised him it would work cooperatively with investigators.

"The City of Perth is the flagship local government of Western Australia, so it needs to be the leader in governance," he said.

"I don't think it's there at the moment, so we're going to work through that and we want the city to be able to return to providing good governance for its community."

In a statement, Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds said he welcomed the inquiry and had always supported independent oversight.

"Importantly, the Inspector noted the council has the inherent institutional capacity to perform effectively. That is an important foundation to build upon," he wrote.

"We welcome the inquiry as an opportunity for the matters raised to be independently examined, the facts to be established and, where required, clear pathways for action and improvement to be identified."

Mr Reynolds said the council's focus remained on "delivering for the people, businesses and visitors who rely on the city every day" and that he believed it would emerge stronger from the process.

'Conflict spiral'

Problems began emerging in late November, when the City of Perth's acting CEO resigned after labelling an attempt by Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds to order a workplace culture review unlawful.

Mr Reynolds later backed down on those plans and announced he would ask the inspector to review the city's culture.

City of Perth Council will be investigated. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Less than two months later, the leaked report made 18 recommendations, which the mayor said he supported.

The report found relations between the CEO and Lord Mayor were in a "conflict spiral", which required "immediate intervention".

Mr Reynolds said at the time the council could "absolutely" get its house in order.

Historical problems

The City of Perth has run into problems before.

In 2018, the entire council was stood down after years of scandal and infighting.

A later inquiry found the city's culture had become dominated by self-interest, complacency and a lack of accountability and transparency.

The report that was leaked in January found "concerning parallels" with the situation at the time and the 2018 collapse of the council.

World.title: SA Health employee reprimanded for accessing Tony Modra's medical records
World.content:
One SA Health employee has been reprimanded for accessing AFL legend Tony Modra's private medical records after he was seriously injured in a truck crash, while two other employees remain under investigation, the health department says.

In a statement, SA Health said another six people were no longer being investigated.

"The number of employees under investigation for potentially accessing a patient's medical record inappropriately has been revised from nine individuals, to three," the statement said.

"Of these three, one individual has been reprimanded and two are still being investigated.

"Six individuals are no longer under investigation for this matter."

Any sanction imposed becomes part of an employee's permanent record.

Tony Modra spent time in hospital after the crash, and later shared a photo of himself in intensive care on Instagram. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

In July SA Health said nine staff were being either investigated for alleged inappropriate access to the records, or "assessed" to determine whether their access was "always appropriate".

At the time, the department also apologised to Modra's family for "any distress caused".

Modra underwent facial surgery and was in hospital for days after a truck crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, on June 18.

In July, the Crows legend posted an update of his progress on Instagram. In that post he said he was now able to get "out and about", and shared photos of himself in intensive care and recovering with his family.

In a statement earlier that month, he said he was "overwhelmed by the kindness and care" that he, and his family, had been shown.

Modra played a total of 165 AFL games for Adelaide and the Fremantle Dockers, after debuting for the Crows in 1992.

Police were called to the scene of the truck crash, near Victor Harbor, on June 18. (Supplied: SA Police)

The probe into staff accessing Modra's records is not the first time concerns have been raised about SA Health staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving well-known people.

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after they were caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh.

Cy Walsh had been charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed a SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

The department has also previously said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

World.title: Minister flies to Pilbara after report of up to 15 kids living unsupervised
World.content:
Western Australia's child protection minister has been dispatched to the Pilbara amid reports her department is failing to address the neglect of vulnerable Indigenous children.

Jessica Stojkovski flew into Port Hedland, 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, on Monday in the wake of reports in The Australian that up to 15 children, some as young as five, were living unsupervised in a home in South Hedland.

The newspaper reported WA's Department of Child Protection (DCP) had failed to take action, despite multiple complaints from residents, police and other agencies of the children's neglect, and failed to address separate complaints of sexual abuse of children in WA's East Kimberley.

The latest reporting followed claims the Department's Pilbara staff failed to heed warnings about the risk posed to the children of Port Hedland mother Margaret Dale Hawke, before she murdered them in 2022.

Jessica Stojkovski was picked up from the tarmac at Port Hedland Airport. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Ms Stojkovski was picked up from the tarmac at Port Hedland Airport after touching down about 4pm on Monday and left the airport without taking questions.

In a written statement provided by a spokesperson, Ms Stojkovski said child protection was a "complex" issue.

"It is unacceptable that children in Western Australia are living this way," she said.

"No child should have their safety and wellbeing put at risk.

" I am seeking urgent answers in relation to the children concerned and what actions are being taken. "

The furore has sparked renewed questioning of the DCP's culture, resourcing and alleged failure to protect children at risk across regional and remote WA.

Elders say neglect a pressing issue

Kariyarra elder Pat Mason said children left alone to fend for themselves was a major issue in South Hedland.

"Children need to be in a home, and be safe in a home," Ms Mason said.

"If you can't feel safe in a home, then we as adults, no matter whose child it is, have to make sure they are safe, some way or somehow.

"We can't leave them like what's happening in South Hedland."

Pat Mason says neglect of children has become a consistent problem across the Port Hedland community. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Ms Mason said the situation was the worst she had seen it, and that the system was failing.

"I reckon the perpetrator should be removed, not the child … the child should be left in the home, with the home that they love being in rather than taking them out," she said.

"When you remove them, they end up suiciding or turning to horrific things like stealing cars, destroying someone else's property because they haven't got a property of their own."

Nyamal elder Linda Doogiebee-Dridi (Milbugana) said the department needed to work with the community to address the problem.

"We don't have a place where my people can go to, to sit down and have a yarn and say, 'Look, I need help. Can you help me?'" she said.

Linda Doogiebee-Dridi (Milbugana) says a whole of community approach is needed to address child neglect in the community. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

"How do we make government departments change? By reaching out and saying, 'Let's co-design this department that has Aboriginal Affairs to the way that it's going to be culturally appropriate.'

"Until we actually have that talk with each other, we're not going to move on and create something that's beneficial to our people living in the Pilbara."

Latest concerns for under-fire department

Speaking earlier on Monday, Premier Roger Cook said the information that had come to light was "distressing".

"The Department of Child Protection works in very complex and difficult circumstances, made even more complex and difficult in a town such as Port Hedland," he said.

"We'll continue to ensure that we're doing everything we can to keep the kids of Western Australia safe."

The reports are the latest in a string of issues for the DCP and its care of vulnerable children across the state.

Child Protection falls under the Department of Communities, a so-called "super department" responsible to five separate ministers.

Roger Cook says the reports of neglect in South Hedland are distressing. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

More than 400 children in the department's care suffered emotional, physical or sexual abuse between 2020 and 2023, when the child protection and foster care system was described as being in "dire crisis".

An inquest into the suicide of a 15-year-old boy in the Kimberley heard the teenager had 30 different caseworkers prior to his death, while the timeframe for investigations of abuse or neglect had blown out to 60 days.

In 2024, the department left 170 vulnerable children without a dedicated caseworker.

Critics have accused the department of maintaining a nine-to-five culture in the face of a persistent problem, with the police union accusing it of outsourcing its functions to overstretched regional police officers.

Unveiling a journey of despair in WA's troubled child care system When a child isn’t safe with their family, they are placed into the care of the WA government. But some of these children and their foster parents are shining a spotlight on conditions they say are putting youth back in harm’s way.

Allegations taken 'seriously': department

The department did not answer specific questions about how it responded to the reported neglect in South Hedland.

A department spokesperson said it worked with multiple community and Aboriginal agencies to respond to at-risk individuals and families in South and Port Hedland.

"Communities' leadership also meets regularly with South Hedland and Port Hedland Aboriginal leaders, to listen to and address local concerns and discuss available supports," the spokesperson said.

"Where safety concerns for family visitations are raised, Communities engages with Police to ensure appropriate arrangements are put in place to allow contact visits to occur safely.

"Communities takes any allegation of child sexual abuse very seriously. Where concerns are raised, Communities will report to Police who are responsible for investigating alleged criminality."

World.title: Yemen's Houthi rebels seize more key islands in Red Sea to grip shipping route
World.content:
Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have captured more strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, government and Houthi officials say, strengthening their control of a major maritime shipping route.

The capture of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish came as Saudi-backed government forces attempted to rally over the weekend, attempting to fight back after the rebels' lightning advances around the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces react during what they say to be clashes with Iran-aligned Houthis in Al-Hazm, Yemen. (Reuters: Media Centre of the Yemeni Armed Forces)

The Houthi rebels deployed fighters on the Hanish islands, 160 kilometres north of Bab el-Mandeb, after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew from the archipelago, according to two government officials and a Houthi official.

The officials spoke on condition of anonymity on Monday because they are not authorised to talk to journalists.

Grasp on shipping tightens

The Houthis' new gains further enable the group to threaten Saudi crude oil shipments, which have used the Red Sea as a substitute to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking shipping.

The escalation, especially Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and its shipping endeavours across the Red Sea, adds to mounting pressure on global oil supplies and prices, which could give Iran leverage in its war with the United States.

Trucks explode during what the Houthis say was an attack targeting vehicles coming from Saudi territory, at the Al-Wadiah border. (Houthi Media Centre via Reuters)

The new capture of the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands comes after the rebels last week seized the port city of Mokha on Yemen's mainland, and the island of Mayun, located inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthis' advances also put them just 32 kilometres from the US military base in Djibouti, on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi air base attacked

The Saudi Civil Defense sent an all clear early on Monday after issuing alerts for potential danger in the southern cities of Najran, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Abha. It also later issued warnings for Khamis Mushait and Abha a second time before lifting them again.

Yemeni civilians celebrate while riding in the back of a utility vehicle as they follow a convoy carrying Houthi prisoners freed in Mokha following the Houthi takeover. (STR via AP Photo)

The Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen said they fired dozens of missiles and drones on Monday at a Saudi military air base in Khamis Mushait, hitting aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots.

The rebel group described the attack as retaliation for hundreds of Saudi air strikes on Yemen in recent days.

Renewed fighting between Houthis and Yemeni forces Renewed fighting has erupted between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemeni government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia.

The advances came with little resistance from forces of the internationally recognised government. But over the weekend, those forces sought to regroup, and the Yemeni military advanced toward the strategic town of Dhubab, north of the strait.

The fighting is pushing Yemen back into full-fledged civil war, after a truce that largely proved to be successful during the past three years.

Gulf meeting called off

Arab states called off a meeting with Iran planned for Monday.

Oman was due to host the meeting with Iran and Gulf states to discuss negotiations aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

But Oman's Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi announced overnight that the meeting had been postponed "in the interests of consensus". Iran said the postponement was at the request of Saudi Arabia.

AP

World.title: The 'kooky' show that lured Celeste Barber back to the theatre
World.content:
Comedian Celeste Barber is set to return to theatre for the first time in 20 years in "kooky" comedy play The Book of Liz.

While her last stage role was in 2006, the comedian and actor, known for Wellmania and Colin from Accounts, told ABC Arts in 2023 working at Sydney Theatre Company (STC) was "on the bucket list".

As the company launches its 2027 season, she says starring in The Book of Liz is "a dream come true".

It's a full-circle moment for Barber, who worked at the theatre's restaurant back in 2003, the year after she finished drama school.

She recalls her then-roommate landing a role alongside Hugo Weaving in Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing that year.

"I was cleaning cutlery at the end of the shift and looking down the corridor at them in the green room together running lines," she says.

" I remember thinking, as I scrubbed crusty pasta off a fork, 'One day that will be me'. And now it's happening. "

STC artistic director Mitchell Butel was impressed by Barber's comedy and dramatic chops in Wellmania. (Supplied: Netflix)

Premiering Off-Broadway in 2001, The Book of Liz is a play by American siblings Amy and David Sedaris — Amy best known for Bojack Horseman and surreal sketch show At Home with Amy Sedaris, and David for his comic essays.

Barber will play the relentlessly positive Sister Elizabeth Donderstock, who decides to leave her cloistered community after she's forced to give up her treasured cheese ball recipe.

She soon finds a job as a waitress at a family-run restaurant, with help from a bizarrely Cockney-accented Ukrainian couple. They're just two of the eccentrics Liz encounters as she adjusts to life away from her community.

It was the opportunity to work on a play by the Sedaris siblings, who write together as "The Talent Family", that lured Barber back to the stage.

"I loved [The Book of Liz] as soon as I read it," Barber says. "It made me laugh.

"I feel like a Sedaris play about an Amish cheese ball maker who is on a quest to find herself is exactly what the world needs: something funny, with heart."

Stepping away from theatre for 20 years wasn't deliberate, the comedian adds, but a "pivot" because she "couldn't book a job or even get an audition".

To play Liz, Barber plans to draw on the skills in character comedy she's finessed over more than a decade as a stand-up, but is most excited by the chance to work collaboratively.

"My favourite part of performing is diving in and picking apart a character and finding out what makes them tick, what makes them laugh, cry, fart, scream," she says.

"That's where the juice is.

"I plan on approaching this play in the way I approach most things: panicked. Then as soon I step into the rehearsal room I'll take on the form of a human sponge.

"I love rehearsal rooms; I love working and performing with other people. I love actors and I love notes!"

The Book of Liz is one of 13 plays in STC's 2027 season, which also includes a Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries play, and an adaptation of Jenny Hocking's The Palace Letters, starring Georgie Parker (Dalliance), about efforts to unseal papers about Gough Whitlam's dismissal in 1975.

The season is artistic director Mitchell Butel's second, with his leadership steering the company to its first surplus — of $765,759 — since 2022.

Butel says Whitlam's dismissal is still relevant in terms of "questions of nationhood". (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

That success is expected to continue, with ticket sales for 2026 already surpassing last year, thanks to new John Farnham musical Whispering Jack and An Iliad, starring David Wenham.

"There's always work to do and we have massive targets to keep the door open," Butel says.

" But hard as it is to produce theatre that's commercially successful, it's a great privilege and honour to do it, and we should celebrate it. "

Companies working together

An Iliad will tour Melbourne in 2027, with more cities expected to be announced. It's just one example of STC collaborating with theatre companies, festivals and venues across Australia in 2027 to extend the life spans of local productions.

In another modern adaptation of an ancient Greek text, Oedipus becomes a political thriller set on election night. It will star Richard Roxburgh and Heather Mitchell and will head to Adelaide Festival.

Roxburgh and Mitchell haven't shared a stage since 1992. Next year, they star together in Oedipus. (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

Keeping with the theme of reinterpreting classic plays, STC also co-produces John Proctor Is the Villain, with Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC), which interrogates Arthur Miller's The Crucible through the eyes of high school students.

In one of the season's literary adaptations, STC and State Theatre Company South Australia (STCSA) will collaborate on The Bookbinder of Jericho, about twin sisters working in a bindery during WWI, from the same team behind the sell-out success of The Dictionary of Lost Words.

Logan St, about an unlikely friendship between an Aboriginal woman and an Afghan cameleer in Adelaide in the 1940s, transfers from STCSA.

Co-produced by STC, Queensland Theatre Company (QTC) and Jones Theatrical Group, Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair is set on a boat and takes as its starting point one of the late Kerry Greenwood's novels not previously adapted for TV.

English writer Jack Thorne's reinterpretation of A Christmas Carol, which has played at Melbourne's Comedy Theatre every year since 2022, will come to Sydney for the first time, starring Tim Minchin in his first play since 2013.

A Christmas Carol will reunite Minchin with Matthew Warchus, the director of Matilda the Musical. (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

Butel says collaborations across Australian theatre like these are "really important".

"Because you're sharing costs, there's suddenly an ability to up cast sizes," he says.

"Bookbinder's a cast of eight, John Proctor is a cast of nine. Oedipus is a cast of 11, A Christmas Carol is a cast of 18. They're pretty large-scale shows for us."

A theatre for actors

Cast size isn't the only thing determining the scale of a production: The now-international "cine-theatre" hit The Picture of Dorian Gray will return to Australia, with Nikki Shiels (Colin from Accounts) playing all 26 characters.

STC's 2027 season Oedipus by Sophocles; adapted by Robert Icke

Logan Street by Jacob Boehme

Becky Shaw by Gina Gionfriddo

The Palace Letters by Melanie Tait

Amah and Nanna by Disapol Savetsila

Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair by Deb Cox

The Book of Liz by Amy and David Sedaris

The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde; adapted by Kip Williams

The Fifth Step by David Ireland

John Proctor Is the Villain by Kimberly Belflower

Vanya by Anton Chekhov; adapted by SImon Stephens

The Bookbinder of Jericho by Pip Williams; adapted by Verity Laughton

A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens; adapted by Jack Thorne

It's not Shiels's first time in the role, having been the alternate performer, or understudy, for the Australian tour since 2022. Next year she'll be taking over full-time from Eryn Jean Norvill, who originated the production.

Norvill will star in a one-woman show of her own as part of STC's 2027 season: Vanya, a new adaptation of Russian playwright Anton Chekhov's play, first brought to the stage by Andrew Scott (Fleabag).

Vanya is another example, along with The Book of Liz, of how Butel likes to program a season.

"I'm finding actors I love and want to be on our stage and asking 'What's going to float your boat?" Butel says.

That approach also led to Andrea Dimitriades (ABC TV's Return to Paradise) starring in the Australian premiere of Gina Gionfriddo's Becky Shaw, loosely based on William Thackeray's Victorian satire Vanity Fair.

Co-starring in Becky Shaw is Lincoln Younes (Last King of the Cross), in his first theatre role in a decade. He's just one screen star coming to STC, alongside Erik Thomson (Packed to the Rafters) in West End hit The Fifth Step and Gold Logie winner Lynne McGranger (Home and Away) and Annette Shun Wah in Disapol Savetsila's road trip comedy Amah and Nanna.

In 2017, at 23, Amah and Nanna writer Disapol Savetsila became the youngest-ever playwright to debut at STC. (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

Developed by Bathurst's Arbour Theatre Company, co-founded by Savetsila in 2020, Amah and Nanna was the winner of this year's Patrick White Award. Earlier play readings were hosted at Bathurst Memorial Entertainment Centre.

"It actually shows the benefit of funding regional arts centres to do this kind of work, because they have the ability to workshop stories that are of the regions," Butel says.

STC's 2027 season feels notable for its sheer breadth, which might account for the company's success since Butel took the reins.

"We're often accused of being elitist … but it's not all high art," he says.

"For every Uncle Vanya, there's also this kooky, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt-like fall into the rabbit hole [like The Book of Liz].

"Some people like KFC; some people like caviar. We'll provide it all for you."

World.title: Prominent pork industry identity charged over alleged multi-million-dollar fraud
World.content:
A Queensland pork industry heavyweight has been named as one of the people charged over alleged large-scale financial crimes that authorities claim resulted in tens of millions of dollars being funnelled out of businesses for personal use.

Darren Gary Wilson, 63, alongside Cameron Ronald Wilson are alleged to have kept $10 million in sales records off the books for personal use and moved more than $30 million in cash between New South Wales and Queensland between 2017 and 2026.

The men are facing multiple charges each including receiving and possessing tainted property, destroying records, fraud, making false declarations and fraudulent omission of entry in record.

They have also been accused of fraudulently relabelling frozen meat products to alter production and best before dates.

Pork industry financial crimes charges Police allege about $10 million was funnelled out of businesses in the pork meat industry for personal use.

Authorities have confirmed the changes did not pose a risk to food safety.

The pair were not required to appear in person on Monday and their bail has been extended.

Darren Wilson is a prominent face in the pork industry, starting Wilpak wholesale meats in Ipswich in the 1980s.

The company has since expanded to include meat processing and pig farms in Queensland.

He is also widely known in the racing industry.

Darren and Cameron Wilson are to return to court in coming weeks.

The pair were charged following a joint investigation involving the Queensland Crime and Corruption Commission, the New South Wales Police Anti-Money Laundering Unit and the New South Wales Crime Commission.

World.title: ‘Hollywood star’ in a Hummer accused of masterminding $50m drug run from Victoria to WA
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACourts ‘Hollywood star’ in a Hummer accused of masterminding $50m drug run from Victoria to WA Rebecca Peppiatt September 15, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police pulled over a motorhome in a rural West Australian town five years ago during an apparent routine traffic stop that allegedly uncovered almost $50 million worth of drugs stashed under the vehicle’s bed. However, they claim there was more to the story. A court sketch of Mohammed Charif Oueida, who is on trial in WA accused of masterminding a foiled drug-smuggling operation. Anne Barnetson The rental van had crossed the border into the state from Melbourne in April 2021 and was being driven by a man and woman who were so overcome with anxiety after being pulled over by police, they had to be taken to hospital for treatment. But police allege a third person masterminded the smuggling attempt – and at that point he was halfway down the highway, bound for Perth in a big, black Hummer.



That man, 50-year-old Mohammed Charif Oueida, is on trial in Perth’s District Court after he was charged with trafficking meth with the intention of selling it. Oueida denies the allegations. Last week, his lawyer told the jury that police spent “considerable time and expense” trying to pin a crime on the Victorian man, having placed a tracker on his car a month before his arrest, and were now tenuously trying to connect him to a crime he did not commit. Why the tracker was on Oueida’s car has not been made clear to the jury, but last week they were shown footage of his cross-country trip, which involved stops at various service stations and roadhouses. One employee gave evidence that seeing the Hummer pull in, number plates reading “HUMR2”, was like “something out of a Hollywood movie”. Others testified that there were three people staying in accommodation that was paid for in cash where the Hummer was parked outside.



It had travelled through before, they told the court. The manager of a remote Ceduna roadhouse told the court she had no trouble remembering the Hummer pulling in for fuel because it was “really impressive”. The black Hummer seized by WA Police in 2021. Peter de Kruijff “[The driver], he was a big bloke,” she said. “He looked like a Hollywood star – tough. He was nice, but very standoffish.” Prosecutors allege Oueida was travelling “in convoy” with the motorhome, maintaining a 30-minute distance and communicating with the motorhome’s driver – Khaled El-Moustafa – through an encrypted app using the code name “Air Force”.



After his arrest, El-Moustafa admitted his role in the drug smuggling plot and identified himself on the Ghost app as code-name “Trouble”. He’s now a serving prisoner, prosecutors told the jury. Police allege a third communicator, code name “Infinite”, was Oueida’s brother who allegedly owned a set of storage units and a panelbeating business on Somerset Road in Campbellfield, about 13 kilometres north of Melbourne, where CCTV allegedly captured the drugs being loaded into a van before the big trip west. Text messages between Air Force, Infinite and Trouble showed an intention to avoid detection on the trip, the court was told, but one read: “I’m at Norseman ... at the back of the BP, hotel room 26. See you soon.” Prosecutors told the court they checked the hotel’s records, and Oueida checked into room 26 at the motel in the remote West Australian town on that date. Further messages shown to the jury include, “Pick up motorhome find the best hiding spot”, “I have a back up female if needed”, “Leave normal phone here with me turned off”, and, “Highway patrol is out ’n about be careful”.



The messages then read, “Meet at Airbnb – Coolbellup”, referencing the suburb in Perth’s south where police later found Oueida and arrested him. Editor's pick Courts Watch: The horrifying moment roof collapses at Curtin University worksite An interview was played to the jury that was recorded by the organised crime squad as they were searching the property. In the interview, officers ask Oueida about his multiple mobile phones, and he tells them he sold encrypted phones for around $1800. “Why would someone want an encrypted phone like this instead of a normal one?” he was asked.



“Privacy,” was his response, before going on to explain that, “a lady who wears a scarf, sends me photos – to protect her privacy”. He then adds that a lot of people who buy the phones “have a problem with corrupt governments ... using their information”. The trial continues.

World.title: Bob Mackie, fashion designer to the stars, dies aged 87
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Bob Mackie, the iconic American designer to the stars who dressed Cher, Dolly Parton and Madonna and defined ’70s Hollywood glamour, has died aged 87.

“It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr. Bob Mackie passed away today,” a statement on Mackie’s Instagram account read on Monday (US time).

“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do. His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”

Mackie won nine Emmy Awards for his designs and was nominated more than 30 times. The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are being held in Los Angeles on Monday night (Tuesday morning AEST).

World.title: City of Perth faces yet another inquiry – this one, with teeth
World.content:
The City of Perth faces yet another inquiry as it battles to overcome “fractured working relationships” and “ongoing governance issues” plaguing the council Local Government Inspector Tony Brown revealed the commencement of his formal inquiry after addressing councillors and city staff at a behind-closed-doors meeting on Monday evening, where he presented them with the findings of a five-month probe that began with the appointment of former Kwinana mayor Carol Adams as a monitor in January. Local Government Inspector Tony Brown outside the City of Perth’s Council House on Monday evening. Cameron Myles Brown told media the fresh inquiry would take about three months and cost about $120,000, however he was confident it would be a “short and effective way of providing an outcome for the City of Perth community”. The council has been in the headlines constantly this year after Adams was appointed to monitor the local government amid a relationship breakdown between councillors and the city administration.



Brown said Adams’ report was not a public document, however the inquiry report would be, and could include recommendations for the council to implement. “We could recommend to the minister for local government that the council be dismissed, or certain individuals be dismissed,” he said. “So that’s the worst-case scenario, and I do not want to pre-empt what the inquiry will find.” Legislatively, Brown cannot take action on Adams’ monitor’s report, which paved the way for his inquiry. Brown listed breaches of confidentiality, a breakdown of public working relationships, and city officers “inundated with way too many questions and requirements” as issues raised during the monitor’s inquiry.



“The City of Perth is the flagship local government of Western Australia, so it needs to be the leader in governance,” he said. Related Article Local government Perth council blocks CEO return as investigation continues “I don’t think it’s there at the moment, so we’re going to work through that, and we want the City of Perth to be able to return to providing good governance for its community.” The local government inspector pushed back on suggestions bureaucracy was hindering meaningful action, noting the previous, well-publicised inquiry into the city ran for more than two years and cost $7 million, while his and Adams’ inquiries should be wrapped up within the space of nine to 12 months. City of Perth chief executive Michelle Reynolds was suspended by the council in May after councillors and city staff received a briefing on Adam’s report from Brown, during which he put the council “on notice” regarding the monitor’s probe.



The development prompted an angry response from Local Government Minster Hannah Beazley who in turn raised the spectre of council amalgamations. Last month, a motion to bring Reynolds back from suspension “effective immediately” was voted down, with councillors opting to defer the decision until after the completion of a workplace culture review. The City of Perth was the first West Australian local government to be allocated a monitor, just two weeks into Brown’s role as the head local government watchdog at the start of the year.

World.title: A cure for loneliness? Hayes Theatre backs the power of live performance as new season launches
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows A cure for loneliness? Hayes Theatre backs the power of live performance as new season launches Lenny Ann Low September 14, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I’ve just realised,” says Victoria Falconer, co-artistic director, with Richard Carroll, of Hayes Theatre Co. “People are talking about the loneliness epidemic and this is a cure.” “You want connection? You want humans? Come to the theatre. We can give you that. It’s here. Why am I not yelling about this more?” Joel Granger in his Phar Lap costume, with Hayes artistic directors Richard Carroll and Victoria Falconer. Sitthixay Ditthavong Launching Hayes Theatre Co’s 2027 season, their final one as co-artistic directors, Falconer and Carroll have many thoughts about the power of theatre. As the arts industry grapples with the cost-of-living crisis, including recently curtailed seasons of several high-profile Australian musical theatre productions, new and original stage work remains vital. “In the hope for humanity, in the hope for learning, in the hope of connection,” Falconer says. “All of that is why we make art in the first place.”



Falconer says parts of the sector, including financial support and opportunities for artists, have been broken for some time. But she sees hope. “People have been struggling for ages,” she says. “People from non-privileged backgrounds find it very hard to get into the arts. That should have been the canary in the coal mine, always, but it’s not. Big things need to change. “But I feel that is coming. Whether that’s the government finally giving artists a living wage, or from something more grassroots. That’s where Hayes came from, a bunch of indie producers with no money persuading the council to give them a building and to put some shows in it. “That can never die. In the darkest times, for hundreds of years, people are drawn to theatre. Why would we be any different?” The 2027 Hayes season will be Richard Carroll and Victoria Falconer’s last as co-artistic directors. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Small but mighty, Hayes Theatre Co is known for a stream of successful new and reimagined musical theatre works and next year some of its shows will venture beyond the company’s Potts Point base. Under the banner Hayes in New Places, the soldout 2025 hit Phar Lap: The Electro-Swing Musical returns for an expanded production at Carriageworks and a multicity tour, including a Melbourne Theatre Company season. In October, Mack the Knife, a new work by Falconer and Carroll, transforms the Foundry Theatre inside Sydney Lyric into a multiroom, immersive rock-cabaret musical based on The Beggar’s Opera by John Gay and The Threepenny Opera by Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill. Carroll says Hayes Theatre Co’s Potts Point home remains integral to its identity but sharing work with wider audiences, in Sydney and beyond, has been a longtime aim. “This season reflects the journey that we want to be taking Hayes on,” he says. “It is a massive thing for us to be transferring and touring Phar Lap, a new Australian work that’s such a Hayes show in terms of its invention and being silly, funny but also weirdly moving. “And Mack the Knife, it’s important for us to make clear that although it’s based on The Threepenny Opera, it’s a whole new script with a new story and some different songs. It’s an original work with the first section a fully immersive [experience], where people will be making their own way through different spaces, before the show itself.”



Joel Granger as Phar Lap, which is showing at Carriageworks next month before heading out on the road. Sitthixay Ditthavong The 2027 season also features new productions of the musical farce Lucky Stiff, folk epic Swept Away and Pulitzer Prize and three-time Tony Award-winning rock musical Next to Normal, an exploration of family and illness, loss and grief. And then there’s a world premiere, Peter Allen: Not the Boy Next Door, a work honouring the acclaimed Australian singer-songwriter’s legacy and songs. “It’s a new cabaret-concert celebration similar to Barbra, this year’s smash sellout Hayes hit,” Falconer says. “It’s high time we celebrated such an influential person across musical theatre and cabaret.” Opera fans are catered for with director Matthew Barclay’s Bridgerton-style, reimagining of Mozart’s Così fan tutte: School for Lovers, before Sydney Theatre Award-winner Cameron Mitchell delivers coming-of-age sci-fi satire Be More Chill and Rachael Beck (Cluedo, Beauty and the Beast) stars in the Australian premiere of Flowers for Mrs Harris, based on the Paul Gallico novel which also inspired the 2022 feature film Mrs. Harris Goes To Paris.



House of Rot, starring Paul Capsis and Adam Noviello, returns as does the Festival of New Work, extended to three weeks, and the Winter Cabaret Festival now called Flare: Winter Cabaret Festival. Related Article Stage shows ‘A really stupid and fun idea’: There’s a Phar Lap musical, and it’s not horsing around “We ask our audiences what they love about Hayes and they always say, ‘I see things here that I’ve never seen before’,” Carroll says. “Being able to surprise, that’s something we don’t take for granted.” Falconer agrees. “People really just want to come to a space and watch another human do some stuff,” she says. “And the more thrilling, the more inventive, the more skilful that is, the better.”

World.title: No taffy for Albo
World.content:
In reflecting on then-transport minister Anthony Albanese’s gaffe in quoting a fictional character in a 2012 speech to the National Press Club – US president Andrew Shepherd, played by Michael Douglas in the movie The American President – Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls wonders, “Which other fictional presidents and PMs might do well in today’s opinion polls?” For the record, Albo escaped censure from then-prime minister Julia Gillard because she loves Douglas and “he’s married to a Welsh woman”.

Janice Creenaune of Austinmer has more on the curbside nature break (C8): “While living in Oxfordshire, we had to drive the A34 north to school in Kidlington to the west of Oxford. Accidents were common and the two lanes were often blocked for sometimes four to six hours, depending on circumstances. Men found relieving themselves fairly easy. For women, not so much. I was advised that it was acceptable to open both car doors on one side and pee between them. Leaving the car to go elsewhere was not an option, but I did wonder about the MGs that were still very popular and once made in Abingdon-on-Thames where we lived.”

Granny wished she’d heard this piece of advice from David Prest of Thrumster a number of decades earlier: “My dad told me never to put a tyre valve cap in my mouth while inflating a tyre as you never knew if a dog (or a person) had peed on the tyre. ‘Always put it on the ground,’ he said.”

“Rumour has it that a prototype of a coffin (C8) made from toadstools was rejected because it was too small and could not cater for larger people,” reports Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “Evidently, there was not mushroom inside.”

With golf cart-chasing US political aide, Natalie Harp, having a moment in the news, Kevin Hunt of Kenthurst notes that “the Daily Mail reports that Melania Trump’s ‘top spokesman’, Marc Beckman, in an interview with media host Stella Inger Escobedo, complained that the liberal press was obsessed with the first lady’s private life, as well as the ‘hardworking, very talented, very intelligent’ close aide to the president, aka ‘the human printer’. ‘The press,’ Beckman said, ‘just keep harping on with these subjects.’ If the pun was intended, it was quite a good one.”

World.title: ‘Not eliciting that duty of care’: AFLW player hit with three-game ban for jaw-breaking bump
World.content:
A Port Adelaide defender has been whacked with a hefty three-game ban over a head-high bump described by one expert as “probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen” in women’s footy.

The incident in Saturday’s game between Melbourne and Port at Casey Fields left Melbourne defender Eliza McNamara needing surgery on a broken jaw.

Port player Ella Heads caught her opponent high early in the last quarter of Melbourne’s 51-point win. McNamara left the field immediately and was taken to hospital.

The front-on hit was deemed by the AFLW match review process to be careless conduct, high contact and severe impact, leading to the three-game suspension.

World.title: Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future Daniel Lo Surdo September 14, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of the star Sydney university student shot dead in a case of mistaken identity has recalled the moment she held her “beautiful” son in her arms as he took his final breath. Marco Tapia, 23, was killed in bed at his Glen Alpine residence in the early hours of September 1 after a group of assailants stormed his family home and sprayed bullets at him. It would become the first of three underworld shootings in Sydney’s escalating gangland war. Sergio and Claudia Tapia say “hate came to our house” the night their son was killed. A Current Affair Parents Sergio and Claudia Tapia recounted the “nightmare” attack that claimed their son’s life, telling A Current Affair on Monday the violent onslaught happened “so fast”. “I remember him taking his final breath,” Claudia said. “There was hate that came to our house.”



Sergio said the attack had been forever etched in their memories: “It’s amazing I didn’t have a heart attack when that happened … when you close your eyes is when you see everything again and again, and again and again.” Marco’s sister, Cassie, will be without her “big little brother” when she gets married in November. Invitations for her nuptials were due to be sent the day he was killed. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine residence on September 1. Sam Mooy “He’s my best friend, and the fact he’s not going to be there as one of the groomsmen is heartbreaking,” she said. “He was just such a warm person.” But the Tapia family has chosen peace over anger, suggesting they could one day forgive the people behind Marco’s death.



“I thought in this situation I would be seeing fire and brimstone and looking for vengeance. Certainly, there’s no anger in our heart. If you have anger, you cannot have peace in your heart,” Sergio said. “Right now we are striving for peace, and forgiveness will come.” The Tapia family have chosen peace over anger following the death of Marco. A Current Affair Tapia was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, where he had won awards and volunteered for Engineers Without Borders. His only known brush with the law was a minor traffic offence. Tapia’s death was the first of two mistaken identity murders orchestrated by Sydney’s underworld in as many days.



Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home one day after Tapia’s murder as he arrived at the home with two children. The owners of the residence, where Macdonald didn’t live, are known to police and are linked to organised crime. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News The attacks triggered the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years as it worked to stave off suggestions it had lost control of Sydney’s streets. The reforms, announced by Premier Chris Minns on September 7, promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings.



Louis Meehan, a 32-year-old boxing coach linked to the Alameddine crime family, was shot dead in an ambush at a Punchbowl carpark on September 9, two days after the suite of reforms was unveiled. Meehan, who was known to police, was sprayed with gunfire by an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Meehan died in the carpark while onlookers prayed for his welfare. Louis Meehan was shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Escalating underworld violence comes as the warring Alameddine crime family and the Coconut Cartel jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities away from Australian jurisdiction. World.title: ‘Hollywood star’ in a Hummer accused of masterminding $50m drug run from Victoria to WA
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWACourts ‘Hollywood star’ in a Hummer accused of masterminding $50m drug run from Victoria to WA Rebecca Peppiatt September 15, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police pulled over a motorhome in a rural West Australian town five years ago during an apparent routine traffic stop that allegedly uncovered almost $50 million worth of drugs stashed under the vehicle’s bed. However, they claim there was more to the story. A court sketch of Mohammed Charif Oueida, who is on trial in WA accused of masterminding a foiled drug-smuggling operation. Anne Barnetson The rental van had crossed the border into the state from Melbourne in April 2021 and was being driven by a man and woman who were so overcome with anxiety after being pulled over by police, they had to be taken to hospital for treatment. But police allege a third person masterminded the smuggling attempt – and at that point he was halfway down the highway, bound for Perth in a big, black Hummer.



That man, 50-year-old Mohammed Charif Oueida, is on trial in Perth’s District Court after he was charged with trafficking meth with the intention of selling it. Oueida denies the allegations. Last week, his lawyer told the jury that police spent “considerable time and expense” trying to pin a crime on the Victorian man, having placed a tracker on his car a month before his arrest, and were now tenuously trying to connect him to a crime he did not commit. Why the tracker was on Oueida’s car has not been made clear to the jury, but last week they were shown footage of his cross-country trip, which involved stops at various service stations and roadhouses. One employee gave evidence that seeing the Hummer pull in, number plates reading “HUMR2”, was like “something out of a Hollywood movie”. Others testified that there were three people staying in accommodation that was paid for in cash where the Hummer was parked outside.



It had travelled through before, they told the court. The manager of a remote Ceduna roadhouse told the court she had no trouble remembering the Hummer pulling in for fuel because it was “really impressive”. The black Hummer seized by WA Police in 2021. Peter de Kruijff “[The driver], he was a big bloke,” she said. “He looked like a Hollywood star – tough. He was nice, but very standoffish.” Prosecutors allege Oueida was travelling “in convoy” with the motorhome, maintaining a 30-minute distance and communicating with the motorhome’s driver – Khaled El-Moustafa – through an encrypted app using the code name “Air Force”.



After his arrest, El-Moustafa admitted his role in the drug smuggling plot and identified himself on the Ghost app as code-name “Trouble”. He’s now a serving prisoner, prosecutors told the jury. Police allege a third communicator, code name “Infinite”, was Oueida’s brother who allegedly owned a set of storage units and a panelbeating business on Somerset Road in Campbellfield, about 13 kilometres north of Melbourne, where CCTV allegedly captured the drugs being loaded into a van before the big trip west. Text messages between Air Force, Infinite and Trouble showed an intention to avoid detection on the trip, the court was told, but one read: “I’m at Norseman ... at the back of the BP, hotel room 26. See you soon.” Prosecutors told the court they checked the hotel’s records, and Oueida checked into room 26 at the motel in the remote West Australian town on that date. Further messages shown to the jury include, “Pick up motorhome find the best hiding spot”, “I have a back up female if needed”, “Leave normal phone here with me turned off”, and, “Highway patrol is out ’n about be careful”.



The messages then read, “Meet at Airbnb – Coolbellup”, referencing the suburb in Perth’s south where police later found Oueida and arrested him. Editor's pick Courts Watch: The horrifying moment roof collapses at Curtin University worksite An interview was played to the jury that was recorded by the organised crime squad as they were searching the property. In the interview, officers ask Oueida about his multiple mobile phones, and he tells them he sold encrypted phones for around $1800. “Why would someone want an encrypted phone like this instead of a normal one?” he was asked.



“Privacy,” was his response, before going on to explain that, “a lady who wears a scarf, sends me photos – to protect her privacy”. He then adds that a lot of people who buy the phones “have a problem with corrupt governments ... using their information”. The trial continues.

World.title: Bob Mackie, fashion designer to the stars, dies aged 87
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Bob Mackie, the iconic American designer to the stars who dressed Cher, Dolly Parton and Madonna and defined ’70s Hollywood glamour, has died aged 87.

“It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr. Bob Mackie passed away today,” a statement on Mackie’s Instagram account read on Monday (US time).

“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do. His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”

Mackie won nine Emmy Awards for his designs and was nominated more than 30 times. The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are being held in Los Angeles on Monday night (Tuesday morning AEST).
