World.title: No taffy for Albo
World.content:
In reflecting on then-transport minister Anthony Albanese’s gaffe in quoting a fictional character in a 2012 speech to the National Press Club – US president Andrew Shepherd, played by Michael Douglas in the movie The American President – Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls wonders, “Which other fictional presidents and PMs might do well in today’s opinion polls?” For the record, Albo escaped censure from then-prime minister Julia Gillard because she loves Douglas and “he’s married to a Welsh woman”.

Janice Creenaune of Austinmer has more on the curbside nature break (C8): “While living in Oxfordshire, we had to drive the A34 north to school in Kidlington to the west of Oxford. Accidents were common and the two lanes were often blocked for sometimes four to six hours, depending on circumstances. Men found relieving themselves fairly easy. For women, not so much. I was advised that it was acceptable to open both car doors on one side and pee between them. Leaving the car to go elsewhere was not an option, but I did wonder about the MGs that were still very popular and once made in Abingdon-on-Thames where we lived.”

Granny wished she’d heard this piece of advice from David Prest of Thrumster a number of decades earlier: “My dad told me never to put a tyre valve cap in my mouth while inflating a tyre as you never knew if a dog (or a person) had peed on the tyre. ‘Always put it on the ground,’ he said.”

“Rumour has it that a prototype of a coffin (C8) made from toadstools was rejected because it was too small and could not cater for larger people,” reports Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “Evidently, there was not mushroom inside.”

With golf cart-chasing US political aide, Natalie Harp, having a moment in the news, Kevin Hunt of Kenthurst notes that “the Daily Mail reports that Melania Trump’s ‘top spokesman’, Marc Beckman, in an interview with media host Stella Inger Escobedo, complained that the liberal press was obsessed with the first lady’s private life, as well as the ‘hardworking, very talented, very intelligent’ close aide to the president, aka ‘the human printer’. ‘The press,’ Beckman said, ‘just keep harping on with these subjects.’ If the pun was intended, it was quite a good one.”

World.title: ‘Not eliciting that duty of care’: AFLW player hit with three-game ban for jaw-breaking bump
World.content:
A Port Adelaide defender has been whacked with a hefty three-game ban over a head-high bump described by one expert as “probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen” in women’s footy.

The incident in Saturday’s game between Melbourne and Port at Casey Fields left Melbourne defender Eliza McNamara needing surgery on a broken jaw.

Port player Ella Heads caught her opponent high early in the last quarter of Melbourne’s 51-point win. McNamara left the field immediately and was taken to hospital.

The front-on hit was deemed by the AFLW match review process to be careless conduct, high contact and severe impact, leading to the three-game suspension.

World.title: Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future Daniel Lo Surdo September 14, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of the star Sydney university student shot dead in a case of mistaken identity has recalled the moment she held her “beautiful” son in her arms as he took his final breath. Marco Tapia, 23, was killed in bed at his Glen Alpine residence in the early hours of September 1 after a group of assailants stormed his family home and sprayed bullets at him. It would become the first of three underworld shootings in Sydney’s escalating gangland war. Sergio and Claudia Tapia say “hate came to our house” the night their son was killed. A Current Affair Parents Sergio and Claudia Tapia recounted the “nightmare” attack that claimed their son’s life, telling A Current Affair on Monday the violent onslaught happened “so fast”. “I remember him taking his final breath,” Claudia said. “There was hate that came to our house.”



Sergio said the attack had been forever etched in their memories: “It’s amazing I didn’t have a heart attack when that happened … when you close your eyes is when you see everything again and again, and again and again.” Marco’s sister, Cassie, will be without her “big little brother” when she gets married in November. Invitations for her nuptials were due to be sent the day he was killed. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine residence on September 1. Sam Mooy “He’s my best friend, and the fact he’s not going to be there as one of the groomsmen is heartbreaking,” she said. “He was just such a warm person.” But the Tapia family has chosen peace over anger, suggesting they could one day forgive the people behind Marco’s death.



“I thought in this situation I would be seeing fire and brimstone and looking for vengeance. Certainly, there’s no anger in our heart. If you have anger, you cannot have peace in your heart,” Sergio said. “Right now we are striving for peace, and forgiveness will come.” The Tapia family have chosen peace over anger following the death of Marco. A Current Affair Tapia was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, where he had won awards and volunteered for Engineers Without Borders. His only known brush with the law was a minor traffic offence. Tapia’s death was the first of two mistaken identity murders orchestrated by Sydney’s underworld in as many days.



Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home one day after Tapia’s murder as he arrived at the home with two children. The owners of the residence, where Macdonald didn’t live, are known to police and are linked to organised crime. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News The attacks triggered the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years as it worked to stave off suggestions it had lost control of Sydney’s streets. The reforms, announced by Premier Chris Minns on September 7, promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings.



Louis Meehan, a 32-year-old boxing coach linked to the Alameddine crime family, was shot dead in an ambush at a Punchbowl carpark on September 9, two days after the suite of reforms was unveiled. Meehan, who was known to police, was sprayed with gunfire by an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Meehan died in the carpark while onlookers prayed for his welfare. Louis Meehan was shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Escalating underworld violence comes as the warring Alameddine crime family and the Coconut Cartel jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities away from Australian jurisdiction. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: KiwiSaver: Would Labour or National make you better off?
World.content:
When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

KiwiSaver is on the table as a major issue of this year's election.

But would you be better off under National's KiwiSaver plan, or Labour's?

National is promising to make participation compulsory, with a 6 percent employee plus 6 percent employer contribution required by 2032.

Labour would only make the employer contribution compulsory, rising to 6 percent, and would remove any minimum employee contribution so that people could pause or reduce their payments.

National would automatically enrol babies at birth and give them $1500.

Both parties would require employer contributions for people who are over 65. National would provide a government contribution for people who are on paid parental leave and not contributing to KiwiSaver. Labour would require employer contributions to continue when someone was off on parental leave.

Labour would ban new total remuneration packages.

As a general comparison and not including the impact of income tax over a person's working life, a 25-year-old currently earning $60,000 a year and making contributions at the default rate could end up with $1.014 million in their account under Labour's plan and $1.241 million under National's.

The worker would have given up more of their own salary over their working life in the National scenario.

A 45-year-old earning $100,000 would end up with $340,000 under Labour's plan and $424,000 under National's.

A 25-year-old not contributing themselves could still end up with $561,000 under Labour's plan. National would require them to contribute.

The $1500 baby payment could grow to be worth about $8000 over 25 years.

Infometrics managing director Gareth Kiernan said it was hard to compare the two policies.

"We can effectively ignore the higher contributions being required of employers because they are set at 6 percent across both parties' policies.

"The question then essentially becomes, are workers better off if they are forced to save 6 percent of their income rather than 4 percent of their income? If people were rational and planned appropriately for the future, the answer would be no - because allowing people to choose what to do with their income would enable them to make the best choices for their individual circumstances. For example, people with a mortgage could decide that the best way to improve their long-term financial position is to prioritise paying off the mortgage first rather than investing, and then save and invest at a faster rate later.

"However, it's questionable whether many people act in this way. I won't say they are irrational; rather, that they have a high discount rate, which means they place little weighting on events a long way in the future when making decisions. Put simply, spending money now is a more attractive option than saving money to use in 40 years' time. Thus outcomes could be better from a broad societal point of view if the government legislates that people must save so that retired people are less of a drain on society in the future. The alternatives to legislating higher KiwiSaver rates now might be, in the future, higher tax rates or reduced levels of government superannuation - outcomes that might not be fiscally achievable or could provide insufficient support for future retirees."

He said there would also be questions about whether forcing people to save more would eventually result in less universal government superannuation in the future.

"If that is the case, then a 25-year-old saving 6 percent now achieves a larger KiwiSaver balance at retirement but it might be offset by less government support after they retire.

"Nevertheless, even this part of the argument becomes nuanced when one considers what an appropriate level of retirement income might be. It could be argued that even the current superannuation rate of $44,400 per annum per couple after tax is not enough for a comfortable lifestyle, let alone any possible future reductions in support as fiscal settings become more stretched. In that case, some level of forced private saving by the government to top up this amount would improve people's future wellbeing.

"Essentially, which policy makes people better off comes down to the trade-off between current personal spending and saving for retirement -and lower-income people are likely to have less room in their budget for saving, how bad people are at planning for the future, and whether they need to be protected from themselves and any differences in future government policy that might see higher-wealth people receive less government superannuation support."

Pathfinder Asset Management founder John Berry said it was disappointing that KiwiSaver had ended up being an election issue rather than a wider discussion about retirement settings and where NZ Super would fit in.

"The bigger question for people in their 30s and 40s at the moment is what is NZ Super going to mean for them in retirement? Are the settings going to be the same or less? That impacts how much they need to save in KiwiSaver."

But he said it was important that New Zealand moved towards matching Australia's contribution rate of 12 percent.

"We're not all saving enough for retirement. The Retirement Commission is saying 40 percent of people over 65 have virtually no other income besides NZ Super. That is quite astonishing. Forty percent of New Zealanders are relying on NZ Super for retirement. We need to fix that. The best way to do it and give people the sort of lifestyle they want from retirement is larger KiwiSaver balances, saving small amounts compounding over a very long time frame."

He said there needed to be cross-party support for a different approach. "People in their 20s are kind of in a difficult spot at the moment where they're saving for their own retirement and their taxes are paying super payments to retirees, but they may not or are unlikely to get the same benefit when they get to retirement."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said the difference between the two policies came down to National requiring people to save more, but that could mean people had less take-home pay.

"Under the Labour scenario you are going to save less but you have more flexibility. Those who can save more will save more."

He supported delinking employer and employee contributions. "If you are going through a hardship, it doesn't mean the employer should suddenly experience a lower cost of employing you. It doesn't make sense."

Read all of the election policies released so far in our full guide

World.title: Flu season hitting children's hospitals hard, extra paediatricians called in
World.content:
Extra paediatricians are being drafted in and elective procedures are still being called off in the busiest flu season for Auckland's children's hospitals in years.

PHF Science figures showed there had been about 70 children with the most severe respiratory symptoms admitted each week for the past four weeks to Kidz First and Starship hospitals.

That was an 85 percent increase since the end of July and did not reflect the total number of children in hospital with respiratory symptoms, or emergency presentations.

South Auckland paediatrician Dame Teuila Percival said this winter had been the worst for years - and the busiest she could remember.

It had been all hands on deck at KidzFirst.

"People do extra shifts, we have senior medical officers like myself, and others who work in places like psychiatry coming in, helping out doing more time in the ED," Dame Teuila said.

Children were being admitted with a wide range of symptoms including dehydration, confusion from fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, difficulty breathing, a bad cough and needing oxygen, she said.

Some were in intensive care - usually because they needed high levels of support with breathing, she said.

Starship Hospital had deferred elective procedures because the space was need for acutely unwell children. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

"They're taken care of very well when they're there but its very stressful for parents and families to see their children so unwell," he said.

RNZ understands Starship also remained very busy, with elective procedures still regularly deferred because the space was need for acutely unwell children.

More help needed next year

Dame Teuila said many of the sickest children were Pasifika or Māori children.

It was great that the flu vaccine had been made free for under-fives earlier this month, but she would like to see it free for everyone next winter, she said.

Flu often made its way around a family, and more vaccination would help.

"It's not uncommon that the whole family come to ED - and we see all the children and the mum and the dad and everybody's sick," she said.

Dame Teuila said there needed to be more resources for general practice to be able to help more people get in to see their doctors before they get sicker.

"I do think getting to primary care is a barrier for a lot of families particularly if you have got two, three, four kids all sick. Its very hard to get into see someone at the moment in a timely way," she said.

"My colleagues in primary care work really hard. They're just under the pump when I speak to them on the phone as we all are. They just need more people," she said

RNZ asked Health NZ for figures for children in other main hospitals in New Zealand, but it said they needed to go through the Official Information Act process which could take several weeks.

But PHF Science kept combined figures for the two dedicated children's hospitals in Auckland, which is why they were readily available.

A spokesperson said the figures which went to 6 September were part of its severe acute respiratory surveillance which only covered some of the sickest children.

World.title: Fears jobseeker benefit changes could trap young people in abusive households
World.content:
Incoming changes to the jobseeker benefit could trap young New Zealanders in violent households, advocates say.

From November, some 18 and 19-year-olds will need to prove their parents are unable or unwilling to support them before they can qualify for the benefit.

The change - passed under urgency just a few months before the election - meant parents would be expected to support their children in the first two years of adulthood.

But Aaron Hendry, the general manager of youth homelessness charity Kick Back, feared for those in abusive homes.

"There's absolutely a risk that for some young people, if they're in a situation where they are unsafe, that they will feel trapped and unable to leave," he said.

"That will put those young people at risk of either experiencing homelessness, or they feel they have no other choice but to stay and continue to be victims of abuse and harm."

Child Poverty Action Group spokesperson Isaac Gunson said the jobseeker benefit was vital for young New Zealanders trying to escape bad situations.

"Especially in households where abuse is a problem and children need to get away from their parents, this policy will fall even more harshly on those people," Gunson said.

"It creates a higher level of dependency on parents who may otherwise need to be escaped."

In a statement to RNZ, Ministry of Social Development spokesperson Fiona Carter-Giddings said there were options for people who could not rely on their parents.

"We will need evidence that a parental support gap exists. This could be an official document or a supporting statement from a health, education, justice or social services professional who can confirm the young person's situation," she said.

"If we are made aware that a client is in an abusive situation, we can also offer specific services to help them into a safer situation."

Isaac Gunson. Supplied

Hendry said that was little comfort.

"Look, I appreciate that the ministry is attempting to create a pathway there, but when you create layers of bureaucracy and regulate these systems there will be young people that slip through the cracks," Hendry said.

"And just due to the nature of it, there will be some young people that are fearful that they won't have an opportunity to get out in the first place."

Child Matters chief executive Megan West said the changes limited the options available to victims.

"One of the unintended consequences could be that young people don't get the support they need when they need it," she said.

"If you've got a young person who wants to get out of an environment, it really limits the options for them, and options are pretty limited already."

Gunson said it should not be left up to young people to prove they were victims of abuse.

"There is a huge difficulty with expecting a young person to obtain evidence to prove a breakdown in their relationship with a parent," he said.

"It places the burden on them to disclose that abuse to the state, or to contact or confront the abusive parent who they are avoiding for their safety."

He said abuse came in different forms, and some of it was intangible.

"Circumstances can be difficult to prove, especially when it comes to psychological abuse, coercive control, family rejection, or even just longstanding dysfunction within a family unit," he said.

"How does someone prove those sorts of things? That would be my question to MSD."

The changes were set to kick in from 2 November, just one week before the election and a week after voter enrolments closed.

Hendry said it was awful timing.

"Coming up to Christmas is one of the most dangerous periods in terms of young people in dangerous and abusive environments," he said.

"This is also the period where a lot of services go on leave. A lot of those key support systems in the community won't be there to support those young people to navigate that."

Social Development Minister Louise Upston. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Hendry and Gunson both urged the government to reconsider the policy.

In a statement, Social Development Minister Louise Upston said where there has been an irreconcilable breakdown in a family relationship, there is a carve-out for 18- and 19-year-olds to become eligible for some supports.

"Where possible, it is expected parents support their young people if they are not in training, education or employment. This is better for their future.

She expected MSD to communicate the policy so that people were aware of what they are entitled to.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki staff were present during 'walking the line' assault
World.content:
Oranga Tamariki has confirmed staff were present during the assault of a young person by his peers in a ritual attack known as 'walking the line'.

The ministry told RNZ the "action or inaction" in this case was being addressed and it could not provide further details about why staff did not stop the assault.

RNZ revealed last month that a young person had been slapped and hit by other teenagers as he was discharged from youth justice residence Korowai Manaaki in March.

Official Oranga Tamariki (OT) documents seen by RNZ confirmed that a 'walking the line' assault took place.

That was explained as a situation where young people stand either side of the internal door of the main entrance to the unit and wait to farewell the young person being discharged.

In this instance, three young people stood on one side and two on the other.

The document described the young person being discharged as standing at the top of the line. It said "he appeared nervous and was hesitant to walk towards the door".

The incident was referred to police and an employment investigation had commenced.

RNZ requested further information about the assault, and was told that at the time of the incident in question, "kaimahi were present in the unit with the rangatahi".

OT also confirmed police had closed their investigation with no charges made and no further action, advising OT they found "no evidence of criminal offending by either the rangatahi involved or the kaimahi".

At the time of the request made to OT for further information in mid-August, OT said an employment process was still underway regarding the matter.

RNZ then asked why staff did not stop the assault from happening.

Oranga Tamariki Youth Justice Services and Residential Care deputy chief executive Dean Winter responded, saying "staff action or inaction in this case is being addressed appropriately and we cannot provide further details".

World.title: Fundraiser launched for children of woman who died in Nelson
World.content:
A fundraiser has been launched to help secure a stable home and future education for the two children of a woman who died in a suspected murder-suicide in Nelson.

Tracey Schroder has set up a Givealittle page for her nephews, Ryan and Josh, following the death of her sister Nicola Yvonne Perry, 48.

Nicola and 49-year-old Brendon James Perry died at a property on Parkers Road in Tāhunanui on 4 September.

RNZ understands their deaths are being treated as a suspected murder-suicide.

Nicola Yvonne Perry, 48, was killed in a suspected murder-suicide in Nelson. NZ Police

The alarm was raised after a shotgun was stolen from Hunting & Fishing on Quarantine Road in Annesbrook.

In a message accompanying the fundraiser on Facebook, Schroder said her family was trying to cope with the loss of her sister, and she wanted to help her nephews.

"My family are trying to cope with intense grief from the tragic loss of my sister Nic Perry, and right now the best way I can support my nephews is to help their futures, Nic would have wanted us to."

The fundraiser page said the money raised would go towards providing Ryan and Josh with a safe and stable home, as well as supporting their future schooling and study.

The fundraiser has raised more than $12,000 for the family so far.

World.title: Environmental imprint of new jeans 180 times higher than second hand pair - research
World.content:
The environmental cost of a new pair of jeans could be enough to make a shopper blue.

Brand new jeans can have an environmental footprint that is 180 times higher than pre-loved ones, according to new research.

The data from Planetary Accounting Network uses a dashboard to calculate the environmental costs of everyday purchases, breaking down environmental data for a product, such as the amount of carbon produced, water used and waste created.

Planetary Accounting Network says by 2030, carbon needs to be limited to six kilograms per person per day - and waste to 2kg.

Secondhand jeans far more eco-friendly than new pair - research Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Recycling champions Wanaka WasteBusters commissioned the research and general manager Gina Dempster told RNZ they wanted the data to figure out a number for the environmental benefits of second hand jeans over new ones.

"And what they found is that if you look at your average per-capita budget for a healthy planet, buying a second hand pair of jeans from WasteBusters uses about three percent of my daily budget, whereas just the fabric for a new pair of jeans could use up to five full days of my planetary budget, which would leave me nothing for food, transport and all the other things I have to do every day."

She said the environmental cost of denim came from the water usage, the deforestation, and the use of nitrogen fertilisers in producing the denim.

"The reality is that if you buy a pair of jeans from an opshop, that pair of jeans has already been made, and then the environmental cost of just bringing those jeans into an opshop and running the shop and selling them is extremely low.

"So essentially they are kind of free for the environment."

Gina Dempster from Wastebusters. Wastebusters

She said it was well known that jeans used thousands of litres of water in their production, but knowing the footprint was 180 times higher "really makes you think about every pair of jeans that you've ever owned".

Wanaka WasteBusters receives a "massive" amount of jeans with a huge rack of available pants, mostly selling for about $10-$15, according to Dempster.

"If it was a really high quality pair of jeans in new condition you might be paying up to $30, but that would be a pair of jeans that you might be paying $300-$500 for new."

Dempster said it was hard for people to get a feel for the sheer amount of textile products that were going on to the second hand market.

"That's one thing for our team, working at the drop-off every day, we see the amount of textiles that come through one opshop in one small town in New Zealand, and it's honestly overwhelming.

World.title: Father of Dunedin party victim says supermarkets share blame for drinking culture
World.content:
Coroner describes death of student as 'senseless' Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A man who's daughter died at an overcrowded party in Dunedin says it's devastating to hear a coroner's report into another alcohol-related death in the city.

A coroner described the death of an Otago University student, who died after choking on his own vomit in 2023, as a "woeful illustration" of the country's youth drinking culture.

Partygoers had carried him to a bedroom after he was found passed out and "pretty much unresponsive" in the kitchen.

A witness described people later trying to clear vomit from his throat. Emergency services were called and took over doing CPR, but the student could not be revived.

Sophia Crestani died at an overcrowded house party in Dundas Street, Dunedin in October 2019. RNZ

Bede Crestani, who's daughter Sophia was crushed to death at an overcrowded house party in Dunedin, told Checkpoint that supermarket companies Woolworths and Foodstuffs had some responsibility for the problem.

"I would like them to get into a room, in Selwyn College, where we met the tenants the day after Sophia died with other parents and family of people who have been victims of excessive drinking, and front us and say that what they're doing is legal and all OK."

He stopped short of saying supermarkets should not sell alcohol, but he said the supermarkets should look at their own part in the issues relating to binge drinking.

"They need to look at the problems and have a look at some of those streets down there - and look at some of the broken glass after different events ... and go 'what is their part of the damage that's resulting from that?'''

Crestani said New Zealand had a youth drinking culture which encouraged people over consume alcohol.

"There is a drinking problem in New Zealand where it's cool to drink too much. It's not victimless, people die and it causes many other health problems as well."

He said people needed to be responsible for their own and their friends drinking.

"There does need to be responsibility for people who hold parties or events ... and I advocated for prosecution of the tenants in Sophia's case."

A Foodstuffs spokesperson told RNZ their thoughts were with the family and friends of the man who died.

"We also acknowledge the advocacy of families who have experienced the loss of loved ones and understand why these issues are so important to them.

"This is a deeply sad situation, and we do not think it would be appropriate for Foodstuffs to comment on or debate the views expressed by grieving families. Alcohol harm is a complex issue involving a range of factors, individuals and organisations.

"We support efforts to promote the safe and responsible consumption of alcohol and comply with all applicable laws and regulations governing its sale."

The University of Otago extended its thoughts to the student's whanau and friends following the tragic loss..

A spokeswoman said safety and wellbeing of students remained top priorities.

She said as well as proactive and regular communication with students about responsible consumption of alcohol - the university had a range of dedicated services, including clinicians with specialist drug and alcohol harm expertise.

World.title: Dangerous copper, metals thefts causing millions in damage
World.content:
Spike in copper thefts causing millions of dollars in damage Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The growing problem of the theft of copper and other recyclable metals is causing millions of dollars of damage to infrastructure and endangering perpetrators and the public.

Police said the thefts - which often occurred at night and in remote locations - could be hard to detect and urged the public to report any suspicious behaviour.

Thefts put KiwiRail projects back months

On a cold, windy night on the rail corridor near Featherston - north of Wellington - KiwiRail's Andy Lyon was overseeing crews working to replace cabling stripped from within steel pipes near the tracks.

He said nearly 5 kilometres of cable had been stolen from the Wairarapa network this year.

In July, police arrested a 36-year-old Featherston man in connection with a series of thefts of signalling power cabling in the area.

"We're right in the throes of installing a new signalling system so the damage that's been done here just puts the work back months. We're having to bring people in on night shifts to make repairs and be able to keep ourselves on target," Lyon said.

Lyon said - across KiwiRail's network - nearly 90 instances of intentional damage had cost over $2 million to repair this year.

Andy Lyon, Kiwirail General Manager Wellington Metro. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said people were putting themselves in extreme danger in their attempts to source recyclable materials for quick cash.

"The rail corridor is a hugely dangerous place. It can be a kilometre for a freight train to be able to stop. The cable can have high voltage running through it so it's incredibly dangerous and we really don't want to see anybody get hurt.

"But unfortunately, that's the risk people are taking when they chose to come into the corridor and steal cable."

Kiwirail workers repairing sections of the Wairarapa trainline damaged by thieves. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Further north, lines company Vector had logged 630 instances of vandalism and theft from their networks during the last eight months.

General manager operations and maintenance, Marko Simunac said staff were discovering tell tale evidence of high voltage discharges as thieves cut into live cables.

Danger signs included charred and scattered tools - where people are attempting to steal materials from their network. SUPPLIED

"We are finding hacksaws which have been melted into the cable because there was a flashover. We are finding tools just left scattered in a place charred. So those people, very likely, are presenting to the medical centres," Simunac said.

In March, a man died after he was electrocuted in what police believe was an attempt to take copper from a transformer in Christchurch's Red Zone.

But it wasn't just criminals who were at risk.

Simunac said some instances of tampering were shutting down network fail safes leaving homes open to appliance damage and fire risk.

Tubing, discarded by thieves, after they have removed the copper cables within RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Others were leaving powerful connections open to the public.

"They have stolen the locks from our transformers on the roads. [They] just walk away and you've got live electricity exposed on public walkways. Kids are curious ... I just don't want to even go that way cause that would be horrific so I can't even think about it," Simunac said.

Simunac said two recent - but unsuccessful - attacks on cables beneath a motorway overpass created more than $500,000 worth of damage.

"Ultimately it is a lost opportunity. This half million dollars - in this particular instance - we could have put into a resilience project or a community project. We could have put it into a community battery somewhere. We could address those climate change impacts as well," Simunac said.

Andy Lyon inspects where thieves cut open metal pipes to steal the copper cables within. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Both companies were investigating adding forensic tagging of cabling to better allow police to determine where items they recover had been stolen from.

Police director - prevention, Inspector Natasha Allan said police were working to bring district team's intelligence together develop a more detailed national picture of the problem.

A new scheme being trialled in Christchurch was also allowing police to analyse patterns and trends by having metal recyclers share details of their purchases with police en masse.

Operation Scrap was launched at the beginning of the year and involved monitoring transactions across all metal recycling businesses within the district.

But Allan said catching people in the act was a challenge for police.

Woodside train station, Wairarapa. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"These offences often occur in remote or isolated locations and under the cover of darkness, which can make detection difficult.

"In some cases, offenders leave limited evidence, making identification and prosecution challenging. Successful investigations often depend on timely reporting, witness information, CCTV footage, and cooperation with infrastructure owners and industry partners," Allan said.

Allan urged the public to be on the lookout for individuals in restricted areas - handling equipment without obvious authority - and in locations or times that seemed out of place.

World.title: Star Hawk's season over after ACL injury
World.content:
Three-time All-Australian Emily Bates will miss the rest of the AFLW season with a knee injury in a huge blow to Hawthorn's chances of snaring a maiden premiership.

Scans have confirmed Bates tore the anterior cruciate ligament in her right knee when the leg twisted awkwardly in a tackle during the Hawks' win over the Western Bulldogs on Saturday.

The 30-year-old club captain also damaged the meniscus and will undergo surgery.

"This is clearly disappointing news for Emily," Hawks AFLW general manager Keegan Brooksby said.

"The playing group and wider club will support her through the recovery journey.

"We have no doubt she'll approach her rehab with the diligence and professionalism she's always been known for.

Emily Bates played her 100th game for the Hawks against Adelaide. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

"Although Emily won't return to the field in 2026, she will continue to play an important off-field role in our program, as our captain."

Hawthorn face a huge test against AFLW juggernaut North Melbourne in Cairns on Friday night without Bates and Laura Stone (concussion).

Fellow midfielder Daisy Flockhart also has to prove her fitness after suffering a knock to her chest against the Bulldogs.

"We've been playing different players through [the midfield] and trying to build some versatility in our side … we're confident in the players we'll have in there," Hawks coach Daniel Webster said post-match on Saturday.

"It'll be a good challenge next week with who we're playing.

"We'll probably have some sort of different look in there with different players and that's OK. We'll keep getting to work."

Hawthorn (3-2) sit eighth in their quest for another finals berth, while North Melbourne (5-0) are in familiar territory on top of the ladder.

AAP

World.title: 'Bittersweet' Swans captaincy call for Rampe
World.content:
Dane Rampe didn't think Sydney would still be here, let alone that he'd be tasked with leading the Swans to an unlikely AFL premiership again.

A heart-and-soul player, veteran defender Rampe will stand in for an injured Callum Mills and captain the club in Friday's preliminary final against Fremantle at the SCG.

Rampe had led the Swans to the eventual 2024 grand final loss when a luckless Mills suffered a hamstring strain before that year's preliminary final.

But the circumstances surrounding this year's premiership push wildly differ.

Mills's vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five Swans players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Many in the AFL world had written off Sydney in the lead-up to finals, with even club chairman Andrew Pridham believing their chances had been "torpedoed".

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

A gutsy 53-point qualifying final win over Brisbane went some way towards rebuilding respect for the club, especially after Mills suffered an ACL injury in the first quarter.

Sustained by the grit displayed against the back-to-back reigning premiers, Rampe was given the nod by Mills, coach Dean Cox and club leaders.

The former Swans co-captain is chasing his maiden premiership after playing in four grand final defeats (2014, 2016, 2022 and 2024).

"It's a thrill. It's a privilege. And yeah, it's a little bit bittersweet," Rampe said on Monday.

"The overwhelming emotion is probably just gratitude to be back here.

"Probably a month ago, we weren't sure what was going to happen with the team and with the club and with the players.

"To be here and challenging in a prelim is just something, particularly being at the back end of my career, I'm really grateful for."

Callum Mills may miss all of the 2027 season, or at least a sizable portion of it. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Rampe's return to captaincy comes after being re-drafted as a rookie by the Swans with fellow defender Jake Lloyd at the end of last year.

While Lloyd has signed on for a 15th season, neither Rampe nor the Swans have made a call on whether he will continue next year.

But the door is open, with defender Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season.

"I haven't had a chance to think about that. I don't think it [being captain] does much," Rampe said.

"We'll wait and see. I'm just happy to be where I am at the moment and to have that little bit of hope and belief is, I feel, a real luxury."

Drafted at age 22 in 2013, Rampe was named co-captain with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker for the 2019 season.

The trio handed the reins to Mills at the end of 2023, but their successor endured a tough 2024 season pockmarked by injury.

Mills was restricted to seven games, hurting his shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate before being ruled out of finals.

Cox's selection conundrum for Friday's clash is further complicated, with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) near full fitness.

Rampe said the Swans were playing the cards they were dealt.

"You've got one or two ways you can go in these circumstances," Rampe said.

"You can get the 'poor me' and feel sorry for yourself, or you can do something about it."

AAP

World.title: Jordan Petaia returns to Wallabies squad after NFL stint
World.content:
Jordan Petaia has been selected in his first Wallabies squad since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Les Kiss braces for the sternest test yet of his brief coaching reign.

A one-time teenage Test debutant, Petaia has been included in Australia's 34-man group for the upcoming showdown with back-to-back world champions South Africa in Perth.

The 26-year-old has been plying his trade in France and Japan since the end of the 2024 Super Rugby Pacific season, after seven seasons at the Queensland Reds.

He left the Reds in 2024 to pursue a career in the NFL, signing briefly for the Los Angeles Chargers in 2025, before being waived later that same year.

He then signed for Perpignan in the Top 14 before locking in a long-term spot at Urayasu D-Rocks.

Petaia made his Wallabies debut at just 19 at the 2019 World Cup in Japan, scoring a memorable try against Uruguay, and has since pulled on the gold jersey a total of 31 times.

With now just a year before Australia hosts the 2027 World Cup, Kiss says it's time to see if Petaia is ready to make a run at a third appearance at the global showpiece.

Jordan Petaia is set for a return to Wallaby gold. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

"Look, we've got a lot of good back-three players here in the country. We made sure we looked at all of them," Kiss said on Monday.

"It was just the ideal opportunity to see Jordan. He's been out of the system for a couple of years now. He has played in two World Cups. We just wanted to touch base with him, get him to come and work out with us, see how he's going.

"We haven't selected that team yet, but it was just a good opportunity to see Jordan back in the environment and him to have a good look at us with the new coaching structure and all those sort of things.

"From the team perspective, there was a lot of deep discussion about where we would go with that."

The classy utility back is one of three new faces in the squad that won back the Puma Trophy in an undefeated tour of Argentina earlier this month.

Another is Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, who has been named in his first official Wallabies squad, replacing Carter Gordon who suffered a fractured calf bone in Mendoza.

Born in Toowoomba and raised in Gunnedah, the 22-year-old flyhalf was part of Australia's 2023 and 2024 World Rugby U20 Championships and has featured for the Reds on more than 35 occasions.

Queenslander Zane Nonggorr is back in the squad after completing a successful return to the field in Saturday's 2026 Super Rugby AUS opener having picked up a minor calf strain in Japan.

He replaces Wallaby number 1,000 Massimo De Lutiis, who is being managed after playing three straight Tests to kick off his international career.

Outside back Filipo Daugunu is also being managed due to a minor knee complaint.

"We've learned a bit more about ourselves as a group over the last four Tests and we know we still have a lot to work on to get to where we want to be," Kiss said of the Springboks challenge in Perth on September 27.

"South Africa have been the benchmark team in World Rugby for a long time and we're motivated by the challenge of meeting them in our own backyard in two weeks' time."

Wallabies Squad:

Forwards — Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Zane Nonggorr, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw, Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (capt).

Backs: Jock Campbell, Ben Donaldson, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Jordan Petaia, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

World.title: World Athletics firm on Russia ban, Coe acknowledges need for solution
World.content:
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has said the governing body's position on the exclusion of Russian athletes has not changed ahead of an upcoming Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) case, while acknowledging the need for a resolution.

Russian Athletics last month filed a fresh appeal with CAS challenging sanctions imposed by World Athletics, which has barred Russian and Belarusian athletes from international competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Our position hasn't changed, and this isn't about politics or passports. It's about the integrity of competition," Coe told reporters on the final day of the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second Australia's Nicola Olyslagers finishes second in the high jump at the new Ultimate Championship competition.

"From the age of 18, I believe that every position I've taken … it's about integrity and it's about competition, and that matters to me."

Coe declined to discuss the federation's legal strategy ahead of the arbitration proceedings but said World Athletics would continue to defend its stance.

"So our position won't change," he said. "And look, yes, this does need to be resolved, and I'm acutely aware of that. (But) I don't think our legal teams would be particularly thankful if I laid out our approach on this."

The comments came a month after Russian Athletics confirmed a new CAS filing, following an initial filing in July, aimed at overturning sanctions it says prevent it from fully representing Russian athletes internationally and participating in World Athletics decision-making processes.

Despite reaffirming the federation's position, Coe said he recognised the importance of ultimately restoring full global participation in the sport.

"We want a full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport, and that has to be our overall objective. Of course, it does."

The Lausanne-based CAS serves as sport's highest arbitration body and is expected to hear Russian Athletics' challenge in the coming months.

World Athletics has maintained one of the toughest positions of any international federation since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while some sports have gradually reintroduced Russian and Belarusian athletes under neutral status.

The International Skating Union has established a pathway for selected Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete as neutral competitors, although it confirmed earlier this week that Kamila Valieva and three other figure skaters had their neutral status revoked.

Russian state news agency TASS quoted Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev as saying that all the skaters affected by the ruling would appeal to CAS.

Reuters

World.title: Mas 'fulfils his destiny' to win historic Vuelta
World.content:
Enric Mas has finally delivered an expectant Spanish public an overall victory at the Vuelta a España, his win confirmed at the end of the final stage into Grenada on Sunday.

Mas finished safely in the peloton during the 21st and final stage of the race, won by Norway's Tobias Johannessen.

The 31-year-old from Mallorca held off four-time Vuelta champion Primož Roglič to become the first Spaniard to win the Vuelta since Alberto Contador in 2014.

Mas finished 2 minutes and 15 seconds ahead of Roglič overall, with Austria's Felix Gall finishing third at 2:44.

"It's just special," Mas told reporters after the race.

"It's been a day to remember, a special Vuelta, and it has been wonderful.

"There's always tension about what could happen, but you've seen it all went smoothly, so we're delighted and we enjoyed every kilometre today.

"It was a long wait and a long way to today. But to be honest, it was always special Vueltas, and this one I think is the special one."

Primož Roglič (left), has won four Vuelta's, while Enric Mas (centre) finally claimed his first aged 31. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogačar had come into the race as the overwhelming favourite for victory, building an ominous lead of 3 minutes 50 seconds by the end of the seventh stage.

The freakish Slovenian star had won three of the six completed stages at that stage and looked set to claim a win of unparalleled dominance in the modern era.

However, the two-time reigning world champion badly crashed on the eighth stage of the race, breaking his collar bone and fracturing his neck, ending his season.

From that point though, Mas, who had tested Pogačar on the mountainous fourth stage in Andorra, dominated the race alongside his much-maligned Movistar team.

Mas had finished second at his home grand tour three times, in 2018, 2021 and 2022, and also finished third in 2024.

When he finished second to Simon Yates in 2018, triumphing on the queen stage at that year's race, there was an expectation that Mas would become the heir to seven-time grand tour winner Contador as Spanish cycling's next big thing.

Mas even spent his junior years racing with the Alberto Contador Academy, indicating just how high hopes were that he would excel.

And although Mas has achieved plenty, finishing in the top six overall at grand tours eight times over the course of his career, the expected Contador-like dominance never eventuated.

It is telling that long-time AS reporter Juan Gutiérrez entitled his post-Vuelta piece: "Enric Mas cumple su destino", "Enric Mas fulfils his destiny".

Movistar switched their usual blue jerseys for red ones to honour Enric Mas's achievement. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Contador wrote in Spanish newspaper AS that he was "very happy and incredibly excited" to see Mas achieve his potential.

"I know how hard he's worked these past few years and how much criticism he's always faced," Contador said.

"Instead of letting it get him down, he turned it into motivation to demonstrate the talent he truly possesses.

"Every cyclist develops in their own way and, in Enric's case, it was fast because he finished second in the 2018 Vuelta a España.

"Then, when he didn't quite seal the deal, well, we all know how sports are — it seems like if you don't win, nothing has any merit.

"That's why cycling will be fair to Enric Mas for winning this Vuelta."

Contador acknowledged that Pogačar would likely had claimed victory had he remained in the race, but that Mas thoroughly deserved his victory.

" It's not a gift," Contador said. "It's thanks to his hard work and his form. He was the strongest. "

Santiago Buitrago of Colombia and Team Bahrain Victorious claimed the king of the mountains jersey, while British rider Oscar Onley won the white youth jersey.

Wout van Aert added some personal closure by claiming the green sprinter's jersey, and the super combative prize, after he crashed out while leading both the points and king of the mountains classifications in 2024.

"In a way this is finished business," van Aert said.

"After the near miss two years ago and the big injury I had afterwards, it was quite a disappointment.

"It makes it more special to be here, to come completely to the end, and to wear this beautiful jersey."

World.title: NRL hands down decision on Cleary after finals sin-binning
World.content:
Nathan Cleary has avoided a ban for dangerous contact, with the Panthers star now just sweating on a foot injury ahead of Penrith's NRL preliminary final.

On Monday, Cleary was handed a grade-one dangerous contact charge for collecting Hugo Savala's leg after the Sydney Rooster kicked in Penrith's 19-12 qualifying final win.

But that charge only carries with it a $1,000 fine with an early guilty plea, meaning Cleary can breathe a sigh of relief with no ban in place.

Had Cleary been handed a grade-two charge, the Penrith halfback would have been facing a one-game ban and the reality of being rubbed out of the preliminary final.

Manly prop Josh Aloiai and South Sydney forward Jacob Host received grade-two charges in 2024 for making contact with kickers.

Canberra's Zac Hosking was fined for a similar incident in last year's finals, while Melbourne's Harry Grant had a charge overturned at the judiciary in 2024.

Loading Instagram content

With the threat of a ban now out of the way, Cleary can focus on his foot and the two weeks he has to be fit to take on the winner of the Warriors and Newcastle.

Cleary was easily Penrith's best in the win over the Roosters, but his sin-bin at the end of the first half for the contact on Savala was only the start of his worries.

The 28-year-old limped through the final 10 minutes of the game with a sore right foot, and opted to give Dylan Edwards the Panthers' last conversion attempt.

Cleary also appeared to say to a Penrith physio after kicking the match-winning 72nd-minute field goal, "my foot is f***ed".

The star half did attempt to play down the injury to his right foot after the game, but his father and coach Ivan admitted there was "something wrong with it".

"I just copped a little bump on the foot," Nathan Cleary said on Fox League.

"It was a pretty important kick, so I just wanted Dyl [Edwards] to take it. I wasn't sure how it would hold up goal kicking.

"It was just precautionary."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Antonelli edges closer to historic title as teammate concedes the fight
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history, while his nearest rival says he is out of the fight.

Antonelli's win in Madrid on Sunday night (AEST) was his eighth grand prix win of the season, extending his lead in the drivers' championship over teammate George Russell to 81 points.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton is a further 20 points adrift with eight or nine race weekends remaining, depending on whether F1 can race in the Middle East to end the season.

Piastri hit twice on first lap, Antonelli wins thanks to safety car luck Oscar Piastri and George Russell made contact with each other twice before the first corner, as Kimi Antonelli took full advantage of a fortunate safety car to win the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix.

Mercedes have lived up to pre-season expectation that they would be the best team in 2026 but Russell, in his eighth season, was expected to win a maiden drivers' championship.

But Antonelli, in just his second season, has been brilliant all season and has a massive lead in the championship.

After Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix, where Russell placed fifth and conceded a further 15 points to Antonelli, the British driver conceded his hopes of winning the title this year are all but gone.

"We [Mercedes] are in a great position to win the constructors' [championship]. Realistically, I'm not in the fight for the drivers'," Russell said in Madrid.

" That just allows me to focus on race-by-race, and try to focus on just getting some good results. "

Sebastian Vettel became the youngest F1 world champion in 2010 when he claimed his maiden title at 23 years, 133 days.

Antonelli took the mantle as youngest driver to lead the championship earlier this year — but when asked if he could relax with an 81-point lead, the young Italian said he would not be taking his foot off the gas.

"That's exactly what I don't want to do," he said.

"I want to keep pushing race by race, keep delivering and keep enjoying all the way."

F1 heads to Azerbaijan for a grand prix around the streets of Baku on Saturday, September 26.

World.title: 'It's for you, Mum': Cooney-Cross makes emotional Arsenal home return
World.content:
Matildas star Kyra Cooney-Cross has shared an emotional message from her late mother with fans as she made her return to the women's top flight in London.

The Australian star midfielder played her first Women's Super League game for Arsenal since late last year.

With the blessing of the club, she had taken personal leave early this year to be with her mother Jess.

Arsenal shows support for Cooney-Cross Arsenal players and supporters pay emotional tributes to Matildas star Kyra Cooney-Cross following her return to Australia to be with her mother, who has been diagnosed with cancer.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother was diagnosed with terminal stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

Before the game against Crystal Palace, fans and teammates gave Cooney-Cross a big welcome.

In the end, Arsenal drew 0, leaving the club fifth on the Women's Super League table.

But it wasn't really about the result.

In the Arsenal match day program, Cooney-Cross wrote a personal note to the fans, thanking them for the "outpouring of love and support we received", saying it would never leave her or her family.

"Coming back to the UK was made easier because I have a family here," she wrote.

Cooney-Cross said her mum was very good at sending her messages before games, and so she shared a message from Jess "for all of us".

Loading Instagram content

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it,' the message reads.

"Back then, it wasn't about proving anything … it was about the feeling, the freedom, the creativity, the joy of pushing yourself.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Cooney-Cross finished her message with a simple line:

"It's for you, Mum. Love," and then her signature.

Tech.title: Volkswagen’s slippery new EV breaks a bunch of efficiency records
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

No, that’s not a Tesla Cybercab. That’s Volkswagen’s Mission Efficiency, the world’s slipperiest electric vehicle. The near-production 2+2 seat electric coupe prototype was built on VW’s MEB+ platform, incorporating front-wheel drive components from the upcoming ID. Polo and ID. Cross models.

True to its name, the mission of Mission Efficiency is to break records. With a drag coefficient of a scant 0.158, the prototype claims to be the world’s most aerodynamic road-approved vehicle. It also claims to have broken the record for energy efficiency, consuming 6.48kWh of energy per 100 kilometers during a constant-speed (68 km/h) test-drive on flat terrain with secondary features like AC deactivated. And lastly, the Mission Efficiency is “the most economical near-production electric car in its class” thanks to its platform sharing with the ID. Polo.

What does all this mean in practical terms? Well, think vast distances traveled with little thought paid to charging stops. Volkswagen recently completed a real-world 1,278.36 km (794.34 miles) trip from Wolfsburg to Vienna on a single charge of Mission Efficiency’s 54.9 kWh (net) battery. The EV used only 6.89 kWh/100 km (7.51 kWh/100 km including charging losses) at an average speed of 67.72 km/h — and still arrived at its destination with 164 km of range remaining.

Previous Next











1 / 7

Given the prototype’s teardrop shape and wheel coverings, it’s not difficult to imagine the Mission Efficiency breaking all of these record. This won’t win any design awards nor cause any stampedes at your local VW dealership. This was designed to slide through air molecules with barely a disturbance. The underbody is covered, the windows frameless, and the door handles flush.

In fact, it gains efficiency the faster it goes. A helpful comparison is VW’s ID. Polo, with which the Mission Efficiency shares its 99 kW front-wheel electric motor, high-voltage battery, aluminum structure, and high-strength carbon fiber materials. At speeds above 80 km/h, the prototype uses over 30 percent less energy than the ID. Polo. At 140 km/h, it consumes the same energy as an ID. Polo traveling at 100 km/h.

Where VW couldn’t optimize for aerodynamics, it slashed weight. The paneling is more lightweight, while the infotainment system is decidedly “bring-your-own device,” including a portable Bluetooth speaker and a smartphone/tablet dock in place of a central touchscreen. Integrated solar panels on the roof can supply up to 30 km of added range for all the auxiliary electronics.

The takeaway is that VW isn’t relying on some super exotic motor and battery to achieve these record-breaking numbers. It’s really a design challenge. This is basically just a re-bodied ID. Polo supermini out there blazing its way into the history books.

And it’s not just some design challenge that will get filed away and forgotten. Automakers across the industry are wracking their brains over how to boost efficiency as a way to attract more people to the EV life. Ford is using design challenges to shave drag off its new, next-gen EV truck. Everyone from Mercedes to Audi to Porsche is obsessing over aero. The question is: What makes it into production? And how will consumers respond to these slippery shaped vehicles?

Tech.title: Adam Conover explains how YouTube ruined everything
Tech.content:
Today, I’m joined by comedian, podcast host, and YouTuber Adam Conover.

Adam is a familiar face to anyone who’s spent time on the internet. He got his start, like so many successful comedy writers, at CollegeHumor back in the day. That was before transitioning into cable TV with Adam Ruins Everything, then onto Netflix, and all the way back to YouTube again, where he posts videos and hosts a podcast called Factually!

That is exactly the kind of career path that fascinates me, and it also happens to touch on basically every major Decoder theme there is.
