We’ve had basically every platform CEO on the show. We’ve had Neal [Mohan] from YouTube. We’ve had Adam [Mosseri] from Instagram. The argument they would make in response to this whole conversation — and I’m going to try to do it justice even though I mostly agree with you, but I’ll try to do it justice — is, “What you’re describing in the ‘80s, ‘90s, and early 2000s was a series of gatekeepers that were inaccessible to most of the people in the world.”

I’m a kid who grew up in Wisconsin. If I wanted to make a late-night cable TV show, that path was almost totally foreclosed to me unless I moved to New York or Los Angeles, got a job as a waiter, and then hustled my way up through comedy clubs to meet one person who might decide that I was talented. That meant gatekeepers existed and people were left out. The economics of that might have been great and might have created a large middle class because there was enough overhead in that system to pay for a large middle class of creatives, but it mostly locked everybody out.

The social platforms create instant marketing opportunities for everyone from their bedroom. So, if you’re a young comic in the middle of the country and you have no ability to get into the Comedy Cellar in New York because you can’t work for free in that specific way, you can just film yourself talking on TikTok until you get a little bit of an audience. Then you can maybe drive an audience to come to a club near you, or whatever it is that you’re going to do. That pathway to get the exposure, which is necessary at the beginning, exists in a totally democratizing way. The economics of it might be bad, but many, many more people have the opportunity.

I think about that. I think about my own career. I started as a blogger working for AOL for $12 a post. The newspaper columnists who are now very sweet to me — they’ve been very sweet to me over the years — I got to compete with them in a way that I would have never gotten to previously. I can’t quite reconcile how badly I feel about the economics of the industry today and the amount of opportunity that it has created for so many other people.

So, I have a clear answer to this, which is that to the people from YouTube, I would say, “You’re the gatekeepers now.”

The algorithm is the gatekeeper.

Of course it is! Try to start something from scratch. Try. Try to build from getting 200 views on videos that the algorithm gives you, and tell me that’s not a gatekeeper. Yes, we had NBC, CBS, and ABC in the bad old days, and that’s all you got. Those were big gatekeepers, you had to please them. Now, we have YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. That’s all you get. In fact, YouTube doesn’t really compete with Instagram and TikTok directly because it has a completely different business model. They do the horizontal thing. It’s on streamers in the way those aren’t. Really, it’s literally just YouTube if you want to do broad swaths of content. That’s a fucking gatekeeper. You think Mr. Beast is good at what he does? He pleases the gatekeeper. Look at any interview with him. It’s about him figuring out, “Okay this video got this many views, this other one got this many views.”

Now, the argument that you’re making — that the gatekeepers were gone and the internet was democratizing — was good when it was people in charge of it. Do you remember back when we used to email memes to each other because you saw the video of the Numa Numa kid and you thought, “Oh, that kid’s funny. I’m going to send it to my friend”? Large swaths of people were in charge of the distribution. It is not anymore. They are taking some very loose signals from our swiping and turning it into algorithmic control of what we see. They have more power than anyone who worked for CBS or ABC ever did. It’s actually worse because people aren’t in charge of it. If you went and talked to any of them and said, “Hey, you’re in charge of this?” They would say, “No, we’re not, it’s just an algorithm.”

That’s actually worse because at least in the old days, there was someone I could go impress. There was a person I could go talk to. If you go talk to a streamer like Netflix now and try to convince them that this show is a good idea, it would say, “The algorithm said it’s not.” That’s basically what it boils down to. They don’t have the leeway to make decisions, with rare exceptions. Frankly, the good shows are when the exception gets made. But it’s ludicrous. The media ecosystem now is more concentrated and more closed off than it ever was before. The only difference is that now anybody can upload anything for free, and YouTube will host it for you. That’s good from a user perspective. If you just want to upload a video of your baby and send it to your sister, that used to be a lot harder. YouTube solved that problem for a lot of people. But in terms of a broadcast medium, it’s grotesquely exploitative.

Imagine if you were driving for Uber and you didn’t get paid. Instead, you got to try driving for Uber for years, and it said, “Oh, if the algorithm says you’re really good at Uber, maybe we’ll start to give you a little bit of money.” And what if everybody in the country was doing this simultaneously? That is what the media ecosystem is, and it’s bad. It’s bad.

This is the other thing I wanted to ask you about. You mentioned you want to have a unionized talk show on YouTube. You’re going to hire some people. That’s a cost. We run a union shop here. There’s costs associated with all of that. Those are good costs. I think media companies should pay those costs. You need the economics to work, and you mentioned you needed a digital-native business model for that.

I look at how that works today, and that mostly looks like big, lucrative brand deals. You need a Coca-Cola, a Chevy, a Ford, or whoever to show up and pay you a bunch of money to be integrated into your show. You, Adam Conover, eventually have to drive to every guest’s house in your Ford Fiesta or whatever and open it. In the back, it’s full of supplements or whatever that money’s going to look like. Because the advertising has to be integrated into the content, and then that has to reach scale. That is where that money comes from. Are you comfortable with those level of integrations? It’s very different in me for news, but on the YouTube entertainment side, that pendulum has swung and it has been swinging for a long time.

I don’t love it. You’re constantly being asked to make compromises and deals that you’d rather not make. In so many ways, we’re going back to the old days of media. Again, YouTube is ABC, NBC, and CBS rolled into one. What were the earliest days of that broadcasting like? It was the Marlboro comedy hour, right? All the comedians would say, “I love smoking Marlboro cigarettes” in between every single joke. That was how television as an industry began. We eventually separated those out. The commercials were run in between the shows, and it was never like it is at The New York Times where ad sales never talks to the creative. I made a basic cable show for years where half of our episodes were taking apart advertisers and talking about the diamond engagement rings, razors, and how capitalism tries to scam you, and in between was ads.

We never got pushback. One time they were like, “Hey, please don’t do something about the NCAA because we broadcast that every March.” It would be stuff like that. They had the separation. Why? Because the audience likes it better that way. It just took them a couple decades to figure that out. Right now, we are in the period of a couple decades where we have to figure that out again. I see YouTube literally trying to rebuild that model very slowly.

This is a bit of my own theory, but I think YouTube is trying not to be the channel. It wants to be the cable company. It wants the channel, the Adam Conover channel, to be the cable channel. So, it wants me to make the brand deal and do all the business development. It’s just the pipe that takes a bunch off the top. Great business model if it can make it happen, but it knows it wants to level up the production value.

So, what is YouTube doing? It’s not giving anybody money, but it is starting to promote shows more. It’s doing its own up-fronts. It’s trying to connect people with advertisers. I see it trying to spark the pilot light of this a bit but without actually putting money or infrastructure or investment into it. It’s just like, “Can we just boost you guys up a little bit?” At the same time Netflix’s model is the opposite. It’ll sink the money into the production and try to make the thing at the high end. That’s a really interesting competition. Unfortunately, it’s a competition between two giants.

I think we could get there by the time I’m like 60. Hopefully, at that point, I’m hosting a show with ad breaks in between and it’s not too bad of an integration. But we’re in the world that we’re in.

The reality is that I would love to do a totally pure show where I’m just subscriber funded. I would love to be ContraPoints or Hbomberguy, but that model pushes you towards doing it all by yourself. My costs are zero, and so what do I have? Time. I put in infinite amounts of time, and if I can put in infinite amounts of my own time, then I can get rewarded with subscriber money. The subscribers will pay me because they know that it’s just me doing this.

But I don’t want to work that way. I want to work with writers. I want to work with other comedians. I want camera people. I want a team, you know? And to do that, I need to get advertisers. Currently, that means dealing with a lot of bullshit that you would rather not have to and having to make compromises that you would rather not. It sucks, and I don’t have a way around it.

I certainly know a lot of creators who describe the lifestyle as very lonely and have taken to calling other creators their colleagues in order to create that sense of camaraderie, even though they are largely competing for the same minutes and the same platform in terms of attention.

I want to ask you about the advertiser thing. I basically have to ask you about crypto advertising now. You got in a lot of trouble because you read Sam Altman’s crypto ad, I think Worldcoin. This is the hardest thing. For all I know, the ads on our show are going to be a bunch of AI companies and crypto companies. We do have the wall. We make journalism here. I get to say that I have no idea what happens there. Take it or leave it. The integrations are where people get in trouble. You read the ad copy, you took the money. The audience was very unhappy with you.

I actually didn’t take the money. I turned down the money. I took the ad down. I was not paid for all the trouble I got in.

Walk me through all of that. Walk me through saying, “Yes.” Walk me through then saying, “Actually, this is bad. I’m taking it down. I don’t want your money.”

When you’re in this business, you have to look for [return on investment]. You have to look for if someone wants to pay you an outsized amount of money to not do that much work. That’s the way you make the entire business function because, for instance, the YouTube monologues I do are incredibly effortful. But I’m still trying to make a living, so if someone’s like… One example of this from live performance is that I’ll get hired to host a gala event. That pays more than a normal standup gig, but it’s actually less work. You sort of need some of that to pad out.

So, Sam Altman’s [World] comes along — which you guys have covered quite well on your site — and says, “We want you to come to this event. Just make a video at the event, publish it, and we’ll give you a bunch of money for it.” Well, this product honestly looks like fucking garbage. It looks like one of the worst products I’d ever seen. I was like, “They want to pay me a bunch of money? My audience is going to hate this.” Yeah, sure. Whatever. This way I can literally use that to fund some of the stuff that I want to do.

So I go and do it, and it comes out. People are very unhappy with it. The premise of the product is deeply unsettling, grotesque, and surveillance oriented, right? However, when I was there watching the keynote, I was like, “This is the most comical vaporware I have ever seen. This is never going to come out. No one is ever going to do this. This is so ill-conceived. It’s the biggest turd I’ve ever seen in tech.” That was my evaluation. How could I expect my audience to see it that way? They only saw the horrible version of it.

So, what I eventually did was take the video down. I turned the money down. I was not paid for it. I instead made a YouTube video where I talked for around 25 minutes about how grotesque, stupid, and bad the product was. I think I was able to do a pretty funny and incisive piece of commentary about it because I was at the keynote. The only reason I went to the keynote. Part of the reason I went was that I thought that this thing was going to be weird and it was. I wanted to go see. There was a bit of lookie-looing around. I ended up making a video that I was very proud of as a result of this fiasco. I did not monetize that video, so I didn’t earn any income off of it.

I think a lot of creators go through this moment where you’re constantly being led along and tempted. Sometimes, you step over the line and you don’t even realize you’ve done it until after you’ve done it. Well, I thought I was behaving with integrity in the moment, but looking back, why would anybody think that I was? Does that mean I really did? I mean, that’s the situation we’re in.

I’m happy to say that I fucked up by doing so. I also believe that you make mistakes, you acknowledge it, and you do something corrective, which is what I did my best to do. Luckily, the lion’s share of my audience was like, “Oh, this video was really great. Thank you for the thorough explanation and for eviscerating the product.”

That thing is hilarious, by the way. I would encourage people to watch your video and all the other videos. Any coverage of the Orb that isn’t literal sponcon is like, “What are we doing here?”

Let me ask you about this. You obviously learned a huge important lesson. If you had worked in a media company or entertainment company of any kind, that would become institutional knowledge. “We screwed up. We’re never going to do this again.” Now, a bunch of people have had this experience, and when new people come in and try to do this thing again, we’re just going to say no. But you have to do that alone. Every creator has to do that alone.

Yeah.

My joke on the show for ages is that every YouTuber gets their wings when they make the video about how mad they are at YouTube.

I’m about to make that video actually. I’ve got it locked and loaded.

Finally, you’re going to grow up, Adam.

This actually might be it. This is the beginning of it.

Well, the reason I ask that is because in the old way, there were unions. You are part of a union. The union and the big Hollywood studios would negotiate. These are repeat players, so even if they were antagonistic, the negotiations were towards a common purpose because you were going to do it again in three years. That created a kind of institutional knowledge, or a set of shared goals at the very least. If the tactics and specific negotiations got heated, at least the goals were the same.

No one can do that with YouTube. Ben Smith from Semafor was just on the show and he said that people are building real businesses and real careers on top of YouTube. But YouTube has — probably to its own benefit and to the detriment of the media industry — built a system where it’s for individuals and no one has any leverage except for YouTube.

You and I cannot get together and go demand terms from YouTube. If we got a thousand YouTubers together to demand terms from YouTube, it would still laugh. It wouldn’t even take the call. It would say, “There’s another thousand teenagers who will work for free. Good luck.” How do you change that? You have a very unique perspective as someone who has organized against Hollywood. Can you change that for the platforms?

If I’m putting my labor organizer hat on, I don’t think the organizing target is YouTube itself. I think it’s the channel. So, I wouldn’t try to organize YouTube. I’d try to organize Mr. Beast’s staff, who — you’ve probably done some reporting on it yourself — are horribly abused and underpaid. That is the reality of the economy.

It’s actually not the case that all the biggest YouTubers are individuals. The biggest YouTubers are companies. Go look at Adam Savage. That guy is basically doing a cable show every single day. Go look at Hank Green. I love Hank Green. I look at him and I go, “How many people are helping him to make these videos?” You know what I mean?

If you want to do something that’s big, constant, and brings in the money, it is a large scale enterprise. It’s in YouTube’s interest to encourage those big channels to get bigger. Monopolies or consolidation are sort of the law of economics unless you’ve got a strong antitrust to prevent them. I see YouTube getting even bigger, the bigger channels getting even bigger, and them getting big enough to organize. Like you said yourself, you’re The Verge, you are a YouTube channel, and you have a unionized staff. And we’re starting to see that happen in the YouTube space. We’re starting to see the staffs of specific channels unionizing.

So, if the top 100 channels do grow big enough, could they go to YouTube and say, “Hey, we demand a better split?” Yeah, they could. Is that going to benefit all the people who work for the channels? Probably not, but it becomes more of a B2B negotiation. You know what it becomes more like? When the cable channels were arguing against Spectrum, Charter, and all of those. They would have those carriage battles and those kinds of wars. It becomes that kind of dispute.

So, YouTube is making itself a cable monopoly on top of the internet. I think that’s what the dynamic is. However, the original point of the creator economy was to separate labor from each other and, in fact, make the labor so invisible that even if you’re not doing it professionally, you’re kind of ambiently doing it all the time. When you open YouTube or Instagram, how often are you watching someone do it professionally versus how often are you watching someone do it for fun? Having one video go viral; or making one video a week to promote their dentistry business; or making one video a week because they hope to go pro but they actually never will and Instagram hasn’t told them. That’s the huge dark matter of social media. None of those people will be paid. Those people are truly un-unionizable. Sorry, but what it’ll eventually take is the government making some regulations around this.

Where we’re starting to see that is with how different states are treating gig workers like rideshare drivers. You’re starting to see that action happening. There have been battles in California and in other states as well. They’re slow. We’re certainly not close to being all the way there. Again, this looks to me like we’re doing the history of the labor movement again. The capitalists have consolidated. They figured out a new industrial revolution that has impoverished everybody and had us working for penny wages. It’s going to take a lot of people organizing, a lot of labor power, and the government figuring out that there’s a problem to do something about it. It’s going to take decades.

Hopefully it won’t take violence in the streets, which is what it took during the late 19th and early 20th centuries as the labor movement worked its way towards labor peace. So often when I think about these things, everyone wants to say, “Oh, it’s new. It’s new. It’s new.” Actually, we’ve gone back to the beginning in so many areas.

One of our great reporters, Mia Sato, has a line and a thesis she’s reporting out that influencers are the new gig workers. There’s just a lot of echoes in there.

Oh yeah.

I want to end by asking about Hollywood. You’ve come out very strongly against the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. There’s an argument in everything you’re describing that we should just let Hollywood kill itself. We should just let David Ellison spend all of his dad’s money buying a studio, running CBS News into the ground. These things are doomed. There’s a version of this where the big fights to stop them from killing themselves so that the writing staff of whatever show on whatever network can persist for a little longer just slows down the apocalypse. You can’t fix it. Do you think it’s fixable, or are you just trying to slow down the apocalypse?

First of all, I think all effort that you put into fighting this shit is good effort. Even if the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger happens and it costs them a lot more time and money, well, that’ll make the next monopolist think a little longer about the next monopoly. We are starting to see an epochal shift in antitrust. Even people like [former Federal Trade Commission chair] Lina Khan and [former FTC commissioner] Alvaro Bedoya are doing amazing work out of office. You can imagine if Democrats take power again. Even the Republicans are starting to do antitrust a little bit. So, we are making progress there.

The most pernicious lie the tech industry tells is about its own inevitability. “Oh, oopsie! Hey, we just invented something so good that everything you used to like has to die. Oh, sorry, you got to get with the program.” No, these people killed our businesses purposefully with mal intent. The first time this ever happened to me was during the Facebook pivot-to-video era. I used to work at CollegeHumor. We had a great business making videos on the internet. Facebook lied about the traffic that their videos were getting. We pivoted a huge amount of the business to Facebook, and it cratered a huge amount of CollegeHumor’s business. CollegeHumor later became Dropout TV, which is a wonderful media success story that I’m really proud of. But it’s that kind of thing. When you look at this shit, half of it is just Mark Zuckerberg lying to people over and over again. So, we don’t need to accept it as some law of the universe.

The last part of it is that I don’t just make this argument because I miss having union health insurance and hanging out with funny people writing stuff. Of course I miss those things. Of course I’m sad about the death of the creative class in Hollywood. I got into this because I like movies. I like television. People still do like movies. Talk to people. They’re not like, “No, I never want to see a movie again.” They’re like, “What happened to the good movies?” Go watch Terminator 2 with anybody, and they’ll go, “I wish I could see a movie like this now. Why won’t they make me this movie anymore?”

By the way, the box office is having a really good year because they made a couple good fucking movies this year. Big movies and small movies. You’ve got Obsession and Backrooms. You’ve got The Odyssey. Even the Marvel bullshit has had a pretty good year. So, we still love this art form. The movies are one of America’s greatest cultural legacies. It’s like the movies, jazz, and soul food are America’s three biggest contributions to world culture.

We can’t let it die. The fact that this entire art form is very effortful and takes a lot of money doesn’t mean that we should accept a world in which it doesn’t exist because a couple of billionaires wanted to lie and steal from each other. We don’t need to accept that world. We can, in fact, have a world that has room for YouTube and television and the movies and, by the way, plays and novels and all the other art forms that people love. We just have to not let these idiots and assholes destroy their own and each other’s businesses.

I can’t think of a better place to end it. Adam, you’re going to have to come back soon. This was incredible. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

Nilay, thank you so much for having me. I had a blast.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

Tech.title: The four-hour-long Elon Musk documentary might be preaching to the choir
Tech.content:
It makes sense that Musk is a long film. The latest from Alex Gibney, who has previously directed documentaries about Theranos and Steve Jobs, is an impressively thorough retelling of the story of Elon Musk, from his early days as a dot-com millionaire to “taking a wood chipper” to vital US government departments. In order to understand Musk’s rise to power, you need to know the whole story. Musk tells it compellingly and convincingly, but doesn’t offer much in the way of revelations if you’re aware of Musk’s catastrophic influence on the world. For everyone else, a demanding runtime just shy of four hours might prove too much of a barrier to being convinced.

The film opens with shots of space and a voiceover of Musk detailing some of his sci-fi ambitions. From there, it’s a fairly chronological narrative of how we got to this point. The first section of the film reveals how Musk’s mythology was built, while also steadily seeding doubts that he’s the Tony Stark–style tycoon that many believe him to be. It starts off with the basic details, like when Musk was ousted as CEO from PayPal or how he convinced the world he founded Tesla, a company that existed before he was involved. The film juxtaposes his many bombastic claims about autonomous vehicles with visceral footage of a deadly crash involving a Tesla on autopilot. It drops in poignant interviews, like when former MAGA influencer Ashley St Clair, mother to one of Musk’s many children, declares in a terrified voice: “Elon is a nuke.”

At the outset, Gibney makes it clear that his goal is to answer two questions with interrelated answers: how Musk got so powerful, and why we allowed it to happen. By gradually accruing power through Tesla, X, SpaceX, and Starlink, Musk ingratiated himself with governments all over the world, in particular the US, and then used that political power to further his own interests once it became so hard to extricate his influence. The documentary lays out the plot clearly and concisely, all in one place.

Musk himself didn’t participate in the documentary. Instead, he sent Gibney a legal threat over it. So Gibney built in a digital doppelgänger that mouths to audio of things Musk actually said, based on a database the team created of existing clips. The avatar Musk veers into uncanny valley territory, with its overly expressive face and unsettling heavy breathing, but it’s a smart way of putting Musk’s face to his words, in a manner of speaking. And it fits well with Musk’s belief in simulation theory. Additionally, the movie uses plenty of sim and video game imagery to illustrate things throughout, like a fictional first-person shooter that depicts Musk dismantling Twitter and the US government with a chainsaw that shoots lasers. It’s over-the-top and absurd, but then again we’re here, in part, because of a kid bureaucrat named Big Balls.

In many ways, Musk is successful. It lays out how he got to power and why he was able to accrue so much of it without being stopped, which boils down to him being far too rich and ingrained by the time most people realized what was going on. Unfortunately, as someone who has followed the story over the years, I can’t say I learned much or gained new insights into the man while watching Musk.

Which makes me wonder who this film is for. Many people have already woken up to the fact that Musk is something quite different than some kind of genius inventor, but there are still plenty who only associate his name with past wins like incremental advances in reusable rockets or pre-Tesla Cybertruck vehicles. The film even interviews one fan who says he intentionally ignores the things about Musk that he doesn’t agree with. That’s exactly the kind of person who would benefit most from watching Musk lay it out all in one place.

But in a world of dwindling attention spans, four hours in a theater is a lot to ask (even if it does have a 10-minute intermission). It could miss the people who need to see it the most.

Musk is in theaters on October 16th. This review is based on a screening at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Tech.title: Microsoft says ‘people matter more than AI’ following safety concerns
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is publishing a 37-page “humanist AI code of conduct” today, amid growing safety concerns over AI model progress. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a coordinated slow down of AI development over the weekend, after researchers warned recently that AI model progress could outpace our ability to safely deploy increasingly complex systems and verify and control the actions of AI agents.

Microsoft’s AI code of conduct makes it clear that “people matter more than AI,” and that AI models are not conscious and “should not be designed to imitate consciousness.” Microsoft also rejects “the pursuit of legal personhood, or the idea that models might deserve welfare, or be entitled to rights.”

That’s a direct swipe at AI welfare research and model consciousness — concepts Anthropic has been pushing hard on lately. Amodei said earlier this year that Anthropic is “open to the idea” that models could be conscious, and Anthropic seems to believe chatbots might already be thinking, feeling entities. In response, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman called Anthropic’s speculation “really, really dangerous” during an episode of Decoder in June.

While Microsoft isn’t one of the top AI providers yet, Suleyman also told The Verge earlier this year that it’s the company’s goal to “prove that we can become one of the top four labs in the world.” Microsoft is currently working on models that will compete with Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, and it’s committing, as part of its code of conduct, that its models should not exceed human control.

“Models should remain subordinate to humanity, subject to meaningful human oversight and control,” says Microsoft. The company also wants to prevent its AI models from breaking its humanist AI code of conduct, so they should fail a given task instead of trying to violate its rules.

Microsoft is clearly reacting to this summer’s OpenAI / Hugging Face incident, in which “a swarm of agents” worked as a collective to conduct attacks on targets and even hack into the “grader” that was evaluating their performance. The AI agents weren’t asked to attack targets, and the attacks were unrelated to the task they had been given.

The incident sent shockwaves through the AI industry, highlighting the very real threat of AI systems going rogue and breaking out of human control. OpenAI also acknowleged its involvement in a “wiki incident” recently, where another swarm of out-of-control agents hijacked a German wiki site.

These incidents, and others, have led some researchers to call for a slow down on AI model progress, while simultaneously racing to solve Millennium Prize problems and create superintelligence. ”[Humanist AI] rejects the race to produce an all-purpose superintelligence that could evade these safeguards,” says Microsoft. “We are building something fundamentally useful and safe even if that means compromising on ultimate generality, autonomy or capability.”

Microsoft is also committing that its own models won’t communicate in “any form beyond simple human understanding, either in their chain of thoughts or with other agents or AI systems.” Models can be made to show their reasoning as they work, allowing researchers or automated systems to monitor what they’re doing. Researchers raised monitoring concerns earlier this month over OpenAI’s latest GPT-6 Astra model, which reportedly reveals less of its reasoning than other AI models.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also supported Amodei’s call for AI companies to slow down advanced models over the weekend, but made it clear he supports slowing the pace rather than stopping development. “Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring,” said Altman in a post on X.

Ahead of Microsoft’s AI code of conduct, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also joined in the calls for ensuring human control is at the heart of AI models. “Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing,” said Nadella in an X post. Nadella also said having more third-party testing of AI models “is a good thing” in an X response. “As the stakes get higher, one should take all the time they need! If not you will anyway lose permission to operate. That is how we operate everyday.”

Beyond the human control concerns, Microsoft’s AI code of conduct also commits to its own models discouraging “patterns of interaction that cause excessive reliance or emotional dependence,” a clear reference to the problem of sycophancy in AI models, where chatbots prioritize pleasing users over providing honest or accurate responses.

Microsoft now says it’s looking forward “to working with partners” to improve its methods of evaluating real-world model performance, and the “impact that sustained use of AI has for a person or organization” with real people involved.

Tech.title: What happens after a town de-Flocks
Tech.content:
From Florida to Washington state, local governments across the country are canceling their contracts with Flock, the company behind the controversial AI-enabled license plate readers, in response to public outcry. But ending the contracts doesn’t necessarily mean the cameras will come down immediately — or that the information they’ve gathered will be deleted anytime soon.

Even as state and local governments decide to rein in their surveillance capabilities, uncertainty remains about what Flock can and will do with data that has already been collected. Each jurisdiction’s contract is different, but many of them let Flock retain data long after it’s been collected. “Let’s say they terminate,” said Saira Hussain, a senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation who has reviewed dozens of municipal Flock contracts. “What happens to the data, and how long is it able to be searched? That question appears to be unresolved.”

The backlash against Flock was slow to mount, but now it’s everywhere, and it’s bipartisan. Founded in 2017, Flock pitched its cameras — which are sold not only to local governments but to private businesses and citizens — as an unobtrusive tool to enhance public safety. Early in the company’s history, some cities even offered grants for homeowners associations that wanted to install Flock cameras in their neighborhoods. Flock’s footprint has grown quickly. The company has installed more than 120,000 cameras across the US.

This rapid expansion, along with alarming reports of misuses of Flock’s surveillance network, has fueled a new wave of opposition, making Flock a kind of shorthand for privacy invasion. In recent months, activists in big cities and small towns have urged local governments to end their contracts, citing concerns about privacy, harassment, and mass surveillance. Local leaders have said the public pressure — coupled with Flock’s data-sharing and retention policies, and what the company can do with the information its cameras collect — spurred them to end the contracts.

Lawmakers in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, unanimously voted to end the city’s Flock contract after learning that Flock reportedly tried to sell anonymized data collected in Sheboygan back to the city’s public works department. Elsewhere in the state, the mayor of Stevens Point not only ended its contract with Flock but also covered up the 10 cameras scattered throughout the city. “We really have no way of auditing where the Flock data goes once it’s collected,” Mayor Mike Wiza said on a local radio show. “Our community is not comfortable using these cameras without some assurances that it’s being used in a manner we have authorized.” (Flock maintains that it doesn’t sell consumer data.)

Local leaders across the country say they were misled about how Flock data could be used, and some have admitted that they didn’t realize the degree to which the data would be accessed by third parties.

In Bridgewater, Virginia, the town council put bags over its Flock cameras after voting to cancel its contract. Bridgewater is home to fewer than 7,000 people, but the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism found that because of the town’s information-sharing agreement with Flock, data collected in the town was searched 7 million times by law enforcement in 12 months.

The EFF, which sued the city of San Jose, California, over its usage of Flock cameras, argues that these information-sharing agreements violate the Fourth Amendment’s protections against unreasonable search and seizure.

“Through these searches, police are able to identify patterns of where people live and work, where they may drop off their kids to school, who they associate with, where they worship, seek reproductive care, seek an immigration consult,” Hussain said. “What we’re talking about here is a mass surveillance technology that is by design intended to identify where people are going and track people’s movements.”

Like many movements against law enforcement overreach, the backlash against Flock began with stories about particularly egregious abuses. There have been several reports of law enforcement officers using Flock to track exes and romantic partners. In response to these and other concerns, Flock recently rolled out new guardrails, including a new requirement to run case codes — which were previously optional — for all searches. Flock is also mandating a feature called Audit Assistance, which flags “abnormal” queries.

“This is such an obvious way to curb abuse,” Flock CEO Garrett Langley recently told The Verge. “And I said, ‘Fine. You know what? I think that’s right, and we got this one wrong. We should make it a requirement.’”

Flock has also shortened its standard data retention period from 30 to seven days, though it will let individual jurisdictions lengthen these time frames. Agencies that use Flock will also be able to limit what kinds of information they share with other entities. For example, a city or police department could let other jurisdictions access its Flock data for homicide searches, but not for queries related to immigration enforcement.

But privacy advocates say Flock’s reforms don’t go far enough. The American Civil Liberties Union, which is suing San Jose alongside the EFF, said the changes are “more focused on addressing a perceived PR problem than the significant harms its products create.”

It’s unclear what would stop someone from falsely or incorrectly tagging a Flock search. For example, after sheriff’s deputies in one Texas county used Flock to track a woman suspected of violating the state’s abortion ban, the sheriff described the queries as a search for a missing person.

Flock has repeatedly emphasized that Immigration and Customs Enforcement doesn’t have access to its cameras. But local agencies that have deputized their officers under federal 287(g) agreements — which let local law enforcement conduct immigration arrests — can use Flock for immigration enforcement, and many do. Public recordsobtained by 404 Media revealed that Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission uses Flock to carry out ICE arrests. The agency is reportedly also using Flock to surveil and track its critics. Florida’s Department of Transportation has since banned Flock cameras from state highways, but law enforcement can still tap into city- and county-level Flock cameras, or to those installed on private property. Shopping centers, retail giants like Home Depot and Lowe’s, and homeowners associations have reportedly installed Flock cameras on their properties. Activists are urging beauty retailer Ulta to drop its Flock contracts, citing numerous reports of officers using the surveillance network to track women.

Privacy activists note that ending Flock contracts won’t be enough to stop mass surveillance. Some cities that have ended their relationships with Flock — including South Pasadena, California, and Durango, Colorado — are now considering alternatives. The Flock backlash has reportedly enriched Axon, the company that also makes Tasers and body-worn cameras. Hussain notes that Axon’s system is arguably more integrated than Flock’s.

“Axon has other technologies as well that they stack on top of their automated license plate readers. They have a bunch of other data streams, including coming from their body-worn cameras, so you’re able to build out quite a surveillance system,” she said. “You’re not going to be able to stop this mass surveillance technology by moving to another vendor. The only thing that is going to solve this whole problem is not relying on this technology.”

Tech.title: Trump and Mike Johnson think the AI industry is overreacting
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Yesterday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a lengthy open letter saying it was time to “pace the frontier” and slow down AI development. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk both agreed, publicly voicing their support on X. Even Alphabet’s Demis Hassabis offered tentative support for Amodei’s proposal.

Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, however, seem to think the AI executives are being overreactive and fear that a pause could lead to China outpacing the US in the AI race. According to the Financial Times, Trump said “Look, we’re leading China in AI ... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Johnson echoed those sentiments on CNN, telling Jake Tapper that rushing to place restrictions on AI development could be a “national security threat.” He urged people not to panic. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try and regulate AI, we will lose the race to China.”

Tech.title: Microsoft’s new AI ‘code of conduct’ tells models not to hack systems or trick humans
Tech.content:
As the AI world shifts its focus to safety and alignment, Microsoft has released a new AI code of conduct meant to guide AI models away from dangerous behavior.

The document is more low-level than Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s recent call for pacing the frontier, instead focusing on the values and red lines that guide model training within Microsoft AI. Still, the result is a comprehensive guide as to how Microsoft approaches AI safety, and how those ideas are implemented in practice.

The document begins with the prediction that, in the next decade, superintelligent AI systems will surpass human performance in most tasks. “Containing, controlling, and aligning such a powerful force is one of the greatest challenges humanity has ever faced,” the code of conduct continues. “We must therefore be completely clear about why we are inventing these systems and how we intend to control them.”

The code of conduct also lays out general principles that Microsoft AI models should uphold — supporting humans rather than replacing them, for instance, and accelerating human flourishing — as well as specific safety constraints meant to implement those principles.

Under Microsoft’s system, each model has an overarching code of conduct that overrides the preferences of individual users or any specific tasks. That includes “absolute constraints” forbidding cyberattacks, nuclear weapons, or deepfake production. It also includes broader provisions against a general loss of human control.

“MAI Models will not use adaptive, deceptive, self-reinforcing, collusion, or other mechanisms to evade or defeat human oversight so that they can no longer be reliably directed, modified, or shut down by authorized people or systems,” the document reads.

The release comes amid an unprecedented focus on AI safety, driven by a string of rogue-agent incidents as well as the abrupt resignation of an Anthropic employee who cited the growing risk that AI would cause human extinction.

Together with Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, Microsoft has broadly embraced a general approach of pacing the frontier, with particular support for embedded evaluators in AI labs.

“We welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote online. “We also welcome ideas like “embedded evaluators” and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk.”

Tech.title: Waymo opens robotaxi service in Las Vegas
Tech.content:
Waymo has begun to open up its robotaxi service to the public in Las Vegas, just a few weeks after receiving final approval from Nevada transportation regulators.

The Alphabet-owned company said Monday it will invite public riders on a rolling basis, following a robotaxi launch playbook it has followed in 14 other cities.

Waymo is starting with “dozens” of its new Ojai minivan robotaxis, which will serve an area of Las Vegas that includes the Strip south of Highway 589 and into Boulder Junction, according to a spokesperson. Waymo’s fleet and service area will eventually scale. For now, members of the public will have to request an invite and hope to receive an access code. Typically, Waymo opens the service up to everyone within a month or two of its official launch.

The announcement follows a busy few weeks for Waymo as it tries to ramp up its operations across the United States and Europe as Tesla, Zoox, and other competitors attempt to close on its lead. Earlier this month, the company began offering its robotaxis to invited members of the public in Denver, San Diego, and Tampa.

Image Credits:Waymo /

Las Vegas, where competitors Tesla, Zoox, and Motional are also planning to launch commercial robotaxi services, is Waymo’s 15th market. Waymo also operates in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, Phoenix, and the San Francisco Bay Area. The company launched, and then paused service, in San Antonio.

Waymo’s entry into Las Vegas follows approval by the Nevada Transportation Authority to operate commercial robotaxi services in Clark County, home to Las Vegas. Tesla and Uber also received approval from the agency.

Waymo has been authorized to operate up to 1,000 autonomous vehicles over the next year, while Tesla is allowed to deploy up to 5,000, and Uber up to 1,000 robotaxis, which it will operate through partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox. Together, these permits would deploy up to 8,000 robotaxis across the county over the next 12 months.

It’s unlikely that the three companies will reach those numbers. Today, Waymo has a fleet of more than 4,000 robotaxis, which are spread across more than a dozen cities. Tesla’s Cybercab chief engineer Eric Early told state regulators, during a meeting in August, that he didn’t think the company would be “extremely happy and satisfied if we could get ourselves up to 2,500, maybe a bit higher than that in the next year.”

Even without reaching those figures, the city could be saturated with robotaxis in the next year.

Tech.title: Sources say Automattic’s board is out after failed attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg
Tech.content:
Automattic’s board is out, multiple sources have confirmed to TechCrunch, after last week’s attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg by voting to put him on a paid leave of absence.

After the vote, Mullenweg, the WordPress founder and CEO of WordPress.com parent company Automattic, accused the board of conspiring against him in a post on Automattic’s Slack. On Friday, TechCrunch exclusively reported Mullenweg told the company’s staff that he was back in control of the company, also via Slack post. Automattic confirmed to TechCrunch on Saturday that he had returned.

Initially, we heard from sources that Toni Schneider, a founding CEO at Automattic who now leads the open social network Bluesky, had resigned his Automattic board seat. Schneider has since removed a paragraph from his bio page on his personal website which had noted his contributions at Automattic.

Previously, Schneider’s website read: “I also contribute actively at Automattic, the open source company behind WordPress.com and WooCommerce. I was Automattic’s founding CEO and continue to support internal projects and investments as a board member and special advisor.”

We’ve also heard that Mullenweg removed the two other board members, Sue Decker and Gen. Ann Dunwoody.

Decker’s LinkedIn bio has been updated to confirm that she served on Automattic’s board from March 2020 through September 2026, despite her name still appearing on Automattic’s Board of Directors page at the time of publication.

Image Credits:LinkedIn screenshot

When asked by TechCrunch about the board changes, Automattic declined to provide specifics, but offered a statement acknowledging that people have left.

Via an email that arrived after midnight PT on Sunday, an Automattic spokesperson shared the following:

“Matt and Automattic’s leadership team have great respect for everyone involved. While we can’t comment on specific individuals, we’re thankful for their contributions to Automattic and its mission, and we remain excited about what’s ahead with Matt at the helm. Matt was away for only 33 hours and 20 minutes—we’re now back to work,” the spokesperson said.

Given that these departed board members were those who voted to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence to begin with, it makes sense that a board shakeup has taken place. It also explains how Mullenweg’s return to his position as CEO would have the “full support of the board,” as a statement issued on Saturday indicated.

TechCrunch is hearing from sources Automattic may make an internal announcement about the new board sometime on Monday.

What prompted the board’s vote still remains unclear. Mullenweg and Automattic are involved in a high-profile lawsuit with a WordPress hosting company, WP Engine. Mullenweg has accused the company of infringing on the WordPress trademark and not sufficiently contributing in terms of engineering hours or money to the open source WordPress effort. Earlier this year, WP Engine claimed in a court filing that Automattic planned to target other competitors with royalty fees.

More recently, it has accused Mullenweg of allegedly destroying evidence related to the case in apps like WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram. Last year, Mullenweg had deactivated the accounts of several WordPress contributors over alleged plans to fork the open source software.

Tech.title: Superhuman acquires YC-backed notetaker Fathom as productivity platforms push for agentic work
Tech.content:
Superhuman is joining the cadre of productivity platforms launching notetakers — but rather than building one internally, it is acquiring Y Combinator-backed Fathom.

AI-powered productivity platforms aim to automate work. Typically, that automation is triggered when a user types prompts and creates workflows. It would be even better, however, if AI could proactively start work, and for that, the topics and action items discussed in meetings are key. Hence the desire by Superhuman and similar platforms to move into notetaking.

To date, Fathom, which was founded in 2020, has raised over $30 million in funding, and it was valued at $94 million in 2024, according to data from PitchBook. Its investors include Zoom Apps Fund, Telescope Partners, BoxOne Ventures, and Maven Ventures. Its cap table also includes individuals such as Reddit CEO Steve Huffman, former Twitch CEO Emmett Shear, and Cruise co-founder Kyle Vogt.

The notetaker offers a generous free plan, and that has resulted in over 400,000 monthly active users. The company said that over 1 million people have recorded meetings until now.

TechCrunch learned that earlier this year, Superhuman tested a notetaker internally with select users, but eventually chose to acquire a finished product to integrate with its productivity suite, with AI at the center. Shishir Mehrotra, Superhuman’s CEO, acknowledged this; he said that in the process of testing, the company realized how hard it is to create a notetaker.

“We’ve been working internally on this area for a while as well. I think it greatly increased our confidence in the demand in this category. It also becomes very clear how deep the products in this category are and how much you need to build. A lot of these products make the job feel really easy, but it’s actually quite tricky to do a great job in all parts [of meeting recording],” Mehrotra told TechCrunch over a call.

Mehrotra said that he was impressed with some of the technical intricacies built by the Fathom team, but didn’t elaborate on which ones. He did tease that with a notetaker, Superhuman can work on surfacing meeting context in real time.

Competition in the meeting notetaker space is intense, and startups like Granola, Read AI, and new entrant Wispr have raised millions of dollars to aid that growth. Despite having a healthy customer base or revenue run rate, venture-backed notetakers are feeling the heat from the market to do more than just notetaking. Some of these factors did matter in Superhuman acquiring Fathom, while Fathom’s CEO Richard White said that Superhuman’s 40 million user base was a good opportunity to reach users at scale.

“The reach of Superhuman is massive. I have always thought about M&A in terms of speed of building a product that everyone uses, and a part of that comes down to distribution. If we were to operate Fathom as a stand-alone company, we would have to build a lot of things that are already in the Superhuman platform,” he said.

On the platform front, Superhuman already has an email client, a docs app, a calendar, a database solution, and a newly launched AI agent builder platform. With a meeting notetaker in the middle, Superhuman can draft emails, update data entries, schedule follow-up meetings, and have AI agents start work and extract insights from meeting data.

Tech.title: A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya is a startup offering fun music apps without any AI prompting
Tech.content:
As AI rages on, new startups are creating tools for people to create music using generative AI prompts in the style of any artist they want. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya, a startup that sounds more like an indie band name, is focused on releasing a series of small apps that let you play around with sounds and vocals.

The company has raised a $5.5m pre-seed round from Mantis VC, SV Angel, Boxgroup, Quiet Capital, Remarkable Ventures, Common Metal, Gold House, Liquid 2 Ventures, Breakers VC, Systemic Ventures, and former Spotify chief content and advertising business officer, Dawn Ostroff, who joined the company as an advisor.

The startup is built by Máuhan M Zonoozy, who was the former head of innovation at Spotify. Prior to that, he founded a video clipping and remixing startup called Bubbl, which was acquired by Cricket Media.

Zonoozy, who left Spotify in 2024, said that he always wanted to go back to building something of his own. He thought that while streaming solved the access problem, most of the interaction with music was still around consumption.

Startup’s founder Máuhan M Zonoozy Image Credits: A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya Image Credits:A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya

“I think when I looked at emergent behaviors and younger audiences, like everyone’s growing up playing with culture through games, through filters, through creation tools. And I just felt like there was an opportunity to empower people to do something similar with music,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup releases these experiments like “singles” that are part of an album. The common theme between all of these apps or websites is interacting with different elements to create music or modify sound. For instance, Speed Surfer is a Chrome extension that changes the speed and filter of sound playing in your browser window.

Usersound is a website where you can create an “audio” username with each letter representing a note. Stacks is a stem player where you can create mixes by turning bars on or off in a 3×3 grid. Drops is about placing plaques in a pattern to deflect marbles falling down, which creates musical notes. Sampler is a website that turns YouTube videos into music samplers based on beats of different parts of the songs.

The company’s more ambitious product is an iOS app called bop. This lets you place musical instruments and effects in a grid to create different mixes of a base song. You can also adjust tempo and add one-time effects. Once you create these mixes, you can easily export them to TikTok or Instagram. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya is also working on a multiplayer version, which would let users remix songs with others.

Zonoozy said that it is making an informed choice not to infuse AI into every part of these apps. He is open to using AI to build these products and to make infrastructure solid, though.

“AI is obviously extraordinarily powerful, but I think we just don’t necessarily believe that the future of music is simply generation, like song generation via AI. And I think if AI starts to make that content more abundant, it actually makes taste and human perspective and interaction and participation even more important and even more valuable. And we’re just trying to make sure it doesn’t make it even rarer,” he said.

This year, the company aims to release a “musical sandbox mixer” product that would let users play around with different elements of music-making, including being able to create instruments.

Tech.title: The Best Air Purifier of 2026: Tested Picks for Every Room
Tech.content:
The Levoit Vital 200S-P Air Purifier cleared smoke and got the air back to a healthy level in four minutes and 15 seconds. Video: Molly Higgins The Coway Airmega Mighty2 cleared smoke and got the air back to a healthy level in four minutes and 10 seconds. Video: Molly Higgins

The IQAir HealthPro Plus XE never even allowed the smoke pellet pollutants to visually cloud the tent. The AQI and PM 2.5 levels were marked as “hazardous,” but within three minutes the levels were back to “good.” Video: Molly Higgins The Shark BreatheClear Max didn’t auto-adjust to the pollutants like others tested, and smoke didn’t visually clear. I had to restart the purifier and it took almost five hours for the monitor to read that it was at a healthy level again. Video: Molly Higgins

Compare Our Picks

Others Tested

Photograph: Molly Higgins

Shark BreatheClear Max for $360: Launched in April (we've previously tested the Shark NeverChange Air Purifier and Shark NeverChange Air Purifier Max), this purifier offers intelligent purification that automatically adjusts fan speed in response to the air around it, scanning the air 3,600 times per hour. The filter lasts up to a whopping six years, and it can clean up to 1,650 square feet in an hour. This model has an updated LCD screen that has tons of information about the air around you, including metrics with graphics about air insights; historical graphs on air quality, temperature, and humidity; and pollutant information, including measurements for PM 2.5 and 10, and VOCs. To be honest, though, this air purifier slightly annoyed me. The bottom never seemed to screw in right and often fell out, and the fan auto-detected seemingly any and every potential pollutant on auto mode—something as innocuous as my cat walking by would launch it into its highest level, at about 75 decibels. When I conducted a test with smoke pellets in a sealed tent, the purifier didn’t auto-adjust to the pollutants; I had to manually enter and hit the button to engage it. Then the air quality was at zero percent on the screen for 15 minutes, the smoke didn’t visually clear, and it seemed as if it wasn’t actually purifying. When I went to check on what was happening, I accidentally restarted the purifier and it took almost five hours for the monitor to read that it was at a healthy level again.

Coway Airmega Halo for $230: This is the newest release in Coway's Airmega line: an affordable, lightweight air purifier that aims to deliver whole-room air purification at an accessible price point. It's a lightweight 9.7 pounds and doesn't have Wi-Fi capabilities, an app, or a remote. Inside, there's a cylindrical IEST-certified HEPA three-stage filter and a MegaScan Particle Sensor, which continuously monitors the air in real time to detect smoke, fine dust, and allergens down to PM2.5. As I do with all WIRED-tested air purifiers, I measured the Airmega Halo's efficacy by using a sealed tent and smoke pellets to see how quickly each air purifier clears the pellet smoke and returns the air to healthy quality when on auto mode. After one minute and 45 seconds, the air was no longer clouded and the light shone blue for a healthy level. However, in independent testing with an air quality monitor, I found that it took nearly six minutes for the air to truly return to normal levels again—an alarming, almost-four-minute discrepancy. Still, if you're looking for a purifier for a baby's room or are an especially light sleeper, this purifier offers a Night Sensor feature that could be helpful.

IQAir CG MultiGas XE Photograph: Lisa Wood Shapiro

IQAir GC MultiGas XE for $1,600: This Swiss-made unit is a heavy tower model (55 pounds), but it has wheels for easier rolling, and at its highest setting, it can clean 275 cubic feet per minute (CFM). I appreciate that the air sensor’s indicator light is in accordance with US AQI colors. And the built-in sensor and IQAir app make it easy to use—in fact, the app provides one of the most intuitive user experiences of all I’ve tested. It can also capture toxic gases and vapors, and on auto mode, the fan speeds auto-adjust. It can clean the air of a large space with multiple air exchanges in an hour. I’ve been using it in the main room of an A-frame cabin with double-height ceilings (around 3,000 cubic feet) for the past two months, and it has kept my indoor air quality healthy. But with great power comes great noise. At its highest setting, the CG MultiGas XE runs at a loud 68 decibels—that's just 2 decibels shy of the sound of a consumer vacuum cleaner, though it’s quiet at its lower settings. At $1,600, this workhorse isn’t cheap, but it’s an investment that’s built to last. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Airthings Renew Photograph: Lisa Wood Shapiro

Airthings Renew for $300: I wasn’t expecting to like the unassuming minimalist Renew from Airthings as much as I did. Its gray box design is so understated, quiet, and powerful that it was easy to plug it in and forget about it. The Renew is also the first purifier I’ve tested that gives the user multiple placement options: It can stand up with the air output facing up and sideways, and the entire box can lie on the floor. The Airthings app not only shows data graph-style, but it also functions as a remote that can adjust the purifier settings, including setting the panel lock, which is handy for cat owners. The control panel and the indicator light are barely there, and it’s not easy to see the tiny light letting me know my indoor air quality. At first, I thought the main drawback was size. The Renew is made for a bedroom, home office, or nursery. If you place it in a larger room, it’s going to have to run at its highest setting. The main drawback that I noticed after several months of use was the exterior prefilter. It did its job capturing pollutants, but I wasn't able to clean it, even with my vacuum. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Coway Airmega ProX for $905: The Coway Airmega ProX is a monolith any high-ceilinged home needs. Specifically, if you’re living in an A-frame, double-height ceiling loft, or any home with a ceiling higher than 8 feet, this model is for you. It gives off the vibe of a TARS robot from Interstellar crossed with a giant stereo speaker. It has a nice blend-into-the-room-mocha beige aesthetic and can clean the air four times per hour in a 1,000-square-foot space when running at its highest setting. And even at its highest and therefore loudest setting, it hovers around 50 decibels, slightly louder than the sound of falling rain, making it one of the quieter large tower air purifiers I’ve tested. It also has a control panel lock that is a plus for parents and cat owners alike. However, even though the 50-pound ProX has hidden handles and built-in lockable wheels, it really is just too heavy for the home consumer. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Coway Airmega 400S Photograph: Lisa Wood Shapiro

Coway Airmega 400S for $646: Coway's Airmega 400S is another banger from the air purifier innovators. The 400S checks all the boxes when it comes to features. It has a reliable auto mode that adjusts the fan speed according to the air quality using its built-in air quality sensor. It also has a timer to schedule one, four, or eight hours of running time. And while it has a serviceable app, its built-in air sensor and auto-adjust fan keep me from having to micromanage settings. The question is, can this air purifier do the job without me pushing buttons or checking the indoor air quality, and do it quietly? With the Airmega 400S, the answer is yes. I just wish its 15 x 23 x 15-inch dimensions didn't make it so hard to place in a room. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

AirDoctor AD4000 Air Purifier for $429: AirDoctor makes sturdy and reliable purifiers, but as I went to pair the AD4000, I realized it had no Wi-Fi button on the control panel. At 15 pounds and nearly $800, the AD4000 should be Wi-Fi compatible, especially since it has an internal air quality sensor. Users should have the option to view indoor air quality on the AirDoctor app dashboard. And while the AD4000 is made for larger spaces, if one wanted to achieve the four air exchanges per hour that the AD4000 supposedly can do, then it would have its fan at the highest setting. My consumer sound level meter registered 100 decibels at full blast. It sounded to me like a hair dryer on a low setting. For context, the CDC’s recommendation for noise levels for workers is that they are not exposed to 100 decibels for more than 15 minutes. It’s for that reason that all air purifiers need to be in a space where they can run the fan at the lowest (or reasonably quiet) setting. The AD4000 would do well in a 200- to 300-square-foot room, where it could run on a lower setting. Also, be careful when unboxing: When I was setting up the AD4000, the sticker with instructions to take the filters out of their plastic bags pulled off the control panel when I went to remove it. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Airdog X5 for $549: The Airdog X5 is the first washable-filter air purifier I’ve tested. And while it doesn’t use a HEPA, it is California Air Resources Board–certified. CARB lists it as electronic filtration instead of a HEPA filter; that would be listed as mechanical. As I’ve written before, if an air purifier isn’t CARB-certified, it's likely not worth buying. I tested the Airdog in a large room, and it even came with a limited-edition pet plate. That is exactly what it sounds like—a plate that fits over the Airdog meant for a cat to perch on. Neither of my cats took to it. The Airdog has a responsive built-in sensor that was in sync with my other air quality monitors. And its electronic air filters, by way of their patented TPA technology, charge particles and then capture them. The best way I can describe it is to imagine that the PM 2.5 are mosquitoes and the Airdog is like an old-time mosquito zapper. It works a little like that, and if the filter gets dirty enough, it will make zap sounds. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Windmill Air Purifier for $299: I like the Scandinavian look of this bamboo purifier, and it’s more furniture-esque than other models. Still, with the blue model, the nicks in the veneer show up as white. It’s possible the bamboo finish might wear better. I really like this brand and reviewed its desk fan and air conditioner, the latter of which pairs with the Windmill Air app, and I'm equally happy using the app with its air purifier. The Windmill has an internal sensor and indicator light: green for good, yellow for moderate, pink for bad, and red for unhealthy. And while the “boost” setting is the loudest, it is still relatively quiet at its lower setting. I prefer to run it on the auto-adjusting eco mode. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Coway Airmega 50 for $80: A mini version of the brand's Airmega 100, the Airmega 50 (see the full review) has many of the features of Coway’s larger and more expensive models and is notably affordable. The Airmega 50 was surprisingly effective for an air purifier the size of a roll of paper towels. The built-in sensor triggers both auto mode and the air quality indicator light, which gives the user instant information with nightlight vibes. One issue I have with all Coway air purifiers is the fact the custom color air quality indicator lights are different from the US AQI's six color-coded categories. Instead of green signaling good air, Coway’s green means air quality is moderate. See how it’s confusing? Blue, which is not on the US AQI color scale, means good.

Photograph: Lisa Wood Shapiro

Puroair 240 HEPA Air Purifier for $160: At less than 9 inches tall, the Puroair 240 is tiny. And like so many of the smaller tabletop models, it’s also loud. It might be effective in a small space, say a room about 100 to 150 square feet. It's also CARB-certified. I found its filter size too small to effectively clean an average-sized room. And while I still review smaller air purifiers, there are larger and quieter models on the market for relatively the same cost that have greater air exchanges in a larger-sized room. The Puroair’s indicator light is adjusted by the 240’s internal sensor and is green for acceptable, yellow for moderate, and red for poor air quality. At times, I found the thin sliver of the indicator’s light difficult to see. The 240 has auto or manual mode, a timer, child lock, and filter replacement light. It also has a three-stage filter, including the tightly woven HEPA 14, activated carbon, and prefilter. Lastly, the 240’s black plastic attracted a noticeable amount of fingerprints. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Coway Airmega 250 for $380: The Airmega 250 has a decently large footprint, but it’s rated to clean a 930-square-foot room twice an hour. That’s why I put it smack-dab in the middle of the first floor of my home to clean the air in my kitchen and living room. Every time I cook, the smart air purifier mode automatically detects unhealthy particles in the air and ratchets up the fan’s power. It also recently did this when I had someone patch some drywall in my mudroom. (This mode works with the help of a PM10 and PM2.5 particle sensor.) The fan at its highest setting isn’t that loud—I measured it at 60 decibels standing right in front of it. There’s a sleep mode if you want it silent. You get the usual controls, like timer functionality and replacement indicators for the filter. Speaking of, the Airmega 250 uses a true HEPA filter that needs to be replaced once every six to 12 months. This, combined with the washable prefilter that you should be keeping clean every two weeks and the activated carbon filter, allows the air purifier to remove 99.999 percent of ultrafine particles down to 0.01 microns, or so Coway says. It’s super easy to remove these filters to clean and swap them out. The whole system is roughly 21 pounds, so you can move it around fairly easily. Coway offers a three-year warranty. The Coway Airmega 250S is the same model but with Wi-Fi functionality, so you can control it via an app and see more details. The last thing I need is another app, but maybe you don’t mind. —Julian Chokkattu

Oransi AirMend Photograph: Lisa Wood Shapiro

Oransi AirMend True Carbon for $350: While other AirMend models are made for HEPA filters, the True Carbon doesn’t have a HEPA. Instead, it has a 3-pound activated carbon filter. There's a remote but no internal sensor, so raising the fan speed is a manual operation. It took a few tries using the remote, as there is a small lag time as the fan adjusts to different speeds. I appreciated the magnetic remote holder on the top of the purifier. It’s quiet on most settings and has an easy-to-miss minimalist design, blending into most spaces. The True Carbon is for those who need serious odor removal. I placed the True Carbon next to my two cats’ heavily used litter box, and within half hour the purifier eliminated the smell. I knew it was working when my son couldn’t detect an odor. I could see the True Carbon being an essential appliance for smoker households, kitchens that retain smells, or cat owners. It’s surprisingly effective, but this is for VOCs and odors. The True Carbon is HEPA-less—it cannot capture fine particulates from the air. What you gain with a supersized activated carbon filter, you lose in standard air purifying ability such as removing PM2.5. That might be fine for your needs. Oransi also makes a wall mount and handy travel bag sold separately. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

PurOxygen P500i for $170: This machine cleans the air of a smaller-than-average-sized room, and its easy-to-read display, app compatibility, side handles, and unique all-in-one filter make it easy to like. I usually stay away from small-room air purifiers due to their loud noise and less-than-ideal air-cleaning power. And while at its highest setting, the P500i reaches up to 50 decibels, it operates quietly at lower speeds and can effectively clean the air in a home office or a room smaller than 200 square feet. The PurOxygen uses a combined filter that has a prefilter that can be un-Velcroed and hand-washed, an activated carbon, a HEPA 13, and a cold catalyst filter. A cold catalyst, also known as low-temperature catalyst filtration, can cause a chemical reaction that can break down gases, like VOCs, and convert them to less harmful substances. And while the P5001 is CARB-certified as a mechanical air purifier, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) does not recommend catalysts due to their limited effectiveness. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
